Valdis Story is a 2D side scroller with plenty of beat em up action. If you enjoy Castlevania games, you're going to like this. The controls can take a while to get use to if you're using the keyboard, just remap them to your liking. I prefered playing with a Playstation 3 controller and DS3 tool, it was fantastic. There are times when doing the precision platforming can be painful but all you have to do is take your time and feel it out.
There are currently two playable characters, Wyatt and Reina.
Wyatt plays more of a strength/dark and light magic character. He's a bit slowered than Reina when it comes to combos, but overall I believe Wyatt plays easier for a new player (especially if you like to jump in on the hardest difficulty). He comes with the ability to use his sword or fists (fists take -40% attack dmg in exchange for +25% exp).
Reina is a monk and begins the game with only her fists (No negatives, just +25% exp) as a weapon. She employs magic as well, but doesn't realy have "dark" magic. She's not as easy to jump in with, as the ability to break guards is obtainable at level 4, where as Wyatt begins the game able to do so with his strong attacks.

Ridge is a first person adventure game where you walk around exploring a world filled with evil balls and using runes to combat them and the many traps spread throughout the world.
With a tutorial that teaches you the bare minimum, a picture of the controls instead of actual bindings, and the expectation that you'll figure out how to play it eventually, Ridge is not a very easy game to get into. Even the instructions to the tutorial were lacking. They'd tell you to use an object but not tell you that you need to go grab an object first and then use that object on a different object before you could do what they were telling you to do. And even then, they didn't tell you how to do it.
Once you get past the tutorial you're welcomed into what I would call a very charming looking world, but the graphics of this game have a lot of effects that stop you from enjoying them. For one, there's a random depth of field that will continuously change and adjust as you play that will blur out everything as close as ten feet in front of you to way off in the distance. Good news is I didn't notice any large objects popping in, but the bad news is that the flora all pops in fifteen feet in front of your face even on the highest settings. Also if it's raining? Don't expect to be able to see a damn thing. Your face apparently has a camera in it instead of eyeballs because your first person perspective will get drowned in raindrops, making it very difficult to see anything combined with the fog effects the game likes to use on occasion. Also, I can't see my body when I look down so maybe you do play as a floating camera as opposed to a real person, who knows?
My favorite part of this game has got to be its music. Its music is amazing. During the calm moments there's soft versions of unfortunately only two popular songs. Jingle bells, and Sweet dreams; the latter sounding more like a cover of Marilyn Manson's version of it. It then has a typical orchestral sounding soundtrack for combat and other moments of action that is also very good.
HOWEVER, this game is no audio masterpiece. The sound effects are horrible. Often times they're too loud, sound distorted, and repeat endlessly. The sound effects in the tutorial were consistently bashing against my ears and making me want to take my headphones off for the duration of the tutorial. And once you get into the open world it kind of continues with a distant 'thunder' that repeats every ten seconds and sounds more like someone bashing a pot into a toilet and letting that ring out.
The gameplay is barely a thing which is why I saved this for later. It's basically just a walking simulator where you use three buttons. The goal is to investigate the game world and collect runes and charge them and use those to defend yourself. It's supposed to be an investigation on a real place but investigation is minimal. Most of your time is spent running away from the evil balls of light that can outrun you unless you sprint (Which is limited by stamina equivalent to someone with asthma) and will kill you unless you have enough runes to combat them all. Oh and occasionally you step on a trap but that's basically the same deal. Use a rune or die.  It's really very boring once you get past the first ten minutes of the game.
The story is...there I guess. There's no real voice acting, just some words that pop up on your screen. There's some explosions. You find some things. But there's not really any motivation to deal with the game's flaws.
Ridge is just the worst game I have played in over a year. It gets a 1/10 because of that. I'd give it a zero if it were buggy and broken too, but at least it works. So long as it works, someone might like it.  So there's your pro, it works. The cons? The rest of the game. Don't buy this game unless you want to gift it to a friend as some sort of twisted April Fools joke.

Well, this is gonna be a long one.
First of all, despite all of its flaws and nasty quirks, Istrolid is a good game. It has balanced gameplay, well hosted servers, and most importantly- It is fun. The main game mechanic and selling point- building one's own ship- is a good idea overall, and you can spend quite a while mixing and matching different parts and weapons. Now, with that over with, let's head into the bad parts of the game.
The first thing that came to mind when thinking of all the bad things about this game was the $1000 build limit. This essentially prohibits you from creating any massive, overpowered ships do decimate your enemies. While this may seem like a good thing, trust me- it's horrible. Just when you think you can fit in ooonnnee more thruster on your ship to get rid of that nagging little sign saying "Warning: Movement Speed is Very Slow", the screen flashes bright red and a message pops up "Warning: Ship Too Large" and you have to redesign the whole ship from the turrets up.
Another incredibly bad thing about the $1000 build limit is the fact that your enemy doesn't have to follow it- and in many cases it doesn't. Nor, for that matter, does it pay any attention to actually paying for the ships that it is creating: until you're in a multiplayer 2v2 with only an AI as your companion.
This leads me into not really a massive problem with the game, but more of a personal gripe about it: the money, as previously mentioned, should be given a definitive place where it is produced, such as a factory- and yes, it does explain in the first level that you get money based upon how many points you control, but there's no indication of it throuought the rest of the game.
Another little gripe that I have with the game is it's highly boasted  variation. Of course, there is quite a lot of aesthetic variation between ships, with everyone adding their own personal touches to their fleet- but other than the small fighter ships, there really isn't much variation between your most powerful battleship and your medium missile corvette, leading to you misinterpreting what class of ship to use to best combat the enemy.
Two quick things before I wrap this up are: 1) more colourful backgrounds. Now I'm sure the devs are working on this, but it kinda bugged me with the lack of, well, anything really in the background; and 2) There should be different level styles. There is only one mode in the game, which is basically a version of 'domination' except whoever captures all of the point immediatly wins. This is, I admit, quite a fun gamemode, but there's no variation whatsoever, which really put me off the game. Another huge gameplay feature or rather the lack of which, was the story. There are a few bosses. There are enemies. No connection between them, no force or ideals supporting you morally and no sense of defeat when you lose a battle, more the kind of 'whatever, I'll just fight them again' vibe.
Overall, I believe that Istrolid is a good game, and with the upcoming patches and updates, it'll be really good. For now,  I'd wait a while until the game is fully fleshed-out with a story and all.

Ridge is an indie atmospheric first person puzzle adventure title developed in Unreal 4 engine.
The game feels solid enough, specially when you consider that it is a one-man project.
Gameplay:
You start stranded on a location, arriving via a rowboat. A quick tutorial shows you the basic gameplay.
You can move around, gather runes, charge them at certain locations and use your 2 powers, light and armor, to explore and survive.
Nothing too complex and it works. I feel the waiting period on the charging stations to recharge your runes was something not really needed in the game and feels like a gimmick made to extend the duration of the game by making you wait and wait in order to charge your runes.
In order to save the game you need a charged rune. This is rather annoying at the start of the game because until you find your first one, if you die, you have to watch the rowboat animation sequence and experience the, albeit short, tutorial again and again.
All in all, the atmosphere of the game is good but I also feel like some things could be done in a better way. For example some hints you find as notes stuck on a cavern wall would make much more sense, and would be much more immersive, if they were something like a journal left on a stone, or abandoned campfire, and the actual hints part of narrative in said journal.
Graphics:
The game utilizes the Unreal 4 engine so it looks rather good. The textures and meshes are rather low resolution though, which is something to be expected, really, from a one-man indie project. It is not really bothersome.
I felt the waterdrop effect on your screen when it rains (and it rains a lot outside) was a bit overdone making rather difficult to locate the runes and caves you need to. This is made a bit more difficult by the low resolution textures.
One minor bug to mention is that the game refused to save my graphics settings. And the fact that the menu you get by hitting escape, you can't exit by hitting escape again. You have to click continue. I found that rather hard to get used to but at the end it's just a minor annoyance.
Music/Sound:
The music is absolutely great and so is the sound design. These are very carefully done and are very immersive.
Pros:
-Very interesting premise. You are exploring a place that is supposedly modeled after a real location. I have no idea if this is actually true or a statement meant to provoke certain feelings (Blair Witch Project style ;), but the environment is certainly well structured.
-It's an atmospheric first person puzzle adventure with action elements. It's refreshing to see more of these games.
-It doesn't hold your hand. You actually feel alone and lost in a desolate place while playing it.
-Music and sound design are very well done and fitting the concept.
Cons:
-Low resolution textures and doesn't take full advantage of the capabilities of the Unreal 4 engine. That is to be expected though of an indie, one-man project.
-A few minor annoyances such as the graphics settings reverting to the default every time you run it.
Conclusion:
It is an interesting game but you can't help but think that it would be much better if the developer had a bigger budget to work with.
I certainly hope it sells enough so we can see a remaster at some point.

I came to this game having just completed The Vanishing of Ethan Carter.  Sometimes I don't feel like playing games that require lightening reflexes, or involve running around shooting the crap out of stuff.  Sometimes I just feel like chilling out, wandering around, looking at some beautiful graphics and solving the occasional puzzle.  The Vanishing of EC was one such game and, from what I've seen of it so far, Ridge may just fit the bill too.
I have played it for 92 minutes according to Steam and to be honest I still haven't got an actual clue what I'm supposed to do yet.  There are stone runes, you have to charge them up (this seems key to survival); there are clues on notes left dotted around and I've found a notebook containing cryptic drawings which probably are trying to tell me what I'm supposed to be doing if only I was smart enough to interpret them; there are orbs of light that follow you around and will kill you; some "control towers" that the game also hints are key to surviving; and that's about all I can fathom at the moment.
Some of my 92 minutes were spent messing about with the graphics settings, as this game does seem to hammer the GPU heavily.  On my GTX 960 4GB it runs at around 30fps with regular dips into the 20s at 1080p with everything on "ultra".  After turning things down and gaining only a few extra fps at the expense of making it look f-ugly, I decided to leave everything on ultra.  It does look quite pretty and is certainly not unplayable.  I think it could do with some serious optimisation though.

For a free-to-play early access mod, this is actually
Gameplay and shooting is fluid and smooth throughout, with only a slight number of small glitches, though that is to be expected in this development stage. Level variety and overall graphics could be improved, as CURE does use mostly Half-Life 2 assets with very simplistic-looking levels, although the length and dynamic layout to the 4 that are available offers good replayability for each, even with bots. Despite the lack of the detail in these missions, it does help support users playing on lower-end PCs.
I played through all 4 levels a few times each, and I found it to be fun and challenging every time, even with bots on an Easy difficulty. That being said, the overall feel of CURE is very much like L4D. When running through a level, you'll stumble upon many situations where you have to wait something out in order to proceed, like a door opening slowly. During these times,
spring up. Hordes are triggered by a loud scream/yell as zombies storm into your area from every entry point, making for very tense and chaotic situations. I had lots of fun combating these onslaughts with my AI buddies, and many times I was saved by them as well. Friendly-fire is also a factor in CURE, so being wary not to blast a hole in your friend's back is paramount, especially for the few times I had played online with other people. The lack of dedicated servers is a slight problem, as well as the usual trolls, though I got about the same teamwork (possibly better) offline with bots. What I think makes this game so enjoyable is that it's able to recapture that co-op experience that L4D did so well. It's feels very similar to L4D, yet it still feels new and different in a way.
Though it's starting out well, it can use some major updates.
would be excellent additions to CURE, with perhaps maybe a Workshop for this. The lack of these things is what will make it boringly repetitive after a while. As of right now, I am able to create levels for this game by using a customised version of Hammer found within the game's directory, but also
would help mapmakers (like myself) add more to this game, without the hassle of manually editing Hammer's config settings to do so.
To sum it up, CURE plays great, especially as a team game. Don't let the overall appearance sway you from thinking otherwise.

This game is fantastic, there are no microtransations or anything in this game.
This game is pretty unique, it is a 2D strategy RTS where you build and design all of your own units!
The most impressive thing is that for every unit you build, you can give it it's own unique AI. This means that you can design your units in such a way that you do not need to micro their every action. The AI system is robust and simple. You simply arrange actions you want your unit to perform in order of preference and it just works!
Due to the cap on how expenisve each ship can be, you need to build specialist ships that excel in different fields. Ships with generators cost a lot more than ships that just run on batteries, however you can build ships that recharge the batteries of nearby ships. This allows you to build carrier style ships that recharge the batteries of your nimble fighters.
There is a large amount of different weapons to put on your ship, the combinations are endless. Ships have a wide variety of stats, from their turn speed to their weight to their DPS. Ships that are heavier have more HP and they can have shield generators, however they are slower and less nimble.
Nimble ships can dodge enemy fire whilst dishing out damage in return. There is long range artillery, plasma cannons, machine guns and even self-destruct bombs that you can use to outfit your ships.
All in all a fantastic little indy game that offers the creative mind and the tinkerer limitless possibilites whilst still being easilly accesible and fun.

The Finch family is cursed. Or maybe they're not. It may just be horrible luck, and the family has found a special way to cope and find meaning in tragedy. Either way, in What Remains of Edith Finch, players take control of Edith while she explores her families abandoned home in search of answers. It plays similar to something like Gone Home, while tonally feeling similar to something like the Tim Burton film Big Fish. This can be seen in the games vignettes, in which you take control of one the other Finch family members, and learn about their untimely deaths. This usually involves magical or fantastical elements. Each vignette also has its own simple but unique gameplay mechanics. There are some other nice touches, like how text from the narration will appear on surfaces like walls, or perhaps the top of a table. Then there's the addition of the Finch family tree on the pause menu that gets filled out as the game progresses. It's obvious that Giant Sparrow put a lot of love into this game, and it’s an easy recommendation for fans of this game genre.

As a fan of RTS's, space, and unit design, I was actually pleased to find that a space-based RTS with unit design exsisted. Even better: It was for FREE.
So, setting Guild Wars 2 off to the side, I booted this game up, partly expecting it to be similar to a few other games I've played in the past. I was pleasantly proven wrong, as I was quickly thrown into battle, and shown (sort of) the ropes.
I LOVE this game so far. It's fun, it's often hectic, and getting that victory over a tough, seemingly unstoppable opponent (be they AI or player-controlled) is the sweetest thing.
That said, there are some things to take note of, especially for players who aren't the best at micro-managing (myself included). Firstly, your ships don't have any sort of AI to dictate how they move. If they stop somewhere, they'll sit there and, if an enemy wonders within range of your weapons, fire at passing enemy craft. This means that it's easy to get absolutely pulverized by torpedo-ladden ships (a VERY common and frustrating thing, I assure you).
Second, loading up on weapons and armor will only do so much. Sure, you could build a hulking behemoth and spawn in two of them, expecting to make mince meat of anything and everything that gets within range, but it won't help you. See, you actually have to THINK about your next move. If you're fighting to hold onto that last captured point on your side, you have to start thinking about how to break the siege. You also have to take into consideration HOW your ships are built. Having some good bruisers on the field is a plus, but even wars are won with peasant troops. Fast, lightly-armed and armored 'gnats' can give you the distraction you need to move your forces forward in relative safety, harass that slow-moving flagship coming your way, or even capture that much-needed control point and slow your opponent's rate of ship spawning. In other words: Brains over brawn, until you're ready to crush some skulls.
I will GLADLY admit: I'm far from any good at this game. I'm still learning, still playing with different designs, and still struggling to make progress in the game's single-player campaign (a fairly good way to learn the controls, mechanics, and all that lovely jazz). But I am VERY glad to have come across this game when I did. It even has a fairly decent and often-helpful community.
TL;DR
10/5, definitely a great game so far.

My thoughts on Castlestorm:
You'll be playing the good guy knight who's charged with the heroic task to defend the king's castle from the evil attackers. To do so, you're given four tools: an army, a ballista, yourself and the castle.
Let's start with the castle editor. You'll be given a set of pre-made castles that you can use or edit, but you can also build your own castle from scratch. To do so, you have several rooms, each representing a certain kind of soldier or creature that may only be used in battle if its room has been built into your castle. More rooms are unlocked throughout the campaign, and you'll have some sctructures for visual und defensive purposes.
During the campaign (or multiplayer) you can now use all those units whose room you've added to your building to fend off enemy units. The are knights, archers, birds and dragons, rock giants and other cool stuff to throw at your enemies gates. The stronger the unit the more expensive it is, so summoning the right amount of them and the right composition is crucial.
Speaking of throwing: Your ballista does not only shoot arrows but can also be equipped with rocks to damage the enemy castle, rainbow farting sheeps, exploding apples and several other things to defend your gates. At some point I felt like the ballista was too strong of a weapon because if used correctly it can kill some of the most expensive units by itself.
If things get harsh you can summon one of several heroes onto the battlefield, controlled by yourself, to slash through the enemy troops. After a certain amount time or once your hero dies you'll be back to shooting the ballista and summoning units.
The game is won/lost, once an army has managed to either break into the opposing gate and steal the flag, or a castle has been destroyed to the point where no room is left and thus no units can be summoned anymore.
Throughout the campaign you'll have some limitations, like you'll only be able to use the ballista, or you may only use soldiers, but that's as far as variety goes. There are some levels with a special boss, and some where you have to fulfill a certain task, but that's it.
Each level gives you gold depending on how well you perform, and you'll get some extra gold if you could complete a challence like never miss an arrow, let the flag steal by a certain kind of unit and so on.

Where to start...
When i first loaded up this game i was instantly assaulted by wild colors, flashing lights, weird aliens and strange music. The game world is a very vibrant place and really seems like the chaotic and lawless spaceport it sets out to portray. The aliens are equal parts weird and funny. From meowing cat-men to oozing slimes to bleeping old school robots, it is a feast for the eyes and ears. The different days introduce different states and change the way the spaceport feels. There is a dedicated festival day, when the bands come to town and play all sorts of weird and catchy music to days where rain is hammering down and not much is going on. The different merchants sell and buy a wide variety of goods (most of them unreachable) and food stalls try to fleece you with bad food that makes you throw up all over the place. This game is a delightful excursion into a wild and vibrant world.
That being said, the gameplay is a bit simple. I get the developers tried to capture the monotony of being a hated spaceport janitor and they did that very well. You get ripped off buying food, your money gets stolen by corrupt guards, bad stuff happens to you all the time. The quest you get at the start of the game seems pretty interesting at start and while it retained it's urgence for a long time for me, it dissapeared when i had to set out on yet another quest. One of the problems in here is the fact you can only complete some parts of these quest by chance. Sticking numerous candles at appropriate shrines (hello Lauster) does seem to do a job, but nothing much is explained in this regard. I understand this is part of the reality of the spaceport janitor, so i can't blame the devs for this.
All in all, this game is a definite must buy if you like your games weird and interesting, if you don't mind much about long term gameplay or if you are looking for a great concept of a game with a vibrant and fun world to explore. If you are looking for a RPG style game where gameplay takes a center stage, don't buy this. I like this game because of its incredibly quirky atmosphere, its fantasticly weird and detailed world. Not because of its gameplay.
I really like these sort of games, where the devs have tried something new and came up with a interesting and weird game. That's why i think 10ish euro is a right steal. Regardless of the somewhat lacking gameplay.

I wanted to like this game, I really did. The concept is interesting, the art style is unique, and the surrealist humor seemed up my alley. Unfortunately, all that is marred by technical problems and a poor UI.
The biggest issue is that save games appear to be completely bugged out, so if you quit and restart the game, everything you've done and all of your inventory is wiped. (update: apparently the save file bug has been fixed since this review was posted) In addition, this game seems really unoptimized despite the simple graphics. I'm able to run other more graphically intensive games like Fallout 4 on max settings at 60fps, and this game still frequently dipped into 30fps for no apparent reason, so I can only imagine how poorly it would run on lower-end PCs.
The user experience is also pretty bad. You're dumped into a world with little to no explanation of core mechanics, which, when combined with the fact that most of the game world looks identical and has no map of any kind, makes it incredibly difficult to find specific NPCs for quests. Also, at one point, the janitor started vomiting profusely, which is apparently solvable with medicine, except there's no direction on where to actually find it, and is only made worse by the slow movement and graphical effects that sickness causes.
Overall, meh. Seems like it's trying to go for a Jazzpunk vibe, so it's worth checking out, but don't be surprised if you end up requesting a refund.

I'm gonna start by saying that this review contains spoilers for what I'm assuming is about mid-game content.
This game has a whole lot going for it. The environmental art is densely detailed, captivating, stylish, charming, I could go on. The gameplay has a decent foundation, with the player's nine to five dictating the way they interact with the world, as well as where they fit into it. The combination of the two results in a feeling of this really humble sort of poverty, which in its own way, especially at first, works really well! However, that changes as the game continues.
The game sets up this expectation that the world is deeper than it seems, more or less literally in the form of the sewer-dungeon. Characters talk about the extensive ruins tunneling throughout the planet, full of scavengers, adventurers, and monsters. The markets are teeming with spells, armor, weaponry, and other goods that in any other game would seem like the setting's various dungeon-diving necessities. Further endorsing this expectation, the very beginning of the game has the player purchase an eye from a unique vendor who sells nothing but these eyes, which are required to enter the sewers. The player walks forward a little bit, through the uppermost level of the dungeon, to a door which the game makes a lot of ceremony out of as it creaks open with a lot of light and sound. The player retrieves a skull from behind the door, and they're shunted back into the overworld, now cursed both with this skull that gnaws away at their luckiness as well as with the expectation of a deeper, more involved game.
While all this points toward the start of some dungeon-crawling RPG portion, the game outs itself as a million times shallower. To remove the curse of the skull, the player has to collect three fragments of a tablet. One of the pieces is hidden behind an unimaginative fetch quest, the second behind an even more monotonous nine-part fetch quest, and the third in the lifeless, bland sewer beneath the city. The "deeper" sewer in particular bothered me, because not only was it starkly free of detail compared to the part the player explores in the intro, but it's trivially easy to just walk diagonally and evade the only barrier the player faces down there. After that, the player is left with what is esentially a ten part grind to acquire the other two pieces of the tablet, which due to the game erasing all my progress as I was about halfway there, I didn't bother to complete.
I've played other altgames before, and often the point is not so much to complete some sort of objective as it is to merely soak in the game's world, interact with it in interesting ways, and just have a nice time of that. Where Spaceport Janitor fails compared to peers like Crypt Worlds or Goblet Grotto is that once you've taken in the setting and spoken to the maybe five unique NPCs, there's simply no incentive to keep going.  To add insult to injury, the eponymous diary is entirely bugged, cloning whatever I wrote each night into all the previous entries.
Overall, Diaries of a Spaceport Janitor is like a feature-poor Harvest Moon or Animal Crossing. The game could almost be considered a deconstruction of the other two, and other games like them, if only it did more than just reduce those formulas to the most joyless parts. After teasing the player with a vibrant and colorful world, it shuts them down with gameplay that reduces the overall experience to one of shallow pointlessness.

To summarize the prologue: I picked up trash and burned it, ate an eyeball, tripped hard, and woke up with a screaming skull following me around.  Oh yeah...and later I changed genders.
In the little bit that I've played of Diaries of a Spaceport Janitor, I can already tell I'm in for a huge treat.  From the first 30 seconds of the game, you can already tell you've just planted yourself right in the middle of an incredibly original and tasteful universe full of people, creatures, and objects there's no way you'll ever understand.
Let me just say up front that this game is extremely abnormal.  There's nothing about it that seems familiar.  In reality, nobody can start up this game expecting to know what in the world to do.  Diaries of a Spaceport Janitor is an anti-adventure, meaning there's no way you can lose and there's no real plot or direction to the game at all.  That might be a turn-off for some, but to a person like me, who loves openendedness, variety, and overwhelming amounts of opportunity, it's a blast of an experience.
There's so much mystery to this game that I can see it being a brand new experience every time the game is booted up.  This is definitely a gem for the right type of person.  If you want something straight-forward, hand-holding, nice to look at, and full of plot depth, look somewhere else.  But if you're looking for something unique, unfamiliar, and full of incredible gaming opportunities, look no further.
Diaries of a Spaceport Janitor is a gem in hiding.  I can only hope this game gets more exposure.

The relative joy of Theday music and streetlife. It being the second day after starting a game went a long way to making the game not seem too oppressive, I think.
The promise of True Adventure just below the mundane is a hollow one. I'm sure it feels (or ends up) this way for a lot of people IRL.
Gemstones, esoteric scrolls, pleasure chips, are all basically worthless. It seems more worth it to incinerate interesting and inspiring found objects than to keep them.

I'm honestly surprised this game is being sold at the pricepoint of $2.99...  I understand it's essentially a Dojin, but there are a myriad of /free/ games that are far superior.
There's no resolution options, no way to make it windowed (that I know of), and always crashes if minimized.  Despite being made in 2005, the sprites and backgrounds are worse than a Newgrounds game.  The music may as well just be some free samples from Fruityloops Studio looped.
On top of all of this, they didn't even bother to translate the script, meaning the minimal story appears as Japanese characters only.  (It'll actually appear as gibberish if you aren't in JAP system mode)  Though I doubt we're really missing out on anything there since it's some nonsensical tale of battling Vampires in the future or something - granted, story doesn't matter in a game like this.
Ultimately gameplay matters most in a bullet hell game, and eXceed falls short there too.  Despite looking like awful, the FPS fluctuates down to 30 and back up to 60 mid boss fight even on a system with exponentially more power than the recommended amount.  This leads to a massive issue in that bullet patterns literally shift speed at an unpredictable pace, making the boss fights impossible to perfect.  On top of this, the bosses are also incredibly health spongey, taking far too many hits before becoming tedious, even at the easiest difficulty levels.
All in all, this is a game that you should only bother with if you bought it in the eXceed triple pack, or some bundle somewhere and want to collect your steam trading cards.  Also good if you enjoy experiencing train-wrecks of games.  Even if you're a hardcore shmup fan, there's just so many better options out there.

Men of War: Assault Squad has been my favorite computer game for awhile. There is just so much more to it than you would think at first. You land on the beaches of Normandy, Operation Overlord. A beautifully written visual novel about the ways queer people are taught to hurt each other, the ways we're made to be strangers to ourselves, and the ways our caring for each other, and learning to accept others' care and love, can let us heal and fight back. The story is set in a Midwestern summer camp and focuses on three teenagers who have formed a bond of necessity; none of them fully understand themselves yet, but each of them knows that somehow, ineffably, they are bad, wrong, and monstrous. The main way you influence the game is by choosing which of the teenage characters spend more time with each other. Over the course of one night, they bond closer with each other, come to understand each other better, and also hurt and alienate each other, sometimes by ignorance and sometimes by trained reflex. At the end of the night, in one way or another, their inner monstrosity is fully revealed. Your choices determine who is included or excluded, and whether, at the end, the characters are able to see their monstrosity with compassion and clear vision.
Recommended to anyone who grew up gay or trans. Especially recommended to anyone who finds themselves hanging out with gay or trans people a lot, or following queer art scenes, or hating themselves for reasons they can't quite explain to themselves.

Valdis Story is a prime time 2D action game.
If you were ever in love in Castlevania/Mertroid games, this is definanetly something to you.
GRAPHICS: Graphics are up to date and well-made. I would like to make a distinction between strictly technical performance of the graphics and the overall feeling: sprites are not full HD and this might feel lackluster when you played modern Rayman games or Dust:Elysian Trail, however overall design is top notch from the artistical point of view. 8/10
MUSIC: Slashing sounds of destruction are done well and I really enjoyed them - during the whole game they did not tired me, and that's a lot. Music keeps up and gives some nostalgic vibe when it's necessary, pumps up during the fights and keeps you on your toes. 8/10
STORY: It's good. You are exploring remnants of the city that is lost in time and space. It might feel somehow lackluster, especially when you compare it to other aspects of the game but the game is not about story all that much. Still, I would say that it's better than in any other game of that type I had ever played. 7.5/10 Only because it still has huge potential and I feel I want more.
GAMEPLAY: It is basically a 2d action game similar to Castlevania series. You fool around the map, find the new places you can go and explore. You fight, pick up goodies, fight again, go back to town, pump up your skills/lvls/items, rinse and repeat. The game is all about nimble fingers and fast decisions, fighting is the real name of the game and it's core difficulity lies in action. This is where the game really excels and broke me into pieces. You have passive trees that let's you decide wether you want to be magic wielder, relentless sword fighter or unkillable juggernaut - and believe me, they are not just a ball of stats but they force different playstyle. The same goes for armor you can wear. It does not only give you different stats, it also alters the way your character behaves. Did I mentioned that different weapons behave completely different as well? Giuve oyu different animations, attacks and such. Side note: you can play unarmed as well and it is a viable option. On top of that, there are currently TWO different characters that can be played, gameplay experience differs DRASTICALLY. Did I mentioned about assistants that can be summoned any time during the brawl? Well, I just did. Amount of complete builds, gamestyles and possibilities just makes your head spin. 10/10 all the way.
FLAWS: It might feel ... short? I am not sure. I really liked the game, it sucked me in and I played until I finished. It took me about ~18h and I really, really wanted more. Experience was really intense, I wouldn't mind if it would take a little bit longer.
Valdis Story is still under poroduction and it takes a lot of time. Game is totally playable in it's current state and gives full experience, yet the polishing takes a really long time and if you expect update every week you will get dissapointed.
Still only two from total of four characters is playable. Don't get me wrong - in one character there is more depth than in any other Mertroidvania games I have ever played, still I would really like to see the 3rd and 4th character being playable.
Overall I do not feel like giving the final score, it's really up to you wether you will like it. If you ever enjoyed any 2d action game - you will be happy. If you are additionally an action RPG junkie trust me, you will love it.

When I first heard of this game, I thought it sounded like a Reassembly clone - creating unique spaceships to take over enemy bases. But where Reassembly is more of an open world sandbox, this is strictly an RTS.
I was never much for RTS games. I could never play them for more than 10 minutes and not think of doing something else. But this game doesn't feel like an RTS. I guess it might be the creative aspect of the game, being able to build your own ships and then command those ships into battle feels great.
Overall, I'd give this game a 9/10, for a beta version. There are some features missing, like being able to rotate parts (which would reduce clutter in the ship builder, however your ship's turning speed is a factor when designing said ship, so I guess I can see why you can't.) But what this game lacks in features it makes up in its simple, nice graphics and fun gameplay. I haven't tried the multiplayer, but I can safely say I think I'l have fun with that, too.
I would also like to note that I have barley even scratched the surface of the game, but from the reviews I've read, I can see it gets much, much harder. Oh well.

Wow. This game took many ideas that i had in my head that could make a good RTS, and executed them so elegantly and perfectly. I fell in love from the moment i saw the trailer, and i have played it for two hours straight, wishing i didn't have to go to sleep, ever.
This game managed to streamline the RTS combat really well, and the different blocks and parts you can build your ship with are well thought and simple to use, but add a lot of depth to the gameplay without adding complexity. Thats a beautiful thing: depth without complexity. Its easy and intuitive to understand, and can lead to a very interesting gameplay and strategies. The strategy aspect of the game is really simple regarding the battle system, and the greatness of this game comes from how important positioning, army composition and ship building is, rather than fast reflexes and multitasking.
The campaign starts a bit slow, teaching you each block individually in each battle, but the promise of unlocking new blocks in every mission is an awesome insentive, and a really satisfying reward, as each mission gets a bit harder, and not every missions can be beaten with the same ships, you are forced to refine your ships and your tactics.
Love it. As of now, two hours in, it gets a genuine 10/10. Try it now! Its really light, its free, its relaxing, its satisfying, and overall really fun. And i haven't gotten to multiplayer yet!
Oh, and also, props to the developer. Its nice to see a free to play game made solely for the love of games rather than as a money grab. Congratulations on your game, i think its gonna get a really nice community behind it pretty soon.

Codename CURE is not necessarily original, but it is far from being a rip off of any game. Codename CURE is a game which requires teamwork in order to succeed, as you need your teammates to watch your back, and cover for you while you reload. There's something about this which makes it fun to play, as strategy varies depending on your team compositon since the classes are diverse and provide neat tactics each and every game.
You can either play "casual" mode to have a taste of the game, or/and work your way up to "insane" where the sheer amount of infected test your skills and strategies to the limit.
Overall, the game is lacking in content, with only four "official" maps, one set of weapons per class  along with only one gamemode, it can be quite repetitive. However you can make up for this by downloading custom maps. Keep in mind it's in early access but still quite polished besides the buggy A.I. by the infected at times.

I played DOW I and loved the strategy, the units and the low need for buildings. However, I don't think I enjoy DOW II as much (But I do like Last Stand). I believe it's mainly due to the map and gameplay repetition.
1. Lore
More Warhammer 40K lore in game. Interesting story except for the "Unknown Primarch" nonsense. No surprise that it's going to be Chaos orchestrating everything in the end.
2. Less "buildy" Multiplayer
No need to play base tetris or resource farmer. Mostly combat.
3. Cut Scenes
Very short. Not exactly a cinematic but it's okay. I would have preferred a full 3-minute cinematic.
4. Characters
Quite interesting to see all the different characters from
a. Force Commander
b. Tactical Marine
c. Heavy Assault
d. Scout
e. Assault Marine
f. Dreadnaught
g. Librarian (Psyker)
1. Campaign Map and Gameplay
So repetitive. Go to point A, kill the Boss. Rinse, repeat. How do I describe the monotonous feeling that I get when I can predict what I am going to do on the next map already?
I know that there is going to be a few "yellow circles" telling me to attack those locations and kill everything there. I also know that I am going to kill a boss.
The rare defense maps are pretty boring too. Defend the generators from being attacked. There. That sums up the defense maps.
The objective is just to kill, kill, kill. No escort missions, no tech upgrades, no mixup, no buildup. I'm sorely tempted to just skip the optional missions just to create more chaos so that I can have some fun.
2. "Unloading"
Very long unload times. Posted in the forums, seems it's a forced save replay that happens.
3. Multiplayer Unit Building
It takes too long to wait for sufficient resources to build a T3 unit. Even if you control ALL the resource nodes, the time required is just way too long. In a 1v1 or 3v3, you can't wait to build a full army.
Don't forget that I've not even added in the upgrades on each unit.

Plays much like Scott Pilrgim Vs The World: The Game but on two planes rather than a 2.5D plane.
Constant progression of characters gives a nice sense of accomplishment.
Rather addictive beat'em up game play that can lead to hours lost and leave thumbs sore.
The sprite work and animation really sticks out with not only each character but also with every enemy you encounter. Overall very smooth animations that link to one another very well. The environment has a nice 3D based style to it giving everything depth despite being played on a pure 2D plane. The art work from sprite to background transfers well. Everything is busy with color but it never distracted me from the gameplay. Not until all the combat had stopped and I took a moment to appreciate the little details helping the world feel full of character.
Everything is very flashy without ( yet again ) being distracting. The feedback of lights and hit animations are really satisfying.
Everything comes together very well.
My one gripe would be the minor gaps you can see every so often in the polygons of the world and the transfer screens. But this is a very minor thing that asshats like me will notice.
Much like the title gives away, this is Steams version of a Kawaii as hell Scott Pilgrim Vs the World.
The combo system isn't anywhere near the same though. Were Scott Pilgrim plays more like a classic side scroller ( Streets of Rage etc ); This title has a double linear 2D fight path. What I mean by this is that fighting happens on 2 planes but not at once. You can only move right or left and switch between high and low planes. It does take some time to get used to after putting so many hours into S.P., but once you get that hang of it it becomes second nature. It allows the player to get out of the way of spamming enemies and make strategic choices on how to attack.
Back on the subject of the combo system. It may seem like a mindless button masher but this isn't the case.  Just mashing away will get you beaten down. Fast. While it may work for the first couple of levels, you quickly need to figure out how to block, when to use specials, when to use emergency mode and so on.  Comboing needs to be timed or you'll be struck in the back and need to figure out how to recover.
The more you learn about comboing and getting high hit combos, the more you'll end out leveling. The game rewards you for doing well and not losing combos much like Devil May Cry.
After a full playthrough there is very little negative about the tittle.
The enemies can be a little spam happy at times. Seems the devs relied a little on juggling and a.o.e. attacks to give the illusion of difficulty. These attacks aren't hard to get around, but once you've been caught in the later levels you'll see your health dwindle down with little to nothing you can do about it aside from waiting for the right moment to counter the hoard.
The game actually isn't too difficult either. This isn't a bad thing as it makes it addictive, but as stated above, it's moments of difficulty come from rather cheesy tactics from the AI.
It's rather short too. Only a few levels that can be beaten in around an hour or less. This one isn't really a BAD thing though! For what the game offers in terms of addictive gameplay and really fun combat, I personally didn't mind the length. Hell, anything longer may have felt a little dragged out. The short play time is also offset by high replayabilty with bonus characters and 50 levels of XP for each.
I've been having a lot of fun with this one! After the take down of Scott Pilgrim I've been craving a really solid and fun beat'em up and this game does a great job at scratching that itch while giving you something totally different yet extremely familiar!
Definitely grab it if you're into S.P./ Streets of rage/ combo based games or anything like River City Ransom.

Let it be known that, while I don't think WKTD is bad, and it has some good morals to tell, I don't think it's worth 8$.
Pros:
-I like the theme of the route being based around who gets left behind, and the true end being everyone sticking together.
-There's at least a positive message in here for people. I understand this work is particularly pointed towards those who are among LGBT+ (and I appreciate that there are works like this willing to tackle the subject matter", so I suppose that hopefully someone who does go through WKTD can get something from it.
-While they aren't around for long, I did enjoy the interactions between the main three characters throughout and they create an interesting dynamic for the story.
Cons:
-It doesn't really feel like the paths to the endings had a consistent rhyme or reason. Yes, you "leave behind" a character, but the tasks are at times menial, to the point where getting locked out of the true end didn't really fit the theme of "leaving someone out".
-It feels too short to get its point across. Even in doing all the endings, it spends so little time developing the characters, that I didn't really get to really know who they were. There isn't much backstory or really much of anything to really get someone invested beyond their personalities and their actions, and the short length such little room for individual character development or actualization. The antagonizing forces of the story had such little presence in the plot until I got my first ending, where it just left me confused. I'm all for some ambiguity, but the game felt like it rushed towards its eventual goal, and is paced in a way that's bound to lead to some confusion.
-The actual game script really could use some work. At times it feels like it was written via stream of consciousness, and while this worked on occasion, other times it just creates confusingly written sentences with poor syntax and grammar.
-The music at times was just... loud noise, and while at times that fit, at others it felt as if it just was trying to make a scene more dramatic than need be.
Overall...it's just okay. There are positives to be taken from this, and I think that there's potential to expand on the good ideas here. It took me about 2 hours to go through, which is honestly a harmless amount of time. But at a price of 8$, there are better things most of you can do with your money.

TL;DR: A fine middle ground between mechanical depth of a fighting game and satisfactory button-mashing of a beat-em-up. Neither the worst nor the best port I've seen, largely depends on your expectations and opinion towards a few particular points.
The Good:
- reasonable mechanical depth without insane learning curve of a true fighting game. If you're looking to practice some basics or get a friend into the fighting mindset without scaring him by overwhelmingly complicated move lists and combos, this is a good place to start.
- plenty of characters and fighting styles - rush, poke, zone control, jumpy tricks etc.
- nice background art/soundtrack (obviously per personal taste)
The Bad:
- "GHJBY" for default keys that can't be rebound? Uh... yeah. Because it makes sense. You can rebind what button does what attack, at least.
- Some random single-digit frame drops upon game launch until you've clicked through 3-4 menus. Nothing critical and totally fine in game, but still.
- Difficulty levels are gated by stats. As in, they're balanced around a certain character level. Mostly a problem with bosses, as not having enough stats makes every mistake really painful.
The Ugly:
- DLC gating character progression? Guess what, you're not getting fully unlocked move tree without it. Just consider it a part of the game's price, really. At least it's one and only gameplay-related, the 2nd being OST.
- No online mp/coop functionality from the original game. To quote: "we're still working on other updates to the game, including the planned online multiplayer update and other revisions. Development has been slow because much of the PBBG dev team has been preoccupied with the upcoming PS4 version". That's not a good excuse for PC gamers folks. It's been like 4 months since release. I'll give it a pass for the first time just because the storefront is honest about coop being local, and I did have fun with it regardless of MP.
UPD: online MP added on 19/08/2016.

MoW: AS is a very tough RTS. You have the ability to control anything from a single soldier to an entire platoon. Combat is intensely realistic as a platoon of infantry in the open can be cut down in seconds. Tank on Tank combat is excessively realistic to the point where most players learn why many strategists would only use tanks with infantry escort. Tracks can get blown off, guns can get destroyed, crew can get sniped from inside of the tank, and ammo racks can detonate, all depending on where a shot is placed. If a tank is damaged, it can be abandoned, or the crew can leave the tank to repair it and get back in.
Aside from Tank on Tank combat, Infantry combat also feels very fleshed out. Units can and will be suppresed (however, there will be no alert, they will all simply just fall to the ground and crawl to the nearest waypoint you set for them), as well as realistic logistics. No unit has infinite ammunition supplies, and if you're running low, your best option is to loot an enemy's corpse for extra ammunition, as ammunition types are universal amongst weapons with examples such as: Rifle Ammo, Pistol Ammo,  Shotshells, Machine gun belts, ect. This may not be completely realistic, but it's enough to keep the game steamlined just enough to keep gameplay fun, but not mindless.
My only complaints are:
- There is no Players vs. AI settings in the game
- Server connection is absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ You will constantly get a message saying "Connecting to server" every fifteen to twenty second. It lags the game for a half second to two full seconds, and is definitely enough to ruin the intensity of a big firefight.
- Units are hardly autonomous. Unless you purposely want units to sit in a defensive position, you have to intensely micromanage your troops and vehicles. If you leave any unit sitting idle for long enough, it WILL be killed.
- In multiplayer matches, there is no "deep striking" infantry unit (like American paratroopers in CoH) that can spawn where you click on the field. 173rd Airborne and Fallshirmjager are just basically elite infantry units, and hold no strategic value over your typical run-of-the-mill G.I.'s or Grenadiers.
Overall the game is great, but the lack of the Player vs. AI option kills it imho. I'd recommend this only so a friend can have a taste of what a true WWII FPS should feel like, only to go back and play with what MoW: AS had failed to compete against.

I played AVA back when it was released under the game company called ijji. When the switch was made, the community hoped for some improvements. Its all they could really hope for. Hackers had gotten the better of ijji and the game wasn't really progressing at the level it needed to be. Regardless of that, it was still a very good game at the time and I think the community felt like the game had potential to grow. Thats when Aeria Games stepped in and literally dropped the soap on this game. We were ♥♥♥♥ed. Hard. Weapons became timed, extreme pay to win weapons were released, and unncessory changes were being made to the game that made no sense at all. Hackers came and went like it was nobody's business. I myself just play for the nostalgia and because I have a good account.
In the end, the game is dead. Simple as that.

I'm writing this review right after finishing the game for the first time.
Metroid, Castlevania, Devil May Cry, Megaman...  If any of those names fill you with fond memories of wanting to throw your conroller at the screen (as opposed to unfond memories of wanting to throw your controller at the screen), then you need to play this game.
Valdis Story has elements from all of them, but most reminds me of the original Castlevania: Symphony of the Night on Playstation.  If we're honest, the whole game is probably much smaller, but it is absolutely beautiful.  Many of the exploration elements are very similar, certain areas requiring you to have specific items or abilities before you can access them.  A new twist are timed platforming segments, wherein you have to hit a switch and then traverse the necessary route before the door you opened closes again.  Many of them demand a great deal of precision, which can be quite frustrating at first, until you get the knack.
The combat system is fairly deep, combining weapon combos with spells and dodge-cancels.  I've seen less complex combat from games that were supposed to be primarily brawlers.  And you will need to make the most of all of them when you meet the game's bosses.  There's no overpowering a boss through sheer button-mashing prowess.  You'll need to pay attention and attack, defend or run away at the right time.
If you enjoy games that demand precision, practice and determination on the part of the player, then Valdis Story will deliver in spades.

I bought this game because it reminded me of a board game about child poverty I played when I was young, crossed with Harvest Moon. The main thing I remembered about the board game is that the mechanics tended to enforce poverty and make escape from it very unlikely, and this seemed like it was doing something along those lines, with a HM-like time management/commerce/quest framework.
The game basically consists of a daily Harvest Moon like routine-loop with a single main quest for a story. The main quest is composed of 3 smaller fetch quests. One of these three is broken. Given how simple the structure of the game is, it's not a good look to release in this state.
-environments are fun to look at and navigate
-character designs read well
-basic loop is fun to do for a while, often seems as though there is a lot to do (more on this below)
-collecting items and reading descriptions has a katamari-like feel for a while
-some mechanics like floor patterns affecting character's luck, or redscarves stealing money, are immersive
-some grinding poverty feels altho usually more on grad-student-level than menial-worker-level
-main quest is broken
-quickly becomes clear that most items (basically all interesting ones) are usually irrelevant to the character (they rarely pop as trash and can't be purchased because the price is much too high). This includes food items, which are a major focus of the game
-Cheap, filling food (Horka Sauce or whatever) is available at vending machines, which obviates whatever attraction expensive foods might have had anyway
-Eating discarded/rotten/inexpensive food isn't really penalised (you puke a lot, but each puke can be incinerated for MC, so you're eating for free and generating your own waste to burn too). There's not really any mechanical pressure in general, but this one just seems to undermine the basic theme of the game
-saleable items that pop as trash are often worth so little that it rarely makes sense to take the time out to track down a merchant who will buy them. What seems like an interesting decision- "should I keep this item and fill an inventory slot in hope of a later profit or incinerate now for a few MC" usually is after a while resolved by "item is only worth a few MC anyway, burn it" or "who the ♥♥♥♥ even buys fusion batteries, 420 burn em".
-because most items are irrelevant, and because most items that seem relevant aren't actually worth that much anyway, once you've seen most of the common trash items, the basic loop stops being as interesting
-not much reason to talk to vendors after you realise their wares are on the table- quickly realise that 90% of stalls are irrelevant
-"gender" mechanic feels completely shoehorned in. "Mechanic" is maybe too grand a word here- "gender" does nothing in game other than remove a blurry camera effect that occurs every day if you don't take "gender pills". I was expecting some kind of trans/genderqueer commentary on the basis of the game description, so I assumed there was some kind of semi-didactic content here, but it just seems like a total afterthought. Literally the only other part of the "gender system" is a wacky-random mad libs description of your new gender after you take your pill- and it always says "Your gender is now <MAD LIB>, you feel amazing!"
After it set in that the gender thing wasn't doing anything in-game, I briefly thought that this might be a sort of "class burns gender" commentary- that is, your gender-shifting janitor's hormone pills are literally just a secondary addiction (drug use in order to stave off negative effects) that has no effect on her (visually, mechanically, behaviourally etc) except to assign her a fancy new label that does nothing to raise her out of her poverty.
In a forums post the devs indicate that the gender mechanic comes out of their experiences with gender and that it is supposed to represent "the way gender works in the real world" and intended "to do something potentially interesting". It seems clear that they didn't really have any specific didactic intent with this, and I don't think it really adds anything to the game (the blurry camera effect could easily have been rolled into the hunger mechanic and the gender-shifting treated either thru story events or another more meaningful mechanic).
-luck mechanics seem easily gamed. I started at -100 luck and was at +1500 luck in a day or two just by praying at shrines and leaving a couple of candles
-"diary" notetaking feature does not allow you to review previous entries, again undermining a basic theme of the game
tldr;
Good game from good developers

5 hours in, and when I say in, I mean IN. I'm invested and enthralled by this indie darling. By all rights this game should not work. It has a really repetative gameplay loop, progress is slow, and the game actively annoys you with small things like a floating, screaming, skull. However it's a great example of how you can use what should be clunky gameplay to tell a meaninful narrative. You're a poor, cursed janitor. Life's hard. You just want to save up money to get off this planet and maybe lift your curse along the way. Day in, day out, you scrape up the little cash you can week by week, and on a bad day you can just lose money. You need to eat and pray to make sure you don't get unlucky. You'll get sick and exepirence gender dyspohira and fixing that also costs money. Guards are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. You even get catcalled. But that's life. It's the small things in Diaries that sticks with you. A fovorite god you pray to first every morning after you get breakfast at your favorite stall. Slowly learning the layout of the city and feeling more at home there. Getting excited to find a container to bring to your friend the container collector (Still don't know why he wants so many). Find a valuable piece of trash and actually knowing where to sell it, or even hold onto in your house for sentimental purposes. And bit by bit things get better. You get more money, meet more people, dare to explore more, and your routine becomes comfy. I want to get out of this spaceport with my janitor uncursed and happy but while I'm here I might as well find a special kind of happiness and you should too.

Reminds me of using pattern blocks in elementary school to build elaborate starcruisers and space stations. A minimalist 2D fleet building Sci-Fi RTS game. The campaign is a bunch of linked scenarios on a star map of a spiral galaxy. The difficulty ramps up fairly quickly and requires you to re-evaluate your ship designs and add newly unlocked ship parts at regular intervals. Istrolid delivers quick space battle action in bite sized occasionally puzzle-like encounters.
It requires quite a bit of mirco-management and the maps are a bit barren but the colorful art style is quite nice. The basic gameplay is building and battling.  There is no interactive resource collection and there is a fixed cost cap on ship designs so the size of ships is limited. This encourages building ships that mutually support each other and which are tailored to specific roles (Anti-Fighter Flak, Long Range, Missile Attack and Defense etc.). More depth then most games which can run in a web browser plus there is Multiplayer.
Istrolid is a game with potential combining elements of a 2D Homeworld crossed with Kerbal Space Program but lacks the storyline and physics fun of those two titles. Which means it boils down to an easy to play but hard to master space battle game versus the AI or other player fleets.

The first eXceed is a decent danmaku (aka bullet hell, manic) shooter. Although it pales in comparison to its sequels, by itself it is enjoyable, and has challenging boss fights.
Scoring mechanics are pretty simple, with a bullet grazing system to charge up your special attack. The game has an automatic death bomb option, which triggers a bomb (as long as you have one) when you're hit instead of you losing a life. It's a good option for those inexperienced with the genre. Controls and gameplay in general are tight and work as they should. Boss battles are entertaining and challenging, but the levels feel a bit too easy in comparison.
Visually, the game is a mixed bag. It runs only in fullscreen, at 640x480. The presentation is pretty basic, and the game way overuses the colour red (red is my favourite colour and I still feel this way). This overuse is also my main gripe with the game. As all the enemy bullets are the same shade of red, along with many other effects sometimes filling the screen, it sometimes feels like my eyes are twisting themselves in a knot and it's hard to distinguish the tons of bullets flying around for a moment, resulting in a lost life. The UI is also annoyingly hard to read for the same reason. The backgrounds vary from boring, to nice but the same smallish picture scrolling over and over. Certain effects, like explosions and boss phase switches, look good.
The soundtrack is awesome as is often the case with bullet hell shmups.
For replay value, the game has three difficulties, plus three characters with completely different weaponry/abilities requiring different tactics to clear the game. The game can be played in Story, Arcade (i.e. with or without dialogue/story), or Practice Mode, but sadly there's no high score or replay saving.
tl;dr, eXceed - Gun Bullet Children is a solid, fun danmaku shooter covered with a flawed presentation. The original game is only in japanese, however there is a patch to get the official english script into the game (
). It's also more newcomer friendly than many other titles in the genre, thanks to the auto-bomb and relatively simple scoring mechanics. Recommended for both veterans and beginners of, and anyone interested in, bullet hell shmups.

RobotEx is a mixed bag when it comes to reviewing.  It's not an amazing game, but it's not a bad game either.
This is an automatic side-scroller with very little controls, as it was obviously made primarily for a portable platform.  Pressing the spacebar makes you go up, letting go makes you go down.  The only other key is P, which fires your forward rockets.  When you first start the game you're given a controller config screen, which seems to be a bug as the controls are hard-coded into the game so the config screen is somewhat pointless.  Once you figure out that there are only 2 hard-coded buttons your control issues come to an end.  (unless you're one of those spoiled individuals who has to have complete control over their key configs)
Starting out with the graphics, they're pretty detailed and very nice to look at.  I'd say right along par with other games in this genre.  My only gripe here is that initially it can be difficult to tell what's going to hurt you and what isn't.  This can lead to a few accidental deaths, but as you have unlimited lives it's really not a huge hinderance to the game.  Once you figure out what things will hurt you it's not too difficult to spot and avoid them.
Sound in the game is pretty much whatever is absolutely required.  There isn't really any music but there are action sounds (rockets firing, explosions, etc) that will keep your ears from getting bored.  Again, the sound that's included is well done.
The menu was a bit of a mixed bag, as it was obvously developed (again) for a portable system.  You have 3 worlds (colored file folders) to select from on the left and those give you the various levels available (1-1, 1-2, etc.) for you to select.  Clicking on a level begins said level.
I'm a pretty intellgent person so figuring out the "story" wasn't too difficult for me.  It's presented in the form of cutscene-style video, but as there is no text or voices to the story it's up to you to figure out what's actually happening.  From what I understand, the world has come to an end and a fleet of ships has set off to find a new home.  You are therefore the explorer of these worlds.
All in all the game could have been ported a little better for the PC.  It could have included a menu screen showing the keyboard commands (which you now know).  It could have been better fitted to the window.  They could have removed the on-screen button graphics, obviously used by the portable version.  There's a lot they could have done... Rocketbirds: Hardboiled Chicken is a game where you are a literally and figuratively hardboiled chicken that slaughters its way through a fascist/communistic penguin regime.
Shooting works fine, even though enemies are quite bullet-spongey. There is an ammo-counter but I never found myself out of ammunition and thus never paid it any mind.
There are some boss-battles that mostly amount to running around, grabbing ammo, then shooting the bad guy with no trick or gimmick whatsoever.
There are also a few Jetpack-encounters where you float freely in the air, surviving waves of enemies until the story progresses.
Aiming and movement are tricky in this type of gameplay and in these sections I found myself collecting fuel and ammo quite a bit. Rushing all over the screen, grabbing the aforementioned crates, evading heat seaking missiles and trying to hit freely moving enemies got me killed quite a bit.
Simple puzzles are all over the game and are mostely of the "push crates onto buttons" variety. Some sections have you mind-controlling enemies to pull levers you can't reach but the reduced arsenal and the fact that other guards will ignore you until you shoot them does very little to change the usual playstyle.
There are a few collectibles in each level in hard to reach or hidden places. I made no effort of finding them in my playthrough so I will not make further comment on them. Just know that they exist.
I finished this game in about 4 hours and found the experience rather mediocre. The humor about action-hero and secret-agent clichés in a setting of flightless birds did not work for me but might be the strongest point of the game.
Price did not figure into this review.

Although the concept is certainly an interesting one, Bad Hotel fails to accomplish this very successfully, although this is certainly the best game from Lucky Frame.
Gameplay:
Already at the start, you see that you do not place towers next to a road which enemies walk on to try to get to a certain objective, but instead you place towers on top of a central structure(hotel) to defend it. As if that idea was not enough, the towers will generate noise that will serve as the music for each stage you are in.
However you soon realize that despite the potential the game holds, it is overthrown by many complications that soon reveal itself after you finish the first few levels. There are no hotkeys to help select a tower to drag them quickly, which really makes a difference since the game relies on fast reflexes. The levels are structured in a way where the difficulty in completing them will vary greatly, where some of them can be destroyed with a simple strategy, while others require you to try for a good amount of time. Unfortunately musical elements never really have a chance to stand out a lot, as you cannot really mess around to create a nice sound to listen to.
Replayability:
After you manage to complete the game, you notice that there is about no replayability available, which is quite noisy for a $5 game. Although the site claims you are allowed to edit the tower arsenal after completing said level, you cannot modify the tower strength or tower types you are given even after completing all the levels. Shockingly, it also decides to not have an endless mode or level editor to be able to continue the game after you beat the campaign, which could have kept players to not get bored after 3 hours. Even with achievements, they can be done relatively easily, as it took me a day to get all of them.
Graphics:
Although some people will claim that they are stylized, the combination of bright colors with simplistic graphics tends to hurt the eyes. They do stand out from the amount of pixelated games you see, but not enough to create very interesting graphics.
Afternote:
Overall for a $5 price tag, this game is too expensive compared to other games which are more fun. Although this game did have developers who did care about the quality of their product unlike Cartoon Wars 3's developers, you are probably better off buying Legendary Wars or an arcade shooter for the same price or cheaper. Only get this game if you want to check out an interesting idea that never got refined well.

Personally, I really enjoy the topic of flags as a whole and I must observe this game's original idea could very well serve as a base for a very fun and challenging game. The game itself could simply be described as "Incomplete". It shouldn't be too much of a hassle adding a main menu, a way to avoid the same flags being asked again in a short amount of turns, a basic flag format for all, and overall something to even barely promote the continued gameplay, perhaps a counter to responses' accuracy or considering the time expended to respond to each flag question, albeit in the form of Steam achievements or not. I mean come on, was a way to avoid the same country appearing twice in the same question that hard? As of now, this game will grow boring in mere minutes, as you're doing nothing but scrolling continued flags without any real challenge or motivation to perform better. Not to mention the SEVERAL inaccuracies present. After less than five minutes in the game, I can already note that:
-Myanmar's flag is displayed as its former version, changed in 2010
-Czechia is displayed as Czechoslovakia, that dissolved in 1993 in its constituent states (Slovakia is present in the game as well, so WHY such a blatant mistake was let pass in the first place?)
-Poland's flag is sometimes displayed upside down, making it the same as Monaco and Indonesia's ones. Why?
-The country "Cote D'Ivoire" aka "Ivory Coast" is displayed as just "D'Ivoire"
-There is no name distinction between the Republic of Congo and the Democratic Republic of Congo, two different sovereign countries with different flags
