This game has a mod called "Dynamic campaign generator".
This mod adds completely different dimension to the game as it will let You build Your force from the begining of hostilities and follow the war till the end of it on all fronts. Troops will acquire experience and their equipment will follow from one battle to the next (unless You choose to reset their invetories).
My recomendations for a german side starting 1940 - bring Your 88 guns ASAP and capture as many Bren Carriers as You can. You can store a lot of equipment in those carriers. This will let You keep micromanagement to the minimum as "reset all inventories" will not reset captured vehicles yet You will not be forced to micromanage every soldier and every gun as they will have their munitions in each battle. There is no way to resuplay Your own tanks in the mod, for example, unless You reset their inventories.  And those carriers are superb for towing Your 88 flak guns around the battlefield - they have rather low profile and will let flak guns to fire over the carrier and they will provide a good MG cover against attacking infantry.
I hope the creators of this awesome mod will continue with Assault Squad 2 and add more features in the future also.

First off, it is fair to mention that I do not actually enjoy visual novels - I find them rambling and frustrating. I enjoyed We know the devil for all it was not like most visual novels. The story is short (I have played through all the endings including the "secret" one) and it does not offer too much choice. What it does offer however, in my opinion, is exquisite music and writing.
Obviously, if you browse the reviews you can see not everyone agrees. The writing can be quite coy and shy away from saying things outright - which might be annoying to you. The story is also magical realism - symbolic and supernatural occurrences are part of the setting, which is very clearly not to everyone tastes. But if you find these things enjoyable you can find a moving story about internalized homophobia and religious upbringing that is well worth the money.

The story is about 3 teenagers who are sent to a summer camp (as punishment for being "bad") and have to get involved with some weird Christian ritual and... the story climaxes, and... it's really a big pile of... nothing impactful, you know?

This game is cheap. This game is short. This game is truly excellent.
The visuals have a distinct lo-fi aesthetic that I personally enjoyed, with B&W character spites over polaroid-quality photo backgrounds. It probably won't be to everyone's taste, but the sprites are expressive and go a long way to making the characters endearing.
The music is... odd. Not bad, but definitely odd. It fits.
The writing is where the game really shines; I don't want to say too much, but it does a lot with a little, both in terms of subtly drawing the characters and making you care about them, and explicating just enough of the setting to keep the plot rolling. I'm literally angry at how good the writing is.

Commandos 2: Men Of Courage is an action/strategy game set in ww2 in which you are in command of 9 special forces commandos and must undertake a series of missions behind enemy lines. The 9 commandos all have vastly different capabilities some of which may be exclusive to that particular soldier so all of them will be useful at some point or another.
Whilst quite challenging the game is incredibly fun and actually requires some careful thought and consideration on how you go about completing objectives. Also there is not one way of doing things, there are often several ways to approach something and what may work for you might not for someone else so its really up to you to think of your way to deal with the problem.
The levels are really well designed and take you all over the world. You’ll have different commandos available for each mission so the same tactics for one mission might not work for the next. The soundtrack is also fantastic and has many memorable tunes that really fit the themes of the levels and make the game very immersive. I’m not big into strategy games but this was an amazing game and might be the best ww2 game i’ve played. It also took me about 30 hours to finish some missions being 2-3 hours each. Its been one of my favourite games for a long time and would 100% recommend if you can get it running.

TLDR – Dawn of War 2 is real time strategy game that borrows squad type combat from Company of Heroes (same game developer). Despite the RPG elements and seemingly overwhelming odds in each level, the game really isn’t that difficult if you take your time, so don’t let that turn you off. If you like epic sci-fi stories and real time strategy, you should enjoy DOW 2.
In this game, you play a “force commander” in the Blood Ravens, a chapter of the badass Imperial Space Marines. This isn’t just a story line thing, your commander unit is deployed in every level and you run him around shooting and chopping bad guys like a hero unit in Warcraft 3. If you’ve played Warhammer games before you should recognize most of your enemies this time around. The Orks are brutish thugs (as you would expect from orcs) and the Eldar are high tech psychic aliens (kind of like Protoss in Starcraft). The Space Marines as usual have made it their mission to wipe out all aliens in the galaxy, meaning you fight everyone everywhere. This time around you face a new threat, the Tyranid Hive Swarm (much like the Zerg in Starcraft) which is invading your sector of space, killing humans, Orks, and Eldar alike.
First of all, if you’re used to real time strategy games like Starcraft, Warcraft, or Command & Conquer, there are a few key differences you should know right off the bat:
•	This game is more “tactical” than strategy, meaning you do not build anything (buildings/units). You start each mission with all the troops you’re going to get (except missions where they introduce your new squads).
•	You can only deploy 4 squads per mission (total of 6 available), and they are all “heroes” meaning they level up and can be equipped with weapons/armor/accessories. They also all have special abilities and “mana” to cast spells. You’re going to be doing a bunch of micromanagement throughout the game.
•	All of your units have both melee and ranged attacks, and you can toggle which one to use. This isn’t a feature in many real time strategy games and you can exploit it in some cases (suppress the enemy with heavy ranged attacks and then charge in with melee to wipe them out).
•	Between missions, you often get to choose where you will deploy next. Even the story missions can sometimes be played in your choice of order. This became a problem for me because the order I played the missions unlocked a certain unit almost at the end of the game, and he turned out to be my favorite.
•	Note that you will be playing on the same 12 or so maps throughout the campaign, but starting at different points on the map. This is because all of your battles are fought in the same sub sector of space, and you’re competing with the aliens to hold ground. Also keep in mind that most maps have special buildings that you can capture, providing bonuses to your overall war effort. Start early and capture as many as you can because holding these buildings offers special “defense missions” where you try to survive waves of alien attacks (more missions means more exp and item drops).
•	Another thing to note is that you can’t save the game manually during missions, it autosaves between missions. If you quit a mission, you get a loss on your record.
Pros:
+Excellent storytelling and a variety of aliens to pound on. If you’re a fan of Warhammer, don’t miss out.
+Simplified gameplay, just your 4 squads vs large hordes of enemies and occasional bosses. Don’t just charge in or you’ll be wiped out.
+The game has co-op campaign gameplay available. You and your friend can play through the single player campaign, each controlling 2 squads (instead of you controlling all 4). This can be helpful if you’re bad at micromanagement, like me.
Cons:
-Like the Company of Heroes games, there seems to be a lot of luck involved in the gameplay, specifically in gun accuracy. Normally you wouldn’t expect real time strategy games to have units missing their shots so much. It’s not really a bad thing, but it can take some getting used to. Also, the ability to charge in with melee units or throw grenades really negates the “cover” system.
-A minor gripe, but it seems like a bunch of the game’s Steam achievements are for playing ranked multiplayer matches and for the Chaos Rising DLC.
Overall, the game is fun and will last you quite a while (took about 14 hours to beat). Each individual mission is short (you get bonus exp for finishing faster), but the single player campaign is lengthy and you have many variables to choose from when it comes to skilling and equipping your squads. You can’t just mass produce units and crush the enemy like other real time strategy games, you actually have to guide them with some semblance of skill.  Also, if you play the multiplayer, be warned that gameplay is drastically different from the single player campaign. You have to build units and tech up like in standard real time strategy games.

Enigma is a great game in my opinion, and one I highly recommend.
Now, I wouldn't go as far as saying it's one of the best VNs I've ever played, because it isn't. But it's so unique and engaging! It's an experience I'll never forget, for better of for worse. Why worse? Well, I assume you've read the description of the game - this isn't a joyful one. I mean, sure it has funny moments, but it's overall depressing and has lots of very disturbing moments.
An important factor to keep in mind if you want to play this game is that it isn't a game you play for romance, since friendship is the main factor here, even if it has "character routes" like most romantic VNs (though you can read in between the lines and see whatever you want in there).
As for the characters, I really liked most of them, though I must admit Ignis must be my favorite from the ones who got routes. He really hits some soft spots in my heart and breaks it in some of his endings. Now, Lauro is lovely and lovable too, and Chester, the MC, is one of my favorite main characters in VNs. I think I like Envirio a bit less than the others, but I love seeing dolls in games - it's quite uncommon.
One thing bothers me a lot about Envirio, but this isn't a story or character problem. The issue is that most of the characters in the game speak of them using the femenine, while they are genderless being a doll, and they even say it at some point. English has neutral forms, so why not use these? But this is roughly my only complaint.
Other than what I've already said, I also think this game is gorgeous, both the art and the soundtrack are great, and don't even let me start on the opening and the ending!
Overall, it was a great experience I'll be glad to replay once the trauma of the depressing story will subside a bit.
PS: don't mind the small playtime recorded by Steam - I've played offline, and it didn't record the time I've played or the achievements. I was able to get the achievements by loading all of my saves and skipping from the last choice leading to each ending (I save all the time), but well, I can't help the playtime.

Rising world. An epic voxel based sandbox game.
peoples may ask why this game would be so epic, and come with comments like "isnt this just another terriblie remake of minecraft"?
well the answere is NO.
This game indeed has inspiration by minecraft, but again theres a whole lot more to this game than you may think.
As i said this game is a voxel game just  like minecraft wich means that the game is buildt up by cubes. And what i just said is not theoretically and scientificly corect, but i am just going to say that so you understand what i am talking about. an better explaination can be found in wikipedia.
However, what is it really that makes this unrealistic pixelized game as good as it is and how is it possiblie that a game that most peoples would call a minecraft remake could be a good game? well i am going to tell you that.
"The thing" about Rising World is that in this game you are more "free" and have a lot more options to how you can build whatever you're gonna build. yes you can build your house with blocks as in minecraft if you like, but in this game the material isnt blocks by standard. in this game you have to manually craft the blocks from different material wich can be mined in same way as in minecraft. when you cut down your first tree you will see that it drops a wood log as a raw material, with this wood log you can create planks and supporting beams for a "realistic house" and floor/wall panel like you would do in real life. Or if you want to you can craft an wood "block" instead.
The developers of this game have been focusing a lot on the subject "Realism" when you cut down the wood, they dont break in blocks, they break in logs, if you mine some ore they dont drop like  blocks they drop like rocks in real life. Honestly this is actually a really awesome looking in game, the way the grass and everything is made is in so high quality that you wouldnt even belive it.

What a satisfying trip down memory lane.  Loaded it up out of a mix of curiosity and nostalgia, and before I knew it I had beaten the game, and wasted my entire day off.  Of course it's dated and clunky, but every once in a while that very clunkyness will add to the suspense.  There's a very real sense of satisfaction which comes from solving the more challenging puzzles.  Oh god the puzzles.  They range from pleasantly distracting to downright sadistic.  The worse offenders will have you backtracking for what seems like hours.  I found the chess puzzles to be particularly infuriating.  My heart set to racing on more than once occasion, from the challenge alone.  Younger audiences will probably be deterred by just how dated this seems, but I was swept away from the charm inherent to that era.  The acting is just about as broad and cheesy as you'd expect, partially due to the low video quality.  It somewhat reminds me of old silent movies, with actors mugging it as hard as they possibly can simply to be understood.  The live-action video director mentions in the included making of video (nice touch by the way) that the actors were encouraged to 'use their whole body' when speaking.  It's frikkin' great.  Took me about 7 hours to make it through the entire thing, even while attempting to cheat my way through the more head smashy against the wallsy bits, and I'm quite glad I did.  It may be an archaeological exercise, but it sure is a fun one.

The first time I ever stopped playing a game because it was boring.
At first the cute graphics lull you into playing and the controls feel great too.
But then you notice the flaws. The main flaw is that the designers really didn't know how to add 'challenge' to the game so they tried to band-aid it in. Bosses jump in difficulty way too fast and fighting them becomes a battle of attrition.
Most mooks are just a speed-bump and while that is true of most beat 'em ups, here they just palette swapped a few mooks and made them hit harder and have more HP and bam "challenge".
Stun-lock is an issue, you press nothing to block (why can't it be mapped to a button?!) and many enemies push you back when you block so you can never close the distance on ranged enemies in an effective manner.
Boss fights are a joke with your health bar being the punchline, grinding to level up is akin to pulling teeth out armed only with string only for you to realize that you actually are holding a can of silly string and those teeth are actually a giant
.
Overall though fighting the mooks to level up is boring and the boss fights don't feel like they are presenting a fair challenge, they just feel like 'you must be this level to pass, unless you can cheese us' and then you realize that the reason the game is designed like this is because it is so shallow. Their is nothing interesting or dynamic to keep you invested in the game, stage 1 is the same as stage 3 which is the same as stage 5, just mash mash mash away until you fall asleep.
Buy Double Dragon Neon instead, both games are the same price but Double Dragon somehow managed to add
to the formula.

I bought this on a lark and have to say that I'm pleasantly surprised.
The positive aspect of this game is that you have some real nailbiting, epic boss fights that will push things well past the limit. There is an element of trial and error as you learn attack patterns, but nailing a tough boss after a protracted fight is extremely satisfying. The game gives you a large enough toolbox to make fights organic and exciting. A boss' attack can be evaded with a dodge move or a timely jump. You might also be able to block it with your shield or blow through it with a defensive spell. Perhaps you could even be prevent the attack altogether with a well timed big hit. No matter how you play it, it's all very satisfying and deaths are not severely punished the way they are in certain other 'challenging' games.
The main issue with the game is it seems to enjoy doing puzzle platforming sections that rely on basically leaping from ledge to ledge against a timer. Nothing has been too irritating yet, but I can see this being frustrating for some.
The game's skill and magic system is also a bit obscure. You'll get an item that says it needs to be 'patched up' and the game will give no indication about how you might do that. The skill system is also filled with all sorts of terminology that the game doesn't bother explaining in the least bit, leaving you wondering if it's a good idea to inflict Retribution or gain a defensive bonus after dodging.
Still, those drawbacks are set aside by some good old Metroidvania action. It's fun. It had a boss based on Rubick, what more do you need?
The one flaw:
I don't like the game's ranking system though. It's one of those "You got hit, D rank" games that get a bit obnoxious. I don't need some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ judging me after I beat an incredibly tough boss fight. Back off, game.

This game is hilariously badly designed. The UI is clunky; the deck builder screen is actually a genius-level example of how not to design such a screen - you can choose between small icons, which are almost exactly too small to actually read, or large icons, which means you can't fit nearly enough on the screen to make sense of what you're trying to do. And you want to see a graph of your mana curve? LOL no, you get a table instead, only it's not even a useful table because it breaks each mana level down into creatures, spells and artifacts rather than giving the total, which is the number that actually matters.
It sets great store by its PVE play, but the campaign is slow, clunky and suffers from impossibly steep lurches in difficulty unless you're extremely lucky in the cards you randomly receive or willing to play a fight repeatedly to get the lucky draw which give you a small chance of beating it.
The best example of just how utterly awful it is is the desert worm fights. With the deck you have at this stage in the game, you struggle to put a 4/4 on the board by turn 5. The AI is dumping 10/6 creatures with charge on the board as early as turn 4. How to beat this fight? Real easy - you uninstall the game. Or, if you're really smart, you don't install it in the first place. Of course, they hope that's the point at which you'll dump £100+ into their coffers to get cards powerful enough to stand a chance. Don't fall for it.

This is a game I hope more people try, because it is a love letter to Metroidvania fans.  Valids the Abyssal city is very much a Metroidvania clone, with a 2-d world that is large and sprawling, but with many areas locked off until you get the necessary key or ability to get past them.  The story is fairly good for what it is.  It focuses on a conflict between angels and demons where neither is truly good, both are corrupt, and humans are caught in the crossfire.  In an underwater city that they are warring in, you must defeat both sides and find your way out.  The characters are pretty cool and it is engrossing.
The combat is pretty unique.  It focuses on a combo system mixing light and heavy attacks, almost like a fighter, however you can use spells, special abilities, and support characters to shake things up.  Also, the more hits or special ways you fight enemies, the more experience you get, as your consecutive hits or fighting styles give bonuses.
What I absolutely love about this game is the replayability.  Four characters are planned, but only two are unlocked.  That being said, each character plays differently and interacts with the world differently.  Wyatt fights with a sword, but can also unlock daggers and a bow, or twin swords, or even fight with his fists, each being upgradeable with different abilities.  Reina uses her fists to start, but can use dark totems, a quarter staff, or a gigantic mace later on.  They both play differently and have different spells, offering a truly unique playthrough for each character.
Some problems with the game are that to upgrade items, you sometimes have to grind against enemies to drop the necessary components for upgrading them.  There are also sections that seem to be awaiting an update, like the two other characters we can't play as yet.  And some of the items you can buy are near impossible to get because the items they want in trade, this game uses a barter system, are so rare.
That said, Valdis Story is well worth the price.  The graphics are quite nice, the combat is fluid and fun, it is challenging, but not frustrating, and offers a large amount of replayability.  A sequel has been teased in the end credits and I dearly hope we get it.  This game is just fun.  It's not revolutionary, but it is a blast to play.

You will marvel at it's unique and colorful atmosphere and almost rage quit in disbelief at the developer's audacity to include the immediately infuriating Towers Of Hanoi puzzle. Acquire beautiful new desktop wallpapers and shamelessly use a walkthrough to get through half of the game. Boldly play games you forgot you ever downloaded in a desperate attempt to make a dent in your rapidly expanding Steam library.
Buy one of those bundles that gives you 11 F-Tier games for like two bucks and get this - a solid B game amongst the dreck.

WKTD is a short, excellent game about all kinds of abuse, being LGBTQ, being a teenager, and dealing with social isolation. The religious abuse hit me hardest -- it's almost impossible to find good media that addresses how scary and damaging religion can be that actually handles the subject well. The characters are great. This is a very short game, especially if you read quickly, but the writing is sharp enough to make a lot happen emotionally in that time. The music is solid and though there aren't many tracks I listen to outside the game, they build the atmosphere well.
There are some typos and oddly-placed punctuation, as a warning. It's not a perfect game. It's also not actually a dating sim, though I've seen it billed as such. Those are really the only critcisms I can come up with, though.
This is an INCREDIBLE game for the price and it's helped me deal with my own trauma and accept myself as a person. I think that's a powerful thing for any work of fiction to do. I wholeheartedly recommend it to all LGBTQ people and trauma survivors, and to anyone who enjoys a short, gut-punching story about all the things that ♥♥♥♥ed you up as a kid.

If you loved the gameplay for Dawn of War, then you will likely hate this game. Its gameplay is minimilstic and extremely boring.
DoW had actual missions with varying objectives. DoW2's missions are pretty much all the same. Go here, capture this point, then kill the boss. Rinse and repeat until you're dead enough inside that you need to be entombed in a dreadnought. The only break from this monotomy is the occasional defend missions, which are much more enjoyable than the actual campaign missions.
Visually and thematically, the game delivers. Space Marines still look awesome, Orks still look like a bunch of Incredible Hulks that got way into crust punk, and the Eldar still look like teched up Space Elves. Most notably, DoW2 brings the Tyranids to the franchise, which are great looking and have wonderful animations.
However, even the niceties of the game can't save it from the ihghly reptitive missions and the lackluster game mechanics. Even the RPG dressings don't really help.
You only get 4 squad members to deploy on each mission, one of which is always the force commander. So, really, you only get to choose three members of the squad. Choices are: Force Commander, Tactical Squad, Assualt Squad, Heavy Weapons Squad, Dreadnought, and Scout Squad. Once you deploy into the mission, you don't build bases or anything like that. You simply slowly saunter your squads around the map and kill things until you reach the boss. There are points to capture which can replensihg your squad and give you bonuses later on.
After you finish your missions, you get rated on how many enemies you killes, how quickly you completed the map, and how much stuff you captured. XP points allow you to level up squads and give them points to unlock various abilities. You will also find new armor and weapons, with varying stats, for your squads to equip.
I'm sure some love this game simply because it's WH40k. I found this to be an extremely dissapointing sequel. The combat is boring. It's the same crap over and over. Another player in Co-Op means that you control less squads instead of there being more squads. (ie: instead of each player controlling 4 squads, each player controls 2 squads)
If you like building forward bases, tricking the enemy with emplacements, and building up large armies, then you will be completely devistated by this game. None of that is available. Even the Orks feel like their armies are increibly minimalistic and underwhelming when compared to the original DoW. The Multiplayer Annihilation mode is terrible because of the lack of base building capabilities (you always know the enemy base is if you know the map) and the only mode that anyone really plays is Capture Point.

Rocketbirds: Hardboiled Chicken is an adventure game in 2.5D. The player controls the main character Hardboiled Chicken throughout various levels within the campaign, in which they encounter enemies of different ranks along with different weapons. Through the campaign, one gets to know how Hardboiled Chicken turned from a government-friendly to the enemy of state-chicken.
Being a game between mildly difficult puzzles and, due to the weapons, bloody and brutal shootouts, it really is as weird as its name.
The singleplayer campaign takes around 3 hours to completion, though one might not reach all achievements, since, additionally, there are signs to be found, resulting in more achievements to be reached (and one special achievement in connection with the signs).
In the co-op campaign two players, either on LAN or connected through the internet, can complete the missions together.
The maps are the same as in the regular campaign, except the puzzles have to be solved in different ways as the characters are smaller and both players have to help each other to be able to progress.
Rocketbirds: Hardboiled Chicken is a weird game with a weird plot and a weird main character in a weird scenario. Though looking like a comic, it definitely is not appropriate for children under the age of, lets say, 13-14 years

I was greatly dissapointed by this vn. Since everyone was praising it for narrative perfection (and it started out as a narrative  perfection), ended up being shallow, underdeveloped and overall mediocre experience.
The premise of the story starts strong and interesting enough. Throw a man on an uncharted island, give him just a couple days to live and make him uncovered its secrets, and spend his remaining time with the max efficiently along the way.
The path with the first characters (Lauro/Colette) gave me a lot of high hopes even. It was filled with a lot of emotional moments, and it was actually interesting to see how the man who is one foot in the grave already sharing his experience with youngsters, who in addition, know almost nothing about the life on a mainland (the game is happening on a desolate island). I actually liked how my choices can alter the story drastically in this path.
By completing the next path with Ingnis, however, I was already bored. First of all, his character is boring and unlikable as hell (worse only envirio and tai, but we will get to that). Second of all, most of his endings turned out to be a filler. As I can guess his path needed to be here in order to clarify stuff about the world, forest and the desease, but here is another problem comes in a play: we know very little about the world, and we know very little if magic is common here or not and by what laws it actually works, and, as a result, I had a little desire to be invested in the mystery.
The Envirio's path is the worst. It pretty much a filler as a whole. First off, her character is terrible. She is a doll. She wants your color. That's the kind of well-thought-out character you can expect feom her.
Second of all, by the time you get there, the novel itself feels overused not only on assetes but also on plot events (chatting with Genious/Lyona, debriefing of Ignis/Greta/ Collette goes mad etc), its clear that author is running out of ideas by this point.
...and what marks this fact once again is the ending. I want spoil it here, but I will say that it's very, very rushed. Tons of questions left unanswered (
), characters arcs are chopping off in cheapest way possible (Envyrio goes to nowhere, Lyona goes to nowhere, Tai was a turd and remained as turd,
), and the most frustrating factor that it lacks any of final confrotation/moral dilemma/recollection.
Overall... is this worth it's money? Yeah, no, maybe, depends on your preference. I feel myself kinda not in the right to ctitise this novel (i mean it's author's first work after all), but at the same time I will feel wrong if I will praise it with other players either. I believe you will like it with the rather high chance, but for me, it was too little all around.

The last thing I expected to buy today. I forgot how useful Fences is until it popped up on steam.
If you are the sort of person who still uses desktop shortcuts a lot and your desktop is always in a big mess this is for you.
If you are disorganised, and need something to organise your desktop and keep it tidy this is for you.
If you have better things to do with your life than learn how to be organised this is for you.
If you want to flick between separate desktops by clicking a mouse on the edge of your screen  to keep work and leisure separated visually on your computer this is for you.
Pros:
-14 day trial available on the company web site.
-Very light, simple to use then you can forget about it.
- licensed for use on 5 PCs with steam on them. (I guess it is tied to your steam account)
- runs without steam (starts up with windows)
- de-clutters your desktop for good.
- no performance hit when it is running even on low spec
- takes regular snapshots of your layouts and keeps the last 3 days so you can restore to an earlier desktop layout if you need to.
- use multi desktops and multiple monitors
-Cons: may not be an issue for most people but you HAVE to have steam on all the computers you want to install Fences. So this is the difference between the steam version and buying it on Stardock's site.
-No serial number or key available to view on steam.
I used freeware Fences from V1.0 on all my home computers way back in the day, somehow I forgot about it between XP and windows 10, I saw it on steam and remembered how handy it was.  You can configure it as unobtrusive tabs which roll up, fenced-in sections on one or more screens (desktops) and also as an "organiser" of files and folders, you can even set one tab for your dropbox etc.
Cons: the "you aren't a Pro if you need software to orgainse your desktop" brigade.
Any moment some clown will be along to neg the review because "you don't need software to be organised, and who uses desktop shortcuts these days... bla bla... look at me I know everything about I.T. ...". Well, news for you:  there are millions of people who have been using computers long before you were born, integral to their job or business, and there are millions who use desktop shortcuts who aren't IT nerds and have better things to do with our lives than get obsessed with the way other people use their computers, so get over it and jog on. There is nothing for you here, you are probably missing your TV show about fat ladies with rubber gloves  cleaning other peoples houses or hoarders having their homes cleaned out by people like you.
TL/DR for everyone else: works great, does exactly what you expect it to do.  9/10. If you don't want to install steam on all 5 computers you can use Fences on, but it from the developers web site instead of on steam, and then you get the serial keys.
*Yes a cluttered desktop isn't best practice, but this hides it all, and on modern computers a cluttered desktop is the least of your performance worries. I used to use this on a 486 with less computing power than a modern £10 throwaway phone, and it never hurt performance even on that.

I will be reviewing Fences in sections. There will be a TL;DR at the bottom along with pros / cons. This will be kind of long. why? So whoever reads this gets some insight on someone's perspective of this software, along with the developer who gets to read this for feedback.
Note: I am not familiar with formatting on steam. Forgive me.
What is Fences? Fences is a tool. Software. That allows users to easily customize their desktop.
Presentation: As someone who knows nothing about the developer, what the software is, or how this stuff is even created. It is best to make sure your product can be presented in a clear format that people can understand. So people know exactly what they are buying. The developer has done a fantastic job at this. The icon has been well made to what the purpose of the software does.There are videos that explain exactly what Fences is, and how it operates. They are clear, well made, professional videos, clear audio with easy to understand words. This is paramount to getting yourself out there as developer, for your product. No one will buy it, if they cannot understand it. Overall, presentation is very well done, professionally hand-crafted for this specific product! Well done!
Platform: I am usually wary when buying "software" via steam. Because of my unfamiliarity with it. I assume that it would always be running and conflicting with other games on steam because it would always be "running" according to steam. Thankfully, the developers who make software, including this one, make it so when you open it's configuration, steam thinks the software is "running" then. Which makes sense. I am glad to have the software that I enjoy such as Fences, to not have any conflicting parameteres, considering I do a lot of gaming on Steam. Overall, the platform choice is good. It gets the word out to your product, and being on Steam helps with that. It does not create any conflicts and therefore has no drawbacks when picking up this software via Steam.
Guts and Glory: The best bits of software, is "how does it run?" - "How do I use it?". Here I will address these types of questions you may be asking. I find Fences easy to pick up and run it, but hard to master. That said, there are videos from the developer that aid with making your "Fences". Along with clear instructions within the settings themselves, which are VERY useful. I do not need *that* much aid when it comes to remembering that "double click means hide and show desktop icons/fences" - BUT I know that some people would really love that hint there. And the fact that it IS there, really means a lot. It can go away with a click, but stay there if you want (the hint). Setting up Fences is rather easy. Run it, click and drag, open and configure settings how you wish. All of the settings are VERY well detailed on what they do and change. Which is very important when software like this has many options. Not everyone will understand right away what everything does, another good design choice from the developer. There are many different options are you will find the right ones for you!
Pros:
+Amazing software for your desktop
+Platform choice (Steam)
+Easy to setup
+Good reminders and hints, never annoys you.
+Many customization options
+Makes your desktop look good and have YOUR icons where YOU want them to be
Cons:
-Can be a little difficult to newer people who are not familiar with these types of software
-It's easy to click and drag and make your "Fences" but to customize every portion does take time, and understanding of what you are changing
-UI (settings) could use a more modern look
Personal Gripes that do not affect the rating:
-I wish there was an option to unalign the icons within the "Fence" I love having my icons unaligned. Yes I am weird. That is why I have stated this does NOT affect the rating.
P.S. I couldn't think of many cons, so I was really "picking and choosing" and being picky, to at least list a couple.
TL;DR = Great software overall, developer makes everything clear and easy to understand, it's easy to set up, but hard to master.
Would I recommend this software? Yes. Why? I find it amazing. I like what it does, it gives your desktop a new look, plus endless combinations to customize your desktop and make it look very professional but also clear a lot of space up so you can look at your amazing wallpaper.
Personal recommendations / UNRELATED: I would recommend "Wallpaper Engine" with this software as well - They go very nicely and I use both.

What a thoroughly entertaining gem of a VN with a rather neat story structure going for it.
In this game our protagonist is Chester, a man with not a lot of time left to live. There's a disease called Enigma, and it's eating away him and humanity as a whole. He's a man who wants to believe in heroes and heroism, and in his last few moments decides to embark on a solitary adventure by sea, not really to accomplish anything, but perhaps to find a peaceful place to die?
He ends up shipwrecked and awakens on an island not on any map, almost as though it is cut off from the rest of the world. He winds up amidst some rather inviting company in this equally beautiful and mysterious island, a perfect place to spend his last moments... But there is more than meets the eye to these inhabitants. His fate slowly begins to tangle itself with the island in rather surprising ways, as if his arrival was more than just accident.
This is the general synopsis. The game itself has some really interesting things to say about heroism, friendship, love, and death, and has quite a neat way of doing this with the traditional VN route system with multiple endings and a "true" ending. It's nothing that hasn't been done before in VNs, and if you're familiar with popular VNs, you'll probably intuit what the game is trying to go for after going through a few specific endings. Either way, the game does what it does rather nicely and makes for a real fun read.
Chester by the way, is an amazing protagonist. He is an adult and for the most part, he acts like one. For a man who has so little time left to live, he has more chill than your average protagonist in an anime/manga/VN. And despite how easy it could be to, it never tries to go the low route with his dying condition. It doesn't try to forcibly pull your heartstrings with him not having a lot of time left and dwelling on it.
Other characters are also more or less likable in my eyes at least, though there are a few whose motivations for their actions I personally found a bit weaker, especially in some endings...
The multiple endings by the way, are all worth looking at, going as far as to say they are for the most part essential towards the grand finale, as well as better understanding some of the characters. The game seems designed to want you to go through the endings, as the mysterious person at the start of the game can guide you towards new routes.
Unfortunately, despite this person's help, this hunting for endings can be quite a bothersome experience. Which is a shame since all the endings are worth looking at, even if some of them border on the outrageous at times (Boy, some endings can really knock the wind out of you with their brutality and cruelty). This is perhaps my biggest gripe with this game. It has to be this way because of the story it wants to tell, but in the end, it's still a bit of a pain considering how many endings there are. I found myself constantly guessing if this or that choice will lead to a new ending.
Going on to presentation, the music in this game is a rather pleasant surprise. The music starts off as rather reserved, not grabbing your attention, until key parts of the plot come into play. It's then that you slowly grow to appreciate the tracks. Too bad the mini-ost doesn't have more tracks aside from the OP and ED, nor does the game itself have a music mode it would seem. The art in the game nothing ultimately amazing, and sometimes the backgrounds can repeat a bit, but sometimes the game will throw you a curveball and have a rather pretty sight or a new background you haven't seen before. There's also a decent amount of CGs and they complement whatever scenes they are depicting very well.
I sadly feel that this game might get passed on the wayside by many people. It doesn't exactly have much to draw people in aside from its mystery hook. For those willing to give it a try, they might be like me and find a really interesting and entertaining experience that I do not regret having.
I'm glad fruitbat brought yet another interesting VN out that isn't some big name known to many. For this game has a story to tell too, I found it good enough to want others to see it.

I had to spend 20 minutes just to get 5 minutes of in game time by constantly reopening and closing the program just so I could post this review hah. Sadly it doesn't register as running for long after the initial opening.
So I was skeptical about this program, not knowing exactly just how much I'd want it, especially at this price, but I bit the bullet because there are basically no English reviews. Well, 2 minutes into using it and I was already in love. The steam launch for the program launches an alternate installer but that didn't really bother me.
Now as someone with a ridiculous amount of clutter on their desktop, this was a god-send. Upon launching the program it will ask if you want it to auto sort your desktop documents into fences and generally I'd say yes is a good starting option. It will put all your folders in a folders fence, your shortcuts and program files into a fence of a similar name and text documents etc into their own fence, just as a base. Now these fences are as simple as dragging the corners to change their size, but they're all scrollable so they can be  as big or small as you want.
To create your own custom fence, all you have to do is left click on the desktop and drag the selection box to any size you want and release, it will ask if you want to turn that area into a fence and you can put anything in there.
The fences are not treated as separate folders, so don't be afraid of folder shortcuts or things like that breaking, they are still technically in the exact same place, just organized.
Now there are many many many customization settings, but I'll just go through the two or so that I tried at the time of writing this.
You can change the colour and opacity of each individual fence which is very handy depending on how intrusive you think they are, however the option I am using makes the fences completely invisible so my desktop is completely blank and it's as simple as double clicking the background to hide and reveal. You can also choose to keep your fences visible and instead opt for them disappearing after a set amount of time of inactive desktop use.
There is an option to treat the fences like a mobile phone, by swiping with your mouse you can cycle through different fences on different "pages" on your desktop.
The price is justifiable at least to me in the sense that now I have this program forever and it's not like it was an $80 software, it works above and beyond how I'd expected or hoped. If this program is something that even remotely interests you, you probably do want it, especially if you're messy and just can't keep your desktop clean, like me.
I  noticed the English, Chinese mixed reviews mentioned Wallpaper Engine, I also use this program and they work seamlessly together. It's fantastic because I can clear my clutter and see my animated desktop perfectly now.
(For those who don't want to read the comments)
Do you need to have steam running for this to work?
No, it auto starts on start up, before Steam.
Did you notice any hit on your computers performance?
It runs smoothly for me, no lag and minimal CPU usage, this is also corroborated by someone with an average PC that has been using it for years. At the moment the memory and CPU usage is negligible.
I have multiple monitors and lower resolution games throw my icons out of whack, how is Fences with this?
The Fences stay exactly where you put them, no change all the way down to 800x600, completely consistent at all resolutions. There are options for having fences change position based on your resolution changes.
Fences also stay on whatever monitor you put them on, there is an option to have your fences move to any new primary monitors you plug in.

Here comes the nostalgia hate. I did not grow up with this game, and this is the first time I have played it. Being honest here I am not just going to give it a good recomendation just becouse it is nostalgic to a lot of people. This is a opinion based rewiev and if you don`t agree with me, you don`t agree with me.
Presentation:
When you start up the game and click on new game, we get to know the story about a toymaker, and how he build the mansion you are in, and are intocuced to the 7 guests he has invited.
The story aspect was acually very interesting in the begining, but I felt like the game forgot about an important story towards the end.
Other than that I had a problem with the game early on. The save feature was broken, and therefore I had to complete the game in one sitting. This was a problem for me, since I never really found the game interesting enough. maybe your save button is not broken, so this is just a personal problem.
Gamepaly:
This game is a point and click puzzel game, and it is very generic. The walking around is used by clicking at a place, and you have to search the house in order to find all the puzzels to solve. The puzzels veryes for sliding puzzels, maze puzzels, chess puzzels and the list goes on.
Sometimes the puzzels can feel a bit samey, but most of the time the puzzels feel very original.
Now I want to talk about defecullty in this game, becouse I think there should be a difficulty setting. Some of the puzzels are really easy, and others are nearly imposible without a guide from my behalf at least. This really ruined the flow of the game for me, that I had to sit with a guide through a couple of the puzzels, when all they could have done, was making a easyer version of that puzzel, for people that don`t want to spent hours on the same puzzel.
I also found out you can skip all puzzels if you want. This blows my mind that you can remove ALL gameplay for youself. That is really a bad thing for me, since the creator thought this button was nessesary. Eather the game was too hard or they just wanted the game too fell easy. I used this feature on the harder puzzels, but I never felt good when doing it, since I felt like I removed potentioal gameplay from myself. But trust me some of these puzzels would have taken hours to figure out.
I can also understand that one of the puzzels are nearly unbeatable since the AI thinks so mutch faster than an old PC would. This was also one of the puzzels I skiped since I thought the same thing.
Charecters:
So the charecter. you see 6 peaple enter the mansion, you know the main villan is the toymaker, and your charecter has forgotten who he is. All the charecters has visions of them throughout the mansion, but I never really feel like I made a conection to them.
All 6 guest have a dessire, and the toymaker can grant there wish, but they are killed off, in ways that resemble there dessire. For an eksample, there is a woman that wishes she was younger, and she then becomes a baby. I found this story element well made, since it was fun to find out how the charecters dessires would kill them off.
There also is a ghost floting around you never get to know about, and that bugged me. Another flaw in my opinion is that you see that events of the mansion, as you find them, meening that you can spoil some of the ending to start with. This can make the story seem pointless, since you already know alot, before you get to the start of the story.
The charecters never really captured me, and that is a letdown for me.
Visuels:
The animation and grapghics in this game are ofc outdated, but they are still very nice to look at, and the overall house looks very good. All charecters are shown with FMV and the dialoughe are very cheesy. The Chessy charecters combined with the bad FMV makes the game very laughabel at times, and that is a shame for a game trying to be horror themed in a way.
I also need to talk about the lines that are repeated throughout the game. If you play a puzzel to long, the toymaker will comment on it with the same line over and over again. Sometimes this is unavoidable since some of the puzzels takes a long time to solve. I wish I could shut him up, but maybe this is another personal problem
Sound/Music:
The music in this game is pretty good. I liked most of the tracks throughout the game. Now the voiceacting can be a bit off at times, but there are some good moments too.
Story:
So I breifly talked about the story but here`s the deal. A toymaker makes toys that make children sick, then he builds a mansion for himself and invites 7 people. 6 people + you. Every person comes to the mansion with a dessire whether it is wealth youth love etc. The only charecter without a dessire is you, since you have no memeorie, and can`t remember why you are there.
The rest of the game you have to uncover what happend at the mansion through cutscense you find throughout the mansion. This leads to a really....confusing ending that really made no sense to me, but play for youself to find out.
Conclution:
This game was not for me. I know this game ment a lot for people back then, but from a newcomers perspective, I can say the game has a lot of weaknesses and flaws. It is boring at times, with puzzels there are too hard, too easy or too random to solve, with uninspireing FMV and a story that never really interested me. Overall I never really felt the game was appeling to me.

What more can be said about The 7th Guest that hasn’t already been said? It’s a mega classic that’s held up surprisingly well. If you haven’t played it (shame on you) you really should give it a whirl, especially if you can catch it on sale. A few caveats, however: firstly, the then-jaw-dropping visuals now look like they were captured by a child’s first digital camera, filtered through cheese cloth. It’s not a deal breaker, but if you’re not already nostalgic, it can take some getting used to. Secondly, to make up for limitations on how large a game could be, developers made the puzzles quite difficult. If you’re not a puzzle guru, or are new to this type of mini-game, you either need extreme patience or a walkthrough. I suggest at least trying to figure them out on your own, however, or the experience will seem rushed and shallow. All in all, The 7th Guest is a solid piece of the masterful gaming of yesteryear.

You control Ophelia and her tulpa Oliver as they travel through several weird worlds and solve puzzles using the tulpa's ability to manipulate objects from a distance.
Tulpa is a short puzzle game with a pretty great art style and atmosphere that sadly falters when it comes to actual gameplay and content: while the care that went into the game is plain to see its simple nature and extreme shortness make the asking price hard to justify.
-great art style
-the soundtrack is subtle but pretty effective
-the worlds you cross are all fascinating due to how weird and eerie they feel
-some puzzles are interesting
-very little in the way of story, what can be gleamed from visual cues is extremely vague
-controls can feel a bit unresponsive at times
-some puzzles and sections rely too much on blind trial error, also a few puzzle elements can be hard to make out from the background
-very short, expect around 90 minutes
I really like Tulpa's art style, it's simple yet very effective in representing strange and somewhat disturbing worlds from another reality: sadly that's pretty much all there is to the game though. The gameplay is very light fare as you simply walk around- or face basic jumping sections- and face a few puzzles for each level.
The aforementioned puzzles go from ok to annoying as some are quick, logical affairs while others rely on clues or visual cues that can be a bit hard to get and either leave you stumped or require several deaths to pass successfully. It's a quite forgettable experience most of the time and the extreme shortness'd doesn't help either.
All things considered Tulpa is worth a playthrough for the art style and atmosphere alone if, like me, you got it from a bundle: but its price tag and bland gameplay aren't enough to recommend as it is.

What a difficult game to rate with a thumbs up or thumbs down.  Enigmatic, often well written, and quite short. But somewhere in my third playthrough, I kind of started to appreciate it.
It was the next day that I realized that there was something about the storytelling that had infiltrated me and intrigued me, stealth-style.  It crept up on me, and made me think about my sleepaway camp days, and some of the things a writer can do to evoke emotion.  A month later, now that it's had time to set, I appreciate how the game at times tries to bewilder in order to shock emotion into you.
I think if you like interesting narrative experiments, this quick whiff of emotion might be up your alley.  And even if you find it frustrating at first, it may yet end up part of your emotional lexicon.

I fondly remember the Magic: The Gathering PC game in the 1990s. The game let you roam the world and challenging creatures and slowly build up a digital deck. I loved it. Ever since that game, I've always wanted a good PvE card game. HEX fills that void.
Let me start by saying it's not perfect, and it's not as open as that old Magic game was. You don't roam the world freely, you follow defined paths and go through straightforward dungeons. Yet, it scratches the itch I've had for years. HEX lets me create a hero, build a deck, and then go on an adventure to earn more cards and skills. There is enough variety in the races and classes that replaying through the story remains fun. HEX also is loaded with strategic options, and the ever growing card effects are unique and exciting.
The things that have really stood out for me in my 500ish hours of playtime:
- The PvE campaign. It's better than any other TCG I've played. Granted, I have not played most of the newer ones.
- The card variety and artwork. It makes me want to collect them and earn enough dust to unlock the full picture.
- The hero variety, skills, and races.
- The evolving sealed gauntlet. This was the first TCG I played with this system, and it's pretty exciting. For $5 you get two packs and some misc cards to build a 40 card deck. You get another pack at 1 and 3 wins, and you're done if you lose twice. I find it far more exciting than ladder play and you see much more deck variety.
- The variety in PvE bosses and dungeons.
- The animated cards and card backs.
The things I don't love or hate:
- The Frost Ring Arena. I do like the arena, but it get's a bit grindy quickly. The level of difficulty also means you don't have nearly as many options in deck creation. You have to create an incredibly strong/efficient deck if you want to beat it. I guess that makes sense, but it also means a huge portion of my card collection is basically useless.
- Ladder play and the number of active players. Most of the time, I can get a game quickly, but I can't deny there are not as many playing HEX as I'd like.
Things that irk me:
- Tied to the last bullet, the sealed gauntlet. Not enough people play it, and I rarely see it in a position where I'd want to join and wait.
- The length of time between PvE updates. This seems to be a common complaint. I will say though, that when they did release chapter 2, it was a very substantial update. That gives me hope that when future PvE updates come out, they will provide loads of adventuring goodness.
Overall, I've thoroughly enjoyed my experience with HEX. It's not perfect, but it's fun. I seem to keep coming back to it despite all the new, exciting games I'm buying (damn you, Steam sales). So, that must mean they've done something right!

Valdis Story is a great example of metroidvania which, while incorporating all the elements perfectly still has something new to say. Exploring a 2D map while leveling up and gaining new abillities by defeating bossess isn't a new idea. By adding a few features Valdis Story gains its own character. These are : smooth, combo-based battle system with ranking and prizes based on your performance, actual connection between chosen skills, equipment, stats and even spells; and as of now 2 characters with vastly different playstyle.
The music and graphic are beautiful and really make you immersed in the underwater city. However the biggest thing is animation. In a game focused on fighting, jumping, avoiding and running the developers did a great job with bringing it to such high level.
For me the biggest downside was somewhat lacking transport system. The map is quite big and I believe that during the endgame more shortcuts should be made available. There are also some frustrating moments, which require you to really nail such a obscure mechanic like grabbing ledges.
The game is great, long, has a lot of secrets and offers great replayability. I believe it's really worth its value even without a discount.

Valdis Story is a fun little Metroidvania style game, with a fairly solid combat and levelling system.
The visuals are incredibly pretty, and the music is decent as well (though not amazing).
The problem with this game is that it implements a few story branches that will majorly affect certain 'safe zones' getting cleared of NPCs. Often there is no clear way of knowing how your actions will or won't affect what happens later. Nothing is TOLD to you, you just have to get there by luck and a little bit of knowing what's going on.
Finding your way around can be a total pain as well. You have a map, but you can't switch the map to scan other zones for unexplored areas. You have to physically go to those zones to check for things you've missed.
The other problem is that the story is ultimately a little muddled and I'm not given any reason to truly care about any of the characters - not even the protagonist. There is nothing that makes anybody particularly memorable or loveable. They exist, and you can talk to them, but there's no reason to care about them. During the final moments of the game, a few characters even appear and 'assist' you in killing enemies, but there's no reason for their appearance and you can't talk to them. They feel like an afterthought thrown in to help serve the ending scenes.
It's a fun little game; it's not amazing, but it's pretty good.

The Single worst Yu-Gi-Oh Game I have Ever Played.
The Single Worst Card Game I Have Ever Played.
I've already written a review of this elsewhere and one of much larger length and in much more detail so let me just make bullet points.
1. This game uses a large amount of mechanics that seem like they've been ripped out of Hearthstone and given then a thin appearance change. Card Converting, Hero Powers and the exact way they do the small things like emotes are all too similar to their competitor to be ignored, it's to the point where it's much more likely that they straight up stole them from a better game.
2. The rarity system in this game is the most broken thing I have ever seen with cards such as Black Skull Dragon being rated as less rare than cards like Magician of Black chaos despite being more powerful in every possible way and being arguably more iconic. If that's not too far for you Sonic bird, a monster with less than half the stats of both Black Skull Dragon and Magician of Black Chaos, a common in the real game and with an effect which allows you to search your deck for a ritual spell card. Is one of the rarest cards in the game thus by the games logic making it more valuable than cards like Battleguard King (Which has 3000 attack and can attack upto 3 times) and Black Skull dragon. Now in turn if you're thinking that's because it helps you summon out stronger monsters... you'd be wrong, with all the ritual monsters currently in the game there is only 1 more powerful than Battleguard King in effect and more powerful than Black Skull Dragon in Attack. This card happens to be an event card so there's no chance of getting it anytime soon.
And this is NOT an isolated case as many low level creatures with semi interesting effects are considered Ultra Rares in the eyes of this game. There's a monster called "Gaia Soul, the Combustable Collective" which has 2000 ATK/0 DEF And the ability to deal damage to your oppenant by attack defense position monsters as if they were attack position.
If the game were a good game this would earn its rarity as Super Rare however given that it isn't the AI doesn't use defense position monsters, the duels are decided in 2 turns in PVP so nobody will use Defense position monsters there either and Dark Blade (1800 ATK/ 1500 DEF) is a Common, meaning alongside the fact that after levelling Joey to 5 or so and gaining the ability to give warrior monsters + 200 ATK chances are you've made this super rare completely and utterly irelevant with a common.
3. They lie about the era they're in.
Whenever I made the previous review I received feedback stating that there were no Synchro monsters because they were only in the GX era, because Synchro monsters didn't exist then they wouldn't have access to them and they'll be coming in time. This is entirely wrong, they claim they're in the GX era but they have access to Six Samurai which are legendary for the use of not only Synchro monsters but also XYZ monsters. they have Mecha Phantom Beasts, they have the Blue-Eyes Archetype and they have an insane amount of other archetypes which are rendered incomplete because they don't have their boss monsters who are synchro or XYZ. They even have Ghostrick as a level up bonus for levelling up Bonz.
4. If you start of the game as Kaiba you'll notice that Kaiba is a borderline psychopath who loves nothing more than beating on kids, and posing over their defeated remains Jojo style. For god sake the most common thing for him to do upon winning a duel is cackle like a madman, they did not do a good job at representing Kaiba.
5. PVP in this game is Impossible, and I don't mean like the pvp community are advanced or anything but rather the servers are horrible. They cannot keep you in a game for more than four turns, they WILL disconnect you. I have played Ranked a total of nine or ten times and out of those nine or ten times six or seven of them ended whenever the servers disconnected me. For reference at the time of this happening my internet speed was 5.7 mbps. Not great but simultaniously not horrible. I could play an mmo or just about any game online with this speed if they're optimised properly, but apparently this Yu-Gi-Oh! Mobile game cannot keep me connected to a 2D, barely dynamic game for more than four turns.

This game is much more fun that what I expected--especially when you realize your role as a seedy cockroach hotel co-manager.  Not your typical dream job, right?  The game itself is incredibly easy to get into due to the simplistic gameplay and controls. Simply click on which items (rooms) you want to use, and then choose their placement--simple as that!  Well, sort of. You can build your hotel as randomly or as strategically as you want, in any direction or height you want. The sky is truly the limit. Some rooms are used simply to earn money, while others are used for defense weaponry from the various baddies (like rats, seagulls, yeti's, and more).  It's fun to experiment with the different rooms and layouts.
What I enjoy best, though, is the aural features. The game itself is a crazy hybrid of tower defense and procedural music. Each room produces a different "sound" so that as you design the hotel you want, it creates a soundtrack that is constantly changing in tone and pace! You get to be both a composer and strategist. It lends a very organic element to the game, since it's unique to the player's design of each hotel.
The amount of enemies can become overwhelming at times, but the frantic nature just adds to the overall adrenaline rush. The color palette used is vibrant and attention-grabbing, and the in-game dialogue/storyline is quirky.

The 7th Guest is a classic of sorts, there's no denying it, a killer app, yet with the impact it had, its presence in popular culture / gaming lore is very understated. How so? Was it mostly because of its technical merits, with the gameplay actually lacking? Was it not that memorable? My memories of the game are very fond, One of the rare few games that struck me as creepy, and, as a kid, actually somewhat scary, definitely not forgettable. But let's revisit it and see.
First off, for a 22-23 year old game, the graphics have aged remarkably well. Thanks to the prerendered backgrounds, which, though obviously and definitely not as flashy now as they most definitely were for 1993, are actually managing not to look bad, and the house is well designed and, hey, makes sense, with plenty of nice little details. The cutscenes / character scenes, though obviously grainy, are still good enough for what this is. The creepiness factor is still there, helped immensely by The Fat Man's very well integrated soundtrack and great sounds, voices, screams, random spooky sounds, the game is still damn atmospheric - I full well remembered the dread I felt as a kid when white noise would start marking the beginning of the sequences - that change in sound texture, likely brought on by techical issues, like the transparence of actors, actually helped the atmosphere. And that's pretty great.
So yeah, the atmosphere is lovely and delightfully creepy, the game still looks and sounds damn nice for what it is, oh, and the story isn't half bad, though a bit chaotically narrated through randomly triggered cutscenes. But what about the gameplay itself? Honestly, a mixed bag. A major problem and a drag is the lag between the screens while moving, which is "softened", but quite irritating nonetheless. It had its reasons back than, but a faster flow would've been a boon. The game doesn't really hold your hand, at all, which is a plus, but, back in the day, revisiting rooms randomly to find if something new's suddenly unlocked itself actually gave meat to a game you paid good money for and expected to last at least somewhat. Now, it's slightly less appreciated. Which brings us to the puzzles. Honestly - a mixed bag. Simplistic, somewhat varied, but you do see 2 to 3 variations on the theme. The "infection" puzzle is pretty great, with a trickier AI than one would expect, but some, including the last two, actually only function as a challenge by not being immediately understandable. If you like puzzles where most of the puzzle is actually determining what the base rules are, with the goals being far from evident, you will like this. There are apparently hints in the in-game library, but with the screen to screen transitions that slow, it's a chore to go there (and that's actually good). "Ego", your "character", comments on several, and so does Stauf - and it can be really, really effective (especially Stauf's mocking/laughter), but slightly too repetitive in a good percentage of cases.
A major issue with the moving is the fact that whenever you go to the menu, to save for example, when you return, you're dumped back at the "first" screen of a room. While that can function as a shortcut in a few rooms (first hall, upstairs hallway), you really don't want to do that in the maze - as it WILL return you to the beginning - forcing you to start all over and even redo the easy slider puzzle at the very beginning. And that's a major drag. There are shortcuts between floors in several rooms, so that's a plus I guess, though I found I only used one or two.
And there you have it, an atmospheric adventure game that has aged somewhat gracefully and manages to tell a fine story in a chaotic manner forcing you to explore its compilation of puzzles, solid in number, of wildly different quality and difficulty using slightly frustrating movement. You can do much worse in the genre, and it's been nice to revisit it. Just remember, it's 22 years old!

I should start by saying I am giving this a very hesitant Recommendation. Part of me wants to say "NO", but I really feel that - should you find it for quite cheap - The 7th Guest is worth trying at least once.
Back in the 90s this game was rather noteworthy, though some would say that even back then it looked somewhat dated. To me, however, it was a game that I felt quite fondly towards for whatever reason. The music, the interesting way it handled cutscenes and the disjointed way you learned the plot all stuck with me. I actually used to listen to the 20-something audio track on the CD which played through all of the music with an opening and ending song and various voice clips spread throughout.
So, I haven't actually talked about the game itself, have I? Maybe I've been trying to avoid it. You see, even though I remember quite a lot of the game from my teenage years, the strongest memory I have was of this absolutely awful puzzle involving a microscope and the AI was smarter the better your computer was. When it first came out the contest was likely an even match but on anything more advanced it became virtually impossible unless you won by sheer luck. The game's other puzzles are by no means much better but none of them -stuck- with me after all this time.
I have no idea if my younger self was just more patient or if I went and looked up various solutions online. What I know NOW, however, is that they were either really simple or very frustrating with nothing really in between. Part of me honestly just wants to say it's cause I've finished the game before and simply don't care anymore. Whatever the case, I found most of the actual gameplay quite boring and just wanted to see the next scene.
Actually, no, I take that back. There IS another factor in all of this. During puzzles the protagonist and antagonist kept going on and ON constantly. You can't skip any of the disembodied dialogue and if you restart a puzzle you get to hear all of it over again! This, combined with how slowly every single transition was, swiftly got on my nerves to the point where I no longer cared and just wanted to get past the puzzles as quickly as possible. Yes, my apologies. I do have a terrible habit of meandering to my point.
Is the game bad? It honestly is, but it's that weird/cheesy kinda awful you just have to see once for yourself, to know if it's as bad as people claim. In the game's defence, if you can call it that, a lot of its problems lie in all the material that got left on the cutting room floor. The GOG version includes a document explaining how it was supposed to be, with multiple endings and a more coherent plot. If The 7th Guest had been made today it would've likely been a bizarre combination of Professor Layton's "random puzzles" with Resident Evil's "explore a spooky mansion".
I've read there were several Kickstarter/crowdfunding attempts to make a third game in the series which all failed, until a creator-approved fan game came along. All I do know is that, for better or worse, The 7th Guest is one of those games I played and will never really forget. I know some people knock the visuals, but really those are fine. It's the tendency for the voice to drowned out by the music that really hurts the presentation.

Oh my god. Okay, now, first off, let me iterate: I have played a lot of visual novels, and yes, they have all been gay visual novels, except for Sonic's Inflation Adventure, which I may have only played in a dream.
This is probably the best visual novel / interactive story type thing I have ever played. The only ones rivalling it are the Analogue/Hate series, which is only KIND of a visual novel, and I'm not even sure if it counts.
Okay... It's almost 3 AM, so I'm organizing this really weirdly. There's elements, y'see, Story, Characters, and Gameplay.
The story is ♥♥♥♥ing great. Obviously, there were outcomes I didn't really like, but I wasn't supposed to like them, so they worked out perfectly. The TRUE ending is my absolute favorite, but all endings were very entertaining. Hellish, but in the best way possible.
The characters were pretty great too. I definitely saw real people in each of the three main characters (and saw the characters in real people). Of course, I wish some aspects of their lives were clearer and more drawn-out, but the game is vague on purpose and often avoids going into character or background details for the sake of the story. Which is fine. The reason I desire more details about the characters is because I like them so much, not because they're lacking.
Gameplay-wise, well, it's a ♥♥♥♥ing visual novel. My only gripe is that the true ending is a little annoying to get, but that's all true endings, so it's a useless gripe. There are other aspects of gameplay though, like, visuals, audio, that sort of thing. I really like the visuals. "♥♥♥♥♥♥ trash summer camp" was captured perfectly, and the quality of each image imbues just that bit of eerieness when you need it. I liked the music a lot, so much so that I wish there was more of it! But I happen to enjoy weird lo-fi + electronic crap so I don't know how it holds up with other people.
Okay, and then, themes. Obviously, disillusionment (or just plain dissatisfaction) with Christianity is a huge thing here. A little off for me, because I wasn't raised with it, but I happen to really enjoy unorthodox interpretations of witchcraft and the devil and so forth, so it really resonated with me. Probably one of the biggest themes is isolation, or being unable (or unwilling) to "fit in," and the game handles this extraordinarily well. And there's the queer part of it, which is pretty clear and makes it all the better since it's a game by queer artists, for queer people. Plus, what better way to be isolated than to be queer? It all sort of goes together; it wouldn't make sense for these characters to be so isolated in a camp full of their peers in terms of age and background and NOT be queer.
I can barely stay awake and it's becoming even more evident, so I'll wrap this up: It's a great game, even for people who aren't into visual novels. If you're not queer or obsessed with the devil, it probably won't resonate as much with you, but you could very easily still enjoy it.
