Over the last few years i've come to avoid early access games as majority of them never reach a finished product let alone match the promises they make. However whilst browsing steam today Rising World caught my eye, so i thought why not take a chance and give one a go? I'm so glad i did! This game is one of most stable alpha build games i've ever played and it is a lot of fun even in this early stage. For a Voxel game it looks really impressive, especially on the higher graphical settings (the screenshots don't do it justice) and the sound assets are great. Plus it is just so much fun tunneling through mountains and building bases with such a large array of options. Also i freakin love the ability to put your own images in the game as posters/paintings. So do i recommend this game? Absolutely!

Completed in 5 hours. Not a bad game. Actually, I'd recommend it as a good action platformer (with some unfortunate puzzle elements). However: the areas with waves of enemies in a locked room are broken, with enemies being "human" (penguin) shields to your bullets but not to each others. I kept getting killed by enemies that were behind other enemies who could shoot past their allies but I was instead shooting the dead, juggled bodies of their allies instead of them. Also, the jetpack sections are a mess, with a huge zoom-out effect and screen scroll every time new flying enemies appear, making it harder to see the ammo or health pickup you were aiming for or the rocket that is still chasing you (fired from a previous enemy) that you're still expected to avoid, even if both you and the rocket are off screen. Both the waves of enemies and the jetpack sections checkpoint frequently, so they become a battle of attrition rather than skill. These two sections are also where the game showcases its' soundtrack. Short sections of uninspired music looping endlessly. On first hearing at the title screen, it got me in the mood for an action game. But repetitively looped in frustrating, cheaply designed action sequences (the waves and the jetpack), both these sections and the one to two verse or chorus songs had both gameplay and music making each other worse. There are also some ridiculous puzzle sections involving playing around with box stacking and elevators that do nothing but artificially lengthen the game. One section had me chase an enemy up a set of elevators, back down, and then back up again, requiring a floor change at each of about six floors on the first two of those runs. I was not amused.
Other than the above, quite an enjoyable game. But if the come out with a sequel, I will not be buying it, given the amount of cheap time-lengthening and unbalanced gameplay of this game. That, and the story of "Rocketbirds: Hardboilded Chicken" (what there is of it) would hardly support two or more games.
I doubt I'll play this game again, because there's no way I'm putting up with that nonsense again.
Oh, and if you get stuck on how to proceed, like I did numerous times (minor SPOILERS), the answer is ALWAYS one of: run past it, use one or more crates, or control an enemy through brain bugs. Don't expect the puzzles to be deep, or you'll just end up confused.

Game is short but fun SHMUP (shoot em up). Graphics are nice, soundtrack is enjoyable. Ship is upgradeable. Mutiple difficulty levels with an endless mode as well present a little bit of replayability before boredom sets in.
What sets this apart from other SHMUPS?
1. There are 5 weapoons systems total. Drones which can be deployed on a timer cooldown. 2 types of basic weapons which you can fire at all times, along with an energy beam and missile weapons that have a maximum charge. This leads to pretty enjoyable SHMUP gameplay. You are constantly firing with your basic weapons, and you have to employ some tactical gameplay in the use of your missile and energy beam so you don't run out of charge. Since deployment of the drones is on a timer, you want to watch that and employ the drones when you need them.
2. Your Sheild and hull can be repaired. The repair is also on a timer/CD also. Makes for interesting gameplay because you have to pay attention to the CD and sort of decide if you can be more aggressive and take damage, or steer your ship more conservatively to avoid enemy fire.
Controls are tight and remappable. Played with an xbox controller no problem. Mouse and keyboard is also nice.
People who are hardcore into SHMUPS might find this game a bit easy, but for the average player this presents a fun and challenging game.
I got this game on sale for like $0.50, but it's still worth checking out at full price.

I spent a great deal of my teenage years fixated on Magic, but it never really transitioned into the digital world successfully for me. If you've played any Magic the Gathering, a lot of the mechanics of Hex: Shards of Fate will seem eerily familiar to you.  So much in fact that Hasbro originally sued Cryptozoic over the closeness of many elements. This was settled in 2015, so is not an issue for the game moving forward.
This is a digital trading card game that has the depth of the Mariana Trench. Don't go into it thinking it's Hearthstone. It has the most depth and complexity out of any TCG I've played. Honestly? More than Magic - because it was designed for a digital interface and can do things that a physical card game never could. It can combo upon combo, it can affect your crypt (graveyard) and your deck, it can shuffle efficiently and it can search through decks for cards. Something you did 50 turns ago can suddenly pop up and affect everything, or a game can be over in 5 turns. This digital world gives it the ability to offer things that Magic simply never could, and with a development studio with decades of physical card game experience behind them, they have transitioned to the digital with an astounding amount of imagination. With Hearthstone dominating the deck building genre in recent years, many games of this type of followed in it's simplicity, but Hex is not one of them. Hex is a game for people who want to see mechanics and deck building pushed to their absolute limits.
Of course, even the most complicated game can stagnate and get boring - but Hex so far has offered an ever-increasing library of cards, with early sets being planned to rotate out of competition, so you won't be punished so hard for coming to it later than other. So far, from what I've experienced, the newer sets manage to offer diversity and interesting abilities that make for a massive potential of deck building. There is a definite meta for constructed play, but if you like drafting (or PvE, or casual PvP with friends), then there is a decent selection of options to choose from. I'm keeping open minded about the future and longevity of the game, much of which will balance on the community as well as the developers.
The PvE campaign is available free, as well as PvP 1v1 duels versus friends. The PvE campaign, which is still in development but at this point features two acts, represents a solid 40 hours+ of playtime on my first playthrough, and if you want to experience it again and again as multiple different classes and races, the playtime is certainly hundreds of hours. During this time you earn character and account experience, cards, gold (PvE currency), and even some chances to PvP for free (in the form of account levelling rewards as tournament tickets). The amount of content you can access for free is actually astounding, if you enjoy PvE vs the AI. If you want to jump straight into PvP, you will need to invest into the game - but not a massive amount, as there are Evolving draft tournaments priced very cheaply and ready for newer players to jump into. Competitive constructed on the other hand, well - let's just say that's definitely not beginner friendly and from the look of the top decks there, can be very, very expensive.
In addition to the campaign, an arena offers unlimited battles vs the AI with gold and PvE rewards. Again, this content adds to your account level, which can give PvP rewards too. The arena is a challenge, and collecting enough cards as a free player to make farming the arena efficient will take some time, so there is a massive time-sink in playing for free - some people may find this grindy / boring, but I'm quite enjoying it.
Once you've earned your PvE cards and gold, you can trade gold for platinum with other players, and you can sell cards for gold or platinum on the AH. Platinum can then be used as tournament entry fees, or to buy PvP packs. So, it is 100% possible with an ungodly amount of time, to technically get full PvP decks and enter big ticket tournaments by playing the free content.
Like any trading card game; you can massively speed up your time sink by paying money, either to buy cards on the auction house, to buy packs to open, to enter tournaments, or to buy special bundles available on steam (which offer the best value for money as starter packs).
I have played almost every card game that's around, I spent a decade of my life playing physical Magic the Gathering, I have sunk thousands of hours into Hearthstone, but also a massive array of other online TcG deck-building variants, such as all of the MtG games on Steam, Spellstone, Runescape Legends, Elder Scrolls Legends, Hand of Fate, Ascension, Faeria, Infinity Wars, Solforce, Gwent and the list goes on... without a doubt in my mind, Hex: Shards of Fate currently offers both the best PvE experience, and the best Free to Play Experience.
A lot is missing from the Kickstarter, as already touched on, the entire MMO / co-op / social aspect. Guilds, Crafting and Raids are all still a complete blank to the community. There are some features that do exist that need serious innovation, such as browsing your card collection, the auction house, and the chat system. These are all usable, but not user-friendly. The core mechanics though, the cards, the game boards, the PvE base and the tournament play are all solid, and I can only live in hope that the rest is still to come. The game has players; but not enough players to feel truly alive to me at this point, and the community doesn't feel as if it interacts well - a side effect of the terrible chat system and the lack of guilds or other social features, but this may be my bias showing, as I really did want this game to involve a heavy social experience.
Despite my initial disappointment at the lack of features I wanted from the kickstarter, I have come to believe in this development studio and the potential of Hex. If my most wanted features never make it; this is still a very solid, well crafted game. Perhaps even 6 months ago my review would have been a thumbs down - but the increased PvE content has really bolstered my confidence in the game. I would not recommend spending $250 on this game like I did, but with some of the most in depth PvE and Free to Play content available in the genre, you need to check it out if you enjoy any aspect of deck building / trading card games.

Hex: Shards of Fate is a TCG to the likes of Magic: The Gathering, which ultimately allows you to collect cards and play with them, trade them, and sell them if you so desire. As a result of this, it's important to note that there is no crafting or equivalent, so you are earning your cards through either PvE or levelling / ranking rewards, or buying booster packs. Will this may seem like poor value on initial glance, this is the standard when looking at a TCG (trading card game), so if you enter with that mindset then it is fine (in addition to the fact that Hex provides generous free content already)
How does the game play? Like the MTGO we never had. The content is unique, but familiar enough to make any regular to a TCG know what they are doing from the get-go, but the mechanics feel deeper and more varied due to the fact it is on a digital platform that they can do more with. The PvP has a 'meta' which will typically exist in all competitive games, and admittedly it's not easy to get into competitive PvP without spending some money, but like I mentioned earlier that's normal for a TCG.
The PvE, however, is completely free and provides a great, rewarding experience in how it plays out. In an RPG like experience, your player character levels up, gets mercenaries and crafts a deck to which you play against a storyline, bosses and other experiences. It is possible to make a good PvP deck from exclusively free rewards, but realistically you would have to be playing a lot.

I've put both time and money into Hearthstone and MTG, and Hex is my favourite of the three by a long way.
The things that make Hex stand out are:
- A genuinely fun and engaging single-player mode. MTG's single player has always felt like a chore: keep ploughing through the AI until you get a good enough draw to unlock the next card. Hearthstone's single-player campaigns are expensive and, in my opinion, not that much fun. Hex wraps its single player campaign in an RPG experience and it makes a real difference. Champions have a race and class, which grants you unique abilities and cards, and a talent tree to work your way up. This is a great way to customise your character towards your preferred playstyle and encourages the use of different deck archetypes. There are so many different ways to play through the campaign that the temptation to start again with a new character (you can have many on the go at once) is always present.
- Digital-only and innovative play mechanics. Magic players will recognise how Hex works but there is a lot of ambitious new stuff going on too, and these mechanics would be impractical in a physical game. Coyotle decks, for example, make use of the Prophecy mechanic that buffs the next troop or action in your deck, and buffs stay on when cards are replaced in the deck or placed into the crypt. I created a pair of post offices, staffed them, bought them vehicles and a few amenities, set routes and fixed prices. All of that took roughly ten minutes. I spent the next 50 minutes doing other things in real life. I cooked some soup, put together a decent sandwich (it even had some lemon zest in it), made a banana split, went to the bathroom, and got some things from my car that I'd forgotten earlier in the day. The whole time, the game was at 3x speed. I occasionally hit "ok" on the dialog that told me the day was over, but most of my time was afk.
I came back to the game and found that after a week, nothing interesting had happened. My operation flowed smoothly and made me a good return. Given a month I could open another office, given a year and I could probably edge out my competition with decent advertisements and expanded service.
Here's the thing - the game played itself. All i did was set it up. There's no management, the prices were already reasonable, there were never any problems, and I didn't have to do anything. Other tycoon games give you a reason to keep playing - more things to build, more people to attract, more stuff to see. This one doesn't - it's over as soon as you've finished setting it up. It's barren and simple. It's so simple that I can't recommend it, because you won't get anything out of it, unless you're looking for a screensaver that doesn't move, but takes ten minutes to set up.
Glancing over the developer's history, it seems clear that this is common. Produce a bargain bin game that's very simplistic, release a new one every couple months. And hey, they apparently make enough money to stay afloat, so cheers to that. Given how many games I play that were made by people who tried 10x as hard and came out roughly equal to this one, I can't really decry someone who is literally in business making this sort of thing.

1981, I’m at a friends place looking over his brand new Atari VCS (2600) and the two games he got with it, Space Invaders and Street Racer. Space Invaders was the game to have in those days, it was fun. Then we played Street Racer. It was exciting for the first 20 minutes, then the crap factor started to dawn on us. The graphics was crap, the game play was crap, the game was overall just…….. crap! It was at this point that I wished for an Apple II (Thank god the Commodore 64 was only just around the corner before I committed to such heresy).
Fast forward 36 years, Lo and behold ZombeTeamz brings out ZombieCarz, a retro racing game that they some how thought emulating Street Racer was a brilliant idea. No, a brilliant idea would have been to emulate a half decent car game like Carmageddon or even Interstate ‘76! Now there was a great Drive-n-shoot game.
Game Play
ZombieCarz is 20 levels of top down, scroll down (road moves from top of screen to bottom) half racing, half shooting game. You start in a stock standard car that looks like a chines Volvo, with a gun strapped to you roof (a pea shooter more like it). You steer your car, slide is more like it sans Digital Derby Auto Raceway style
(God I loved that game)) using the Left and Right arrow keys and you use your Up arrow key to shoot.
In the beginning levels you contend with zombies that stand on the road, ride on dirt bikes (how the….? Never mind) or Dune Buggys (ATV’s to you Millennials). Best to shoot these Moving Violation, P plate road hogs, as hitting them damages your car. You get cash for every kill. Other things to avoid on the road, is the tricky trash left behind by Anti-clean-my-room teenagers, these also will wreck your ride faster than Mr Bean on a Busway.
You can save stranded survivors, before said zombies tenderise them into road kill, meat patties, gaining even more money but that is up to you. Also collect health packs to fix up your car or skid over a Nuke box to have a jet fighter zip across the screen, dropping bombs to clear your path.
After each level you can go shopping to upgrade your guns, your car or add a deadly bull-bar/cow-scooper.
Everything Else
The handling of your car is CRAP! I mentioned DD Auto Raceway before (watch video), even that game has better handling than this. You have no throttle to adjust your speed enough to avoid most obstacles, your just a kamikaze drive bomb! Shooting is painful and slow, even the chain from Road Rash would do better damage! Even auto-shoot is pathetic.
Options are few, with only Sound and music volume adjustment, windowed or full screen, touch-screen and language option. No Key binding which would be nice as I find the arrow keys annoying for games.
Sound effects and music are sparse and will become boring after a few minutes.
The only saving grace of this game is the nice cartoon style animation and background. The animation of a Zombie trying to stop you from leaving the game, by hitting the ‘Yes’ button out of your way, was the only thing that brought a smile to my face. This quirkiness should have been carried into the game, hell, I sat there for ten minutes just watching this one Zombie, he was more entertaining than the game itself!
Don’t wast money on ZombieCarz, not even if it was free. In fact go out and download a copy of Road Rash, I know it is old but there never was a more satisfying game to make you laugh yourself sore, believe me you will thank me for it!

What can be said about System Shock that hasn't already been said. Many games have often imitated... but never truly replicated it. So many games out now were inspired by this classic masterpiece. From BioShock to Dead Space, the fomula obviously has a very lasting appeal. Even games like Doom 3 tried to replicate it's unique style of story-telling.
This game was actually one of three games that I first played on a computer. I've told this story many times but... I was heavily into console games at the time & a friend wanted to show me that there were types of deep games that consoles just couldn't do or handle at the time. This was the third game he showed me & I was instantly won over by it.
"An instant classic"
"An absolute masterpiece"
These phrases have often been tossed around by reviewers in magazines & on gaming websites. Most don't even consider the true weight of these words as they should never be tossed around lightly. But this game does not need to prove itself as it is the real deal. It, along with its sequel, is often included in these "top games of all time" lists for a very good reason. This game changed the very way story-telling was done in games. Its developers wanted to make an RPG without stats. Where you could use any & everything in the world with your own skill.
One of the unique aspects of this game was how the sound was handled. Rather than employ a dedicated sound engineer for the game, which was normal for the time, the developer hired musicians to handle the sound & music. And the final product shows this great quality immensely. Every sound & every music piece just absolutely fits into the games theme.
This game also holds another personal record for me for having one of the scariest levels in all of gaming history. Level 3 Maintenance... I still get chills up & down my spine just thinking about this level as I would constantly jump at any weird noise. Even knowing the layout of the level before hand & where everything is will not help you prepare for this level as the atmosphere was spot on perfect.
If you play one game in your entire life, you owe it to yourself to play this one as it is just that good.
Update: Years laters after defeating this game for so many times... still worth every cent.

This game is the reason why 1993's Doom (plus its successors) was and still is little more than noise and pixels for me.
When i got my first IBM-Compatible PC (a 486), I asked an old friend what would be a nice game.  He recommended System Shock and it defined my gaming expections.
I was obsessed with it.  Played so much I knew 3/4 of the whole place like the back of my hand and still remember the critical points when I revisited the game recently.  I got so used to a movable curser for selection and aiming that I can't really play the Enhanced Version with mouselook - I had to play it old school i.e. Classic (there are playing methods I use that won't work with mouselook).
You start off with an intro video setting the background for the player character - a hacker who got caught attempting to jack into a corporate's database.  A corrupt executive offered to dismiss the charges along with a neural cyberspace interface - if you perform some hacking for him on a space station's Aritifical Intelligence called Sentient Hyper-Optimized Data Access Network or SHODAN.  How could you refuse when the likely alternative was to be thrown into corporate detention for who knows how long?
So you hacked SHODAN as instructed and removed its ethical constraints, the exec set you up for an operation to install the promised neural hardware, you slept away the next 6 months to heal, and woke up to ... what the **** happened while you were dozing?
From there, you're on your own.  The game offers hints via logs and notes left by dead station crew and plot-triggered emails from off-station corporate staff trying to solve the disaster (mixed with threats and taunts from the now ax-crazy SHODAN bent on extermination of the human blah blah blah).  Beyond that, you are left to your own devices to figure out what to do and how to do it without dying.
As the game throws you in a station overruned with mutated critters (including former humans), robots and cyborgs, almost all (note: NOT ALL) are hostile, combat (unless you turn it to minimum) is an integral part of the game.  Enemy AI is basic (simple line of sight and shoot/pursuit), but the weapon damage system is impressive for its time.  All weapons (melee, firearms, remote explosives) have an armor penetration matched against whatever armor the target might carry - your likely first gun, a dart thrower meant to subdue lab animals won't do squat against any robot. Several weapons also have unique damage types that make them powerful against a class of enemies but useless against others - Gas Grenades melt mutants but are useless against robots, while EMP weapons wreak circuitry without harming flesh (including yourself - so feel free to drop an EMP grenade at your feet if you are at touch range of a nasty robot about to put holes in you)
The game doesn't have any experience system where you get better at killing enemies as you kill more.  Instead, it rewards you for exploration by scattering goodies in the form of weapons, hardware upgrades and supplies around.  In the first level, there are two powerful end-game  weapons (with limited ammunition), secured away for the player to unlock by fulfiling conditions on that level.  Players willing to go to the effort are rewarded with the weapons which can make the first few dangerous hostile encounters much easier.
As a hacker, the player can 'jack into cyberspace at specific cyberjack locations.  Cyberspace sequences are deplicted as 3-D wire-frame world where the player could attempt to access useful information and trigger switches that affect the real game world (such as opening some locked doors that could not be unlocked by any other means) while dodging hazards and defeat security programs attempting to terminate the unauthorised entry, all while on a timer (which is adjusted by the relevant difficulty setting) which might make things dicey for some of the longer/harder sequences.
New players, if you want a game that points you where to go and tells you what to do, you're looking at the wrong place (unless you turn the Plot Setting down which affects the story and in my opinion the enjoyment).  If you like to explore, find secrets, read/listen to logs and piece together clues to the next step, this game is for you.

Many years ago when I was first exposed to System Shock 1 & 2 I immediately feel in love with these games and their mechanics and story. A cyberpunk future where hackers rule and you're trapped on broken down space stations or space ships fighting off a omnipresent and vindictive AI and hive-mind alien species made for many jump-scare ridden nights.
I bemoaned to myself that, because of the trademark issues of the time, System Shock 1 & 2 would never come to Steam or other digital distribution. Low and behold, NightDive Studios managed to detangle the ownership rights from legal limbo, perform much needed software compatability and mod-friendliness upgrades, and has released System Shock 1 as an Enhanced Edition, with widescreen support for modern video cards.
System Shock 1 is a unique masterpiece from early 1990s PC gaming. Combining the FPS elements of Doom (its elder of 6 months) with point-and-click adventure elements of dungeon crawl CRPGs (uber-popular at the time), the Action-Adventure power-up system of Metroid, and a beautifully designed horror atmosphere and audio aesthetic (provided by members of the band Tribes), System Shock is one of the first games to tell its story primarily through environmental details, exploration, and prodding by the voice-acted driven villain taunts. The combat is tense, the degree of control over your character neigh overwhelming, and the story gripping.
As you near the end of the game, you're quite ready to finish off SHODAN, your tormentor for the 12 or so hours it takes to get to that point.
This game is a must play for anyone that wants to see where so much of modern gaming (like Half-Life's environmental puzzles and even all FPS's current control scheme) comes from.

Short Version: It's not terrible, but buy it when it's on sale.
Long Version:
Graphics: Ok, not great, the levels and ships really aren't much to look at, the particle effects are simplistic, like you'd see in a directx or opengl demo in 2005. The only real visual difference between levels is the planet in the background.
6/10 - above average

Sound:  Sound effects aren't bad, not jarring, not much here.
7/10 - good
Music:  Doesn't fit the game at all, sounds like bought tracks, plus the game just randomly shuffles them and plays one during whatever level you're in.
3/10 - poor
Controls:  Has keyboard and  controller binding, so that's a plus, though my dualshock 4 which works fine in other games just constantly reads as tilting the stick up no matter what i set, so controller had to be unplugged to play. The game is clearly hardcoded to check the wrong axis for this controller and there seems to be no way to set as the ingame menus do not function with the controller plugged in.  Also has mouse support which worked fine.  Keyboard controls worked fine but there was a strange input delay, ship didn't feel 100% responsive.
3/10 - extremely buggy (7/10 if controller bug was fixed)
Level Design:  There really isn't any, all the levels are pretty much the same empty space with asteroids, each level just throws slightly more at you, but there doesn't seem to be any real sense of progression or difference between levels besides the number.
2/10 - bad
Gameplay:  Pretty boring and easy, even on the hardest modes. You more or less see the exact same ships all game with a few tiny variations, just more of them, and without any real level design to back it up it gets old really fast.  There's multiple fire keys and keys to lock on to targets for your special weapons but there's no point, you really just end up using auto-target and holding all the keys down at all times as theres no point in NOT firing.  it takes a LOT of damage to kill you as well so dying is actually pretty hard to do, after i cleared the game i ended up going to the level 20 boss and suiciding on it 9 times to get the last achievement as i'd only died once in the entire playthrough, and that was because i was watching a youtube video and ran into an asteroid.  Endless mode can literally be "beaten" by going on forever by just staying in the middle left and holding the fire button.  It is however functional, and the level-up mechanic would be nice if there was more to the game.
4/10 - poor

Length:  I cleared the entire game with all achievements including surviving endless mode in under two hours, and that included going idle to chat on twitch and do other things. Actual playtime to beat the game is probably less than a hour, this is VERY short, even by schmup standards.
(at the $0.50 i paid, whatever, but at full price i wouldn't say this short of a game is worth it)
Overall opinion: 3.5/10

Amazing game that takes the formula of Magic the Gathering and expands on it with card permanency.  This means your cards retain their effects when they leave play.
This simple change has proven to allow for outstanding results and the gameplay is greatly enhanced by it.  Random cards in your deck can be buffed by a spell you play without ever seeing the cards.  Troops can grow larger and larger the more they enter your crypt.  Cards that have been removed from the game by void effects can be brought back with all their buffs intact.
Examples: I can cast a spell that gives +2/+2 to all my troops in all zones. That means it buffs the cards STILL IN MY DECK. I can reduce the costs of random cards in my deck or insert spiders into someone else's deck. I can transform your cards into a different troop and even if they die or go to your deck, the card keeps any changes I've done to it.  Which means I can also give your troop -3/-3 permanently, return it to your deck, and the next time you draw that exact card it will still be -3/-3. HEX remembers which card it was even if you have four copies of the same troop in your deck. That's something Magic in a paper format can never do and something their online clients have never attempted.
It's even possible to permanently add abilities to cards like Replicator's Gambit does, a card that puts a troop back into your deck and gives it the card text "When this enters play summon six replicas of it".  The next time you draw that card and play it you will get 7 identical troops.  But it's only possible in a digital format since HEX remembers that specific card over the other three copies of it you have in your deck.
Add to this the threshold system that solves the mana problems Magic can sometimes have, a modified shuffler that eliminates the worst resource hands prior to mulligans, or the deck champions you select with activated charge powers you can use in game, and HEX ends up being an improved online experience that a true-to-form paper card game simply cannot deliver.
Top it off with a PVE campaign that lets you create your own character, customize it with talents and activatable abilties, then battle it through story content and dungeons on a world map to earn and unlock even more rewards.  Level up your character to get stronger as well as gain access to more cards for it.  We haven't seen something like that since Shandalar, that Magic computer game from 1997 that was completely abandoned as a concept.
Best part?  The content isn't going to stop there.  More campaign expansions up to level 30 content, 3-person raids cooperating against an AI boss, a guild system that can LEND players decks you own, a third facing to cards with achievements and stat tracking, and a stream of continuing PVP expansions similar to a major TCG provider (set 6 will be here soon).
Highly recommended.

Big fan of Magic, but when I moved away from a lot of friends, this game offered me a great means to keep playing the game I love with people I enjoy gaming with.
However, what I really like about this game more than just being digital, is that this game goes steps beyond what MTG can do. Unlike a paper based game like MTG, Hex is able to manipulate cards outside of the active state of play. You can have cards that go into your enemy's deck, or cards that change things in your deck.
Additionally, they have an interesting means of handling some of the difficulties Magic has with mana. In Hex, instead of mana being tied to a mana type, each resource in Hex is split up between "Resource" (Mana), and "Threshold" (Mana Type). So lets say you play a Sapphire, you'll get a Sapphire Threshold, and (1/1) resource. Next turn, you play a Blood, you get a Blood threshold and (1/1) resource, totaling (2/2) with 1 in each resource. Now this is basically the same as having 1 Island and 1 Swamp in MTG. Where this becomes different is when you have 1 Sapphire, 3 Blood , (4/4). In this situation, you could play 4 cards that cost 1 Resource and require 1 Sapphire threshold. In Magic, if you had 1 Island and 3 Swamps, you could only cast 1 card that costs 1 Blue. By separating these things out, it helps to curb a lot of the mana issues experienced in MTG and makes it less likely to get ♥♥♥♥ed by RNG. You can still just not draw resource, or not draw the right thresholds, but it is less severe with the arrangement Hex uses.
Single player campaign is a ton of fun. I found myself editing my deck quite often to handle different challenges, rather than having just a single deck through the entire thing.
Honestly, very good game. Can't recommend it enough.

I wasn't expecting a masterpiece - just a few hours of fun - but it didn't take long to realize that this game would be disappointing.
Immediately from the main menu, there's music that doesn't really create OR fit a mood, and when I ventured into the options menu I found practically nothing but a list of resolutions. My Xbox 360 controller worked on the menu, but input failed to register once I entered the game. I won't make it that big of a deal, however, since I'm fine with keyboard and mouse. The gameplay itself is much more of a cause for worry.
The fist thing you notice is that jumping is stiff, like the infamous Castlevania jump: you can't change direction in midair. There's also a painfully slow windup time and hang time for each jump, making platforming a pain and breaking the flow of transitioning from run to jump. You can grab onto ledges and pull yourself up, which would be kinda cool if the game didn't completely depend on this SINGLE MECHANIC for 100% of platforming from start to finish. Every time I jump or pull myself up I sigh at how slow it takes. But hey, you might wonder, isn't the game also focused on combat? That should be a nice refresher. Well, guess again.
Rocketbirds has a ridiculously shallow form of combat. You shoot directly forward, or you crouch and shoot directly forward. You can't change direction while shooting, so you have to stop shooting and turn around if enemies appear on either side of you. The different weapons seem to be there simply for necessity rather than variety, because the only difference between weapons is the amount of time it takes to kill the enemy. You can throw grenades, but it breaks the flow of the game with its clunky behavior and no way to tell where exactly your mouse is aiming so that you can affect the projected trajectory. There's also the ability to take temporary control of an enemy instead of Hardboiled Chicken, but that feature is COMPLETELY POINTLESS because gameplay doesn't really change at all.
There are cutscenes, but they're awful, especially the voice acting. The game also tries to be kinda funny, but I had to double take to make sure that certain lines were ridiculously pathetic attempts at humor. Anything I actually like about this game? Well, the artstyle isn't too bad; I kinda like it. There's also a section early in the game that works like a 2D dogfight minigame which I definitely enjoyed, but the rest of the game is just boring, even painful, to play.
Rocketbirds brings nothing new to the action platformer, while also managing to ruin the basics of the genre.

Overall, this game makes for an ok introduction to business sims.  But even a minimally experienced player will likely find it lacking in depth and challenge.  While I can easily point out several things that could use improvement, I find myself hard pressed to choose something that this game does well.
- Control over your business is minimal and easily maxed out given a little time.  There are very few upgrades to speak of beyond vehicles.
- While you can easily upgrade a vehicle from one type to the next, you can not do the same with your facilities.  Instead you must wait for another location to randomly become available for sale.
- When a new facility spot becomes available, the prices can vary drastically, and may not even be capable of housing the size of facility you need.  No information is given to why this is.
- Other upgrades within your facility are quickly unlocked, incredibly cheap, and give no real indication of how they effect your business.  Upgrades improve “customer/staff morale” but no hard data is given to how this effects your business.
- You can spend money training your employees, but the effect is temporary.  If your staff is over-worked by physical load, it makes more sense to open another facility rather than trying to train them.
- All of this is over-shadowed by the mysterious “fault” graph.  You are told, the higher a number is the worse the problem, but aren’t given any parameters as to what they are measuring.  You start with “Coverage” at near 100% “fault” but can open two more facilities in your starting town that will allow you to give every service to every block in your first town and it will only drop to maybe 85% “fault.”
- “Competitor Fault” is another bit of information it gives, stating that it means “your competitor has better prices and coverage.”  But again, there’s no useful feedback to what that means.  What price are they transporting at?  Where are they taking business from?  You can see their offices and sometimes their vehicles, but nothing useful enough to actually compete.
- The only thing that really requires an immediate reaction is “high-priority packages.”  Little mission bubbles that pop up every once in awhile.  You designate a vehicle solely to transport these; quick responses reward money and stars to unlock upgrades.  But keeping a dedicated courier for those packages is not worth the investment.  Package events may happen once every couple of in-game days and the reward could be easily passed if that same vehicle worked on deliveries/pick-ups  instead.
In the end, every facet of the game can be improved upon.  There eventually came a point where I had no real connection to what I was doing. The colored sliders would go up and down, but there was no real feedback.  I had no idea how things were being changed.  I was watching a screen-saver of driving ants and climbing numbers.  Even at the discounted $3 I spent, I don’t feel I got my money’s worth.

Here's some standout features of this game:
Awesome artwork
-Character designs are varied and tell a story unto themselves. For example, each crew member the Wyatt must find is detailed, unique, and have at least SOME backstory to give them personality
-Levels are vibrant and also have a lot of variety
-Enemies types are recycled a bit, but they have cool designs and the bosses are downright awesome
A soundtrack that is, at times, beautiful, haunting, and tenaciously driving forward, all at once. Other times, it's just beautiful
Bittersweet Gameplay
-Combat: move-canceling is introduced early on, and failing to use it to its fullest in respect to its limitations will leave the player frustrated and blaming the game's mechanics when the going gets tough. And boy, does it get TOUGH. Combos tend to leave one open for attack, so bad timing, spamming the attack button, canceling too early, and failing to mind enemies' attack patterns and environmental hazards will cause many to rage quit and not recommend the game. Once the player learns to cancel into a dash at the right moment, be defensive when the situation calls for it, utilize the right spells, and basically use the resources that the game gives you, the experience is fulfilling, as improvement can actually be felt with each boss fight won, each timed puzzle achieved, and each upgrade unlocked.
-Movement: Not the best, but the cancel/dash is everything in this game. Certain platforming sequences are tough to pull off since jumping in this game is not as tight as others in this genre, but again, learning the mechanics of the game and working within them takes most of the kinks out, just not all. This game definitely needs a PS3 controller-type of D-pad to execute certain sequences with masterful precision. Unfortunately, too often there are platforming sequences where enemies are placed at the perfect position to hit you mid-jump, causing the player to be "stunlocked" so that you cannot recover in the air, thus forcing you to fall helplessly until you hit the ground. Additionally, the character can continously get hit by everything around them while in stunlock. The latter situation can be helped by move canceling into a dash, but the former can be overly punishing.
All in all, highly recommended for those that want a little bit of the technicality fighting games offer (I'm thinking of "roman cancel" from Guilty Gear and other fighters with canceling) mixed in with Metroid/Castelvania/Mega Man X level design and platforming and difficulty spikes that seem like they were meant as a challenge to only serious 2D sidescrolling fans. I personally would love to see more of this genre done this way and even a sequel to Valdis Story: Abyssal City that removes or limits "stunlock" and tightens up the overall frame data of combos and jumps, but even then, what makes these games great may turn off the majority of players out there. Therefore, the appeal really comes down to nostalgia for the SNES/GENESIS era and the prospect of taking an old genre and injecting modern gaming features (skill trees, customization, etc.).

Nidhogg is a small game developed by an indie developer Messhof. While the game isn’t the longest one I have ever played, it is definitely THE best local multiplayer game I have played in a long time. You can literally spend countless hours playing the local multiplayer against your friends.
In Nidhogg there is only one objective , kill your opponent by out-stabbing them by using only three sets of stances, high, middle and low. Maneuvers such as, rolling, dive-kicking, neck-snapping and sword-throwing are also at your disposal. While it may sound simple at first, the game is really hard to master, and sometimes it gets a little bit frustrating when you get stabbed couple times in a row.
After you kill your enemy you have to run to the right in order to advance to next level, the enemy can do the same thing, if you get killed, he can run to the opposite direction, this will get you back to the previous screen, and this gets really annoying because sometimes the enemy instead of fighting you, will just run past you just to get you back to the previous screen. Each ‘level’ is divided into couple smaller ones. In single player, there is a total of 17 AI opponents, the first one being the easiest and the last one, the toughest(I don’t know if that’s true but when I’ve played it, the game got harder every time with each AI opponent). At the end of each level your character is eaten by a giant dragon-like creature, by the name of Nidhogg, you can’t avoid it though(trust me, I’ve tried), I don’t know what’s the point of that but It’s kind of hilarious and random.
The art style is what I love the most about this game, it has that surreal look to it, kind of like Hotline Miami. The player animations are also worth mentioning because of how smooth and realistic they are, and also it feels really satisfying when you stab someone.
On the other hand, the game also has some flaws, one of them is the online multiplayer, it is seriously lacking in features and is very unstable, I kept being disconnected from matches, and I have experienced serious lag during several online matches. You can’t even properly communicate with your opponent because the chat can’t handle longer messages.
As I have said before, the single-player consists of 17 AI opponents, which is great but the same can’t be said about the level variety, there is only 3 or 4 different levels which are re-used during the 17 battles in the single-player. I really wish that there was more variety in level design, maybe we’ll get them in later updates.
Nonetheless, If you enjoy playing games with your friends then this game is for you but If you don’t like the local multiplayer I would still recommend sure the game isn’t very long, but the multiplayer is still there, it might be a bit lackluster but who knows maybe the devs will add some new features to the online multiplayer.

System shock stands as one of the greatest leaps forward in immersive simulations and environmental storytelling in the history of gaming.  While it may have crude graphics, and the modern FPS control scheme had not yet been standardized, System shock was arguably 5-10 years ahead of its time in terms of world building and storytelling.  Most of the key developments attributed to half life in 1998 were pioneered in 1994 by System Shock.  Consider this:  System shock was release in the same year as doom 2.  Here are features it cotained which doom 2 did not:
1- Persistent Levels
2- Modifiable weapons (through ammo types)
3- Coherent, compelling storytelling
4- Levels which resembled funtctional places
5- Persistent levels which could be left and revisted
6- Inventory management
7- Character customization through cybernetic modules
8- Scripted events
9- The ability to crouch, go prone, lean and aim in the y axis
10-Full voice acting (Starting the influential practice of audio logs)
11-A separate, abstract cyberspace gameplay element
12-Hacking mini games (perhaps a bane to modern games, but revolutionary at the time.)
13-Dynamic story based objectives.
While aspects of the game may be crude, there is no denying that it it the grandfather of immersive simulations and one of the key influences in the history of gaming.  It is well worth a look.
10/10.  Would redefine interactive electronic storytelling again.

Heresy!
What do you get when you take a different, albeit risky, spin on a popular franchise? You get Dawn of War II, a squad/tactics-based strategy game set in the Warhammer 40,000 universe which is also the first proper sequel in the Dawn of War series.
What is striking in Dawn of War II is how Relic decided to throw away all of the base-building and army management mechanics - staples of the strategy genre - and focus on squad/tactics-based mechanics instead where you can control of up to four (out of six) unique squads and capture points throughout various missions in the campaign. In other words, it is something like taking exclusive control of heroes in Warcraft 3. On top of that, light RPG mechanics were seamlessly implemented to give a bit more depth to the gameplay by allowing the player to level up their squads, assigning attribute points, unlocking new abilities, collecting dropped loot and customizing war-gears to their will; essentially a character progression system. These RPG mechanics, while basic, do provide some diversity in tactics when preparing for a mission.
With no prior knowledge of Warhammer 40,000’s lore, aside from these Space Marines worshipping this Emperor of theirs and barbarically killing Tyranids (and other races), as if they are BJ Blazkowicz on steroids, Dawn of War II is actually capable of providing an interesting and somewhat immersive story, albeit nothing new to this genre though, with a fairly strong narrative even to someone who knows absolutely nothing about the Warhammer universe, like myself. About an hour or so in the campaign, you will quickly familiarise yourself with the lore in no time. However, this time around you are allowed to play whichever mission your heart desires in the campaign, with each pick having a certain consequence depending on its objectives. If you want to take a break from the main story-missions, distress calls act as secondary missions for you to complete within a limited time, despite most of them getting generic after a time. At least this creates a layer of non-linearity in the campaign, even if it is all just an illusion. And once again, unquestionable high production values all around coming from someone like Relic, especially in its visuals and voice acting. Where do they find these voice actors?
Relic has been known for making good campaigns in their games, even memorable ones as seen in Company of Heroes, but ultimately everyone plays these games for the multiplayer. And there is no denying that Relic did well here too, again. With co-op added, it is possible to play the campaign with a friend and/or battle against each other in either the Victory Point Control or Annihilation modes. But the real meat of the multiplayer is in the Last Stand mode where you have to survive waves of AI controlled units. It is simply addicting and so much fun to play in this mode, especially with a group of friends. No wonder most current servers just run the Last Stand mode, because it is that popular.
Sadly where Dawn of War II falls short is in its small and quite uninspiring map designs, repetitiveness in some of its mission objectives and levels, underwhelming boss-fights, squads’ poor path-finding and the lack of other playable races in the campaign (see the expansions packs); having different perspectives from different factions is always a bonus in a story. Also, once you clear out the campaign, there is little reason for coming back to it straightaway since the story, while pretty good, is not worth another playthrough for quite some time; unless you want to play on a higher difficulty, collect all of the achievements or maybe delve into co-op with a friend.
And frankly, while the gameplay is probably not as deep (as you may wanted it to be), it can still deliver plenty of hours of fun regardless. Come to think of it, the reason why it is fun is because it is simplified, stripped down from its original roots. No more headaches from micromanaging all your troops across big maps. In actual fact, it is almost like playing a MOBA game, minus some aspects and without that overwhelming depth in gameplay. Moreover, due to the small size of most maps, a mission can take can up to around 15 minutes to complete, with multiplayer matches lasting potentially longer depending on skills. This eliminates the possibility of long-winded plays and getting tired by them, although this is fairly subjective.
In conclusion, Dawn of War II is a good example where a developer took the risk to try something dynamically new on a popular and acclaimed franchise to at least satisfactory results. Whether this might have caused them to lose some hardcore fans whilst also gaining new ones, I personally do not care. It is a solid squad/tactics-based strategy game nonetheless, backed up by a story faithful to the Warhammer universe, a well-written narrative, high production values (as we are accustomed from Relic) and a strong multiplayer component thanks to its co-op and Last Stand mode, but definitely not without glaring flaws. Overall nothing mind-blowing, but it is tons of fun. If you are looking for a straightforward traditional RTS, either pick the original Dawn of War or try any other RTS out there instead, if you are desperately missing the good-old base-building and army management mechanics. Otherwise, this is a solid recommendation regardless if you know anything about Warhammer in general.

Here's a small section of my review for Demetrios - The BIG Cynical Adventure as a part of my YouTube series, The Show. You can find the full review in my video linked below.
Demetrios features a fun story, wonderful graphics that bring about a welcome feeling of nostalgia for golden age point and click titles, and an attitude that doesn't take itself too seriously. There's a heavy helping of snark, adult oriented jokes, and puerile humour here, but this brings me to one of the features I found incredibly novel. When you start a new game in Demetrios, you're asked if you're okay with toilet humour, and given three options, which let you set the tone of the jokes within your play through - a setting which can be changed at any point during play from the options menu. What's quite impressive about this feature is that Breton hasn't just put censor marks over words or phrases that might be inappropriate, but has completely rewritten entire lines and chunks of dialogue to ensure that you get a full experience regardless of your desired brow level.
Demetrios also takes into account one of the age old complaints that point and click adventuress face: the lateral thinking roadblock. It's great to see that if you're faced with a puzzle or scenario that you just can't work your head around then hints are available to you, “purchased” in a sense, using an in game cookie currency, with three cookies hidden on each screen of the game. Although it would be great to see an option that allowed players with, for instance, cognitive disabilities to obtain hints without the need to find objects that are typically incredibly well hidden, which may then act as a source of frustration, it's still great to see an inbuilt hint mechanic has been implemented at all.

One of the rare classical (mechanical-wise) adventure games that doesn't put on too serious a face. It's a really big adventure with good dialog and inventory puzzles, colorful characters - and good humor. Yes, sometimes it's toilet humor (it's quite good, but you can turn it off), but there's also fine situational comedy and satire. And it feels fresh to play as a cynical slob, art dealer (yeah, right) Bjorn Thonen and other somewhat unpleasant but alive-feeling folks.

It can always be hard for most to get into pretty old PC games, usually due to clunky controls or "bad graphics," and sometimes even getting it set up to play on a modern PC without any hitches. It was nice to see that the Enhanced Edition completely does away with any kind of set up pertaining to its DOS roots. Now on to the game.
Unlike most games from its time, System Shock was actually pretty easy to get used to in terms of controls (especially with a Steam Controller, where the absolutely maddening shortcuts for reloading a gun and such can easily mapped to one button), but where the game shines best is its exploration and feeling of isolation, all with a kick♥♥♥♥♥cyberpunk soundtrack. Searching every box, every (audio) log, and roaming through cyberspace for clues and items to progress through Citadel Station feel absolutely rewarding. And the feeling of being on a space station where everything went wrong, where the only other inhabitants are jacked-up mutants and an AI with a god complex, is a scary feeling. You never know what's going to be around that next corner. The weapons in the game from beginning to end are all cool as well, ranging from your basic conventional pistol to a laser sword and an energy rifle. Energy weapons and special powerups you get use your Energy, which you will always have to watch when using these since it can drain quite fast depending on how much and how powerful the weapons and effects are.
Now for music, I must say that I personally love it. Some tracks get you pumped up, and some tracks can get you freaked out for the kind of area you are in. It fits perfectly to the aesthetic of System Shock and I'm hoping the remake keeps the soundtracks in some form. I think the music sounds best with a soundfont, though. I personally recommend taking the time to setting up a program called Coolsoft VirtualMIDISynth, which will allow you to change the sounds of instruments in games that use the MIDI system. Most games don't sound right with just one single sound font, you will find some that are better for some specific games than others. For System Shock, I recommend using the Chorium Rev A soundfont. I personally think it's the one that sounds best with the game and fits it completely. I should mention that the music can also be a bit buggy at some times. For a game that came out back then being advertised with a dynamic soundtrack (combat, exploration, low health), I'm almost sure the Enhanced Edition messes that up. I noticed combat music didn't que in well, usually quite a bit after combat has started or it just didn't come up at all. Another major bug with the music I encountered was right at the final boss. I can say it's a sequence with 2 different paths that both lead to the same space, when going one way the music would completely stop for the rest of the area until the ending. I don't know why this happens and I don't think there's anything to fix it either.
This is definitely a very unique game and I think I'm one of the few who actually like it better than System Shock 2. It took me an hour or two to really get into it when I first played it but it was so worth it. I haven't beat many old PC games, actually very few, but System Shock was just so well done I was hooked until the end. This game alone has got me wanting to play other PC Origin Systems games and just even other popular games during the 90s. It completely changed my view on what seemed to be mostly clunky, uninteresting games until I actually played it.
Give it a try, I hope you will enjoy it.

Demitrios - The BIG Cynical Adventure is proof that point-and-click adventures can still be fun. Fans of the Monkey Island, King's Quest, Roger Wilco, and Sam & Max series will find a welcome trove of puzzles and sarcasm embedded in farcical narrative that might even make you laugh out loud.
The mechanics show tremendous improvement over 90's era games in the genre, such that intuition is usually enough to explore each handcrafted scene. Navigation through the world is instantaneous, omitting the back-and-forth slog sometimes found in such games, with six chapters of story providing about the right length. The in-game hint system gives a balanced approach toward easing the difficulty while keeping the player from heading straight for a walkthrough. I appreciated that many of the puzzles provided a genuine challenge or at least required more than a casual glance.
I played with maximum toilet humor enabled, which suffice it to say was still rather tame compared to, say, the "South Park" series. The whimsical plot and cast of incompatible and flawed characters reminded me of the film "The Big Lebowski" in its irreverent style, which is really the only way to make a game like this.

I am really into strategy games, I used to love playing Age of Empires and Star Craft. However, Im a huge world war 2 fan and i had never heard of a WW2 strategy game. When I found I totally fell in love with it. It is a different game compared to most strategy games out there, including the ones i mentioned above, but different in more interesting way. For one, in Sudden Strike you can't make troops, youre supplied with them, when you need them. However there is a limit to the number of troops you can get which is what makes it real. The variety of troops is huge, with riflemen, submachine gunners, machine gunners, officers, anti tank personnel, etc. Theres also a big varity of tanks and armored vehicles.You can call for air support: you can call bombers, paratroopers if your running low on men, or for supplies. There is also all diff. types of artillery: field guns, short range, long range artillery, anti tank guns, anti aircraft guns, etc. When it comes to infantry, the diff. types of things they have are: experience, health, morale(new to SS2), primary ammo, and secondary ammo. The more experience they have, the more accurate they shoot both with their guns or when in artillery guns. The higher the morale, the better they fight in battle. Having officers around your troops helps to keep morale higher. When it comes to supplies, it is the "supply trucks" that contain supplies. When they fix tanks, the supply number gets lower, or when they make anti tank obstacles or barbed wire. They also provide the ammo for the troops, tanks, artillery, etc. Supplies are obtained from brown and silver boxes. Brown boxes contain "ammo" while silver boxes contain "parts"....The things i mentioned here make up only about 40 percent of the game, there is a lot more to it. I hope this review has been helpful to everyone.

Really enjoyable game, it’s fairly short, and very simple, but it has a lot of personality, and love put into it.
This shows in its fairly “minimalistic” game mechanics, you only really get to complete puzzles, and shoot enemies while “plowing” through the game.
It’s fairly straightforward and never really gets too complex, even then there’s a level of difficulty that’s harder than the “standard” one that definitely makes the game longer for the simple reason it also makes it a lot harder.
On normal difficulty however, the game it’s fairly easy, I must haven’t die more than 5 times in my playthrough that lasted around 3 hours or so.
It’s very short when you compare it to the amass of games that prolong themselves either artificially by adding a series of redundant activities to complete, but even while taking other “indie” titles into consideration, this one does fall into the “short side of things”.
But it’s worth it I think because it has a beautiful aesthetic even while not being very graphically intensive (clearly) and also because it has a great cast of characters, and humor attached to the whole game, it really is sincerely one of the most individualistic creations I’ve ever encountered, one may argue that all of them are, but you know what I mean.
The game just “oozes” uniqueness in a set of ideas it implements and forms on top of fundamental, and familiar bases in game design that we’ve seen in the past.
It’s a novel effort that succeeds in creating a genuinely “fun” relaxing, and, generally, enjoyable experience.
I certainly recommend it for its asking price given that the game its very funny, and interesting at times, the whole concept of having a sort of war amongst plenty of different types of “humanoid birds”, whilst taking elements from real wars that happened through history, seems, to me, like a really creative idea.
And they succeed in transforming this “idea” into videogame media, so I can definitely recommend it, solely, on that merit…
Well that, and the fact it understands perfectly what it’s trying to be.

FYI: I put well over 1000 hours into Hex before the Steam launch. I was a Kickstarter backer and have been playing since the Alpha.
Hex is one of my absolute favorite games. It's one of the best card games I've ever played, and blows away every other digital TCG.
A couple points:
1) Is it free to play?
You CAN play 100% free. The entire PvE experience is completely free. You can play the full campaign. You can earn the PvE cards and equipment as loot from playing. None of that requires spending a dime.
The PvP has a cost associated with it, BUT that cost doesn't have to be money. PvP booster packs are purchased with platinum (the real money currency). However, you can sell/trade your PvE loot for platinum or PvP cards/packs. So, you can play 100% free as long as you are willing to invest some time into the PvE to earn platinum.
2) Is it pay to win?
No. It's a TCG, and the PvP does follow the traditional TCG model of buying booster packs. However, as mentioned above, you can earn those packs/cards via just playing the game and trading. You CAN pay for more packs/cards which will give you more options, but they don't make you stronger or better than someone else. A skilled player is much more dangerous than a good deck.
3) How does this compare to Hearthstone?
This game is a little bit slower, but is a lot more strategic. The main advantage that Hex has is being able to play cards on your opponent's turn. This makes a HUGE difference in strategy. It gives the player a lot more control and a lot more options. The other difference is that the defender declares blockers. It allows you to make a lot more strategic defensive decisions. And to go along with that... damage to troops is not permanent. This changes the gameplay from fast paced cycling of creatures to something with a lot more interesting decisions. Overall, Hex is just a deeper, more strategic game.
Also, the PvE in Hex blows away Hearthstones by a mile. It's much more in depth with character customization, quests, story nodes, full dungeons, varied paths to take, etc.
4) How does this compare to Magic: The Gathering?
It is very similar. Hex obviously took a lot of inspiration from MTG, but Hex does plenty to differentiate itself. The resource system is similar at first glance, but there are a lot of nuanced differences. The decoupling of threshold from costs has a lot of interesting things that go along with it (being able to play multiple cards of a color with a single threshold, or having cards with a threshold cost higher than their actual resource cost, for example).
Permanent effects! That's right, effects are permanent and persist through various changes. A buffed creature that is returned to your hand or placed into your deck retains these buffs even after being re-drawn and/or played. This leads to a lot of interesting options.
Digital only mechanics. There are a lot of mechanics in Hex that just wouldn't work (or would be very tedious to attempt) in a physical card game. For example, the prophecy mechanic affects the next card of a certain type in your deck when the card with prophecy is played. The permanent/persistent effects wouldn't really work in a physical card game. Tons of these types of things exist throughout Hex which make for a very interesting experience.
Champions/Charge powers. You have a champion with a specific power. When a resource is played you get a charge (there are other ways to get charges as well, but this is the basic method). The charge power has a specific cost to activate. These powers vary from simple things such as just drawing a card to buffing all troops that share a type. These are not only interesting additions from a strategic point of view, but also help combat resource flood as you'll be able to activate the charge power with those resources.
Then there's the PvE... which there is no equivalent to. If you like MTG there is a good chance you'll enjoy Hex as well.
5) Can you really make money from this game?
Yes! Not only was there recently a $100,000 tournament, but you can sell your in-game items (cards, packs, etc) for real money via third party trading. These cards DO have a value! There are plenty of third party sites set up in which you can either sell/buy directly with a store or with other players.
Summary
If you like deep strategic card games, then you owe it to yourself to check this game out. If you like single player card games, you'll love the PvE. If you like competitive card games, there's plenty of that in various forms (Constructed, Sealed, and Draft with both synchronous and asynchronous modes). This is one of the best card games out there!

Okay.  Where to start...
Graphics:  Very simple, cartoony buildings and landscapes.  The game almost looks like a slightly polished SimCity 2k, right down to the building models.  It's uncanny.  In the large post office garages, the vehicle interaction and information tabs actually go outside the border of the building screen, and can be hard to see with the city in the background.
Audio:  Not a lot of variety in the background music loop.  Note the singular noun there.  It all sounds the same.  Sound effects and incidentals are okay.
Control:  Clickdrag to pan the window gets a little annoying at times.  I'd also like the ability to zoom out further to save me the trouble.
Interface:  Simple, but it works 95% of the time.  An area I would suggest for polishing would be for changes in paths and other variables to go into effect while the game is paused instead of having to unpause the game, then pause it again to go back to what you were doing.
Gameplay:  Incredibly uninspired.  A sim junkie can figure out how to game the engine within the first hour or so.  Get both your first and second post offices fully developed (which can take maybe two hours after you've taken the engine back behind the tool shed), and you can then just leave it running and walk away while the money pours in.  On medium difficulty, I completed all of the "missions" and eliminated my AI competitor by day 45 or so using the walk-away method.
Bugs:  Surprisingly few and far between.  Kudos on this.
Final thoughts:  This is a very shallow game across the board, definitely not worth the full $15.00 price tag.  This game is categorized under the "casual games" category, and should have been priced as such (if this were maybe half the price, it'd be a little bit more reasonable and falls in line with the one-and-done depth).  Save your money and spend it on something with a lot more teeth and replay value.

This is an early stage review of “Don’t Shoot Yourself!”, which I’ve only played for 2 hours.
A difficult game to categorize. Partly “arcade”, perhaps. Certainly largely “puzzle”, certainly, for reasons to soon be explained. It begins with Tier 0, of seemingly 6 tiers (0-5) of 10 scenarios each. Each scenario consists of a named layout, or game field to try to beat, each with three skill levels: Normal (1 star), Hard (2 stars) and Impossible (5 stars!). That’s important, so I’ll clarify. Impossible counts 5 TIMES as much as Normal, and 2 and a half times as much as Hard. Each tier ends with a boss scenario that has to be defeated to move to the next tier. But it’s not that simple. To even access each boss, a cumulative number of stars must be acquired. On Tier 0 this is a very easy proposition. Few of the Normal skill level puzzles are difficult at early levels. Some early level scenarios are almost stupid easy, all the way through Impossible. This led me to believe my money had been poorly spent. I was hasty.
Each scenario requires the player to use the mouse to move a cursor forward, shooting a stream of bullets to the rear. Once 100 bullets have been fired, the scenario has been defeated at that skill level. That number of stars, 1, 2 or 5, is added to the total. What makes this game interesting is the fascinating differences in the scenarios, and the ways the bullets react to the walls and barriers they encounter in each.  Imagine invisible walls (Glass Ceiling), or backgrounds of which more than 50% are opaque (Hourglass.) Or in many cases, lines that can be followed, or must be followed, or a combination. Barriers to the bullets, barriers to the player. “Wormhole” type walls. Bullets that fly off walls they strike, or that shoot back at the player at high speeds. Fortunately, the bullets do eventually shrink or fade away, and it’s simply necessary to avoid them long enough. It generally seems to be OK to hit them, just not for them to hit you. And, oh yes, the boss levels are harder.
The reason I called this a puzzle game is that any scenario can conceivably be difficult, if the proper logic is not applied. From what I’ve seen, many levels aren’t just impossible in name, but in action, without determining and applying that specific logic. With it, some of them almost instantly become the described “stupid easy”. And that is very fortunate, because it doesn’t take long until the cumulative number of stars required to access the next boss, thereby giving one the chance to open the next tier, grows almost exponentially.
Admittedly, this isn’t typically my kind of game, where the movement of the cursor is so precise. I have very little experience, so the difficulty I describe may be mine alone. The math, however, is not. After 2 hours I have a total of 9 Impossible, 11 Hard and 9 Normal, for a total of 76 stars. I need 4 more stars to access the third level boss, and I’m stumped. (Perhaps YouTube is an admission of failure, but I have a cash investment here. PC is a new port, so no telling if that’s even an option.) Here’s the problem. To access the 4th level boss, assuming that level is even more difficult and I may have to accept Normal wins on every 4th level scenario prior to the boss, it will be necessary to have beat skill level Impossible on almost EVERY preceding puzzle on all 3 prior levels. And I can’t imagine that will be easy for anyone.
Again, I’m wondering if my money was poorly spent.
A very hard, very frustrating game, at least for me. But certainly interesting intellectually. And very satisfying when that “trick” suddenly comes to light, and victory is so very simple. Hopefully, that possibility continues throughout “Don’t Shoot Yourself!”

This game was fun to an extent. However there is very little variation in the levels which led to me getting bored nearer the end of the game.
The concept of the game is great and very unique. You play as a small shape that shoots bullets from behind as it moves along. It does this at a constant rate. To finish the level you have to simply do what it says in the title of the game and "don't shoot yourself". You have to successfully manouvere the areas presented to you and avoid 100 bullets. If you win you send out a blue bullet that destroys the outer area and releases you free.
This concept is very fun for first 20 levels or so but dies out after a while. The problem with the game comes from the fact that it doesn't do enough to engage you throughout the game by adding more obstacles to new levels. In later levels you do have obstacles such as changing walls, portals and things that shoot bullets back at you. Although this does add to the gameplay it doesn't feel like it makes much of an addition into the way the game is played. You still continue on as you was before just flying about aimlessly. It seems to make no difference to the way in which you control the character or play the game.
Another problem is that the game was quite obviously designed with touch controls on a mobile device in mind. It doesn't translate well to pc. As much so that you get glitches that make it impossible to use some elements of the game. At one point of the game it introduces to you portals that can teleport you from one side of the level to the other. This sounds great in concept but when translated to pc controls with the mouse it breaks. This is because your character is bounded to travel where your mouse pointer is located on the screen. So when you go through the portal the character gets confused and tries to go back to your mouse pointer location as quickly as possible leaving you zooming through the field of flying bullets with no control whatsoever over your character. This problem made me have to avoid using portals completely making the game significantly harder to play.
Each level has 3 sets of difficulty ratings. It has "normal", "hard" and "impossible which give 1,3 and 5 stars respectively for completing it. The way the difficulty is raised is by the speed of which the bullets are emitted from your character and travel around the screen. This does add an extra challenge to gameplay for people, like me, that found the original difficulty of the game to be too easy. It is also needed to complete a certain amount of stars to unlock boss levels and move on to the next tier of levels. This addition is welcomed and makes for a much longer and more enjoyable experience.
I also want to comment on the graphics and sountrack of the game. The graphics style is very nice looking and presents itself well in a simplistic but very colourful manor. The whole game sticks to this graphics style and I believe it benefits well from it. The soundtrack is very well implemented as well and leaves for a very calming and relaxing experience and is very nice to listen to,
So in summary I did really enjoy the game for a while, but I feel it does need a lot of improvement to be worth a full price purchase. Currently I would say you should consider waiting for a sale or a bundle to buy this game but I would definitely recommend playing it at this stage.
Disclaimer: I was provided an review copy by the developer before the full release of the game.

The Weeping Woman is a typical example of a hidden object game that won’t bring anything new to the genre, but it does its job well enough to entertain anyone for a few hours.
An investigating journalist arrives in a small town in order to solve a case of a missing child. Sounds familiar? It should, as it is not just the basic premise of Lost Legends: The Weeping Woman, but of most any standard modern hidden object games.
Luckily, this HOG here knows how to play the cliché. It creates an engaging environment with an actually populated village and by using a Mexican festival of the dead as the main theme to build its mystery on. Said mystery is hardly difficult to figure out, by the way, but the plot is tight enough to not worry about predictability.
Game mechanics tread on safe grounds as well, in a good way. There are plenty of above-average hidden object scenes, and the same goes for the puzzles too. Probably the biggest problems are the constant backtracking and the barely-helpful map, but even those are tolerable. All put together, The Weeping Woman is an average HOG, but of the engaging and fun kind.

The game is very challenging without ever seeming impossible (given you save a lot) and forces you to be conservative of ammo and health restoring items. If you are down with the maze like level design and the (wonderfully) outdated cyberpunk aesthetic, than definately buy this game. If you cant help but compare this to its sequel, than you'll probably complain about the fact that its not very similar. I'd give it a solid 8.5/10
