System Shock: Enhanced Edition is an amazing retro FPS, horror, cyberpunk game that's released in September 22, 2015. In rough comparison, the DOS version of System Shock requires DOSBox, or even MS-DOS in order to play it, but System Shock: Enhanced Edition has its said requirements utterly removed, and you are free to play without the DOS systems to do it.
The Negatives
Because the game is rather fun to play, there's a certain amount of flaws that I'd rather want to point out.
I. Certain levels are rather semi-cryptic, and it always takes some time to know what to do, or else look up walkthrough videos or internet pages every time.
For example, the Enviro-Suit is locked inside Greg MacLeod's office, and you need to guess the keypad combination. I don't know how the player really needs to get the code from, just guess it! The code is 838. That shouldn't be necessary though. Who thought that this is a good idea? That's possibly the dumbest idea for a keypad puzzle ever. To be doubled, certain levels are mazes, which is considered to be the worst part of the game.
II. Another striking example is the Reactor room where you first encounter the Security-2 and Flier-Bots. Once you've entered, you will quickly realize that the room is highly irradiated, and you need to upgrade your Enviro-Suit to resist the Radiation Poisoning, use Detoxication Stimulants and eventually you'll run out, or use cheats, which is not considered to be recommended, no matter how much you find it necessary. Now, you DO have a reviving machine or whatever it is, to help you, but you will always have to run to the reactor room every time you've been revived.
The Postive
I. The in-game's functions, also known as controls, are rather strange, and takes some time to get used to, but once you've managed to get the hang of it, its epic. If you are feeling uncomfortable about the controls during combat, you can press e to enter shoot mode, also known as crosshair mode.
II. The enemies and bosses are rather unique and interesting, especially the Cyborg Assassins, Cyborg Elite Guards, Virus Mutants, Cyborg Enforcers, and the Inviso-Mutants. In System Shock 2 however, the enemies from System Shock are no longer present, except for the Cyborg Assassins. I'd love to see all the enemies from System Shock to return in the third sequel as a retro throwback to the first System Shock game.
III. The music is rather hype-inducing, combined with synthesizers, technological ambiences, and much more. In consequence, the music is rather good to listen to.
IV. From System Shock 1 to 2, the storyline is rather fantastic and unique, and the game does a great job in thrilling gamers, especially on how it brings the said games to life. I wont be writing the whole plot of the game here since its long, but you can look online and read for yourself, which is what I don't recommend due to spoilers.
CONCLUSION
Needless to say, System Shock is one of the best games ever made to make its way onto Steam as I've wished, but ingame, it only has a couple of negatives that are easily sprouting out like pond weeds, and they will smack your face repeatedly over and over and over again.
For those who are reading this review, its your optional choice, go play this game; and it will give you a retro throwback. Enjoy.

I am a veteran Ultima Online player, and I loved the hardcore elements that made the game challenging and rewarding. Where UO was like a sandbox world with severe consequences for those who chose to PK, this game has none. In UO, becoming a PK was taking a big risk so people didn't just try to murder everyone they saw. There was actually a virtual society in that game world where PK's were notorious but not so rampant that the world was unbelievable. Darkfall is not a virtual society. It is simply a murder simulator. Everyone you see outside of the newbie zone just rushes at you to try and kill you and loot your corpse. This game is just a deathmatch MMO.
If all I wanted was to fight everyone I saw, then I wouldn't waste time grinding for gear and levels in an MMO, I would just go play a competitive shooter with way better gameplay. I go to MMO's (particularly of the sandbox variety) for a virtual society and community. Again, I loved UO's unforgiving nature, but it was balanced. If Darkfall added a reputation/criminal system then the game would be a much better environment for a fully fleshed out world that I would enjoy spending more time in.

It really only serves to prove how bad the actual card game is in terms of balance and design.
The actual application itself is terrible. Almost every action while dueling has a delay on it. Got to wait for the PNG image of the monster to spawn overtop of a card everytime it is summoned, got to wait for the character to cycle through their dialogue literally everytime you do anything. You can mute it, which speeds up how fast the subtitles go by, but they still delay everything by at least half a second and serve no actual purpose. The process of cycling through turns is awkward, especially when you have to initiate the battle phase manually every single time. You cannot just activate it automatically by choosing to attack, you have to click a prompt to activate the battle phase then you can attack. Outside of that, there are tiny loading or delay times on performing all kinds of actions in the hub world. For no reason. When you first log in the game spams you with probably over a dozen different pop up screens none of which you will remember what they were informing you about when they are all gone. It is just an obnoxious, slow and tedious application with absurd amounts of meaningless padding or delays all throughout its functionality.
And the character dialogue and world presentation is absolutely terrible. It makes the entire thing look like a badly written elementary school writing project.
I was starting to get into it regardless of the terrible application until I met the meta.
Fill your deck full of monster cards with high base attack that require no tribute summon. Fill your deck full of spell or trap cards which boost your monster attack power even more. You win.
If you actually want to make a real deck which involves strategy, element types, monster types; you naturally have to accept all kinds of none-meta cards into the fold because they all play a role in the overall theme and strategy. This straight up loses to spastic meta decks which are just filled with cards that have all the high end attack power but can be summoned instantly. There is no balancing or sacrifice for doing this, you can just do it. So now all your cards are literally more powerful then your opponents, and you can keep making them even more powerful using generic spell or traps cards which also buff your monsters with no sacrifice.
There is nothing your opponent can do to stop this short of getting lucky draws which link together to allow them to pull off a big comeback. Because if you just keep spawning monsters with the highest base attack for a none-tribute summon monster, you perpetually will win every confrontation unless your opponent gets lucky. Since the only way your opponent can make their cards stronger then yours, is through their own buffs or special effects. So they need to work or get lucky just to be able to match the amount of power your deck has from the start which you can make even stronger through your own buffs.
Unplayable. You either have to adapt to the spastic meta and foresake actual strategy and thematic deck design or hope you do not encounter the meta or get lucky when you do. Because there is absolutely zero drawback to exclusively choosing monsters with the highest base attack to fill your deck. There are numerous cards that are capable of being effective without needing monster or element type synergy, so even if your deck is full of overpowered monsters of all different types you can still pull off chains and tactics using generalized effects.
Because the attack power of immediate summon monsters massively varies, yet they are all classified under the same umbrella of being immediate summons. So there is no disadvantage to picking all the strongest ones. It is even more hilarious because there is a pre designed tutorial which actually simulates this. The tutorial is for showing the player an Elemental Hero deck, versus a Warrior deck. The Warrior deck is filled with buffs and almost all the Warriors have near or more base attack then the Elemental Heroes. And all the Elemental Hero deck spell or trap cards are utility. So winning is borderline impossible because your Elemental Hero deck is fundamentally weaker then the Warrior deck and there are zero restrictions in place to stop this.
This is a scenario the developers coded into the game; which is an actual example of the most fundamental balance problem in the game. The ignorance.
Beyond that, there is nothing stopping the game from making your starting hand all spell, trap or tribute summon cards so on your first turn you cannot summon anything and thus are at a disadvantage the whole game. There is no actual mechanics or abilities in place which allow players to strategically climb back out of a bad situation, if you get in it you are doomed until you draw a super card designed to counter said situation. And do not forget you even having those cards is random based on if you find them in card packs.
Most of this is not even this application, it is just the fundemental flaws of the card game itself. Which are highlighted massively when you put them on the internet where they are going to be exploited for the sake of winning as much as possible.
The developers could have coded it so the starting hand of each player has at least two immediate summon monsters and three other cards so players always at least can actually start spawn something on their first turn. But the developers could not be bothered. The developers could have restricted the deck building system so that players can only have so many monsters of each attack power type or range so players can not fill their deck full of all the strongest most meta ones with absolutely zero drawbacks. The developers could not be bothered. Just copy and paste a completely imbalanced and short sighted card game into an online setting where every single imbalance and short sighted feature is going to be exploited as much as possible.
Do not forget the classic pay to win elements which give players a bunch of resources to start off but then barely give them any resources to get more cards afterwards thus forcing players to grind or pay to get more cards. Which is amazing considering players only get three cards per pack, packs barely have any thematic organization so if you want to build a certain type deck you likely have to roll the dice to get those type of cards from multiple different pools of cards. Want a zombie deck, well there are two zombie cards in seven different card packs each with a pool of over fifty cards so have fun rolling for those two zombie cards out of fifty; seven different times, with a limited currency. And you cannot create cards manually, the currency you get from disconstructing cards can only be used to buy some from a random small array of cards which changes each day.
Even the gameplay itself is a grind. Players having to defeat low level weak opponents over and over to level up and unlock things, so much so that the game even lets you allow the computer to play for you because there is so much grinding. And you can only fight so many regular opponents in certain frames of time, the stronger opponents cost currency to fight, and the game gives significantly less experience for beating other players online. I grinded for ten hours and I still do not have enough to build a full single type of deck, and there are still numerous ever more complex grinding ahead from there. This is a chore.
So, it is a time and or cash trap; with an obnoxious application that has absurd amounts of padding and delays; all connected to an absurdly imbalanced card game which the developers could have easily fixed through basic coding; if they actually were concerned with something more then making cash.
It is near the end of two thousand seventeen; and developers still are not meta proofing their games. Eventually maybe they will realize you cannot trust the human species to just play fair.

I purchased this game thinking it would be fun.
I was right... for roughly ten minutes. While the tutorial is excellent in helping you understand the basics of the game, the programmers obviously decided to make this thing WAY too difficult WAY too soon out of the starting gate. Granted, I'm playing on a keyboard, and i'm not used to playing platformer games like this on a keyboard. So OBVIOUSLY, i'm a bit out of my depth here. However, My big hang-up on this game is, without a dout, THE DIFFICULTY.
The core design of a good game, say for instance, Super Mario or Sonic the Hedgehog, is the start the gamme off blaringly easy so players have a decent time getting the hang of the controls and getting used to the gameplay mechanics. Graphics, sound and the little moves the spider character put on for the end-of-level theatrics is acceptable, and I could get by with those alone in a normal game. But here, the difficulty comes NOT from a decent, well-paced challenge, but from the game forcing you to essentially crab-scuttle with your head bowed to the ground at ALL times to make sure you
A: Don't miss anything
B: hit all the right jumps and web shots PERFECTLY
C: DON'T. FRIGGING. DIE.
which is AGAIN, where this gae fails: THE DIFFICULTY AND HOW EASY IT IS TO GET KILLED. Once again, looking at Mario & Sonic again. Both main characters have at LEAST a health counter: Mario has one hit in small form before death, 2 if he's powered up, while Sonic MUST have rings in his possession at ALL TIMES in order to stay alive. Not having a life bar is fine if the character is made to die in one hit, but they LEAST the developers/designers/WHOEVER could have done for this game is to PACE the difficulty apprpropriately by the world and current stage. Stage 1-3 SHOULD NOT, AND I REPEAT, SHOULD NOT BE the stage that kills any desire to continue.
I played that one stage for nearly a half-hour, retrying over and over to make SURE I hit everything perfect and NEVER died, and STILL ended up dying close to fifty times, ending up with 0 points before i gave up and shut the game off.
The mark of a GOOD game, folks, is that it is enjoyable, entertaining and makes you WANT to not only finish it, but replay it again and again while NEVER losing its playability over time. This game Is, as I've said, enjoyable ONLY for the first ten to fifteen minutes, is only entertaining while watching that litle spider prance around like he's got something to prove, AND makes me want to NEITHER finish NOR replay this game EVER.
Hints to the developers: Take some time to go back and recode the game. Judging from the reviews and comments you've gotten, this could be a VERY GOOD title, if not for the flaws that have been pointed out. Some hints would definitely be:
1: Adjust the difficulty scaling and retool the earlier stages accordingly. World 1 should start off easy and get to low/mid-grade diffulty by the boss. World 2 should pick up from World 1's ending, bumping up the difficulty JUST enough to keep players on their toes and getting up to mid/high-grade difficulty by the boss. World 3, again, should pick up from World 2's end, bumping up JUST enough to keep attetion strong and finish with a boss that's challenging to beat and will leave a sense of accomplishment.
2: Addition of a display/graphics menu option would be a VERY handy feature. I'm not big on full-screen gaming, as I tend to have multiple things going on over two screens; taking up one SPECIFICALLY for the game and nothing else is annoying, but with no option to fix it, there's nothing I can do save for "alt+tab" every time something happens.
3: ADDITION OF A LIFE METER. Touching a MUSHROOM kills you in one hit? Are tips being taken from the NES title "Action 52" here? Because there was a HELL of a lot of that going on in THAT title; I know because I've played it. Being able to take multiple hits willl DEFINITELY see an increase in playability; would you EVER want to play a game where you have to play the entire game PERFECTLY without dying once? the infinite continues from save points feature is nice and works, but having to start BACK from where I JUST was every time I die AND having to collect ALL the same items again and AGAIN is NOT fun, it's tedious and frustrating.
4: The controls need work in general. I find the character does a lot of gliding after directions to move have halted, and the jumps are awkward and hard to aim. half the time, I end up BARELY making my mark, while the other half ses me plummeting into a death trap. The web shooting mechanics need some tweaking also; as long as I shoot from the ground, i should be able to hit and connect to my target; why would i EVER need to jump to hit a target the size of pea with webbing? I've never seen Spiderman having these problems, and he does everything either from a stand-still or while STILL IN MOTION.
overalll, I'd rate this 3.5/10 due to the numerous game-breaking flaws. And if the save-deleting bug i've read about is real, then the score will be going even further down. You can't make a game, find out it's bugged and in need of work and just decide to leave it as is; people WANT to play this, so come back and fix these problems, for the love of all things GAMES!
Thank you in advance, regardless of whether you read this and/or take action or not. I've said my piece, and that's all that matters.

You are a Chicken on steroids combating evil Penguins.
Honestly I thought this was gonna be a humorous play on Americans vs Germany or some variation on it, just with birds.  While it is indeed similar, the graphic content of the game actually surprised and offput me a bit, and after awhile felt it was way over done just for the sake of being gory or graphic.  Characters are pretty stereotyped, though the animated cutscenes are well done, as is the voice acting.  The dialogue though is really stale for the main cast I felt, though the penguin henchmen you run into had much more amusing dialogue.
The sprites themselves are very well animated (minus sliding boxes around), and the environments are detailed and lush.  The problem is the lack of variety, as you'll either be in a military base, blimp, or forest with the same similar backdrops and details minus a few neat areas that I wish were more prevelant.  Enemy types are also for the most part the same with different colored uniforms.  There are a few different enemy types but you really don't run into them long enough to notice, or they are a boss of sorts and are a one off sadly.
The keyboard personally had a bit of a wonky control layout, but much more response while the controller (which you need to manually go into the options to enable) had better key layout but a weird sluggish feeling to it.  Also rocket levels are a nightmare on keyboard but much more smooth on controller.
I have no clue how some of these mechanics were deemed okay and sent off to the final product.  Maybe I had extremely bad luck in the game, maybe the game just hates me, but beating this game is a bit like gambling.  You can count your cards, do all the math in your head in probability but it still falls down to that 5% chance that the game will have everything against you.  You cannot aim your gun.  You can only shoot left or right, crouch/roll jump and switch weapons.  Later you get neat little things called brainbugs to control your opponent and grenades but god help you if you even think of using anything other then your machine gun in combat.  Rolling does nothing to dodge incomming fire, and the only way to not be juggled around for 5 seconds being shot at is to pray the level designers put a crate (which they never do minus two or three times) or some sort of thing to hide in.  Or just shoot before they do unless luck decides it says no.  You will be put into near impossible situations such as having two enemies on either side of you with no cover, and friendly enemy fire doesn't exist, yet you can kill a penguin, juggle it's body while another penguin camps behind it and shoots through his friend's corpse and at you.  Walking into the next part can also result in death due to them open firing before you can even have the camera slide fully over into what's even killing you and can only hope the enemy is looking the other way when this occurs.  The puzzle element is more aggrivating than most, as you'll most likely need to brainbug and control an enemy (which is cool but the process involved is tedious) and flip switches or slide boxes around cause you're too short or fat.  Aiming the brainbugs is an incredibly slow process and the aim arch moves slower then water boils.  I want to add your grenades use the same mechanic, and also you can kill yourself with them too and make them impossible to use practically in combat as the enemy is either juggling you with fire or in your face punching you.  The only thing they seem to have gotten right is the rocket levels to which there are only three (with a name like Rocketbirds you'd assume you'd just jetpack everywhere, apparently not).  My only qualm is the keyboard control scheme and the fact the camera can have a mind of its own, zooming in close or super far out and you looking like a grain of rice.
Don't be fooled by the endorsed music.  The only time music ever plays is the title screen, cutscenes and very specific places in the game.  Otherwise you're left with the ambience of a military base or jungle with in-game chat sounding like two iron plates rubbing together in the slowest form imaginable.  Even the endorsed music kinda felt like your generic emo-ish indie fair, I personally didn't like it, but I'll leave that up to personal opinion.

Apparently the only easier way to kill that boss is to do the most obnoxious task of finding all the red flags achievement and being gifted a knife to kill it with.  I can't be bothered with that crap, and I'd rather actually play a game that involves strategy then play Russian Roulette.

I am someone who has followed the Yu-Gi-Oh! TCG since 2006 and someone who continues to play the game competitively to this day. I went in to Duel Links thinking... "this game is so different I bet im going to hate it" and to be honest i wanted to hate this game and im not really sure why looking back at it. Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Links is a very fun addictive game with a dynamic diverse meta despite what online critics may tell you. Progression is fair and you never feel like you have to wait on a timer like in other mobile app games. The 3D graphics and the Character Voices are well done and completely optional if you dont want to deal with them, which is a nice touch. I feel like packs are too grindy though... at 50 gems per pack and only 3 cards per pack its really lackluster... i would perfer to get 5 cards per pack instead to speed up the grindy process a bit. Also there is a lack of a Main Phase 2 which irritates me as it discourages alot of "habits" ive gotten from the real life card game such as "Setting Face Down Spell and Trap cards after declaring attacks." its a nitpick really. Honestly this game is pretty good but its not better than Yu-Gi-Oh GX Tag Force Evolution or any of the Tag Force Games Respectively. However it is better than recent titles like Legacy of the Duelist PS4/Xbox1/PC and Millenium Duels PS3/Xbox360. Pick this game up if your a fan of old school Yu-Gi-Oh!, The Yu-Gi-Oh! Tv show or if you are looking to get back into the game without being swarmed by the real life card game which can be overwhelming these days. However i dont reccomend this for people who want an accurate Yu-Gi-Oh! video game as your card pool is limited, and the rules dont match that of the real life card game. In this case i Reccomend YGOPRO, or
respectively. Final score 78/100 that i would gladly bump to a 85/100 if they increased the amount of cards per pack or increased the ease of getting gems in the game to compensate for the grinding even though it isnt as bad as other games.

The game is free. Try it.
Mechanicly it is very similar to Magic, with an improved resource system. It also has some really neat features you won't find in other card games. The community is outstanding. Strategy games in general tend to have a toxic atmosphere but Hex as a pretty mature player base. Granted its player base isn't huge, but there are enough people to find a match pretty quickly and the tournaments have okay match making ranking.
The Goods:
+ Good Mechanics
+ Fun cards/abilities
+ Faster play.
[Priority switches with a click of the button, meaning less waiting around than in games like Magic Duel (which uses a timer). Great for people who enjoy strategy but can get impatient].
+ Awesome interface and UI.
[The UI is both beautiful and efficient. All the information is presented in a clear easy to see manner. Interacting with it is pain free, and casting abilities is hassle free].
+ Beautiful artwork
[Both the background and card artwork is very pleasing to the eye. There are all the flashing lights and moving pieces that give an arena atmosphere, but they are also swift and efficient. The artwork is not quite as pastel as Magic, but it is far from being toony like Hearthstone. If you ask me, hearthstone looks like a learning app you download on your tablet to teach kids how to do math].
+ Ability sound effects.
The Okay:
~ Unique singleplayer.
[Personally I think the singleplayer is a little overdone and doesn't offer good enough rewards].
~ Decently interesting card abilities.
~ Semi-useful auction house.
~ Good social/buddy options
The bad:
- Grind or Pay.
- Not enough starting cards.
- Everyone starts with the same starter deck.
(Personally I think if they varied starter decks from a thousand card pool, it would make the auction house more popular and jumpstart the game. That would be a good player built economy... I'll get to the bad player economy here next.)
- Two currency systems: Gold (earned in game) & Platinum (buy/ trade for only).
The negatives of this game can be summed up together in one paragraph. Obsolete in game economy. Separating the currency you buy from the currency you earn is a poor concept that has ruined games. Yes you can trade one for the other, but only the most invested of people are willing to spend the time that takes-- On top of the time it takes to grind.
If they want this game to be more successful they should make accessing tournaments/leagues and acquiring new cards easier. The more cards people get, the more cards they want, which means the more likely they are to pay for them.
Customization is the biggest selling point on both TCG and RPG genres. If you have to jump through too many hoops to get the variety you need to customize the way you want, it isnt worth it.
I'm endorsing this game because It has exemplary UI with card mechanics I enjoy. A lot. I am endorsing it with the hope that they continue to listen to feedback and eventually eliminate platinum and make the game more accessible.
PLEASE try this game for yourself. It is free, its a small download, and has HUGE potential. Just needs a few tweaks and I believe the devs are very active and want their game to succeed. They view the game as a permenant they intend to buff, not an instant cashpit to be discarded after a quick use.

Unfortunately this review will be quite brief, due to an unexpected issue I ran into. Alien Spidy is, in and of itself, a fairly solid physics puzzler. You swing from anchor point to anchor point, collecting little bits of energy, hopefully in a row, in an attempt to boost your score by reaching the end of the level. At 3 worlds and anywhere from 16 to 24 or so levels per, it doesn't seem exceptionally long, but the game is quite difficult, though not unreasonably so. The web swinging could use some work, which is a shame because it's basically the core of the game, but that isn't the issue here.
When returning to the game to make further progress, having already made it to the end of the 2nd world (no small feat, I can assure you), I started the game only to find the Continue option blanked out. My save file was gone, and according to the forums nobody knows where to, not even the developers. With such a game-breaking bug being so common, and with the developers seemingly planning to do nothing about it, this game gets a hard pass.
If it's ever fixed, it's a pretty challenging game that requires a lot of finesse, but when all of that effort can be dashed in an instant, something is wrong.

First of all: To look at Hex as a Free to Play game is a mistake. Yes, you can play the game for free and enjoy the mechanics and exciting gameplay it offers but you will be restricted to some basic cards and you would be forced to work hard to get fun new cards to play with.
On the other hand, if you change your perspective and look at the price for the in-game currency as the price you pay for the game, you'll find that Hex is a really fun game to play!
Although many of the rules are comparable to many other TCG's, Hex will make full use of it's digital form and will allow you to do things you didn't even dream of in physical TCG's. Duplicating cards, changing the card text, boosting other cards in your deck or just turn some cards in random other cards, it's all there.
The real fun part in Hex is discovering how the mechanics can make the game seriously fun to play. You'll look for crazy combination, explosive boosts, invincible supermonsters and other unorthodox ways to win you your game.
Hex will give you a good time, as long as you know it's a game you should pay for to enjoy it to the fullest.

Imagine you have your white cube. It has real sharp controls. But it's also eternally covered in butter. That you obviously cannot consume. Now imagine the cube
behaving like a cube at all but still retains the hit boxes as one since it
acts as if it is a sphere. Imagine hitting a button that changes gravity. Oh, but not just
button, no no no: it's surrounded by spikes so that if you didn't hit it
right, you'll slide off the edge ever so slightly and restart the level. Now imagine that, if you
happen to hit it just right and the gravity changes, you leave it to dumb luck to fit between two sawblades that will also put you back to start. A pixel to the left? Dead. A pixel to the right? Dead also.
If you

Onechanbara Z2: Chaos is a 2014 Action–Hack and slash video game developed by Tamsoft. It's a port from Playstation 4.
The game is pure hack and slash with good music, regular story and nice but simple combat. You can upgrade your combos and equipment to focus on different aspects of your playstyle. It's a short game (5 hours should be enough to clear the Normal difficulty) with lots of missions/quests to entretain you for a while and you can prove your worth with the Online Leaderboards. Has five difficulties and dozens of cosmetic unlockables.
Good:
+The voice acting is very decent. Some are even excellent.
+The music is quite good for this type of game.
+You can dress your squad as you like.
+Lots of missions/quests to give replay value.
Cons:
-The AI tends to be bad. Sometimes it's Fake Difficulty.
-The backgrounds are very outdated.
-The sound tends to bug every now and then. Common during loading screens.
-The lock-on camera works wonky against certain bosses.
-Game is a bit repetitive. Go here, kill that, trackback a single room, kill these, push forward.
Overall it's a decent game if you can get it at a sale.

To start with this is an arcade game and not a simulator, it was ported from phone to pc I think and they did quite a good job of it.  I personally play it with a joystick and I have to say for a phone port this game has better joystick response than War Thunder when last i played that game.  I had no trouble mapping buttons or with responsiveness in Storm Raiders compared to the buggy and mouse bias War Thunder which is a flight simulation game.  That aside I really have been enjoying this game.
Pros:
-Very easy to fly, it's just throttle up and you're off, this is an arcade game after all.
-3 Difficulty settings.
-Simple 3 modes wingman support: Attack / Defend / Formation
-Multiple control types supported, works great with a flight stick. (I use the Logitech Extreme 3D Pro)
-Good graphics, effects, & atmosphere music with the exception of one of the campaign missions.
-Larger scale air battles with large maps, you'll get into some decent furballs here.
-Three short campaigns filled with fun as well as several solo game modes that mimic the multiplayer games.
-Active multiplayer online matches. (Deathmatch, Capture the Flag, & Destroy the Base.)
-Unlimited bullets with a heat mechanic, recharged rockets/bombs/torpedos mechanic. (Also a con for those who want realism.)
-Toggle Aim Assist, personally I found it easier with this disabled as I could kill enemies from outside the lead que range.
-New aircraft are earned by completing the campaigns and leveling up, you don't have to purchase them like the phone version.
Cons:
-There's only one internal cockpit model used in every plane, very sad. :(
-The campaigns are pretty short, about 5-6 missions long each it wont take long to finish them. (Also a pro for casuals.)
-For those that like realism, there's unlimited ammo & a radar system. (Again, it's an arcade game.)
-The physics are not the greatest but only really is bothersome when landing, if you cut your engine by boosting too much, or running out of fuel via campaign event. (There is no actual fuel consumption.) My first landing in this game dropped me dead from 2 meters up for a successful three point landing vtol style.  If you want a more realistic landing don't try to coast, go in low at 50% and grind the ground, wheels deploy automatically and then drop the throttle back. When you run out of fuel or kill your engine (temp only) you quite literally will start to drop straight down shortly after, there is no gliding in this game.
Really there isn't a whole lot about this game that bothers me, I really like flight games like the Ace Combat series up to game 5. (Assault Horizon was just a disappointment.)  While this game isn't an Ace Combat with an amazing story I found the gameplay engaging and fun.  At $9.99 I feel the game is well worth it.

Wow!  This is one incredibly enjoyable game.  The animation is superb, and the overall presentaion is very well-crafted. Rocket birds: Hardboiled Chicken
Well… This one is weird: The gameplay is shaped like a 2D run-and-gun with a bit of platforming and Sokoban mixed in. It’s reasonably okay and the puzzles are simple enough to get around. The controls are a bit fickle, though, and and shooting, while somewhat satisfying, is hampered by the fact that the automatic weaponry completely locks up whoever is getting shot. That means that when you meet an opponent whoever shoots first wins - and when, later in the game, you end up being surrounded by enemies you’re gonna wind up cursing at the shooting mechanics a lot. There
a cover mechanic implemented, but I didn’t find it to be particularly useful due to the somewhat clunky controls of maneuvering - I mostly ended up rolling past enemies, only to get up and shoot them in the back.
Overall, the gameplay itself leaves a lot to be desired - there’s potential in here, but it needs polish.
Then there’s graphics and sound. The backdrops are mostly grey’ish and boring (like:
boring), although the character designs, and the way birds are framed - from nazi penguins to the chicken prisoners - are amusing and work really well. Animation is notably stiff, but not in any way detrimental to the gameplay.
I guess what the game does best is in the sound department: While the levels are notably devoid of music or ambience - with footsteps (and gunshots) being the only thing heard - the gameplay is interspersed with music videos retelling the story of protagonist Hardboiled to the alternative rock-sounding music by Austrian music project New World Revolution. At first, I thought it really odd and jarring to have the gameplay interrupted by music videos, but over time I actually grew to appreciate this as one of the best parts of the game. The videos are well animated and actually interesting, touching on themes like war and genocide in a way I surely didn’t expect!
Whether my appreciation of the music videos says more about their greatness or the inferiority of the actual game, I’m not really sure about. Maybe both, because, honestly, it isn’t a very good game.
At select times, the game gets serious with the plot, but most of the time you almost forget it’s even there as you run from Point A to Point B to shoot penguins, pick up keycards, operate elevators and move boxes. And that’s a shame because I liked what little plot I saw - like the plot was balancing on the edge of an epiphany in its portrayal of war, sitting right between mature portrayal of the horrors and dehumanizing on one side and a B-movie featuring Arnold Schwarzenegger on the other.
Also, the voice acting is laughable - Hardboiled sounds like he doesn’t even want to be part of the game.
In the end, I’m afraid I really can’t recommend this game. I don’t say that lightly, as it is really,
close to being interesting. The cliffhanger ending even left me wanting more of the story - just with less of the actual game. This is a good story/bad game kind of situation - I hope Ratloop either work out their serious gameplay kinks or find another medium for their potential sequel.
Still… If genocidal nazi penguins sounds like your thing, and you can work past the broken combat system, there are things to love in here.

I really wanted to like this game, but half an hour into it and I'm just done.. it rubs me in all the wrong ways.
Allow me to enumerate my grievances.
First- the music is terrible. Think of the worst prog rock crap you heard in the mid 90's and then layer random chicken and gun sound effects over it. Okay sure, that's mean- and subjective. But what isn't subjective is the fact that it's repetetive as hell! And not just in a "this type of music uses four chords and repeats the same crap over and over again", but the actual system that delivers the music seems to be somewhat broken- often restarting the music for doing simple things like pausing or walking through a doorway. If the music didn't have vocals, it'd be instantly less annoying- but it'd also have the beneficial side effect of masking the fact that it restarts ALL THE TIME. Okay, so you can turn the music off- let's forgive them this point and move on, shall we?
Next, the art. The chickens themselves are actually well designed and interesting- I'll be honest, they're one of the main reasons I flushed $5 down the drain on this one. The hand-drawn look is somewhat unique and appealing- but slap it on some poorly rendered quasi-3D backgrounds that look like something out of a late 90's PSX game and it sucks the life right out of it. But as we all know, fancy art does not a good game make- so again, let's forgive them this point and move on.
Gameplay. So much potential.. This seems like one of those ideas that was designed on paper and then executed from start to finish without any usability testing or gameplay prototyping.. none of that 'find the fun' stuff- because it's just not fun. At the end of the day, that's what kills this game for me and it's tragic because it really does have a lot of potential. Imagine playing contra where your dude took up half the screen, moved at a snails pace, rolled at the slightest touch of a button. Now imagine playing that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ized game, only allow shooting left or right, and make it so you waste tons of ammo juggling dead bodies against the edge of a screen while trying to get the guy who's behind the guy you just killed.
The one redeeming part of the gameplay were the jetpack segments of the game, which plays a bit like MiniSquadron if you've ever played that. HOWEVER- they manage to donk that up too by constantly changing the focal point of the camera to parts of the sky that your dude isn't even in! So you're controlling a flying chicken completely blind while the game spawns more AI into the field- by the time the camera pulls back you waste time trying to find yourself and orient so you can take on the new enemies. When AI flies offscreen there's no offscreen indicators that hint at where they might be coming from.. so you just fly around hoping to cross paths with them (meanwhile the AI knows exactly where you are at all times).
I'm not even going to get into the poorly balanced weapons and ammo system, or the infuriating juggle/stun system.
So I can safely recommend that you stay clear of this one, unless A) you're morbidly curious, and B) it's sufficiently discounted.

HEX: Shards of Fate is everything I have ever wanted out of a trading card game.
Note the emphasis on the "trading" aspect -- your collection has real value, and there is a secondary market via player to player sales/trading and the Auction House. Right from the jump, without even getting into gameplay specifics, that appeals to me as a huge fan of Magic: the Gathering that has had to put down the cards as I have gotten older and started a family.
Magic is great for friendly, casual tabletop games, but back when I played, I loved the tournament grind. I loved min/maxing, trading, tuning those last 2 slots in your sideboard to be able to beat the expected matchups. Not to mention drafting! Modern popular F2P CCGs like Hearthstone are great video games, and fun for quick play sessions, but were unable to sate my appetite for a full-featured TCG deep dive. Hex does that in spades. If you're familiar with Magic, you'll be right at home with Hex, although I do love how Hex introduces some innovations that only work in a digital environment that really alter how games play out.
Drafts, Sealed, a free ladder system with rewards, free weekly tournaments, and a 5K you can qualify for every two months? Compare Hex to something like MTGO where your collection has real value, and Hex's value proposition blows everything else out of the water. Booster packs are only $2 (and can often be found cheaper in trade chat or on the auction house), and there are plenty of reasonable constructed decks you can play PvP with for under $100. It scratches my competitive itch like nothing else in years.
And on top of that, if you're into the world's lore and like RPG progressions, the campaign is 100% free and lets you level your specific character with race/class traits, a talent tree, PvE specific cards, equipment and mercenaries that buff your dungeon runs, etc. PvP is the primary draw for me, but I'm not ashamed to say I've somehow managed to get 3 different characters to level 9 (the current level cap) in PvE as well.
If any of this sounds good to you, give Hex a try! It's totally free to install, and there aren't any artificial paywalls or hoops to jump through. If you're a TCG veteran and don't mind spending some money, you can jump right into the constructed or limited deep end. If you'd rather grind cards for free and play the campaign, that's an option for you as well. There are also gold sinks like Adventure Packs and treasure chests that encourage trading of platinum (the paid currency) and gold (the earnable currency), so you can dip your toes into both sides of the pool if you like!
Enough gushing. Hex is great. Try it! Now back to trying to qualify for the Cosmic Crown Showdown!

Hex is an excellent trading card game. It has depth and complexity but is not overwhelming. There are many different deck archetypes to try and with a recently released 8th set, there's a ton of card variety. Hex also makes full use of its digital nature to incorporate many mechanics that wouldn't be feasible in a traditional tcg, such as prophecy, which alters cards still in your deck.
Hex has an extensive single player campaign that takes 10-20 hours to complete. There are 8 races, each with its own unique theme, and 4 classes, which greatly alter playstyle. This variety allows for a lot of replayability, and I've spent much time trying out different race and class combinations. Once you've completed the campaign there is also a single-player arena that's great for farming gold and playing fun pve decks. PvE also features card equipment, which alters or increases the strength of your cards. You get equipment as rewards from the arena and campaign.
Hex has a number of multiplayer modes that fall into either the limited or constructed categories, so there should be something that appeals to every player. For constructed play, there's a ranked ladder, immortal format, and an unranked mode. There is a also weekly constructed tournament called Hex Bash with a $1000 prize pool and a minimal entry fee. There are also free weekly tournaments with ingame prizes, including a "Rock" format event which only allows commons and uncommons, perfect for new players.
For limited play, there are drafts, sealed gauntlets, and evolving sealed gauntlets. In each of these modes, you enter with packs and platinum (Hex's premium currency) and compete with other players for prizes, which are typically more packs. You keep the cards you open, so often winning just a little makes up for the entry fee, and winning a lot drastically increases the value of your packs over simply opening them. Similar to the constructed format, there is a weekly $1000 Hex Clash tournament that uses a sealed format.
Hex has made great strides over the past few months to reduce the barrier to entry for new players. They introduced an account leveling system that awards free packs, draft tickets, and sealed tickets. The new "Rock" format tournaments are perfect for new players and many experienced players are willing to give out free commons and uncommons to those who ask. For those who want to be F2P, Hex allows users to trade the gold you earn in pve with platinum, the premium currency. Both currencies can be used to purchase cards/packs from the auction house, while platinum is used to buy packs from the store and for tournament entry fees.
The Hex community has also made a number of excellent tools based off of the client and server's robust APIs. There are card browsers, auction house tools, trading posts, match trackers, and meta analysis websites that automatically gather decklists from ranked matches and tournaments. There are also a number of excellent streamers and content creators that can help new players understand the game.
The game has a number of smaller flaws, such as a confusing tutorial and an auction house that desperately need a usability overhall. However, I think the gameplay more than makes up for it. The game also has an excellent community, there are always people willing to help you and answer questions. This is the first tcg I've really gotten into and I'm having a ton of fun. If you have any interest in the genre, I strongly recommend you try Hex.

A very solid TCG for the crowd that wants deeper systems than hearthstone and an interface that doesn't make your eyes bleed like MTGO.
In terms of play it is extremely similar to mtg with the mana streamlined into a much more useable format.  It however does things that magic can't do because they have to adhere to a card game that is physical.  Effects on cards last through that card going to the graveyard for example.  Meaning if you buff a troop you control and it dies, if you have some means of returning to your hand or play it retains the buff.  There's a host of similar enhancements that go along with the digital only format.
The game also has a suprisingly large pve portion in the form of character creation and leveling, multiple classes, equipment specific to cards, dungeons and campaign as well as an arena.  So if you just feel like playing silly decks or have the urge to farm for in game currency or cards you can do that.
PVP is where the game really lives though and contructed format ladder as well as tournements are fast paced and extemely competitive.
Finally, this is a TCG.  I know that seems obvious but with the host of card games coming out constantly it bears repeating.  You can trade and sell cards to other players either in personal transactions or using the Auction house, the cards have value, allowing you "cash out" if you feel the urge.
All in all this has become my favorite card game over the last year and i would 100% recommend it to anyone who's into these sorts of games.

I didn't really expect much from this game, having seen many other games nowadays try so hard to pull off the Metroidvania style with a mediocre result.
That was far from the case on this game.
Attacking feels smooth and many other mechanics make the combat one of the most enjoyable in a 2D world. The story feels JRPG-ish with the way the dialogue is set up, which I personally find as a plus. The leveling system adds several different ways to go about fighting, as does the element system which allows for a combination and easy-swap to counter any monster type at any moment.
While the platforming can be difficult at times, its more than likely that it is for a completely optional item that may or may not help you. I see a lot of complaints regarding the platforming, but most of the "difficult" ones are simply optional.
As far as progressing through the game, there is no hand holding. There is a simple indicator on which area you need to go to and the direction it's in. There is a lot of exploration to be done, especially later in the game when backtracking is essential to completing that old puzzle you didn't have the ability or means to complete before.
What I have a minor issue with is the restricted trading system, as it sometimes feels like it doesn't give anything of use. There are obvious exceptions to this such as the weapon/armor upgrades given later in the game, but otherwise there are only a few other items that you will be looking for each time you find a trader.
My biggest issue though is the lack of "navigation completion". By that, I mean that the maps don't indicate very well that this particular room is complete, giving the feeling that there's always Something left to do it there, when in reality there isn't. It's a little frustrating for the completionist in me because I want to be sure I collect every treasure and complete each room to its fullest.
Overall, a must-get for anyone looking for a Good Metroidvania game. 9/10

What sets it apart: A full-fledged campaign PvE mode and a massive marketplace to trade or sell cards.
Hex: Shards of Fate feels a lot like someone said "what would Magic: The Gathering look like if it was designed to be digital from the start?" With a few exceptions, it plays exactly like Magic, but has a much better client and play experience than any official digital Magic game—making it a better choice for Magic fans than any cards games,  It also does some cool things that paper Magic can't with persistent buffs, copying cards, and transforming cards. It likely has the highest cost of any game on this list, mostly requiring you to trade on its marketplace to get PvP cards without spending real money, but its PvE campaign is shockingly deep and a huge amount of fun on its own.

Most people know about System Shock 2 these days due to its status as a beloved classic, but people always seem to ignore System Shock 1, the game that started it all. To an extent, it's hard to blame them, as the game hasn't aged nearly as gracefully as its sequel - the UI that takes up a majority of the screen is pretty daunting at first, and the tutorial screen that almost entirely buries the screen in arrows pointing at every little dial and doodad on the screen at once doesn't do much to encourage new players. It's easier to get used to than it initially appears, though, and it's helped out by the inclusion of mouse aiming in the Enhanced Edition. Aside from the mouse aiming, not much has changed aside from a slight increase in resolution, so it might take a little time getting used to switching between the mouse aim mode and the environment interaction mode (where you use a cursor to interact with things and pick up items, as well as manage your various UI elements), but once you get past that initial barrier System Shock 1 is a lot of fun. System Shock 1 is clunky, and it's not as good as its sequel, but it's worth trying if you want to see how the Shock series began.

I am just going to take a minute and write down a few thoughts I have had about this game as well as the additional games in this entire franchise. Because it is on a sale at this particular time I am jotting this down, I see from time to time a lot of people who wonder if they should get this game. The quick and easy answer is of course a most definite YES!, and I think for two very good reasons.
I will go ahead and put as the #1 reason is that, given how long this game has been out, the developers Relic Entertainment is in my opinion one the best video game development studios to have ever come along. They have done such an incredible job with the way they made this game. Everything from the production values to the voice over acting is just a perfect example of putting big budget resources to good use.
Another thing about this is, if you take a moment to look at the news and announcements pages for these games, Relic  is supporting this series and franchise to its fullest extent. There are lots of updates and general postings being made about these games on a constant basis to this day. Good communication with your player base goes a loooong way to helping people make good decisions about what games they should buy.
The #2 reason I could recommend getting this series and games, is that the level of polish and overall feel of the games themselves is very top notch. These games run extremely well across a huge variety of PC configurations, low end systems to the very latest PC's. Along with this is that these games play very good without huge game-breaking bugs ruining your playing experience, seems like Relic did a great job with making sure as many bugs were taken care of before they released this series a long time ago, in general I found that all of Relic's older games including CoH, The Homeworld series, etc. were done very well.
Some of the other things I enjoy about this series is that while I don't know a whole lot about the Warhammer Universe, I thought the story and characters are good enough to be interesting. Great campaign play, Good multiplayer action, and just altogether a solid, nicely done game series.
And lastly, I should go ahead and mention specifically that the DoW II games are just slightly different from the original W40K DoW series. The original DoW series had a classic C&C base-building, resource gathering model while the DoW II series switches over and gets rid that in favor of a squad based, heroes model.
Some people were surprised at the change, some liked it while others didn't, in my opinion it looked as if they wanted to go the other direction and that was fine. I would recommend in fact that anybody who wonders what the big difference is, is to maybe watch a youtube game review/let's play video that way you could see for yourself and decide that way because no one but you can decide if you would like that or not.

I'm definitely recommending that you play Nidhogg. The controls and mechanics are simple enough for you to learn them quickly, but they also have enough depth for complex, skill-based play. At first, fighting doesn't appear complicated, but there is a lot going on. Positioning is crucial; standing above your opponent or blocking a doorway can make all the diffence. You also have a few different ways to approach fighting. Fencing is an option, but you could also try tossing your sword and rushing ahead for some melee attacks. One of my favorite tricks is "playing chicken"; I throw my sword and charge ahead, and right before my opponent attacks, I roll past them and just keep on going. Local versus is one of the most intense multiplayer experiences I've had in a long time. The visuals ooze retro style, and I absolutely adore the soundtrack.
As much as I love the gameplay, I can't necessarily recommend that you buy Nidhogg, at least for $15. You don't get a ton of content for your money. Apart from multiplayer, all you get is a single-player mode that is just a series of AI matches. The AI makes it clear that Nidhogg is a multiplayer game at heart, as it lacks the complexity of a human player. Playing with friends is great because of the atmosphere, the intensity, and the psychology. Messing with your opponent's head is just as important as the onscreen action, and when playing against the AI, you lose that crucial component.
If Nidhogg were around $7.50, I would have no reservations about recommending it. I'm still setting my review to "recommended" because the game itself is so fun, but you might want to wait for a sale.

If I want to play the expansions, I will put in my old Heroes 3 complete CD disc into my PC and play those campaigns...or scenarios....never been a fan of random maps because I generally like some sort of story going on with each mission, but to each their own.
As for Restoration of Erathia, (which the Heroes 3 HD edition is all about), the RoE campaigns already offer ALMOST FIFTY HOURS OF GAMEPLAY
ROE.
CAMPAIGNS.

I bought the Heroes 3 HD edition during the last 75% off sale and havent regretted it once. 60% of the Heroes 3 gameplay is contained within RoE. The expansions just give you 1 new town (of which about half the creatures are already featured in RoE's wilderness) with a dozen or so new elemental heroes, a dozen or so new creatures, more powerful artifacts that can be combined ...aaaand thats it.
The main value of the expansions comes from their campaigns which are about the same length as RoE. Of these, the Armageddon's Blade campaigns unfortunately do not allow you to even choose your difficulty, and are super hard so you need to be a pro at this game, a king of resource management and map knowledge or you wont beat them to begin with.

I guess this is a rip off for die-hard Heroes 3 fans who can easily play this game every day for months, if not years straight (yes, there is that much content in Heroes 3 complete)

I loved HOMM 3 since I was a kid; it is the pinnacle of the Heroes of Might And Magic series that started with 1, got better with 2 and reached not only its graphical, but also gameplay and story and creature feature zenith with 3. After that it sorta went downhill with HOMM 4 and I no longer was interested in the story. And the transition to actual 3D with HOMM V and beyond just made things cartoonish. A bit like how Diablo III's look and feel is just not the same as Diablo I and II.
So anyway, i KNOW this is just Restoration of Erathia with redrawn spirits and widescreen support and functioning multiplayer.
i KNOW this doesnt contain the Armageddon's Blade or Shadow of Death expansions. And I know that widescreen support is already available with the free HD mod for the Complete edition of this game (which also contains both expansions) which you can get on gog for cheap. And I am not even buying this for multiplayer.
Hell, I even OWN the complete edition myself!
But on CD. So everytime I want to play it, I have to put the disc in which is a chore.
Also, even with all the additional features of the complete edition, if you want to play RoE there, you wont get any of the new features anyway. And RoE is pretty much 60% of the entire game.
So bottom line is, if you want to replay the RoE campaigns (and there are many), then you should buy this game because playing the RoE campaigns is the same on the complete edition as it is here, except here the sprites (and by sprites I dont just mean the creatures, but also the buildings, the altars, the treasure chests, the towns, the hero portraits, hell even the resource icons and user interface) dont look pixelated when you play on a big monitor, and you have widescreen support without having to install some russian dude's mod and you support your favorite game that defined your childhood.

Sky Gamblers: Storm Raiders is the third game in the Sky Gambler series, previously released as mobile games. As a result, this is turn-and-burn only, but for a WW2 turn and turn, it's surprisingly fun and decently balanced with some interesting complexities should you wish to delve into such.
For a mobile port, this game is actually quite good. Terrain and flying area is nice and big, objects are not oddly scaled (things are tiny in a distance). Details are not PC standard, but quite workable. Enemy planes break apart when you kill them, with a wing falling off, then the whole things spins and twists like a falling leaf. And so on. Ground targets can hide among trees but that's why you have rockets and bombs. Or for naval targets, you have torpedoes and bombs.
The engine can be "boosted" for a short period of high speed, but engine will overheat after X seconds, and may shut down altogether (but it will restart once you cooled off). Guns will also overheat and prone to jamming should you held down the trigger for too long. The temp gauge on either weren't too obvious though.
There's quite a bit of decent single player content (2-3 campaigns, plus survival mode and dogfight mode) as well as full set of mulitplayer games including Capture the Flag, Free for All, and so on. There's also three difficulty levels so rookies can feel free to dive right in.
Don't expect too much realism, as you have P-40 Warhawks fighting the Luftwaffe, or Hurricane carrying torpedoes, and so on. A fighter here do often carry bombs. And many of the scenarios have you attempting to race to the airfield before your fuel runs out on a timer, not on actual fuel consumption. On the other hand, they can be quite exciting, and these missions do have checkpoints so if you fail, you aren't forced to start from the beginning.
Controls are easy enough, though the gamepad support should be better, as there needs to be some custom mapping. For games that supports such, I do "RC controls" (i.e. stick one controls elevator and roll, while stick two controls throttle and rudder) and this game was able to do such, but it wasn't the default.
On some game types you can customize your plane, both paint job and the primary/secondary weapons, and choices are plenty, some are good for ground work, some are good for air attacks.
With four classes of planes (fighter, bomber, jet, and legend), there are plenty of choices and lots of customization options. Legend class contains very iconic fighters as well as some prototypes that never made it into service but were very good planes.
The interface is a little weird as often you have to rely on dragging to show more panels as there are no obvious signs there are more choices below; legacy of coming from a touch interface.
All in all, SGSR is a pretty good game, for the turn-and-burn crowd. Don't expect "realism", flight model, and so on.

You know what the best thing about this mess of a "game" is? The soundtrack...it's awesome. The aesthetics are also pretty nice...a bit different from the usual, so kudoz on that. Let me think...nope, can't think of anything more. What I really don't get is how this game can get reviews like 5/5 or 9/10...on the store page...this is ridiculous. Even if it wasn't so bad, it would never be THAT good. I read♥♥♥♥♥♥like "plenty of content"...I beat this in 2.8 hours!!!!!!! And most of it was being stuck...lol. A pro can beat this♥♥♥♥♥♥in under an hour...this is NOT plenty of content...jesus christ.
Why you should NOT buy this game, not even during a sale, as I did:
You are a chicken...this is cool. You have guns...also cool. This is where cool ends.
You can either run or "roll"...funnily enough the roll move is also the best way of locomotion for 95% of the game. Running was only useful for 1 or 2 precision actions. Rolling can be chained together, it is faster, more responsive, you need it to bypass enemies with shields and 95% of the time whenever you encounter an enemy they will immediately drop down and shoot at you. If you are in "run" mode this means you will simply shoot over their heads, miss and die a gruesome and quick death.
By the way...enemies. There are a few generic enemy types. Enemies with guns, with bigger guns, with shields and melee weapons and those with rockets. None of those is even remotely challenging on its own, however they have the annoying habit of appearing suddenly BEHIND you, which wouldn't be that bad, but for the following:
The game has no continous scrolling background...you move through fixed backgrounds, after about 2-3 seconds you reach the end of a screen and a new screen is instantly loaded. On this screen there can be a number of enemies...you can't know, so I found it best to just be rolling around all the time and instantly shooting as soon as I entered a new screen. Often enough enemies will then enter the screen behind you, while you are already fighting an enemy before you, meaning they will shoot you in the back, which more often than not results in your death or severe health loss and subsequent death on the next screen. The only way to prevent this is to either stick to the very end of a screen, because enemies will not shoot you outside of the current screen or roll behind an enemy and make sure to not have enemies in both directions. They will not shoot one another (the shield guys are an exception, somehow they can be bypassed by enemy bullets).
Enemies are also bullet sponges. No matter the weapon, pistol or assault rifle, they will take a whole lot of punishment. This only changes with the final weapon, which does not have a continuous firing mode, but a burst mode...you get that weapon after you have completed 90% of the game...or even more...have I mentioned that you can only shoot left or right? no up/down...nope.
Puzzles...this game has "puzzles". These puzzles look something like this: There is a Tower with 4 sections and 4 levels or so...the puzzle involves you going from Section A, level 2, to Section B, level 3, collect a card, go to Section C, level 1, collect another card, go to Section D, level 3, mind control a minion, activate some elevator, go to Section C, level 4, ride the elevator down to Section A, level 1, collect another card, lalalalsakgnjfdajkgndfjksgndsjknagjksdnjkganfdgk
I can't even! I understand backtracking...what I don't understand is senseless prolonging of levels. I completed this game in about 2-3 hours on normal...most of that time was spent dying randomly or trying to figure some stupid puzzle out that has you going around the whole level multiple times...I especially loved the crates in level 11...♥♥♥♥ you. All the levels are built like this famous ziggurat puzzle or whatever it's called: move the top layer to an empty space, move the next layer to the next empty space, move the first layer back and forth and so on, until you have moved thy ziggurat/Pyramid whatever from 1 place to another...it's horrible design. The final level has you ride different elevators up and DOWN a rocket again, as the villain tries to flee from you!!!!!! WTF? And that after the most boring boss fight in history that lasted ages anyway and didn't even have music...you have to experience this♥♥♥♥♥♥to believe it.
Between those levels you can use a jetpack...you might think this would be fun...it's not. The level are literally always the same. There are 2 enemy types, each wave spawning more of each. That's it...survive a few waves then blow up the airships with the same procedure as explained above.
You also have grenades, which are pretty useless, because to throw them far you have to stand up. Standing up in a fight usually means you die before you even threw the damn thing. Even behind "cover"...You also have a sort of brain control thing...this isn't a tottaly useless feature but most of the times you can only use it at fixed points in the game to control an enemy and open a door or move a box or activate an elevator...lame, boring...also sometimes it takes 1 hit, sometimes 3...lol weird.
The check points are also a joke. Sometimes you start right after you died, sometimes you have to navigate half of the level again. They are just really awkwardly placed at times. Especially before the final "wave" fight...man those are stupid...if you die at the first wave, you have to ride the elevator upwards again...this takes about 10 seconds or so...it's unnecessary. After the first wave though the game saves after every wave and even respawns you with additional health and ammo...lol.
The voice acting and writing is so bad, that I almost had to switch the sound off. Luckily they did not use a lot of voice acting. They even have some kind of wannabe Schwarzenegger accent in there...wtf. It's so bad. The writing itself is extremely boring. You do not care about most of the stuff. The best you get out of the story are the cutscenes, which evoke at least some kind of emotion. The soundtrack also helps...
You're also being objected to several superfluous text bubbles that you have to endure...nothing really matters but you also can't skip it.
The sad part is that I wanted to like this game...but the more I played the more I hated it, so my final voting if I had to would be 5/10, because the soundtrack and the art and the general aesthetic is pretty nice. Gameplay wise this game is junk...sorry.

Very good game, but with glaring flaws.
First thing I'll say: this game is miles better than Magic Online.  It takes the fact that it's a digital card game and does things physical card games can't do very well to make for exciting games.  (ie. move cards X spaces further to the top)
You can do a lot in the game without spending a dime, like the campaign (use gold earned to buy from the auction house), but there's a reason to actually spend money on this game in the limited gauntlets and drafts.  No paywall seems to exist because you can use gold (albeit a whole lot) to buy those same boosters and cards for your collection.

First, because there's no dedicated trading interface, each player mails their side of the trade to the other player as an attachment. Dawn of War II is a science-fiction real time strategy game based in the Warhammer 40k universe.
When most people think of RTS games, games such as Starcraft and Warcraft typically come to mind. You have workers to build up your base so that you can train more powerful soldiers. Resources must be harvested, but there is a finite amount of them. Indeed, this is how the first Dawn of War functioned.  However, the sequel takes a much different approach.
In the single player campaign, you are given 6 unique squads, and 6 only, to take on missions. No base building whatsoever. These squads can be upgraded with weapons and armour, and can level up to gain bonus abilities. It is a extremely well-executed combination of an rpg and a rts. The story is fairly linear, but you are free to explore the planets and do side missions at your realative leisure (that is, until the space bugs show up. Then you need to be quick or else the bugs will eat the planet).
The multiplayer is also a genre-masher. Each race has three different "heroes" which act similarily to champions in DotA or LoL. They level up, can be upgraded, and can oftentimes turn the tide of a battle. All of your other units are spawned from you one and only building, so if it dies you're out of luck. There aren't any workers, and you must collect resources by capping points. A capped point will grant you the resource constantly. The more points you have, the more resources you'll consistently obtain.
The other huge change in DoW II is the "Last Stand" game mode. Three players, each controlling one of the heroes, must survive wave after wave of enemies (top-down horde mode pretty much). You're heroes level up, get more powerful, and eventually die because Last Stand is hard.
If you enjoy RTS games, but are tired of the same-old same-old style that most RTS's follow, then I would recommend this game (or DoW II: Retribution the stand-alone sequel).

This game aims to be challenging, but doesn't give you the tools to make this challenge fair. Timed platforming puzzles require extreme precision and perfect execution with mechanics such as dash cancel, jump, walljump and platform hanging which are very unreliable, to not say random. You have to fight enemies on tiny platforms but you make a huge step forward every time you swing your sword. Every time an enemy coughs in your general direction, you're stunned for an absurd amount of time, so if there are several enemies (or worse, a flamethrower) any hit will lead to a stunlock, then death.
You can block a boss' special attack from front four times in a row, but the fifth time it might count as if you were hit from behind (which means extra damage and stun, thus death) because the hitboxes are glitchy. Speaking of hitboxes, sometimes you jump over a projectile and still get hit because hitboxes are much bigger than the visuals. I could go on, there are dozens of nitpicks that make the game feel really unpolished. You can't expect perfection from players if your game doesn't respond perfectly itself.
Among other problems, the map doesn't show any useful information (doors, treasures, shops, save points...) so navigating is really tedious, a major flaw for a Metroidvania game. The skills seem unbalanced, I had a lot of trouble with bosses until I unlocked perfect guard, then they became really easy (but still very long ; a boss took me over 20 minutes because of his ridiculous HP bar and teleport spam).
On a positive note, the art (sprites and music) are really nice. Way too many recolors though, there are only about 10-15 different enemies that you will see in every dungeon in a different color.
