After having a blast with the original
I decided to pick up the sequel, and I'm glad that I did.
The Blood Ravens are back to dispense Space Marine justice once again, and this time it's personal!
I don't mean that they have actual personal investments in the story or anything though, this is Warhammer after all.
The main difference this time around is that you only control a small number of hero squads (usually 4) in each level, so the focus is far more on squad management and tactics than the previous game. The previous game had some of that too, but definitely a lot of economy and base building too. None of that here though, this is purely a combat game.
Your heroes level up as they purge the xenos (that's Space Marine for killing just about everything) and each level up grants them a passive stat boost, 2 skill points and access to better gear (which drops randomly from enemies you kill, almost like an ARPG, but fortunately not quite as frequently).
These skill points (and your choice of weapon type and accessories) are your primary means of customization, and you can spend them on 4 attributes. Health, Ranged, Melee and Energy. The first 3 are self-explanatory, and Energy just gives you more "mana" to use your abilities in battle. What elevates this system to something far more strategic though, is that specific levels in an attribute can give very specific effects. For example, putting 3 points in Energy could unlock an additional accessory slot or allow your units to equip plasma rifles.
There aren't enough skill points to get everything though, as the maximum level is 20 (for your units anyway, I've seen enemy AI with level 27 units... I hate it when games do that). This means that you'll have to decide how to develop your units quite early on, and with no way to respec them and a total of 6 (steady) party members unlocked as the game progresses it is possible that you screw up your build and will have a harder time.
In general the game is pretty fair though, and as long as you don't split up your squad or rush into enemy fire unprepared (which will 'suppress' your squad, drastically lowering its movement speed) you should be okay. There is a range of difficulty settings too, though this can't be changed once you start your campaign.
I personally went through the game on the lowest difficulty setting, Recruit, and felt sufficiently challenged (lost 2 optional missions, which I was then able to redo at a later time).
The story is the standard 40k fare. Sub-sector Aurelia is important to every 40k race, and as the Imperium presence is overrun with Orks the Blood Ravens are called in. This quickly escalates into a conflict against the insidious Eldar and relentless Tyranid as well.
In general I had a great time with this game, and I'd definitely recommend it.
You're still only able to play as the Space Marines, and they're still stupidly serious about everything, but as a power fantasy they definitely deliver.

Gunpoint is actually, err, not what it sounds like at all, but at least the developer acknowledges that. Apparently it was a poor choice of a title early on in development, as I was told ingame... by the developer. I guess that speaks for itself about how seriously Gunpoint takes itself.
Gunpoint is a great little puzzle game, on par with games like Mark of the Ninja, and in a style relatively similar, too. It's a mix of stealth and puzzle, and has a bunch of interesting gadgets to help you bend each puzzle to your will. You have the crosslink feature, undoubtedly the most useful feature in the game. It allows you to rewire security devices to trigger different objects, such as doors, lights and elevators. The puzzle aspect comes from rewiring entire godamn buildings so that pressing a simple lightswitch will actually ring an alarm to cause a distraction, throw open two doors that are meant to be locked, then call an elevator right to your floor all in one simple switch. The rewiring is so satisfying, and the game even builds upon it more with upgrades and extra conditions.
As for the progression of the game? It's short. Short and sweet, and very entertaining during that time. It's not too difficult, either. There's an upgrades system in place where you can buy new gadgets over time, but you don't exactly grind through skill trees or anything. It's just a limited selection of upgrades and you'll acquire all of them on one normal playthrough.
The story of the game is actually relatively interesting. You play as Richard Conway, a freelance spy, and take part in a lot of different missions for different people. As you're a freelance spy, anyone can hire you and you don't have any particular allegiences, so the game decides to tear you in two by making you complete missions for two sides. The person you're stealing information from one day might be your employer the next. As such, the game offers moral choices and due to its freelance nature, you can decide on how you want to treat each character for yourself. There is no set "Good or evil". The choices actually made me stop and think for a moment, which is something that most games don't do these days. It's not a basic "Press A to be a d!ck, press B to not be a d!ck" setup.
Lastly, Conway's got a load of quips and funny lines throughout the game which only help to enhance his character.

Some of them are relatively simple, while others can be more than 10 jumps. This can get frustrating at times, but collecting all the armours is not required to complete the game.

The game mechanic is fairly simple, you've got a ball resting at the starting point, which needs to be moved to a goal within the maze. Said ball is moved via the arrowkeys, which unfortunatelly are not rebindable. (This could be fairly hindering for people with a 40-60% Keyboard) Also the ball tends to move two full spaces instead of one, so I ended up missing some junctions and had to try again and again to not mess up the right combo.
It's definitelly not the most challenging game, since I was able to complete all mazes within 32 minutes. Most paths seem very obvious, with exception of the overly bright levels.
This leads me to another point. Every level has it’s own background, which is repeated two to three times during the game. Some are really nice to look at, soothing the eye, others look like ripped desktop-backgrounds and a few are unnecessarily shouty. (For example bright pink)
Actually these backgrounds are the only challenging thing in the game, since they are distracting your eyes of the course.
Another annoying little detail is the sound. You are able to mute the music, but the clicking sound at the end of the level remains at full volume, so I had to turn down my boxes instead the imgamesound.
All in all I hope the above things are fixed in the other aMAZE games and would still recommend them for the sale price of 0.49€ for the short time I played it.
Btw. for trading card hunter: I only got 1 of 3 in the time I completed the game, maybe someday I’ll let it idle for the rest.

aMAZE is a calm and wholesome way to spend a few minutes, but there's a real problem with this game that being comfy doesn't quite make up for. "Surprisingly-difficult" isn't exactly the hyphenation I'd use to describe this game. aMaze is a compilation of 50 mazes divided into "Easy," "Medium," and "Hard" categories, but the simple truth is that all of these mazes are easy. I finished this game in under 40 minutes, and that included a bathroom break. In all likelihood, I will be idling for cards for a longer period of time than I spent playing the game. As such, aMAZE is probably great to plop a kid in front of, but adults will get more enjoyment out of its marginally tougher sequel.

All the stuff it does right (good art, original premise, some fun sections) is negated by its broken combat system, which often puts you in unwinnable scenarios by no fault of your own. There's no Easy mode available outright, which means there's no options for mitigating that. As much as I'd like to say it's worth it to try it out at least, I can't, unless you got it extra cheap, for free or in some bundle.

Wow. I'm amazed. This game is incredible. What is obviously a labor of love for the developers, it was a truly enjoyable experience for me. The story is great, but where the game really shines is in the high level of environmental detail, from the lush surrounding forest, to the incredibly detailed interiors of the house.. I am awed.
Is it short? Yes. Took me about 2 & 1/2 hours to complete. But, is that a concern? Not for me it wasn't. If a game is designed well and keeps me entertained, I'm happy to pay the price for it. The game is just right in length, I think, and it is engrossing and well-crafted throughout. I kept trying to take everything in along the way, but I also wanted to find out what was going to happen next.
Is it exciting? In a way. But it's more like an incredibly detailed hidden-object/point-and-click type adventure, just realized in full 3D. It was a joy from beginning to end to explore the detailed landscapes and poke into every nook and cranny of the mansion. If you like an extremely detailed area to explore, driven by an engrossing narrative, then this game is for you!!
Cons: not many; sometimes the character would get stuck on some of the terrain in an odd place, or a transition area would grab my character's control and I would have to wait until she made it through whatever crawlspace entrance or whatever, to be able to turn back in the direction I wanted to actually go. And there might be a way to fix the non-existent Vsync control issue, but the game is short enough to not really matter.
None of that really mattered, as the game is full of great stuff and nothing that felt like it was just filler or out of place.
Highly recommended for anyone loving story-rich and visually wonderful masterpieces of art. Because this game felt like just that, art. A wonderful journey from beginning to end.

The prequel to the incredibly famous System Shock 2. It's really just as good, if not better, in my opinion. This Enhanced Edition on Steam comes with the standard floppy and CD releases of System Shock 1, as well, so don't worry: If you don't want HD graphics or modified controls in a classic DOS game, you don't have to deal with that stuff at all. A lot of new gamers are s-h-i-t-t-y at video games, so they need mouselook or whatever. If you think you're not terrible at games, the normal, classic controls are just fine. They just take an hour or so to get totally used to, since they are unusual.
Anyway, this game is great.
I recommend playing on the hardest difficulty, since there are machines you have to find and enable on each sector of the space station that are essentially regeneration chambers, things that people who've played System Shock 2 first will easily recognize. Thing is, dying and respawning (with low health) in one of these costs you nothing at all, so you should definitely choose the timed-gameplay setting in the difficulty options as well, where a 7-hour time limit  (part of the story) is imposed on the game. This makes it so the "revive in a room with no consequences" mechanic does have a consequence other than "get annoyed that I have to walk back to some other room". Personally, I just avoided the regeneration things altogether.
Besides that, the game has a great atmosphere, and it has all the complex movements that System Shock 2 had, and more. You can lean, crouch, go prone, jump, sprint, and climb up ledges. You can lean while crouching or going prone, as well. If you play on my recommended difficulty setting, the game is less of a "sprint around hallways and hit guys with shotguns with my wrench before they hit me" type of game like System Shock 2, and more of a Rainbow Six in Space type of game. This is because you really need to lean around corners and go prone or crouch while shooting to avoid getting killed in like two seconds. It's also because there are plenty of grenades/mines that you have at your disposal that explode on impact or just very quickly, so you usually want to throw them around corners and get out of the way fast.
There are no PSI powers like in System Shock 2, but you will find new implants for your "Military-grade Neuro-Interface" that'll do stuff like let you run fast, or fly vertically. These and other implants have multiple hardware upgrades that you will (or not) find throughout the game.
Speaking of PSI, there is no PSI meter by your health, but instead, an electric energy meter. The implants you gain and all energy weapons will use this shared power source, which can be recharged with battery items or static power-stations.
Your interface lets you jack into computers to access cyberspace, which is probably the most 90s thing you'll ever see in a videogame. I'd explain it here, but it's honestly so much more amazing when you play the game and go "OH GOD WHAT THE HELL IS GOING ON"
The story is awesome. The story is explained in the intro cinematic, which I will post a link to here.
So yeah. System Shock is the apex predator of cyberpunk videogames. It's complex and difficult, so any fans of old-school gameplay should love it.

This game is ridiculously fun. It's a Dynasty Warriors-style mob beat-em-up with a DMC/GOW-level combo system that has a steep learning curve, although the basic controls are very fluid and accessible. There is a lot of replayability with an unlockable Violent level and a plethora of missions to play through as well as the main story campaign.
PROS:
- Great main character design. Not just for T&A, the main characters look great even when bundled up.
- Great main character animation. Seriously impressed at the skeletal animattion and accessory customisation - you can hook accessories to various skeletal points and resize and rotate them. Want a comically large cowboy hat hanging off your neck instead of on your head? Go to it.
- Fluid combat system and controls. The combos are very timing-sensitive, and the game rewards skillful play but doesn't punish button mashing unduly.
- Great (Japanese) voice acting. I can immediately pick out Kagura, Saaya, Aki and Aya's voice lines. The English VAs are... not great.
CONS:
- This is a console port, and it shows. Resolution tops out at 1080p, and there are no graphics options to tweak.
- Level design and graphics are beyond uninspired. Environments are blocky with muddy textures; think PS2 level environments. Fortunately, the enjoyment in the game is in beating up enemies rather than gawking at the levels, but it's still a shame.
- Training mode is not very informative, figuring out the combat system takes a lot of trial and error.
I played mostly v1.05 and, contrary to some comments from earlier reviews, had no problems with 120 Hz. I think this may have been fixed from v1.04, where I had speedups in canned movies at 120 Hz. Hooray!

This is a follow-up review to DOOM 1 and 2. Don't let playtime fool you as I've played this before many times.
Final DOOM is the final installment of the 'Classic DOOM' lineage (at least until No Rest for the Living for DOOM II, included with the BFG Edition of DOOM 3 in 2012), published by id Software on June 17th 1996 under the initiative of John Romero and developed by members of a DOOM fan community known as TeamTNT as opposed to id themselves. Final DOOM consists of two authorized DOOM II IWADs, effectively two DOOM II games in one package. The first is TNT: Evilution, which was developed independently by TeamTNT and later purchased by id when it was nearing completion to be included with the Final DOOM package. The second is The Plutonia Experiment, which was created specifically for Final DOOM, after its authors Dario and Milo Casali had contacted id and showed off an incomplete set of levels. While part of TeamTNT and contributing to Evilution, the Casali bros had produced Plutonia independently.
The 'TNT' in Evilution's title stands for 'The New Technology' while also representing the name of the mapping team. Evilution was completed in November 1995 and would've been released for free, but a publishing deal by John Romero the night before its release had resulted in a commercial publication of Final DOOM by id. This commercialization of Evilution had caused a significant amount of controversy within the DOOM community back in the day and is consequently regarded as one of Doomworld's 'Top 10 Infamous WADs', albeit not for reasons regarding gameplay or level design. Evilution's design has a strong technical theme with levels that are akin to real buildings like experimental labs and military bases, unlike Plutonia, whose design tends towards a more naturalistic and abstract landscape style. Evilution features a variety of new textures as well as new music tracks on most of its levels.
Dario and Milo Casali, who contributed a few levels to the Evilution project, accepted the task of creating what would become Plutonia after sending an eight-level PWAD to American McGee, managing to impress him along with the rest of id. Soon after Plutonia had its 32 levels created in a mere four months' time and were submitted to id in January 1996. Compared to Evilution, Plutonia is considerably more difficult due to the usage of stronger monsters like Revenants and Arch-viles in earlier maps and massive amounts of enemies in later maps, especially on Ultra-Violence difficulty. Map designs and special effects that were considered against regular IWAD norms were utilized, such as invisible bridges and hidden Arch-viles placed near groups of enemies, effectively creating infinite respawners that would harass the player throughout levels. According to sources, the Casalis had always enjoyed challenging each other with their creations, and had intended to make Plutonia harder than usual in order to challenge DOOM II veterans. Plutonia has a variety of new textures but re-uses music from DOOM 1 as well as DOOM II.
Each of the two standalone IWADs are presented as sequels to DOOM II, referencing events in their background stories like the invasion of Earth, but without referencing each other in any way so the canon for either story in the mainline Classic DOOM series is unlikely.
Evilution's story has the UAC once again intent on developing and experimenting with teleportation technology, but this time they setup their facilities on one of Jupiter's moons, Io, in the hopes of preventing another Earth-based attack. They come prepared too, with a solid detachment of space marines for protection. Unsurprisingly, the first gateway opened results in an attempt from Hell to invade again, but despite their best efforts to overwhelm they are massacred by the marines. Figuring Hell was unprepared by their quick defeat, research on the gateways continued at a greatly accelerated rate, to which the UAC were also rapidly growing complacent. Later on, the yearly supply ship arrived earlier than expected, and looked strange and unusually large on the radar. The personnel of the base went out to greet it, but then saw the terrible truth: it was a magical construct from Hell, built from steel, stone, flesh and bone. The ship's enormous doors opened, unleashing hordes of demons on the base, quickly killing, feasting and corrupting everyone in sight. The marines from before, despite their battle-hardened status, were of no match to the fury of Hell's armies. The Doomguy, now in command of marine deployment, had been away on a walk, thus escaping death or zombification. He rushed back to the base after a quick exchange with an Imp, where he sees the terror that has transpired. Swearing to seek revenge for his slain buddies, he sets out to rip and tear as many demons as possible, even if it results in him being taken down with them.
Plutonia's story is set after the catastrophic invasion of Earth, with the US government taking measures to ensure no such incident would occur again. The old UAC was refounded under completely new management (what with the previous owners being all deceased this wasn't much of a problem) and given a new assignment: research tools and technologies that would prevent a resurgence from Hell. UAC's scientists began work on quantum acceleration devices, machines intended to close interdimensional gateways from a safe distance. The experiments would be carried out in a secret research complex, with a stationed brigade of marines on-site. Work was going well, but the creatures from the other side were drawn towards the new research, and a gate opened in the heart of the complex, with unnatural horrors pouring out. Miraculously, the quantum accelerator, even in its prototype stage performed superbly, the gate was closed quickly and the potential full-scale invasion halted. Research would continue, more boldly than before, confident in their device's ability to counter Hell's efforts. The next day, a ring of seven portals opened and an even greater battalion of demons arrived. For one hour the quantum accelerators managed to close six of the gates, but Hell's army had grown too numerous and too strong to stop now. The marines were cut down where they stood and the complex was overrun. The final gate of Hell remained open, manned and guarded by a 'Gatekeeper'. The government, frantic that the quantum accelerator will be destroyed or used in some alien fashion against us, ordered all marines available to the site at once. Of course, as fate would have it the reinforcements arrived too late to be of any use now as the demons have them outgunned and outnumbered. The Doomguy decides that he will have to enter the complex and stop this Gatekeeper, alone.
There isn't much to be said about Final DOOM visually as it aged just as well as the prior DOOM games, using the same engine and features. The new artwork is mostly good, I say mostly because some of Evilution's art looks pretty amateur even back when it was released. The new music for Evilution is mostly great though, with memorable tunes on par with DOOM 1 and 2.
Criticisms aren't as numerous as DOOM II's but like with D2 there are some not so great levels here and there, mainly the last half of Evilution which has some stinkers in what's overall mostly pretty great. Plutonia is subjective as a whole since while the mapping is largely solid, the gameplay it provides may not be everyone's cup of tea, and you will grow to hate DOOM II monsters like the chaingunner, Revenant and Arch-vile more-so than you did in DOOM II. Evilution's MAP31 also has a missing yellow key in single player that prevents you from completing it without an official patch.
Other than that you have two very good DOOM II games in one, trumping most of what was on offer in DOOM II itself. Highly recommended to diehard fans of the originals, so grab some pizza and a couple sodie pops and get to blasting some demons!

Game is truely incredible. I can't count just how many hours I played this masterpice with my friends. Allow me to go over some of the positives and negatives.
Pros:
Incredible class balance. For an early access game I had assumed that there would be massive imbalances between the 3 classes, however I found it to be flawless in execution. The Racoon with his burst fire pulse rifle was able to cause accurate and swift death to those afar. The Rabbit with her trusty wrench, swift speed and doublejump (a mechanic I find to be incredible in these kinds of games) is able to bludgeon and evade the incoming projectiles of her enemies. Lastly we have the bear, a true BRUTE of the gaming world. With his gattling gun and incredibly large health pool (a whopping 8!) you are able to lay waste to any Animal that dare stand in your way. Yet despite all of those differences, I never felt as though I was at a disadvantage. Skill plays a very bit part in playing your class effectivly.
The maps. WOW THE MAPS. Never in a multiplayer game have I seen such variety in the maps you play on. From a desert to a jungle, you'll never get bored as every map brings a very welcoming breath of fresh air.
The cosmetics. Now I know what you may be thinking. "Oh no is this just another TF2 clone?" And to that I say NO! Its enough of a system to allow you to look different compared to your fellow players, but not overboard in the sense that it feels overwhelming to a new player as they are unable to identify the classes.
Cons:
No game is without its flaws, however this is not a game, THIS IS A WORK OF ART. FLAWLESS 10/10

A huge and incredible jump following the success of Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines - And still looks just as exceptional
We see a welcome return of much that made the first game amazing: A true David & Goliath situation where, using your wits and the skills of a handful of commandos, you must work your way through heavily-guarded encampments, cities and even Colditz Castle itself - eliminating enemy soldiers as you attempt to neutralise key targets, rescue captives and capture the enigma machine. Gratefully all of the commandos from the first game return, charming as ever, including a few extra faces. This goes way beyond point-and-click stealth - The game requires a lot of patience, careful planning and studying of enemy movements. For 10 missions (not counting bonus ones), there's a huge amount to do - so expect to divulge many hours into this... it's a beast!
There's a ton of new features and abilities too - including completely revamped graphics and a superb soundtrack, the biggie is that you can now enter (and operate) within buildings - bringing huge levels of new scope to the missions. Each Commando also now has an 'inventory' and can carry / exchange any item (even if they cannot necessarily use them) and there's much more this time around in terms of raiding boxes / cabinets for useful items or pinching them off some guards
The missions bring with them an exceptional variety too. Amongst the sneak-and-kill we're used to, the first night mission forces you to play without any killing. Another leaves you with just one Commando having to set free the rest of your companions, held captive in several different houses. You also get a number of 'defence' scenarios where you have to place your guys and a handful of friendly soldiers to defend against an attack force. It's varied and brings refreshing new elements to an already formidable game
I have two small gripes though. The first is that, compared to the original, it's not as difficult where you no longer have garrisons. Previously, patrols would start swarming the place if you set off the alarm - here, the consequence is less fatal. That's not to say the guards are any less dangerous, but you can sometimes ragequit a situation with a few well-aimed shots or explosives if you get fed up. The 'rooms' tend not to interact with each other much, so it splits up the levels into smaller easier-to-manage chunks
The second... Spike the rat (and a castaway with a trumpet). Come on... a specially trained rat that does backflips to distract enemy soldiers? You can get infinite uses, send it through doors and it pretty much distracts nearly any group... Talk about overpowered. It removed a lot of the challenge - not to mention being quite ridiculous
Truth be told though, that's nit-picking. It's an otherwise exceptional title which successfully manages to retain much of what made the first so ground-breaking, whilst valiantly bringing in a cavalcade of new features and dynamics. Superb work

Nidhogg is a game that has been wowing the tournament crowds for a little while and now the rest of us get a chance to see what all the fuss is about. A one on one fencing the game, it is a pure test of skill against an opponent much in the same way Street Fighter or IK+ is.
On the service Nidhogg is a simple game. You have to get your fencer to run across the level and reach your opponents end zone. Here you are eaten by the big worm Nidhogg thing and pronounced the winner. In order to do this you need to repeatedly best your enemy as you progress. Starting in the middle of the level you need to kill your opponent and run, after a short time your opponent will respawn and you fight again. If your opponent kills you they can then run the opposite direction in an attempt to regain ground.
There are four levels to fight on which offer different environmental challenges and obstacles to use to your advantage. The castle has rooms and pits, so you can try and force your opponent to jump a pit and land on your sword or stay in a room so they can’t jump over you. The mine has a low ceiling which nullifies the ability to throw the sword or jump over your opponent, The clouds have disappearing ledges and the wilderness has platforms and long grass which allow for more manoeuvring and hiding.
The only stage that doesn’t really work is the cloud stage as it’s just a bit much for your eyes to deal with; it’s also a bit dull compared to the others. The Wilderness reminded us of a 2D version of Bushido Blade which is certainly no bad thing at all.
The fencer has a range of moves and techniques at their disposal. They can roll, cartwheel and jump which can be used to try and sneak past opponents if they have their sword at the wrong height. You can also perform a dive kick which knocks opponents over and makes them drop their sword. When an opponent is on the ground death can be dealt via a swift neck break.
With the sword in hand you can thrust at three different heights. This works in a rock, paper, scissors kind of way and also defends against things like dive kicks depending on where you have the sword set. If you wish you can also throw your sword, however, if it’s parried you then leave yourself open to almost certain death.
These basic moves form the crux of your sword fighting strategy and can be used in a number of different ways in order to best your opponent. If you are feeling super confident you can also disarm your opponent by moving your sword to the correct position at the exact right moment. Get this wrong though and you will find your own sword flying away.
Essentially, this is a two player game and anyone going into it expecting a lengthy single player component will be disappointed. Single player acts as an arcade mode where you continually square off against computer controlled opponents on the games four levels. It’s practice for multiplayer and while a nice distraction it will only last you half an hour or so.
The game uses a bright, 8-bit styled, colour palette to build its world. The colour scheme is garish but somehow seems to work. As a fencer is slain they explode into coloured dots and quickly begin to cover the arena in pixelated blood. It helps to highlight where the choke points are in each level as well as provide some visual flair.
There’s no denying that Nidhogg is an excellent two player experience. It provides the same sort of adrenaline rush as all the best one on one fighting games and the mechanics work really well. However, we can’t help but feel that more could have been done here. There is certainly scope for a roaring Prince of Persia or Defender of the Crown style single player adventure. Even something like taking the Blood Valley (it’s an old, bad, 8 bit game), template and adding the superior gameplay of Nidhogg could work. Another option would be to have more stages. Having just four levels does make the package feel a little sparse. You could have had stages requiring some basic climbing or less footholds etc.
Anyone who plays the game is going to have a great time and this is some of the best multiplayer action around at the minute. However, it could have been much more fleshed out in both single and multiplayer. The mechanics are great; we just hope there’s some further development of the other elements in the future as it could lead to something really special.

This Arcade-style dogfighting game is a nice change from the horde of twitch-shooters currently on the market. It's one of those easy-to-learn-hard-to-master games that seems simple at first, but over time you'll learn there is depth to the combat. With close to 30 planes, all with varying stats and play-styles, you'll find something you like. The single player places you in one of three theatres of war across the globe during WWII. The difficulty ranges from♥♥♥♥♥♥easy to OMFG-EJECT EJEC-(explosion). You'll fly sorties for the British and the Americans fighting against Germany and Japan, all while utilizing various frames: fighter, bomber, and special role planes. Each with there own unique weapons. Frames are unlocked by perfoming  campaing missions or playing multiplayer. The weapon and plane specifications could use an EXPLINATION, however. I'm not sure what some of these symbols mean, but I'm sure there is a wiki on it somewhere. Multi-player is fun and has several modes: capture the flag, defend the base, deathmatch, team deathmatch, last-man-standing, survival (horde, you and team versus NPCs) and even a free-flight mode for the achievment horses to mingle! In a market thourghly saturated with hyper-violent, grim and sexual content, this game is a breathe of fresh air. I would feel comfortable letting my kids play this game.
Final verdict: this game is good, not great, but with patching it has the potential for excellence. View my livestream at twitch for my first sortie with this game

This game is if Oceans 11 only had a single good guy, who's also an expert hardware hacker, and had boots that allowed him to jump like Superman, and a stealth skill-set akin to Batman.
An absolutely fantastic game.
The one thing I will warn anyone looking at this game about is the relatively short length of the campaign.
However.
I said,
I've now played roughly 7 hours as of this review, and beaten the campaign twice.
And I'm having an absolute blast playing through it a third time.
Why?
Because the game is an absolutely amazing sandbox, that's why.
The AI is extremely well written and you can make them do all kinds of stuff by manipulating the environment.
And I don't mean in the "throw a rock to distract a guard" kind of way. I mean in the "call an elevator to the same floor from behind the floor so that the guard will turn and look at who might be coming out of the elevator that just arrived on his floor, giving you a chance to open the door with the re-wired lighswitch to then hack a computer to find vital information in order to save an innocent person's life" kind of way.
Yes, the story is short, but it's well written, the characters are fleshed out, and no one is quite who they seem to be.
The level design is superb, encouraging multiple approaches to every situation.
Violence is optional.
The soundtrack... wait, is this the first time I'm mentioning the soundtrack?
Jesus, the soundtrack is fantastic. A noir jazz masterpiece, with spot-on electronic composition. The music alone is worth the asking price.
The controls are concise and tight.
The level editor that the game has is excellent. I only wish you could change the shape of certain items, rather than having to build with a set of pre-determined building blocks. However, you can still build almost anything you can imagine. And if you don't feel like building, there is full steam workshop integration.
I absolutely adore this game.
To anyone who liked stealth games, this will be an absolutely enjoyable experience.

A divine voice from
bellows that you "MUST BUILD A BOAT". You must also search the world over for 1 of each monster worth saving, allowing them to board your boat and subsequently reap the benefits from their quirky talents. You’re further required to constantly upgrade your own weapons, shield defence and spell power as you venture the world’s sinister dungeons looking for coinage and monsters worth recruiting. Hence after many significant 3 match battles you will eventually build up your boat from a dinghy to a titanic leisure cruiser.
The objective is to 3 match the necessary tiles in accordance to the obstacles present as your character runs through each dungeon. Each monster you face will require you to match up sword, staff and shield tiles, whereas treasure chests stumbled upon will require you to match up a series of key tiles depending how many locks are on each treasure chest.
The game is a sequel to '10000000' and follows roughly the same premise. Unlike other games which have an intricate woven story encouraging a gamer to push forward, instead the only motivation here is simply the next upgrade to be made.
For achievement hunters there are two achievements which will undoubtedly give you some grief. One requires you to do an 800m run on the last level 'The Gallery'. To complete this I strongly suggest at the end of your first completion of the game to drink a potion that entitles you to more staffs and maybe drink a potion that lowers the danger level somewhat. The second difficult achievement requires you to play the game two more times upgrading the difficulty of the entire game both times.
The game with its wild shenanigans was rather fun to play for the majority, it tested mainly just hand and eye co-ordination and the occasional anger management issues as I held a glass of water precariously over my keyboard and shouted fruitful expressions of displeasure at the 8 bit monsters bouncing up and down my boat like vegetative lemmings.
In final, a cheap game with a catchy soundtrack, which entertained me with the odd chuckle and smirk here and there. It definitely impressed me enough to want to look at all the rest of their games in future. Surprisingly gripping.
The rules are a bit different from the TCG for quicker play (smaller decks, smaller initial hand, lower lifepoints, smaller board space, no Main Phase 2 after combat), and characters can equip a special skill to their deck.
There's a large collection of cards already, representing many different archetypes.
The game also features plenty of AI combat (including a decent auto-duel that can play a large amount of deck archetypes surprisingly well) and a Duel School that not only teaches basic concepts, but later on also showcases different deck types.
Another important plus is that you can use the same save game for Steam and Android, the save is kept in Konami Cloud.
Still suffers from the basic issue that Yu-Gi-Oh! always had regarding having many cards that are flat out useless no matter how you look at them, but the variety of useful cards and playable archetypes is not that bad.
I think my main complain would actually be that the 20 cards deck size minimum is too small, making decks way too consistent. I feel like 25 or 30 minimum would be better. On the other hand, it does make mill decks a lot more viable, so I guess there's that.

So, Hex.
Here's a game that just can't decide what it wants to be.
They marketed heavily as an "MMO" yet there is no functionality at all for any sort of multiplayer interaction in the PvE. Amazingly, Hearthstone has even done a better job in that regard with the occasional "Co-op Brawls".
In fact - on the topic of Hearthstone and PvE - where the Hearthstone "Adventures" have often contained some creative encounters with quality card rewards, Hex PvE encounters in AZ1 tend to be quite bland and largely rely on frustrating the player in some way, while offering almost nothing in terms of value in the rewards.
Which brings me to the second part of, "Hex doesn't know what it wants to be". It's labeled as a "F2P" game - and technically yes, you can download the game and log in for free. You can even play through the PvE campaign (which has not been updated or expanded upon for 3 years now?) for free. However, beyond that, if you want to play the actual TCG part against other players, the game uses a payment system that's almost identical to Magic Online. (Albeit cheaper per-pack)
Now, experienced players will probably read this and jump in to ask, "But Bovinity, what about grinding for gold?"
Yes, you can grind in the Frost Ring Arena for gold which you can then trade to other players for their Platinum which you can then use to buy packs. And this is entirely PvE, you won't even be playing against other players. Just the same AI over and over again. If you're an experienced player with an already-refined (read: paid for) deck, you can grind and get about $1/hour out of the Arena.
Yes, $1/hour for an experienced player with an already-good deck. In other words, a new player is likely to get a better return on your time walking on the side of the road and picking up cans to turn in. With the added bonus that you won't utterly hate the game afterwards, which enough Frost Ring Arena grinding will indeed cause you to do.
Now, what about the software itself? Well, the Hex playing boards are certainly prettier than anything in Magic Online right now at least. The interface overall is much prettier. I don't think that's reason enough to play one game over another, but if that's what you're looking for, then Hex is a good choice for you. The tradeoff is that the interface is horribly laggy. Using the Auction House is a painful experience more often than not, every click can take seconds to process.
On to the game itself!
So Hex wasn't sued by Magic for no reason. The game is extremely similar in many of the core play mechanics. Mostly the same play phases, card interactions and so on exist here. If you enjoy Magic, you'll probably like Hex. If you hate Magic, there's no reason to waste your time in Hex, simply stated.
This brings me to another one of Hex's big marketing points: That they're a purely digital game, while Magic Online is still tied to the paper cards, and therefore Hex is capable of a lot more. This is true, but there's a problem: The design team of Hex just hasn't leveraged it well at all. Many of the mechanics just aren't compelling at all. For example:
Random Effects on cards? No, I don't find that to be a compelling use of the format.
Cards "remembering" buffs placed on them if they're removed/bounced/etc? That's nice, but again - not really a truly compelling use of the format. I don't know that any players thought to themselves, "Gosh, I sure wish Magic did that!"
Prophecy? It's ok. Similar effects could indeed exist in a game like Magic, albeit not in the same way. In fact, most all Prophecy effects are just familiar card effects. (+1/+1 to a creature, Fork on a spell)
I think the only truly interesting concept I've seen the designers use in the format are cards with "hidden" tokens.
In fact, I truly believe that the design team is a big factor in holding Hex back right now. They seem incapable of truly leveraging the digital format, their PvE encounters are bland and uninteresting, and they even seen to be unable to produce cards/effects that encourage anything but the same old Rush and/or Burn styles of play. (If you're a casual follower of Hex, what major decks have you heard of? Yotul and McBombus? No great shock there.)
The upcoming rotating out of all existing Characters and Gems is probably the most blatant, "We have no idea how to fix what we've done, lets just burn it all." move that I've ever seen from a card game. Even with that move, the upcoming 5th set seems to still be full of cards that just aren't very interesting unless you want the same kind of pure burn/rush/tempo style play that Hearthstone offers.
So the bottom line - and the thing that most people probably ask themselves when looking at the variety of card games out there now - is the question, "Why should I pick Hex?" and the answer is simply that there's no good answer.
If you're looking for a deep, complex strategy card game there's simply no good reason to not go with Magic: the Gathering right now. If a clean interface, occasional PvE content, and a more honest F2P system are what you're looking for, there's little reason to not simply play Hearthstone.
If you're looking for something in between, then maybe one day Hex will be what you're looking for, and maybe supporting it today will help it become that game. Right now, it just hasn't met its goals.

I originally got this game in a bundle, and was intending to trade it away because I didn't want it in my backlog. On a random whim, I decided to try it as a filler game, and was very surprised with the quality of what I played.
If you like fairly casual, side-scrolling action, and pump-you-up music, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are quite good - the detail in the environment and characters is well-done, and the art-style pops out nicely. The music is very good if you don't mind rock-style - the cutscenes pump you up, and the story is decent (and comical at times).
The controls are very basic and easy to pick up. The tutorials are quick and helpful, instructing you on new game mechanics as they are introduced. The learning curve is minimal, however, the most difficult part of the game is probably timing your attacks, as you can get swarmed from both the left and right sides at any time. Because you (and your enemies) can air juggle with attacks (popping a character up and stun-locking them with bullet fire), if you let even a single enemy get a shot on you, you can quickly find yourself in a dangerous situation. Choosing both the appropriate weapon and timing your attacks will ensure your survival.
Gameplay is very linear, however, there are parts where you are required to backtrack a bit. Many of the "puzzles" require you to collect various colored keycards and/or push and pull crates to allow you to reach higher ledges. There are collectibles in the form of signs that you can reach for extra achievements - some of which take extra effort and intuition to find.
Some of the weapons you will find as you progress include a submachine gun and a shotgun. The submachine gun is fantastic for juggling opponents, but does very little damage. While the shotgun is deadly at close range, it is an ammo-eating monster, and can cause you to get overwhelmed if you are attack from the opposite side (as its bullets cannot reach an enemy on the opposite end of the screen). Health and ammo crates are usually common throughout the level, and enemies seem to always drop a small amount of ammo. Ammunition is shared among all weapons, and you do not have to reload, ensuring that action is constant and rapid.
Later, you unlock a
Sometimes, I use this weapon just for fun, and to watch the same script over and over again.
Overall, the game can be a lot of mindless fun, will be enjoyed by 2D-platformer enthusiasts. A good game for casual, time-filling gameplay.

This is the first dungeon crawler that I have finished. I am playing Legend of Grimrock at the same time, though, so I have something to compare it to.
The good:
- The progression was OK. It really didn't start to feel like a chore, although some levels did start to get old.
- The atmospheric change from beginning to end was well done for a small team.
- The balance was good. Each character type and set of weapons felt satisfying.
- The art and aesthetic was well crafted.
- The story was interesting to piece together from the various notes and recordings.
- The skills were decent. No matter what you put points into, as long as you picked your skills and stuck with them, you cant really screw yourself over. (I would avoid picking more than 3-4, however).
- There were a decent number of secrets to find on each level.
- Enemy design, difficulty and diversity were pretty good.
The bad:
- Secrets contained story elements, and you had to really work to find some of them. I missed some of the story because I didnt find all of the secrets.
- The voice work was just terrible (probably due to the writing, which was also sketchy). Forgivable, as its understandable for a super small dev team, but terrible. I am unsure if there are other language versions, maybe this was a translated version. If so, that could be why.
- As some others say, the story fell a bit flat. The atmosphere and back-story were pretty well crafted. If you ignore the voice work and writing, it was obvious that this was a labor of love from a small team. There were some obvious questions left unanswered, so make of that what you will. I won't say that I was disappointed, just expecting a bit more at the end.
Solid game. I recommend it if you like or are interested in the genre. Avoid it if you typically are bothered by breaks in immersion, unanswered questions, etc.

Well I think I've put in enough hours on this game to write a review.  The mixed reviews seem to range from the absurd to some valid points.  Development was slow for awhile, mostly due to a lawsuit with a company that made the biggest tcg ever.  I will say I started playing Magic during Beta in my youth and have a long history with card games and video games.
I am one of the people that did almost entirely free to play for the bulk of my play, making a competetive budget deck from pve grinding was not too difficult or too easy, it was a rewarding experience and I learned a lot about the game, trading, and community.
The Good:
-A F2P model that works, but suplementing it with a cash infusion is certianly advantageous.  Even with a 20 dollar purchase of in game currency you can easily make more either through trading or winning competitions.
-A multitude of playstyles.
You can do the campaign with multiple characters, which is not so difficult, but can be far more complex when you tune and try to find interesting combos or increase your speed to the best possible.
A competitive constructed ladder for when you gain some cards to make competitive decks, some of which can be made without using any expensive cards.
Draft for the more experienced players, Evo tournament for the new players (a great way to learn more cards and gain cards witha minimal buy in, also all buy-in can be accumulated without paying cash)
Free tournaments held by community pages (most notably FiveShards) which require no buy-ins and offer great prizes, currently there are two of these that occur weekly, twice each day at different times to accomodate all schedules.
- A far deeper experience than most ccg/tcgs on the market, think more like magic, much less like Hearthstone.  With this being said it is far easier to jump into than magic both economically and the learning curve.  I feel my understanding of the nuances of the game has increased at just the right amount as I continue playing.
-PVE events that can be very profitable even to those that have minimal cards, very good way to earn currency without spending money
-The use of the digital format to do things physical card games cannot is way ahead of any other existing one.
-Lastly a great community, I recommend finding a guild even though there is not a system in the game for them.
Cons-
-The auction house.  The fact it exists is a pro, the UI and system are the con.  Not easy to check current prices and sell cards at same time without going between windows which makes the experience very pain staking
-The lack of new and challenging PvE content which was promised, although some spoilers have been made available and it appears with the lawsuit ending things are progressing quickly.
-The announcements of new additions can be vague or late, it does seem they are learning from this situation though.
-The chat/friends ui coudl be greatly improved.  included in this is the aforementioned lack of a guild system.  Although with outside apps it is not hard to keep a guild cohesive.
Conclusion:  Although I listed quite a few cons, most are simply wishlist items.  The game simply is fun, easy to learn but difficult to master, and f2p is more than possible if you find community articles and writeups.
8.5/10 simply because it can be improved, but it is the best game of its kind on the market currently and I intend to continue playing as long as these things all remain true.

This game seems to have fun combat and platforming until you get stunlocked a million times. How could anyone say this game was designed so well? The jumping "puzzles" are overly precise and not really based on skill, seeing as I seem to get a different jump height every time I walljump. Plus, the wall spikes and such have massive hitboxes. The enemies will even stunlock you midair while platforming with ranged attacks, usually offscreen or too far away to hit. The bosses can go from super hard to super easy in a heartbeat, from one to the next. The Yeti is a prime example of that. Enemies are recycled CONSTANTLY. I don't seem to be doing anymore damage than before after leveling strength, or upgrading a weapon. The skill trees have some really lame filler skills that you have to buy or else you can't get the better stuff. A bunch of somewhat interesting characters are introduced, and then discarded from any importance immediately. You can miss some items because an area is blocked off. Platforming is not very fluid because a lot of it is based on grabbing ledges (Why is this a problem, you may ask? Sometimes your character will stand completely still for no reason during combat (not stunned, possibly a glitch). The controls with a controller AND on keyboard are awful. Sometimes the character will swing more times than you press the button. Speaking of buttons, the hitbox for ground pound buttons doesn't even cover the whole button. Everything is a lame jumping puzzle and you end up having to fall down 20 times to get all the chests that they put under them. Sometimes these chests are anti-climactic, getting Cloth or something. aMAZE (or αMAZE, if you go by the store image) feels like someone’s trial project at coding collision detection on a 2D plane, and, frankly, I wouldn’t be surprised if that is actually the case. The 50 available mazes vary a lot in quality. The first 10 are a joke, but the other 40 offer a few nice ones, where sometimes the intended route is not as obvious as in most cases.
The result is some strange mix. On one hand, the game is cheap and offers simple fun. On the other hand, the low-resolution stock images, high-contrast backgrounds, and bland music point more towards some freebie Flash game. If you do not mind spending a dollar for an hour of simple entertainment, then, by all means, go for it. Just do not expect anything more than what you see on the store images.

VAPORUM a excellent high mileage hack and slash dungeon crawler with quality production values.
Atmosphere is thick and creepy with eerie fog and moody lighting in a metal forged deathscape pulsing with industrial strength inhumanity as one gets a sense of dread as if in some demonic jail forever damned. Puzzles so far have been easy to solve especially for those who have played the likes of DUNGEON MASTER and EYE OF THE BEHOLDER in the 1990s. Tool tips are very helpful and done well never getting in the way as they teach the player the inner workings of the game mechanics.
Audio is rich with cold mechanical precision with the sounds of steam pipes, clanging mettalic doors, the fear inducing foot steps of robotic and non-robotic hostile entities stalking about in the shadows.
Combat is surprisingly smooth and free form creating a situation where strategy and timing as one dodges, make sudden turns and play catch me if you can with dungeon horrors is quite rewarding. Damage taken to one's armor from such encounters can be repaired with kits found in different areas of dungeon floors. Experience is also gained when enough of certain resources gathered from combat are gathered where the player can put the points into many skill ranges from stealth to combat oriented tank characters.
Enemies look fabulous with a mixture of clockwork machine visuals and living fleshy monstrousities from some HP Lovecraft story. Their attacks are graphically impressive giving a sense of murderous power from huge snapping insectoid mandibles to lightning discharging mechanisms. Animations are full of life and a joyful sight to see alongside the excellent creature models.
There is alot of spoken dialogue by the player character as well as from recordings that are found in many places which is quite welcomed to hear another human's voice in this dark vortex of pure isolation.
VAPORUM a place outside. A reality disconnected from life in the same way the dead are from the living. Dare you traverse into this iron mausoleum of misery where terror awaits to tear your soul asunder?

FINAL DOOM is an official commercial release of two community created mega-WADS for DOOM II. Each of the WADS (entitled "TNT Evilution" and "The Plutonia Experiment" respectively) consist of 30 regular levels, and two secrets levels.
"TNT Evilution" boasts a mostly original soundtrack, fantastic new artwork, and incredibly clever level design. While it is by far the easier of the two WADS, it more than makes up for it in character.
"The Plutonia Experiment" also has some good level design, but its strength lies in its difficulty. Even the most seasoned DOOM players will be hard-pressed to complete this WAD without making liberal use of the save feature.
***IMPORTANT NOTE*** As with all Steam releases of the original DOOM games, the version provided is the god-awful DOSBox emulation. If you intend on buying and playing FINAL DOOM, or any other original DOOM title from Steam, I highly recommend looking into using a source port like "gzdoom".

Old fan of dungeon crawlers here, still holding Dungeon Master as an all-time favorite and used to games like Eye of the Beholder, Lands of Lore, Black Crypt, Captive and more recently the two Grimrock. I hesitated a long time for Vaporum: recommend or not? And despite my recommendation, I'm still on the fence. Here is why: on one hand, the production is surprisingly solid and at times impressive. On the other hand, the game falls in the traps that the best titles in the genre managed to avoid. And it repeats its errors, again and again... until you feel like playing something else entirely.
My first big complain would be that the game insists really heavily on putting you in a small closed room and overwhelming you with enemies. Getting stuck between 3+ enemies, while some of them have a very large AoD means you are bound to sustain a lot of damage and reload often. It's good a couple of times, but repeat this too often and it's just a drag. You see, dungeon crawlers are usually all about thinking and avoiding this kind of situation. Here it is mandatory, to some extent like in the last Doom game. But it's a dungeon crawler, not a fast-paced FPS.
My second big complain is about the game's mechanics. While some enemies are organic and others mechanical, you will have to adapt your weapon to the enemy in front of you. And you also have firearms for long distance engagements. So far, so good. However, you only have two quick weapon setups to switch between. Which means you will have to manually go in your inventory and change weapons very often. In games like Captive it is not an issue because you control 4 robots and can have melee characters and shooting (or spell-casting in other games) heroes with other specializations. Here, you only have one guy who has to multitask constantly in combat. Or just give up entirely on shooting, because a firearm-only character will lead you nowhere here (see issue #1).
If you can put up with such frustrating issues, Vaporum has a lot to offer. It is best defined as a Grimrock 1 in a Bioshock-ish setting. It is moody, darkly beautiful and especially dangerous. So much so that the difficulty (already from level 2-3) is closer to Chaos Strikes Back than its predecessor Dungeon Master. The puzzles are challenging, especially the timed ones, but they remain good overall. It is nowhere as good as a Grimrock 2 but if you like the genre you should give the game a try, and refund it if it frustrates you more than it should.

Not a member of top-tier RTS games, but a sincere attempt to bring Warhammer 40K to the genre.
The Dawn of War series struggles from one thing more than anything else. It's not Command and Conquer and it's not Starcraft.

I found the campaign to be fine from a story standpoint, but often repetitive and a bit boring when it came to actual game play.
The multiplayer mode was, oddly, lacking some level of immersion. The scale of the battles was quite underwhelming and while the resource acquisition was fine, the objectives were not enough to make up for an experience that was just not very... 40Kish.
I can recommend this game for what it is, a 40K RTS. If you are seeking some RTS experience that immerses you for hours and really give you a new take on the genre, this really isn't the game you are looking for.

It's really hard to explain the game better than it was made in the "about this game" store section. The trailer video is also helping.
Run the line from left to right, match 3 tiles in a row, complete some quests on the way. Just like its predecessor, "10 000 000" game, "You must build a boat" is a really simple to start causal-style project, that gets harder and harder with every level. And that is the main downside of the game: even with all upgrades farmed, with the top blessings for your run, you're still too hard into luck and not in the skill. I've finished 10 000 000 just out of pure luck, and I've stopped somewhere in the Gallery level, trying to catch the east wind here, in the "YMBaB". It's getting annoying after a while, so I understand some negative votes on the game...
But, as player who have seen much stuff, I really can't call this game bad. No-no-no, in fact, it's good and enjoying - especially if you like somewhat original approach on the evergreen field of casual "match-3-in-a-row" games. "You must build a boat" is fun. It's good, and I can recommend it almost to everyone - especially with a discount or a bundle purchase. It's definetely worth some time and money of yours... If you don't take games too serious and only want to spend your coffie-brake time in some action. Don't expect to beat the game just as easy as you started it, however.
My mark is 6.5/10. Good for some time when you simply can't play some AAA-size. However, if you're choosing a gift for some really casual player (like your Ma, or maybe GrandPa) - I'd go with the more refined "10 000 000". Here, in the "YMBaB", there is too many upgrading which isn't doing you any good. Too much grinding and less actual fun gameplay. Which is sad. But still tolarable, still worth a try.

You Must Build A Boat is all about random numbers and questionable game design; the kinda thing you'd usually see for free on mobile with a banner ad at the bottom.
To put it bluntly, the game is frequently just not very much fun. Everything in the game is essentially up to chance. The developers even seemingly rolled the dice and went with "indie casual", "pixel art", "match-3 puzzle", and "roguelike."
Beneath all the fluff, you're really only playing a strange sort of tile matching game. You watch as your hero passively runs along a path at the top of the screen, and tiles (semi)randomly appear on a playfield at the bottom. As he proceeds along the path, he encounters obstacles such as monsters, chests, and traps. Your job is to match 3+ tiles by dragging any column horizontally or vertically. Successfully matching tiles does damage to monsters, unlocks chests, casts spells, etc.
The game is technically impossible to lose, though you don't always win. Each play board has a certain objective; completing that objective earns resources and access to the next level. Failure yields a consolation prize and a retry. You can opt to undertake multiple objectives at once, but each additional objective adds another difficulty handicap.  It's a little awkward, especially thanks to the mostly randomized playfield. Sometimes matches simply cannot happen.
While somewhat unique, this approach makes any given playthrough totally unpredictable, especially if RNGesus is not on your side. You can curry his favor by grinding for resources with which to upgrade your tiles, making them a few percent better at a time. Keep trying, and eventually you'll get lucky. With some objectives, that's literally the ONLY way you'll get anywhere. With no negative consequences except having to try again, randomly clicking seems to yield the same (or better) results than careful concentration.
Despite the title, you don't ever actually "build a boat." The boat just gets bigger as you progress through the game. You attract NPCs and buy crew members in a set order, though they don't do anything except add a few more percentage perks to your tile matching stats. The grinding can get tiresome if you don't actually enjoy the matching game itself, since everything else is just window dressing.
The most intentionally irritating aspect of the game is the needlessly excessive cookie clicking. When you purchase an upgrade or unlock a treasure box at the end of the level, you are REQUIRED to spam the mouse button anywhere from 20~40 times to open the chest or activate the upgrade. It's super annoying, and I can't imagine WHY they thought it was a good idea.

Wild Warfare has been abandoned and not updated for around 2 years now, and as it stands the game is weak and only fun for a few matches. I used to love this game but as I've played higher calibre shooters like TF2 and CS:GO I have realised it really isn't that great. There are three classes, two of which move a lot too slow to keep your interest and the weapon models are WAY too large. There are a few game modes and maps and they aren't very well designed. The characters themselves are rather cute looking (a bear a rabbit and a raccoon) and can be customisable with items that appear in crates. I rather like the crate system in this game, much more in favour of this one than say something like Counter Strike. You do not pay for keys in Wild Warfare and they come in rather plentiful supply. You level up quickly and killing a lot of other mammals with plasma guns can be quite satisfying. The gunplay its self is not great, the guns shoot some type of plasma projectile instead of bullets and is not exactly fun, the game would definitley benefit from faster projectiles. It is weird how in this game instead of having say 100HP, in this game you only have 3-8 hit points, sometimes it seems you hit them but they take no damage. In some game modes (like CTF) you have mechs that you can drive and shoot in, they are quite overpowered and take a lot of hits to take down, sometimes these mechs get stuck in some areas of the map. The game can be fun but it is not something you will play for hours on end due to the underwhelming quality. But it's cute right?

Perhaps DFUW's lower fps and constant dc's may be due to *bugs with the Steam Overlay meshing with DFUW, I know I was affected by the endless screen shots bug and needed to turn off Steams Overlay, to get to playing a bit smoother. I also deleted all 1378 screen shots!  The loading screens were a bit...long, and I found out early on that I could not simply "ALT-TAB" out during loading screens to desktop without crashing the Program fully.
I had a chance to try out spell caster, skirmisher and settled on the hack n slash nature of the warrior class, for the most part the tutorial was helpful, until I crafted too many items and no longer had the starting gold to complete making a Saddle, and thus breaking my Tutorial, forcing me to find an alternative way to continue.  On a side note I was not able to actually craft any items with my Skirmisher class, I had tried re-logging which I disliked due to the wait times and no ALT-TABing, only to finally find out in the Chat channel that it is a known Bug that you may not craft whilst you have a shield equipped...
A helpful player /W Whispered me from my query's in the chat channel, and offered to give me the gold I needed to complete the tutorial, I declined as I would like to know how to make in game currency and get out of the situation on my own...  the suggestion was to harvest ore from metal deposits in the safe zones, and sell that...
... Thus I went through the new player city mining metal ore deposits until my pickaxe broke!  So I went to the general store, to buy a new one, and double clicked a few times, before I realized I was buying pick axes per double click it was too late, at 5 gold each, I now had 2 new pick axes and 1 gold.  I took my Iron Ore and Inferior bits off to the Smithy, I was able to craft once - as the crafting costs 1 gold per craft.   At this point I felt the only way to make money now would be to sell it on the Market and get what I could...  Unfortunately I did not have enough in game money to use the market left, and this left me to offer a sale via Trade Chat.  I checked market prices for Iron ore at 22g per unit that day, I offered a Trade of 7 Iron ore for 100g, I asked in main chat and was told to bother the people about trades in Trade chat, after re-posting several times over 40 minutes, a player whispered and offered to help me out, they did not want my Iron ore, or anything else, they game me 2,000 gold some advice and told me to pay it forward.
I enjoyed the market system quite a bit once I had some money to play with...   Not having items sent to a mail box and or money was a real treat!
The game play reminded me of early console "Bards' Tale" *STYLE* Games, with accuracy of attacks being counted for where you swing your weapon, and/or if you actually hit your target with a projectile, be it magical or otherwise.  Thus the PVP was no big thing for me either, perhaps my years of Project Entropia playing, makes me think less of DFUW, play style....  there are countless games out there not just the ones on steam, and not just in the America's!  There are non-English mmo's that would blow your socks off, that you may never realize exist.
I explored out of the safe zones, I died out of the safe zones, I PVE'd and PVP'd, I worked with a group to farm prowess, both acting as support and skinning team, I had an enjoyable experience in that style of team play, of which I have had in most other games, thus team play is what I want out of any mmo....  I joined a clan.  I like to do some solo PVE as it gives me a chance to see the world and learn first hand knowledge, I had my request in to join, and went with the farming group even though I was still solo, after 40 minutes I had gained +400 Prow and the system was shutting down for nightly 1 hour maintenance. Our group disbanded... a day later my application was accepted, yet I could not get the attention of anyone in the alliance to tell me how or if I could port directly to the main clan city... in the end I took everything off my character, except the starting weaponry you are forced to keep, and a skinners' knife (I chose to bring), and set out... great way to explore btw - the Green Shield soon was blinking and a 10 second Warning flashed on my screen and counted down... I passed mountain ranges, snowing passes, water falls and fields of blood... the red shield got up to the roman numeral V before I even got half way down the map, leaving a slug like trail of visible land behind me....  at one point another player rode up behind me on a silver bear... I had pressed "Num Lock" and just let my avatar run whilst I worked on my laptop... the player stopped then turned and rode off... I explored a few fields, some structures etc when I fancied a look around, it took nearly 2 hours to *run* to the clans property, and another 5+ minutes to get to the city, then I spent maybe 15 minutes trying to figure out how to get inside!!  I used markers in the city to note where the clan bank, mines, farms, timber lot etc were so I could find them easily.    Not having the ability to taxi from one place to another is a big drawback to me, only being able to be bound to 1 stone also was useless after binding myself to the clans stone, as the only way to get to a world wide market was in a major city, as the clan market was just for the clan!!!
In the end I spent easily 90% of all my time Gathering and hitting Mobs to gain the much needed supplies, armor, gold, prowess, to advance in the game, was it enough to get me to shell out $20.00 a month after exchange rate and taxes?  No.
Ending prowess 8.7k, ending gold 27k, lots of banked resources.
The real drawback for me was TIME INVESTED to ENJOYMENT EXPERIENCED. The scale is heavily weighted on the Time Investment part in this game, however if that makes you happy, go for it... I've invested thousands of hours and dollars of my life in game play, over ten's of years! There is another way to get "real life 3D team experiences".... that though requires you to put some clothes on, shoes too, and head outside, I know that sounds scary, but trust me it's worth every moment of it!

A huge world with a full loot mechanic and the ability to kill anyone and anything at any time outside of safe zones. Its basicly a giant sandbox meaning you can just start doing whatever you feel like from the start. You can start harvesting reasources or killing mobs. One thing to note is this game has no experience bar or levels but instead has a system that uses Prowess which basicly resembles experience but instead of traditional mmorpg games, prowess is used to increase everything from your mining speed, stats and basicly anything you can think of involving character progression. It takes about a week or so before you are ready to pvp. You have a few ways of fighting in this game as well, you can be a warrior that uses melee or a brawler that uses speed, agility and lighter armor than a warrior but who also uses daggers. Or an archer, elementalist or a primalist. Since they removed classes in this game you now have the ability to mix and mash any of these and more that you like so the one character restriction limit they enforce upon you doesn't really matter because of this. If your looking for a giant sandboxy hardcore themed mmo with full loot and have some friends to join you then this game is probably worth a shot with the $15 price tag. If you are someone who gets really attached to items or plans on going solo then your chances of enjoying this game are a bit lower since this game is heavily group oriented. This doesn't mean you can't play alone though it will just take longer to earn prowess, upgrade your character and you have the risk of being overwhelmed by groups of players. Its quite rare to find games like these and the only ones I have found in the past few years have been this and Mortal Online so everyone has limited options/

Coming from someone who was a big fan of Relic COH and Warhammer series, this is definitely way better.
Pro:
Amazing detail and realism. All ballistics are modelled physically. There is no life bar on tanks instead it depends of physics and penetration, any parts that are damaged will result different effect.
A lot of different tactics to try out.
Environments are very detailed and battlefield changes dynamically, building can be destoryed, wreckage block tank's path and create new cover etc. No two game played out the same way.
For me it's a pro, there's a lot of micro management down to the manually manage ammunition of each individual soldier and gas up vehicles manually. Some player might not like this though.
---
Con:
Graphics are functional, but nothing to write home about. Audio gets repetitive after a while, all units repeat the same lines to acknownlege your commands.
The game is very unforgiving, be prepared to save an reload a lot. Even the best tank can be one-shot killed if you are not careful. Sometime feels like a puzzle game where you are carefully removing enemies' defence one piece at a time. At the writing of this review only 8.4% of players completed the first mission on normal difficulty, so don't be shy to start out in easy difficulty.
No stories to speak of, just go from south part of the map to the north that's about it. If you want story you should try other MOW titles.
The game model the ballistic of every bullets, so you need a good CPU, instead of GPUs like other games. Even on my i7 3770 the game can slow down in very large battles. Not game breaking but you should be aware of this if you have older machines.
---
Conclusion, Hardest RTS I've ever played, period. It is so cruel... Anyone up to a real stiff challenge should try this. I'd give it 8/10.

2016.12.08 - I would like to update my below review I've done earlier, as AZII was released, and I returned to the game to check it out.
Positives : new PVE content is great, game balance seems a bit less ridicolous than earlier
Negatives : I can't believe that after all this time, they made 0 effort to make the game less bugged than before. In a few hours I encountered login problems, random crashes, some cards not working at all, valid decks shown as invalid with no explanation (but thankfully still playable). This is simply unacceptable for a released game.
------
I played a lot with the non-Steam version of the game. Since you can find info about the positive
aspects of the game in many reviews, I'll list below why I don't recommend the game.
- bad game balance, with no intent to change it.
- false advertising - features promised still not delivered after years
- major bugs could make the game hard to enjoy in some cases, and it's not only happening for new features/sets. Good example is Arena, where specific bugs were still present (and even reapered) after several patchs.
- PvE content is nice, but short, and have some intentionally unfun parts which can be passed with specific strategy and/or pure luck. Then it still won't be fun, but at least you win the match.
- very bad communication from the developers, which included in the time I played : providing no info on important details, late apologies for repeated delays, false promises etc. Also, the terribly outdated homepage deserves a special mention, since it has some information (for example about champions) which never covered the actual things in the game.
I don't want to mention smaller things, like specific bugs, or my own issues with the community.
The game has a lot of potential, and a few very nice ideas. Sadly, in this pace it will need at least another 2 years before (and if) I can recommend it.

It's okay. I like this game in theory. You don't see many maze games like this. And it works well with simple arrow key controls. Pressing two arrows at once though to try to roll around corners doesn't work well though. It just sort of spasms very slowly or goes the wrong direction.
I made it to the 2nd level of hard before I decided to move on. The first level of hard isn't any more difficult than anything in easy. Instead of there being more branching to wrong ways, the game pretends to increase difficulty by increasing the number of small moves you need to make. Instead of a straight line across half the screen, you navigate the same type of path but with up, left, down, right, up, left, down, right, up, left.... The amount of increased moves and longer, tighter paths make the maze take marginally longer, which creates a false sense of increased complexity.
For a game that is trying to be counter-strike it does alright, my only complaint really is that the loading times are too long and the games lag issue needs to be adressed.
