This game wasn't off to a good start in the opening cinematic, where there was 10 seconds of two unknown characters talking to each other. Except we couldn't hear a word either of them was saying, because the designers decided that playing their "badass" rock soundtrack over the image of two characters talking was more important than any actual context or storyline.
I mean, it's not like a game needs a story to be good. But if you're going to waste my time with two characters talking, at LEAST have them say something. Is this hard to understand? I don't think this would be hard to understand.
That's what I thought, anyway, until the second cinamatic, where characters DID communicate. They managed to say exactly nothing about anything, except that they're going to try to kill me. I don't really know why. I guess I was infiltrating their base?
Honestly, maybe they explained this in the first cinamatic. I skipped it because I didn't feel like watching two people talking without dialogue.
As far as the gameplay goes, you move forward and you shoot guys. Note I didn't say you have to aim, because you don't. And you don't have to move strategically -- forward is the only direction you have to move.
It takes like 10 bullets to kill an enemy. This is probably because the game would be way too short if it took one bullet to kill an enemy.  I couldn't say for sure, though, because in the 8 minutes I actually decided to play this game, I couldn't think of a single reason to keep going.
Maybe it gets good at some point. I figured my time was too valuable to waste time finding out.

aMAZE is a pretty short and simple maze game.
First of all, there is nothing hard about maze games, unless they stack you a super super super super big maze. aMAZE doesn't do that, so the game ends up being relatively relaxing. Right off the bat, I have to bring up this game is about 2 hours long.   Maybe 3-4 hours if you wish to get the achievements but there is little replay value aside.
That being said, this is one of the most memorable experiences on Steam if you enjoy a deep, detailed story with a host of interesting characters.  This is one of the most incredible examples of story telling I've seen in a game or even in recent decades in cinema.
Gameplay is mainly guiding the various characters through their stories.  You do have a lot of freedom to examine and admire the detail and beauty that the artists have crafted for this masterpiece.  You do not have any way to change the result so it's simply a linear story-telling narrative with one set path through each part of the story.
I definitely recommend this to anyone that enjoys an artful, heart-felt story with interesting characters.  It uses an eloquent, artistic and masterful presentation style like nothing I've ever seen before.  If you can set aside two hours to be taken away into this magical world of fairytale-like story telling, pick this up!  It's particularly recommended to play in one sitting if possible.

As with other DOOM ports on Steam, this one isn't much better either. So again, I have to post this:
Takes only a couple of minutes, but with this, you can choose a port of your liking (I like ZDoom) and run it with Steam overlay and screenshots enabled.
Now that *that's* out of the way, let's see what we have here.
This game is basically two large map packs for DOOM II, one called "The Plutonia Experiment" and the other "Evilution" (weren't the nineties great, lol). Both of them offer genuinely challenging levels with a few cool new tricks (e.g. I love how despite the limited verticality of the DOOM engine, they still manage to make "ladders" somehow), and if I had to choose between this and the Master Levels, I'd say this is a much more streamlined experience and it feels more like a DOOM "sequel"/spin-off and less like "here's 20+ maps we didn't put in the game". There were a few maps where I cursed the creator's apparent love (dare I say fetish) for spamming chaingunners (or, as I like to call them, "hitscanning f#%kheads"), but for the most part, these maps really bring out the essence of what DOOM is: learning enemies' attack patterns, prioritising who to take out first, choosing the right gun for the job, finding that friggin' keycard/skull key, the works. It's more of the same, really, but it's done well. Rip and tear!
Oh yeah. There are two secret levels (I'll give you a hint: the entrance is near the end of "The Twilight" map) that will KICK. YOUR. NADS. Seriously, I think that's A) the most time I've spent playing two DOOM maps and also B) the most fun I've had with two DOOM maps alone. It's hardcore, it's difficult, it's over-the-top, it's ridiculous, so yeah... it's DOOM alright.

Onechanbara Z2 Chaos is very, very good. The action is fast, your movesets are fun, it is somewhere south of Ninja Gaiden in terms of speed and action quality, I mean it, it is that good, except that absolutely none of your enemies pose any threat at all.
Onechanbara has been a budget series alongside, and I believe from the same makers of, EDF, and it really has come a long way since the PS2, Wii, 360 era. The protagonists have changed, the maudlin despairing tragedy around half-nekkid action girls killing zombies and killing each other have been replaced with slapstick comedy and half-nekkid girls killing zombies and just trash-talking each other. The combat got the biggest change, ditching the leveling system, ditching the musou nonsense, and really doing its level best to take a swing at the DMC/NG/Bayonetta-esque action fighter.
The levels aren't great, the bosses are all tanks that don't stagger at all, the human form bosses still fight like they did in the last games where you could block but all you can do now is dodge so they are kinda wonky, timing-based Cool Combos are still back (Time your button presses on your main attack combo to get faster speed, damage, etc.), and there are a dozen more little niggling things carried over from previous games that were never released in America.
But the end result is that this game has extremely good zombie slicing action and gives you a lot of opportunities to slice zombies, blast zombies everywhere, with four girls you can swap freely between or call them all in and swap mid-combo for crazy action... it is an absolute blast to play and far better than it has any right to be.

I give it a recommend but this is a 6 out of 10 type review.  The game is functional, it's cheesecake as all hell and it is the best Onichanbara game I've played to date.  However, it is HORRIBLY ported.  For example, when you exit to the main menu it closes the entire game and you have to start it again.  All I can say is whatever needed to be done to make it run on PC was done and literally NOTHING more.  You will need a controller (seriously, you should use one anyways but that's a bit of a faux pas, no?) since the keyboard layout is ... insane?  And as far as graphics options go ... there are none.  So either you can run the game or you can't.
Where the real points are lost is not there however, I would normally just gripe about it if the game was fine.  However, the gameplay is ... well, it's one of these games.  It tries, pretty successfully, to Devil May Cry it's Musou Warriors gameplay but the problem I have is that it's not that fun.  Damn you Onichambara!  The pieces are there but it can just be so frustrating.  The boss of Japan has you fighting a pair of legs that don't damage you, but keep running around so you can't damage THEM.  It's a fight that goes on SIGNFICIANTLY longer than necessary.  A lot of fights have this feeling, like they are just dragging on.  The story exists but isn't a driving force so you'll excuse me if repetetive arena battles don't drive it either.  I also have to say I don't care for the quad-fighter gameplay for a couple reasons.  Perhaps this is part of the charm but you are limited on stat-altering equips since they can only be equipped on one person, fine, but since you have to bring all four girls it either means each girl is kitted differently or you'll just choose to use one or two until forced to switch.  It doesn't help that two of them seem SIGNFICANTLY stronger than the other two.  It's just not satisfying to me, and in fact sort of drives me nuts.  The swapping for combos is cool sometimes but honestly I hated this about Warriors Orochi and Dragon Quest Heroes so while others may not mind, it annoys me a lot.
Of course the cheesecake is fine, the animation is pretty good and I'd be lying if I said it wasn't fun to either finally kill that annoying boss or just decimate some mook with a completely over-the-top and unecessary combo.  It's just the best parts of this game butt right up against what I feel are the worst and that drives me away.  So I give it a recommend even if just barely so.  It isn't 'broken' for me, it's completely playable.  It's just a niche experience that some will like more than others and your mileage may vary but during a sale you could easily do worse.

This game is a classic, and was the precursor to Deus Ex and System Shock 2. System Shock is a Cyberpunk Survival-Horror FPS with Adventure and RPG elements which places you in the role of a computer hacker aboard Citadel Station; a space station owned by the Trioptimum Corporation. Due to a deal with a corrupt executive, you have a military-grade neural interface which allows you to enter "cyberspace" - of course the installation of this device in your skull caused you to be placed in a coma for six months.
When you awake, everyone on board the station is dead or worse, thanks to an AI called SHODAN; SHODAN developed a god complex and is now planning on remaking humanity in her own image. You're the only person with a chance at stopping her.
The game is surprisingly atmospheric even with the dated soundtrack and graphics. SHODAN is a remarkably effective villain, and the gameplay is quite deep.
I recommend this game to anyone who likes FPS/RPG hybrids, horror games, or simply has an interest in legacy gaming.

You Must Build A Boat is a repetitive dungeon runner focused on matching tiles for attacks, skills, weapons and loot so the player can upgrade their boat and proceed to the next hub environment.
While the early game is enjoyable and provides speedy matching options with a barrage of ship upgrades, the late game flips this progression on its head and quickly becomes a slow progression where the player will be tasked with finding a sole match-3 on the board while juggling traps that require matches not available on your board. Thanks to the items that take up matching space, it becomes a deadly balancing game of playing safe with your current items while hoping future encounters work in your favor (rarely do they ever thanks to enemy resistances) or risking the next abysmal sole match-3 hidden somewhere on the board.
The game tries its best to cover this issue up by encouraging the player to re-run dungeons since you "never lose" and the game is made for "quick matching". Unfortunately, these are no more than excuses built into the game's bare dialogue by the developer in hopes to hide the abysmal matching system late game.
10000000 is the developer's previous game. Unfortunately, the predecessor outweighs this game when it comes to consistent gameplay and entertainment.
TL;DR
Get 10000000 instead. You Must Build A Boat is an early game trap that leads to mechanically broken experimentation from the developers that results in a terrible experience late game.

A friend recommended 10,000,000 to me, and I was really impressed. The gameplay was fun and straightforward, the "adventure" was simple if perhaps a bit unexceptional, and the music was delightful. So when they came out with a quasi-sequel to it in You Must Build A Boat, I was excited.
Having played it now...meh.
It's not a bad game. It calls on some of the fun features of the original, and the basic gameplay is pretty much the same. Match three tiles, accumulate points, fight monsters. It's more that everything *else* they put around the basic gameplay is just a little bit worse.
I get the idea behind the change to the item system, but putting them into the board makes it feel harder to make matches while you're sitting on a couple fireballs. There are more rooms where you can spend your accumulated resources, but that doesn't necessarily mean they're *better* (gambling room anyone?). And the designers added unskippable cutscenes...to an 8-bit game...with no real story. They also added a wholly unnecessary clicker-game for most of the unlocks in the game. Maybe some players find it fun, but to me it's just a nuisance.
The game, at its core, is very fun, because 10,000,000 was very fun. And the music is perhaps even better than 10,000,000. But I constantly found myself getting yanked out of my fun to deal with one of these annoying additions. As such, I simply can't recommend the game.

As the spiritual successor to 10,000,000, You Must Build A Boat is a match three-style puzzle game with RPG mechanics slapped onto it.  The goal of the game is, you guessed it, to build a boat to take you across the map that pops up between dungeons.  Its strengths and improvements over the previous title are immediately noticed, but its flaws become more apparent as the game progresses.
Lacking any real narrative, progression of your character and ship are the primary motivators of moving forward.  Each run nets you a handful of resources that you can use to upgrade your boat, your equipments, your spells, and so on.  This is the real strength of the game as there are significant increases to both the quantity and variety of upgrades available.  I found myself compelled to keep playing multiple times as an exciting upgrade always seem to be just around the corner.
Unfortunately, the greatest strength of You Must Build A Boat ultimately breaks down into its greatest weakness.  As you approach the late game, the exciting progression bogs down into a crawl and the monotony sets in.  It's not at all rare to do the same run of a dungeon a dozen or more times hoping for the randomly generated order of monsters, traps, and treasure to be on your side.  The fact that you've now also run out of available upgrades but have managed to amass a wealth of resources only hastens the encroaching boredom.
As negative as some of that may have sounded, I really did have fun throughout the majority of this game.  If you played 10,000,000 and enjoyed it, this one is definitely worth picking up and spending a few hours on.  If you're into puzzle-RPGs, I'd recommend the title as well as it's a solid game for a price that certainly isn't going to break the bank.  For everyone else, I would definitely suggest doing some research on the game to see if it's really your cup of tea.

It's been over 3 years now, and many of the features that people like myself backed this game for are still no where in sight.
Those features you think of for online RPGs, things like guilds, raids, proper levelling content, etc. Yeah, none of those are in yet. The current PvE content can be completed in 4-6 hours with a good deck and it takes Hex more than 12 months to add the same amount of content again.
In short, by the time the PVE side of this game gets anywhere, some other company which actually knows something about developing computer games will have probably come along and done it better.
It basically leaves Hex as an ok PvP digital card game, without much to distinguish it from any of the dozens of others floating around on the market. If that's what you're after them maybe give Hex a go, but I still think you'd be better of going to Magic or Hearthstone or one of the other smaller games out there than sinking time and money into this game.

It's fun so long as you remain a filthy, casual scrublord like myself.  Game has a lot to offer without paying a penny, and the pay elements are fair priced and balanced so it's not entirely pay to win neither.  As it is right now, game does enough that you should get cards you want to play with by just playing or even opening the game from time to time.
PvP elements do suffer from the same ailments as its real life counterpart though with a very clear and distinct meta between 2-3 decks right now with no real sign of being adjusted for this format of the game..... but at the very least older sets of cards you saw on the show get their cards at the right time.  While Red-Eyes Black Dragon is more of a joke with the new releases it gets, in Duel Links, having gotten some key cards in a far more timely fashion, Red-Eyes is viable if not one of the problems of the meta currently
Skills are a love hate thing.  It's REALLY cool to be able to pull off what we saw in the show and really feel like the character we're playing as, but likewise there's ways to abuse the system that isn't as welcome and is more frustrating to play against than it is charming to use at times.  A good example is the Destiny Draw skill that allows you to pick and draw any card in your deck after taking so much damage..... except it just checks for damage.  You could gain a ton of life points prior or even after and still use this effect, and be able to do so several times in a game.  A lesser, but still annoying one is the Restart skill that some people just seem to use as a mulligan on any character that it's available, and kind of gives off the impression that your character choice doesn't matter as much as it'd be cool for it to be.
The return of the old guard is welcome as well.  If you aren't an avid fan of the card game but liked the show, this still has something to offer you here and there just to launch and make believe you are one of the titular characters you're playing as, from Kaiba to Jaden and I'm sure latter generations as time passes by.  Especially Kaiba.  As some have suggested, this is fun just as a "Kaiba is mean to children" simulator.
For those who are REALLY into the card game, this is a refreshing romp, but you'll quickly find not all cards are as balanced as they are in the regular game.  Accumulated Fortune, a chain burn staple, is near unplayable but exists in the game.  There's just some strategies that are not at all viable, like the aforementioned chain burn, even if most cards for the deck are released on the platform.  Red-Eyes is ridiculous having the searcher Insight and Spirit to set-up a slow but fast 2400 monster.  Likewise though, you'll most likely not be staring down as many floodgates in this setting, nor will you be frustrated with the ever apparent power creep and money grab.  Game is reaching its one year mark, and while the ban list may not be as proactive as one would like, one can hope that the game going forward will be far more attentive of balancing the game than the IRL counterpart that just seems to get riddled with "they need to make their sales even though this deck is already doing too well."
7/10:  Has flaws to the game that may affect how far you can get into the game and still enjoy it, but on the surface is a fun casual experience.  For what problems the game has, the free to play model allows for anyone to remain casual or be competitive with a low or near non-existent paygate; you really don't have to pay anything for any level you want to enjoy the game at.

You know, there was a time when "dungeon crawl" felt like something bad and boring for me. Probably more due to disposable boring dungeon quests in RPGs, bad Diablo clones and grindy Japanese action RPGs. I actually didn't play a lot of classic dungeon crawlers, like Ultima Underworld or even newer titles influenced by it like Arx Fatalis and didn't get to understand the good bits of this subgenre of action RPGs until Legend of Grimrock 5 years ago. But since Grimrock, I was highly interested. And there haven't been that many good follow ups to that game, apart from its fantastic sequel. Games usually focus too much on combat, or too much on puzzles, or too much on something else, never really feeling as balanced and as engrossing as Legend of Grimrock games were. Vaporum is one of the better examples so far.
Game does some things differently on a very basic level. It ditches a lot of mechanics and ideas to boil everything down to the core ideas. So you have just one character to control, "magic" is just a set of abilities tied to keys/icons, you don't rest/eat and there are no save crystals, the dungeon is mostly one layer only and secrets and puzzles are usually not that obscure. But at the same time, it attempts to keep all the beauty of exploration, the thrills of encountering enemies and "dancing" around them, the simple joys of skills and leveling up. And it does it surprisingly well.
There are occasional hiccups, which probably will vary depending on how you level up the character (remember to specialize, not spread across everything), but overall game progression in terms of combat and exploration is pretty well paced with just enough challenge to actually feel how powerful you can become by the end, just enough puzzles and secrets to feel smart about figuring them out and just enough variety in levels, that you will probably not get bored. The start can be pretty slow and I feel like some things should've been introduced and spiced up earlier then they do in the game, but when things get going, they never really stop.
Where the game does disappoint is in how... plain and derivative it feels in the rest of things. The plot and story are very heavy influenced by BioShock games, but, more importantly, are just boring and rather badly acted, never even trying to be creative or strange, something that both Grimrock games did really well. The music is "fine". Visually and technologically, the game feels a bit cheap and poorly optimized, a bit too close to the "stock Unity experience" than the style and the setting deserved to have. I mean, there are really beautifully set up scenes and locations, they just could look so much better (and run so much smoother).
But overall, Vaporum is good doze of dungeon crawling that will keep you wanting to play more of it, to explore just one more room, clear out just one more floor. It could've been much better, as Grimrock games show perfectly, but it is still worth a play and I hope the developers get to evolve their craft with whatever next projects they might have.

Simple (but not too easy) take on programming games at a reasonable price
This is an interesting twist on programming games (The first video on the store page is actually a good example of gameplay) . You start with a cube (representing a hacking probe) that can move around a series of rooms like a maze (representing some sort of cyberspace architecture). You need to get the cube to move various locations in the maze (representing data file locations) to complete each level. However all movement is pre-programmed, and you have a limited way to get the cube to do what you want.
You write programs by putting "nodes" of one of five commands together (move Left, RIght, Up, Down, and wait), and setting up different colored tiles within the maze. These colored tiles are branch points for your program, and how you get the cubes to change direction. For example, "move left until land on blue tile, then move down".
There are about 45 levels and the difficulty varies. It takes anywhere from a few minutes to solve most levels to a handful that I've had to put aside for a few days cause I just wasn't seeing how to solve it. Since you're not limited by the length of programs, you can "brute-force" levels by having lots of nodes and colored tiles (but where's the fun in that?)
I should mention that chapter 2 level 6 is a bad idea by the design team IMHO. There are slight changes that they could have made to keep the challenge of the level without having the layout looking like a "good luck cross" (google "fylfot" or play the game if you don't know what I'm talking about). I understand the various historical and non-offensive usages of this particular symbol (various religions, Finnish Air Force, etc) but I still think there there are enough people that might be offended that the designers will lose potential sales by having this level in the game. Again, there is no reason to have a something controversial in such a good game.
When you solve a level, you get between 1 and 3 "multipasses" depending on how well written your code is. So one challenge after you solve a level is to optimize your solution. Also the January update added a global stats board that tells you how well you did compared with everyone else.
There is a level editor and community mazes (I have yet to try these), so you're not going to run out of challenges. As far as I can tell, this game does not do Steam Sync, which is annoying (but alright for the relatively cheap price).
The graphics are on the flashy side for a programming game, but still very functional. There's something very pleasing about seeing the cube move through the maze. I'd recommend turning off the bloom effects and the TV-screen effect. Each chapter of the game starts with a brief graphic-novel narration setting up the backstory.
Overall this game is an 8/10 (10/10 if the designers change Chapter 2, level 6). Ten bucks is maybe pushing the price to value ratio, but if you find it at even a slight discount then I'd definitely get it. 45 levels multiplied by about 5 minutes per level, plus community levels and you can figure out how much game value you are getting.

TL; DR If you like adventure games such as legend of grimrock, and are fine with a single-character story as opposed to a party based adventure, this is definitely worth a look as a solid addition to the grid-based crawler genre. Just surprised I hadn't spotted this sooner.
This game is stylised beautifully as an up-to-date Dungeon Hack (Or single-character Eye of the Beholder / Grimrock) sort of game. I am not too far in (started on hard, my character just got kicked out of a doorway) but the style is very remniscent of classic dungeon crawling, combined with graphics that bring it to the modern era. Being able to customize your characters towards how you want to play is an essential in games like these, and every exoskeleton, upgrade, found item & gadget has been very clear in what it does.
The game has character, and I am intrigued by how far it will go. Vaporum gives you the option of stopping time to plan out your actions, which is especially handy if you keep getting interrupted (damned phone) and being able to shock, burn, cover in acid, stun etc. opponents is useful. Even a basic encounter with multiple enemies in true fashion will be dangerous if you get cornered, so no encounter is trivial. The puzzles so far seem to have been fun, the last one before this current part involved quite the thinking, ended up mapping boxes in my head and thinking for several minutes before finding the solution. The little snippets of story are paced out and some of them being read help keep the tempo of the game going.
Fully worth the price from the experience I have had already. Looking forward to the rest.

Cyber Sentinel is an interesting twist on a Turing machine - instead of a tape that can be moved right or left, a matrix is used allowing for a 2-dimensional puzzle to be constructed and solved.
This game is not for everyone.  If you don't enjoy the kind of puzzle that makes you feel like an idiot until you reach the "Eureka!" moment that makes you feel smart again, you won't like this.  Some of the puzzles border on the fiendish, and I haven't even completed the game yet.  I'm having too much fun optimizing my solutions to use the fewest number of states I can manage.
You don't need to be a programmer, or even understand what a
is, to have fun with this game.  Having a logical mind and enjoying puzzle solving is all you really need and something puzzle afficianaods typically have anyway.  Having done some fiddling with Turing machines in the past certainly helped me understand things quicker, though!
All in all, this is a great game for those who enjoy logic puzzles!  Kudos to both the author, and the genius of Alan Turing.

Overall I would say Cyber Sentinel is not brilliant but it's still pretty good and if you are into programming puzzles you will definitely enjoy this.

This game is something of it's own. Just by playing, it's rather obvious that this is generally just a modded version of Half-Life 2, but it pulls it off. The gameplay is solid, with the shall we say "survivors" having to reach a bomb site, plant a timed charge, and get out before time runs out, all the while forcing through hordes of the undead. The classes and possible combinations of classes make each game interesting. You can take a team of shotgunners and just shred through the zombies, or take your time with a more strategic approach using a variety of classes. The characters are well made too. If you pay close enough attention, you'll notice that the zombies are various Half-Life 2 NPC's with an "undead" effect (pale skin,  claw marks, etc). But there's always a bad side... One problem is that it's very diffficult, even on casual difficulty if you get cornered on your own or run out of ammo, you're done for. There's also the frequency of waves, with dozens of zombies all rushing the players every few minutes. There are also only four maps to play on. There's a few other things to cover but this has already been a very long review. If you can imagine Couter-Strike meets Left 4 Dead, that's Codename CURE in a nutshell. I personally think it's worth it, especially since it's free and a pretty small download.

Great game with much potential.
Things I like:
-Massive world (about 40km2)
*You also need to actually explore, since world maps starts blank. You can vaguely see where land ends and sea begins as well as general look of the terrain from under the blackness. Mobs spawn in certain areas like wooden forts or caves (map has marks for those areas. You can also make your own tags if you find something interesting.
-Lore
*Well, it exists. You need to dig into the wiki or ask the players about it, but a little mystery is nice too. Still, it could use a some padding.
-Openworld pvp (you also drop your items if you get ganked(killed by player while down)/release your spirit after death. You can get them back if you reach your grave before it's looted)
*Also openworld ofc. A bit overwhelming at first, but it's nice to set your own goals and plan your own adventures)
(Quest system is still under development)
Constant threath of other players also makes it much more rewarding to bring a haul from adventure back to the bank (there are also banks around the world near chaos bindstones (respawn/recall points) but they are unprotected. I haven't experienced much playerkilling around them though).
Being chased by another player can be quite thrilling too. It's possible to escape from even high level player since all mounts run at the same speed (there are speed enhancing skills that make you faster than mount, but you can outrun even them if you get enough headstart and manouver well enough (not too much zigzagging to dodge projectiles and using terrain as cover.)
Currently there are no stealth skills, but if you crouch in a bush or hide behind objects and use 3rd person(there is 1st person too, obviously), you can "manually" sneak around players too. Crouching also makes much less noise when walking. You must target player/npc directly and be within certain range to see it's UI.
-Localized markets (still under development, partially implemented)
*Similiar system like EVE online has. You need to travel to different markets to physically get the items you buy
-Monthly subscription
*Yes, It is a good thing. I haven't seen any bots, gold spam or even cheaters. It also keeps the game fair, which is essential for such pvp oriented game. Upkeep isn't free and this is the most fair way to get money for it. Free to play works really well for some games, but this isn't one of them.
-D.U.E.L  subscription extension item
*Similiar to PLEX in EVE. You can buy it with real money and sell it for ingame money, meaning that it's possible to play the game for free. Gold isn't too hard to get. Some mobs drop a lot of it and you can also get lucky with chaos chest (random chests around the world that may have huge amounts of gold or almost none. They may contain other nice stuff aswell. You find tons of them if there aren't much players around.)
-Upcoming feature (Relics: Grand items that you can either haul to your clan's church, which gives clan a worldwide buff, or you can take it to demon altar and destroy for prowess reward.
(Prowess = xp. There are no traditional levels in DF. You buy and upgrade skills and attributes with prowess. First levels are extremely cheap but it gets more expensive higher the skill is. Currently 100 is max for everything. Each level makes skill a little more powerful)
-Graphcis and music
*While graphics may not be highest AAA quality, I think it's very atmospheric. Reminds me of Morrowind. Music on the other hand is epic.
-Clans
*or guilds, how ever you want to call them. Much of the game is built around clan system. They can capture villages (in which you can build your own house) and Cities. Citys have allkinds of nice stuff that clan can build there: crafting area, resource nodes for faster and safer gathering (there are also safe areas in which you can harvest, but clan nodes always give full quality resoruces, while regular nodes may give inferior quality stuff, which you can use to craft reqular quality resources.), skill trainers and shops. They are closer to more exiting places than safe zones too.
-Economy
It's completely player driven. There are only few essential items that can be bought from npc like basic tools and spell ingredients.Mobs drop low quality equipment and you can find better items from random chests/equipment racks around the world. Rest you have to craft or buy from market.
Mixed opinion
-Resource gathering from nodes
*It's time consuming and uneventful(thought it also gives you prowess, especially if you get rarer items while harvesting), but it's easy to do other things while waiting for iron node to get picked or wood to get chopped. Gathering makes distinct sound which can be heard throught video if you set your volume levels right. If the sound stops, you know it's time to switch node/tool or regain stamina. This gets a little harder if there are multiple harvesters around you, but then you just need to be more vigilant. In areas outside safe zone this is a lot more dangerous, since other players can attack you, but with large group emptying nodes is much faster and safer.
I think there could be somekind of minigame for harvesting, but that might not be that good idea in the end.
Things I don't like
-Inventory system (Devs are making an overhaul to it)
*Very crude and quite hard to manage if you are in hurry. At least there are bags which greatly help organization.
-Small playerbase (Game needs more publicity. More positive recommendations and/or less negative (and useless, like mere "this game sucks!" reviews) would help too.)
* This can also be a benefit for new player, since if there are less players around you can gather prowess and resources more freely and thus become more pvp viable faster. The game can be enjoyable even with small playerbase.
-Easy to get away with player killing.
*I don't think there are any penaltys for doing so, expect for being tagged as playerkiller. I hope devs will take a look of this at some point.
> This is not handholding game like wow or many other mmo's there are. While this means the game may be harder for you to understand and play, it also means greater satisfaction once you start to see how things work. Also the game wont treat you like an idiot.
On my experience the community has been friendly and helpful towards new players. There are also currently 2 major clans that actively recruit new players and teach them how to play. There is also mentorship system. Experienced player can take apperentices and teach them how to play. They also get rewards if their apperentice gains enough prowess. <
There are other stuff too, but this is all I can think of currently. If you decide to try the game, be patient and don't give up. Also watch some gameplay videos first to get better general idea about the game.

It's my firm belief that this is the most well-crafted RTS to date. The sheer amount of detail is staggering: Fully destructable environments and morphing landscape, fully realised unit inventories (guns, ammo, grenades, sandbags, explosives, knives, bandages; it's all there and freely tradeable between your soldiers), smart unit AI, direct control over any unit in the field, the best RTS cover system (brick walls actually stop bullets, as opposed to providing a 'defensive bonus') and realistic ballistics and damage models. Starcraft 2 looks like babbies first RTS by comparison.
While good micro is still important, good macro, field awareness and tactical thinking play a more prominant role. Did Colonal T. Awesome get sniped while gunning down Fritz with his 50. cal? Then get Private S. Meatshield to go grab that machinegun, and do his mother proud. Your comms officer get blown up while trying to lay down an airstrike? Lay down some smoke and go grab his flaregun to finish the job!

There's many issues I've seen so far on this game.
-No Fullscreen. Like what the heck, I wanna be immersed into this seemingly great story and universe, while not seeing either the Steam Page or my wallpaper.
-Packs are awful, card navigation is even worse. Compared to Shadowverse, whereby you click a card and there's information about where this pack is from, here, I have no damn clue on where to get some of the other cards that support the current "box expansion". I would like to suggest some letters or something that indicates where the card is from. Anything, other than god awful navigation we have today. In Shadowverse, you get 7 cards in a pack. Here, only 3. And you need to like refresh the box to get another SR if you got it from the first one? Realistic? Yes, very much. Annoying and grindy? Oh yeah.
-Grind for items to create cards/buy packs. Now, I know, I don't mind grinding for cards that I need. You have Hearthstone, that you grind for the Gold and Dust, Gold for buying Adventure and Pack and Dust for . In Shadowverse, you grind Vials for cards and Gold for packs. Here, you grind items such as: Gold for specific cards from a Card Dealer, Gems for packs/structure deck, and keys(Water, Fire, Dark...) for the Gate World, and Stones(Water, Fire, Dark....) for the Card Dealer(specific cards), and Jewel (R,SR...). There's so many to keep track of that I forgot how many currency type this game had.
-Stage Mission. Some people like this, making it sort of a progression system. I hate it though, because it restrict freedom and causing the game to be a bit linear and not making it fluid.
-No japanese voices. Isn't this from a Japanese game? Why is Korean voice included but not Japanese? I love Kaiba's Japanese voice.

-Can't choose the characters immediately. Wanna play Mai? Then you had to stick to either to Yugi or Kaiba to grind it so that you can get her. I actually want to play Pegasus due to my love for Relinquish+Toon monster combo. However I can't because I'm not there yet.

+3x3 Zone with 4000Lp. I don't mind this at all. This makes the game at a much faster pace and make it fresh and appeal to people who never played Yu-Gi-Oh! before.
Unfortunately, that's all the props I can give.

Pure casual titles focusing solely on mazes, aren’t that many on Steam so perhaps developer Blender Games made the right choice in trying to fill that niche. They are newcomers on the platform, yet their aMAZE series (comprised so far of two games) is more than decent for its price tag.
No actual storyline here, it’s just an increasingly more difficult set of mazes which players must guide a colored round object through. You don’t require much explanation for it, since most casual Steam games don’t multitask or offer the kind of diversity to warrant even tutorials. You just pick them up and play.
Pleasant looking 2D graphics and I can’t tell by looking at the game’s files, if it was created through Unity Engine assets or not. It looks the part and that’s really all you need to worry about. The mazes, backgrounds  and the guidable balls shift in color from one level to another, so at least you can’t complain about too much repetitiveness. The fact that the maze structure is just using the classic square-shaped or rectangular form factors, is the main reason why aMAZE is rated lower than its more versatile sequel. At least the game runs in your monitor’s native resolution so there won’t be technical issues even if you’re playing on an older system.

aMAZE uses a repetitive tune which only gives you the option to mute. Not even lower or increase the volume. Just mute it and listen to whatever soundtrack you wish. It can’t be worse than what aMAZE provides you with.
The gameplay itself is straightforward, even if we’re talking of mazes here. You just have to use your keyboard arrow or numpad keys and guide the ball of different colors (shape and size seem to be persistent) through a certain maze that may prove more difficult than the previous one. They still don’t require much time to solve and thus aMAZE can be considered a relaxing distraction from heavier titles in terms of complexity and topic usage. I wish the developer might add a timer and highscore board, to at least offer a more competitive edge to the gameplay.
As it is now, you can complete an individual maze in an hour instead of a minute, and it would still not make any difference. You can’t fail a level on aMAZE, so the complete lack of a challenge may deter some players. There are sufficiently many stages though, to keep you busy even if playing in longer sessions, instead of just a few mazes per day. Just play the game if you’re really interested in 2D classical labyrinths and if you feel like your Steam game collection might use this particular type of casual title.
You can't argue with its pricing since you get to play exactly what the official screenshots from the Store Page, advertise. No false promises, no doctored images. What you see, is what you get and I consider it a decent offer. Picking aMAZE during a bundle or Steam Sale, makes it an even more attractive deal, so I don’t understand why some many folks complain about this title and still praise its successor? I’m reviewing aMAZE 2 as well so be sure to read that article and find out the differences between the two. In the meantime, sit back and relax. Play some mazes, ok? You’re supporting an honest indie dev and you should feel good about that.

So fairly straightforward here - you have 50 mazes, 10 shortish easy ones and 40 called medium/hard of essentially the same level of difficulty and you have to find your way to the finish line. Or sometimes brush past the finish line while passing close by it. Playtime is probably about 0.5-1 hour, with little replayability.
The controls are poor - your ball will stick to wall and has trouble cornering, making long windy passages really annoying to traverse. Which is another problem - instead of having mazes with lots of medium to large branches to choose between, the mazes here are mostly long winding passages with sometimes a fair number of ultra short dead ends you sail past (if you don't get stuck on a wall) without needing to pause or look ahead to decide which is the right way as you can tell at a glance.
There are a few levels with fairly decent branching that actually work as proper mazes, but entirely too many you walk 60%+ of the length of the maze to get to the end because all the branches are so short. Others also make decisions that cut off large chunks of the maze way too trivial - the first screenshot on the store page shows a level where you start right on the bottom, move slightly up and right, then travel right to the top of the maze, splitting the level in half and making the half without the finish immediately and trivially easy to ignore, and there are several more levels that do the same (although slightly less obviously).
So overall the controls are annoying, some of the levels have horrible backgrounds, and the mazes are mostly poor; even by the time you get to do the few decent levels that are interspersed in the later part of medium and a couple of the hard levels you really just want it to be over.

If there was a "meh" rating option, I would have chosen it. I did finish the game, but towards the end I wanted to just get it over with. And I don't really care if I'm going try-hard on a 1 dollar game, at least it's a thumbs up.
Issues:
-Ball controls - Ball gets caught on edges and drags when too close to the walls, which becomes immensely annoying once you get to the harder levels.
-Difficulty between Medium and Hard - Really no difference, the maze just gets bigger.
-Music - Single track that's about a minute-long looping throughout the whole game.
-Color changes between levels - There are levels where you go from black to NEON. PINK.
-Lack of settings and additional buttons - No settings, no key re-configurations, no movement sensitivity changes, you can only turn music off and on. And when you beat a level, you can only click on the arrow to proceed. Allowing the shortkey to be 'enter' or 'space' would have been convenient.
-Finish through walls - There are a couple levels where if you can get the ball close enough to the goal through the wall, it counts as passing.
-Uninteresting later levels - Specifically the latter half of the medium levels and all hard levels. You have to pretty much go through at least 50% of the maze to reach the exit. Some levels have you going through almost the entire maze where it's obvious where dead ends are since it literally takes a couple glances to see that it is sectioned off.
My thoughts throughout the game:
Easy levels: Ahhh, good old nostalgia.
Medium levels: This is fun, but it's kinda getting repetitive. Oh hey, that's a bright co- MY EYES.
Hard levels: Is this actually Hard? It's just slightly longer than Medium. It would be great if I could customize the ball and background.... I wish I could handle these balls as well as the developer thinks I should. Just let me glitch through the frickin' walls, I've got 49 problems and I don't want mazes as innovative as modern-day art to be another one.

A fun little game where you have to program the movements of small cubes so that it collects all the data spread into each levels. The mechanics are really easy to learn but have quite some depth to it.
The game is quite short. There are 45 levels and for each level the threshold to get the maxim rating is very low. It took me 4~5 hours to 100% the game and i only skipped the last level. There is also a level editor and the possibility to play user created levels but due to very few people currently playing the game there are not many of them. Also, just like all games with an achievement to upload custom levels, you can expect some low quality level spam.
The levels themselves are interesting for the most part. There are a few stupid ones and duplicate ones but overall they are very satisfying to solve using the simplest "program" possible. You also have the possibility to upload your solutions and compare them to others but there isn't any leaderboard of any kind which is a shame because in these kind of game optimization is a big part of it. And that's not the low threshold to get the max rating that helps.
In the end, if you like "programmation games" and want something not very difficult and with a different mechanic than the other available on steam i would recommand it. The game in itself is interesting and feels very polished but i still feel that it lacks a bit of content. Hopefully, more people will get the game and make more custom levels or the devs will make optimizing the levels more interesting.

Huh. Final DOOM, huh?
I'm sure id wasn't planning on DOOM 3 and 4, were they?
Final DOOM is a collection of fan-made maps gathered by id and strung along with a story... and god, does it show. The story to both map-packs (TNT: Evilution and The Plutonia Experiment) are pretty much interchangeable. Correct me if I'm wrong, but I'm pretty sure the paragraphs between levels are almost word-for-word the same thing as well. But the difference between these map-packs is almost night and day, when we're talking about the actual levels.
TNT: Evilution is arguably the best 2D DOOM game I've played. It's got everything from DOOM II that made it good, but with much better designed and more aesthetically-pleasing levels. I've gotta say, the people who made the levels in TNT: Evilution kicked some serious a** by using the old graphics on the Doom engine to make some really creative levels. Some locations you go to are just jaw-droppingly beautiful. Well, as beautiful as abandoned space stations and Hell crypts can be.
On top of that the music in TNT: Evilution is pretty damn good. There are several new tracks that keep the same metal feeling of the original games' soundtracks, and they fit in well. If I were just reviewing TNT: Evilution, I'd easily recommend it as my favorite DOOM campaign.
Plutonia Experiment on the other hand... makes things a bit trickier.
I didn't really like The Plutonia Experiment as much. The levels aren't as creatively designed, there's no new music, and a lot of the places you go to are very labyrinthian and cryptic... but not in the good way. As in "The worst parts of DOOM I and II, but in most of the levels of this campaign," kind of way. It honestly feels like more DOOM- which isn't bad, of course- but it feels kind of stale after a while. And once you get to the same final boss as TNT, and get the same death-credits as TNT... you're just kind of tired of playing DOOM for a while.
Now, I'll just play some more DOOM 2016!
For what it's worth, Final DOOM is a solid game. It's just knowing that half of it is like the strawberry half of a sundae with nuts and whipped cream on top, and the other half is filled with cheese cubes. It just depends on what you personally like the most out of the DOOM games, and either TNT or Plutonia will cater to your desires, whether its aesthetic design or cryptic design. It's still worth a recommendation, and I'm giving Final DOOM a 7/10.

As you can tell by my hours on record, I play HEX a lot.  I love the game.  I love the vision HEX Entertainment has for it and I'm incredibly excited for what the future has in store.  I waited to leave a review here because I didn't want to seem like a fanboy who was trying to puff up the ratings for a new release on steam.  Now that a more even spread of good and negative reviews have been left, I feel it is the right time to say my piece which is less of a review than an explanation of what HEX is.
If you like depth and strategy of trading card games, especially Magic the Gathering, you will probably like HEX.  It is very similar to Magic but does have some major differences that sets it apart such as its threshold system, champion powers, card transformation/generation, etc.  Since you are reading these reviews, it is probably safe to assume you are into card games and are thinking about trying HEX so here are a couple of things you need to know so that you will have the right expectations coming into the game.
1.  In spite of what HEX is labeled on steam, HEX is not technically a F2P game.  It has a free PvE campaign that you can play as a stand alone game.  You get something like 250 cards just by creating a campaign champion and then you can earn additional PvE cards by playing the campaign.  You will also earn gold which I will explain in greater detail in a moment.  The competitive PvP side of the game is a standard TCG which does cost money for participation.  Again, TCG.  (Trading card game) Not CCG. (Collectable card game)  Think Magic, not Hearthstone.  While all TCGs are CCGs, the opposite is not true due to several unique characteristics TCGs have that differentiate them from other card games.  So, if you don't know the differences between these two things, please go educate yourself in order to understand what you are getting into.
2.  HEX has two currencies.  Gold, earned for free through PvE and Platinum which is purchased from the in-game Store.  Gold can be traded directly with other players for platinum. Gold can also be used on the auction house to buy things like PvP packs or cards.  Platinum is the paid currency of the game that pays the entry fee into PvP tournaments, enables the purchase of PvP packs off the in-game store, and can be used to buy the more valuable items on the AH that people tend to not list for gold like primal packs.  (If you don't know what a primal pack is, look it up.  They are awesome.)  The players who regularly pay for participation in the PvP side of the game have several incentives to want a ton of gold but may not necessarily have the time to obtain it for themselves.  That creates an environment where the free player can come in and convert time into money.  This is how you can play the game for free, if that is what you want.  It will never be as efficient as just buying the plat from HEX Ent. but it is an option that someone who doesn't want to pay, or can't, can use to still participate in PvP formats.
3.  This game is still in its infancy and development tends to be slow over at HEX Entertainment.  At this time there is only one adventure zone for the F2P PvE campaign but more are on the way.  There are currently four PvP sets and hopefully production will start to pick up so that we can get to a set every 4 months or so.  Many of the ideas the devs have for this game are still in development such as crafting and PvE dungeon raids.  The AH is clunky as hell but I expect they will improve it over time.  The bottom line is that what you see currently isn't where things end.  Not by a long shot.  The future is very bright for HEX.
4.  On the whole, the community in this game is extremely helpful and good-natured.  Don't be afraid to reach out and ask questions.
5.  Ultimately, reviews are just opinions and you'd be better served by forming your own instead of relying on others to tell you what to think.

Visually and technically, What Remains of Edith Finch is good but does not excel the other walking-simulator games to which it might be compared (such as The Vanishing of Ethan Carter). Where it really shines is in telling a story—or rather, presenting a series of haunting vignettes that combine to sketch a deeply affecting portrait of a loving but very ill-fated family. I'm a bit of a sucker for games that create a good sense of melancholy, and this hits the spot as far as that is concerned.

In this programming puzzle game you make your block(s) move through the level by adding movement direction blocks to the program grid, and connecting them with lines. The thing that makes this really neat is that the tiles in the game world can have different colours, which your block can interact with! You can decide to go in different directions based on the floor colour, or you can change the colour of the floor itself. Add in hostile program cubes, laser grids, teleporters and buttons, and the game can get complicated rather quickly. Did I mention you can have multiple blocks going at the same time?
The game features 5 chapters with 9 levels, each featuring a comic book style introduction that tells you the story of why you are solving puzzles. The first puzzles of Chapter 1 act as a tutorial, after which you have to solve the puzzles by yourself. The first chapter is relatively easy, but the difficulty does ramp up to a nice and interesting level. Let me know how you liked Chapter 2, puzzle 8, which took me a while to get to a solution, and then more time to try and optimise it.
Cyber Sentinel has a built-in level editor, and it features community-built levels in the main menu. It is very easy to make your own level and publish it from within the game. Similarly, you can share solutions for the game's levels as well as load other people's solutions from within each puzzle. This is a neat feature that I haven't seen in other puzzle games yet. If you have been stuck on a puzzle for hours, it's nice to have a community solution you can look at to see how it's done!
I received a free review copy of the game before it was on Steam, which is why my played hours are rather low on Steam. Because I enjoyed playing the game, I made a YouTube video to show how it works. I do the first few tutorial levels to show you the basics, then I look at a later problem and solve it step by step, finally we dive into the level editor to see how that works.
If you are on the fence about buying the game, have a look to see if you get a better idea what the game is all about:

FIrst off, yes, it's pretty much a walking simulator. With that out of the way, it's a damn good example of how good a walking simulator can be. It concerns Edith Finch, the last in a family line whose members are "Cursed" or, at very least, have a tedency to die tragic deaths, often at young ages. Edith returns to her family home to discover the secrets about her family she barely knew.
It's short and is pretty much divided into two sections. The main part of the game is the walking tour of the home, where the bedrooms of dead family members have been preserved the way it was when they died and sealed to prevent entry. Finding a way into the rooms is the first "Challenge"(finding secret passages isn't really hard though). The more interesting part is when you find a journal or some such relating to the deceased, which  starts a gameplay sequence based on their lives, often ending in their deaths. Some of the sequences are quite varied and creative and all of them are tragic(Poor Gregory....).
That's pretty much what there is. An in depth look at a family marked by tragedy for generations. The gameplay is limited but on an emotional and character level, it suceeds.  If this appeals to you, buy it.

I've always loved the Commandos series from the beginning. It wasn't until I learned how to properly play the game that I found the beauty in the gameplay. It's not a game you can just run around gunning all the Nazi's down and hope to prevail. It's a game where you rather setup your attack or simply go around the obstacle using whatever gadgets or tricks you have up your sleeve.
That is the beauty in the gameplay. You can make up many different ways to get to your next point. During this time you will spend patiently waiting, hiding behind something out of a guards view as you inspect your surroundings and the entire environment where you plan your move.
Each Commando has his own special abilities and reasons for use so you generally have to mix it up and figure out which Commando to bring to the situation at hand.
While the game can seem brutal hard, there is a quick save and quick load feature which is best to use often. I constantly found myself reloading after making a mistake and trying to figure out the best way to accomplish the task at hand.
While the game has aged quite a bit, it's still a great play for any gamer this day in age mostly because there is none quite like it. The backgrounds are solid looking pieces of work that can be rotated at 4 different angles while the troops, Commandos, and most interactive environment objects are full 3D. You can also go for 360 degrees when you are inside a building. This makes for great planning and inspection of the environments.
Overall, I recommend this game as I consider it one of the benchmarks of this type of gameplay. For those unaware, its' not turned based or pause the gameplay and figure out what to do. It's all in real time and 1 mistake can cost you the mission instantly. Although like I said, there is a quick save and load for a reason and be prepared to use it often. The beauty in the game is making the corrections of the mistakes you made to get by and the rewards for the success upon finally completing a mission. Great game!
For another game similar to this that I think did a great attempt at trying to be like Commandos, look out for the original Desperados.

You choose one of two (eventually 4 with free DLC) characters to hack, slash and magic your way through angels and demons alike.

Valdis looks great, its got rich detailed graphics and some great enemy/boss design.

The story is probably a little short, but I'd like to ask you how long is Diablo 3's story? How long is Torchlight 2's? Or Zelda a link to the past, if you just play straight through the story and don't do anything else?
With all of the hidden items to find, timed puzzles to solve, multiple difficulties and multiple characters, I don't really see Valdis' content being a negative for me. Not to mention the "Coming soon" free DLC/additions.
All in all I'm very happy to recommend this game.

I couldn't decide what to play (too many games, first world problem extraordinaire) so I scrolled down to the final item in my steam library - You Must Build a Boat. I actually obtained 100% achievements on 10,000,000 so I don't know why this game was sitting in my library unplayed - but 18 hours later, I'm happy to give it a reasonable thumbs up.
This is a Match 3 / RPG combo in a very similar style to 10mil. In fact the actual game board is near identical - but the upgrades and premise are a little different. This one has more collectibles, more upgradeables and in my opinion, is harder - especially if you're aiming to 100% the achievements. However, at it's core, they are extremely similar games.
It's very RNG and this makes it a grind, especially towards the final few achievements. In trying to add depth to the previous game, there are some extras like traps, monster vulnerabilities, quests and so on - but by adding so many different things sometimes it's simply not possible to complete a level or a quest without just spamming it over and over and hoping for the right combo. This ends up with you having a ton of resources you can't even use by the end - but still not getting the things you need to progress. There's a fine line between adding depth/strategy and simply padding the game out to give it the illusion of more, and I think this fell a little into the padding category.
Many of the cut scenes / actions for upgrades also seemed unskippable, and they were pretty boring to sit through. This is not the sort of game I play for story.
I must have picked it up in a bundle as I have no recollection of purchasing it - but for those who enjoy the match 3 concept and aren't bothered by a bit of RNG/grind then this is a very fun game. If you're easily frustrated, the simpler concept of 10mil may be more suitable. I wouldn't pay full price for it even though it's only £3.99, but I'd definitely give it a playthrough if you pick it up in a bundle or on sale. I enjoyed it, despite the flaws and I built a pretty awesome boat!

I originally gave this game a positive recommendation, citing its beautiful visuals and fun gameplay. That review was actually based on my time playing it on a mid-range Windows 7 laptop. This review is from my re-download on a gaming desktop.
This game has the potential to be a really great Metroidvania. It's hampered, however, by horrendous performance issues. The framerate is unbearable, with constant slowdowns and overall sluggishness. My computer isn't top of the line, but I have an AMD FX-6300, a Radeon R9 290x, and 16 GB of memory. There's no reason for this slowdown other than terrible optimization.
I WANT to recommend this game a LOT. Theoretically, I love it. But the chugging framerate renders it unplayable, and the best suggestion I've seen in the forums is to edit your registry. When your customers have to edit their registry to try to get your game to work right, you've done something wrong.
If the performance issues are ever fixed, I'll wholeheartedly recommend this game. Until then, avoid it, even on sale.

It's time to D-D-D-D- D-D-D-D-D-DUEL!
Ah, a throwback to when I was a kid collecting the trading cards and watching the anime. (grew up with the original series and GX.) I'll keep it short: You get to start as Yugi or Kaiba (But you don't get to screw the rules like he screws his legendary Blue-Eyes.) and you start off with respective decks for either choice. The dueling is fun and addicting, but I do have some issues: The tall thin screen on which the game is displayed, and the fact that it's not the format of the actual TCG or the anime; it's in the Speed Duel format, meaning there's only 3 summon and spell/trap spaces for each side of the field alongside your deck, extra deck, graveyard and field spell space. Early on duels are one sided in your favor as you just plow through opponents that only summon weak monsters for you to mow down or easily beaten trap or spell cards. You don't really get much of a challenge until you face level 30 duelists, or somebody on PvP. However you can also lose by the sheer luck of your opponent when you don't draw any viable cards.
Finally you can earn gems and use them to get card packs to build decks, but you unfortunately don't get the freshly opened trading cards scent all trading card geeks fondly remember.

Dawn of War II is perhaps the best example of a sequel outside of StarCraft II in the RTS genre. While it tossed out Base Building for a more streamlined approach, it did so with flying colors combining Diablo style loot drops with an RPG leveling system and an extensive skill tree.
Pros: +Decent story with likeable characters
+Excellent loot, weapon, armor, and class variety
+Great graphics and animations that still hold up to todays standards for RTS games, especially for 2009
+TONS OF CONTENT! On top of a 20+ hour campaign that is highly replayable, you have Co-Op on top of that. (The online modes should be played exclusively on DoW II Retribution though as that has ALL the factions and the majority of the community.)
+Fantastic combat with great enemy variety, boss battles, special enemy types, and lots of guns, powers, and toys to play around with
+Huge open maps meant for exploration to find loot and other goodies as well as mop up any enemies to rack the experience points.
+Decent mission variety with story missions being the most focused with optional Assassination and Defense missions to spice it up
+The voice acting is SUPERB with some of the best game actors in the biz working it, including Steve Blum, aka Spike from Cowboy Beebop in this game as a grizzled Sniper expert
+ITS WARHAMMER 40K! If you love the franchise like I do you will be splooging at all the detail, lore, and awesome stuff that helps build upon the license and makes you giddy just to feel like youre in the universe of W40K
Con: -Graphics are great overall, but there is some serious texture quality that is left to be desired, like the ground for instance
-While the maps are expansive and fun to explore they repeat them CONSTANTLY in the game. It gets repeitive doing the same maps over and over, but it's the quality of the gameplay and the map design that save this unfortunate problem
-Cant respec skill tree :(
-Still suffers from bugs. Nothing major, but there are occasional animation bugs where units may get stuck or cant move, and enemies who get killed may fly in circles around the map. It's actually kind of funny when you see that one though
-Along with repeating maps the missions themselves feel very repetitive after a while. It's the differing enemy types and awesome loot drops that encourage you to play these and save this unforunate repetition
-While the writing is passable by W40K fans, most people will see it as stock and cliche. It really is the setting and license that hold it up. The characters are memorable and likeable enough, but fairly one dimensional in personality and you really need to listen to a LOT of their dialog to feel invested
OVERALL: Fantastic
I mean no exageration when I award this a 9.5/10 as a W40K fan. As an RTS/RPG fan, I award it an 8.5 for those not familiar with W40K. An excellent game none the less and one of my favorite games of all time and my favorite RTS alongside StarCraft II. An easy buy.

First off, why did Steam allow a mobile game onto their store? Just because it is popular? You have no reason to get this port. Just get it for your phone, if only it was a good game.
This game's only gimmick is that it is the original format. No synchros. No Xyz's. No pendulums. Just the OG cards, except the fact that Konami had to put in newer cards into the game in order to boost consistency and support. Also you only have 3 monster card zones and 3 spell/trap card zones, which makes some cards and archtypes, like Dark Scorpions, unplayable. Speaking of cards, where are the good cards? 80% of the cards are pack filler garbage, 15% are decent, 4.9% are good, and 01.% are great. Also, some cards from the OG format are gone for some reason. Most of the Element Hero fusions aren't there, some Gladiator Beast are missing, and there are only TWO MONARCHS. And the reason for why the monarchs are gone is the main reason of why this game sucks. The OG format sucks. Almost all of the cards suck and the concept of archtypes was still being figured out so consistency and support is nonexistent.
Synchros, Xyz's, pendulums, and even link summoning was far better than the OG format. Each one helped evolve Yu-Gi-Oh into a better game, except maybe link summoning. Sychros made the extra deck actually worth having, Xyz's sped the game up and allowed easy access to the extra deck, pendulums allowed better swarming, and link summoning helped counter OP extra deck spammers. What did the OG have? A lot of crappy fusions that aren't worth running and ritual monsters that only where relevant due to two ritual archtypes that came out after the OG format. Literally the only reason that you would play this game is for nostalgia. And Nostalgia is the only thing that will carry you through this game.
If you understand this game even a little, you will became to OP for NPC's in no time. You will mow through them so efficiently that not auto-dueling will become torture really fast. In 24 hours, I was almost able to collect all the cards available for one box set of cards that had 600 total cards in it, with the amount of cards you get with each pack being only three measly cards. It only took me around 30 packs to make a deck that was so good that I have to brick in order for my opponent to have a chance to beat me. As for keeping you coming back to the game, the game offers pathetic events and the fact that every "energy" bar, that are the staple for long mobile games like this, fills up really quickly that you have no choice but to keep playing which is bad for games like this. The reason the "energy" bar exists is to keep gameplay in quick, short burst and prevent burn out. If a mobile game forces you to sit down and empty your battery, it goes against the entire point of a mobile game.
Finally, another big problem with this game are the skills. To keep things simple, the skills allow you to cheat and make the game even easier. Skills have appeal because it makes you feel like your playing like they do in the anime, but let it sink in that everyone in the original seasons cheats and the anime had to make up cards and edit existing cards in order to allow the heores win with their terrible decks. Granted you don't have to use skills, unless you want to play against other players. Speaking of which, how is playing against other players? Not that good. The more you face off against higher level players, the more you start seeing the same cards over and over again.
Is this game good? No! Is this game at least playable? Yes, but not for long. There are far better Yu-Gi-Oh games that you could be playing instead that play this is down right stupid. Just play one of the console, handheld, the actual card game, or buy and play Yu-Gi-Oh Legacy of the Duelist on Steam.

Before i jump into things im gonna go ahead and say that this game has a pretty great concept and decent delivery. For the price it is definitely worth it.
To start off, the gameplay essentially goes like this.
You can pick two weapons before you spawn, with a fairly decent selection although if you want to build anything you will have to select the miner gun as one of them, which is almost useless for attacking. You are then spawned into an arena with other players made up of tiny little bricks which can be destroyed, or built on with bricks of your own. The combat is fairly skill based, while still being somewhat friendly to new players, and if you haven't gotten very good at the game yet you will get killed alot, but will likely still have enough moments where you pull off an awesome stunt to make it enjoyable.
The game does give you the ability to build with the minergun, but i find that there isn't really enough of a focus on construction especiallly in the deathmatch mode to really make it worth your time. Not to say it can't be fun to build up a base, but the gameplay is so fast paced that you will likely be killed alot by the other players/zombies while trying to do so.
One thing that is worth mentioning is that i believe this game was originally designed for the Xbox, and then ported over to the PC, so if your playing on the PC the gameplay can feel pretty "klunky" at times and just generally unsatisfactory.
The graphics are nothing special, but they are pretty good for what they are. I especially like the ability to customize your characters colours and helmet.
Listening for the sounds that other players are making can be helpfull sometimes, but can also just confuse you too, since you there is almost no difference between a sound made all the way across the map and a sound that is 30 feet away from you. It only really starts to get louder if a player is closer than about 25 feet to you.
I have heard people say that there aren't enough players on this game, which is understandable considering that this game is very old. However, although i would certainly like to see more people online and hosting games, i have never personally been completely unable to find someone to play with. Especially since my computer is good enough to host games without serious lag issues. However, especially if your computer can't host games, this might be something you want to consider. (By the way the process for hosting a server is easy, no port forwarding or anything.)
Overall, i give this game a 6.5 out of 10. This game is nowhere near perfect, but it can still be a good load of fun to play especially if you've got a couple of friends to play it with. And considering the insanely cheap price, i would say it is well worth your money.

I've always enjoyed TCGs of all types and flavors, but I haven't seen one execute PVE content well yet. Hex is trying, and doing a half-decent job. Cryptozoic makes strong use of digital design space in a typically physical medium. Cards will often have effects (like manipulating stats on cards still in your deck) that are impossible or prohibitively fiddly on a table. The cards are original and fun, but there are real power creep issues which concern me in regards to the game's future. Like most TCGs, expect to spend some money here. I've been happy to do so, but I don't know how good the F2P experience in Hex will be.
I do prefer Hex to Hearthstone for many reasons: it preserves the higher complexity of Magic that I wish they hadn't streamlined out of HS, and the PVE, while still in development, is looking to blow HS's out of the water. Most importantly, I feel like Hex is on track to support more creative deck-building, as opposed to the "deck building as intended by the designers" experience in HS.
If you've got a bit of money to spend and you love TCGs, Hex will treat you right.

A pretty nice dungeon crawler in the same vein as Legend of Grimrock 1 in terms of gameplay, but features a steampunk theme for the dungeon.   The game took me about 15 hours to clear with about half of the secrets being missed along the way.  Leveling up allows you to spend point into various skill trees, all of which have attractive abilities to unlock making them all compelling ways to spec your character.   By the end of the game you will be able to fill out 3 of the trees, so this gives a lot of creativity for coming up with cool builds.  Achievement hunters will find a lot of reason to replay the game.
The game is visually really great looking and features some puzzles that aren't too heavy as to drag the game down.  Some of the more challenging ones are optional, but it never really gets to the point where Grimrock goes in terms of trying to figure out things.  If you like dungeon crawlers you will probably love this game, and there's enough meat in terms of content to justify the asking price.

The mood is dark, but there are some pretty fantastic lighting / volumetric effects and although assets are reused, every single level felt unique with its own atmosphere. Great job there. Sound is also good, with lots of ambient noise, machinery, gears.. love the Steampunk setting. Voice lines / messages are pretty well acted for an indy game which is definitely a good surprise.
In terms of gameplay however it is a bit disappointing. You only control a single character and the skill tree is quite limited. I liked the guns / ranged weapons and still had to alternate with melee weapons when ammo was sparse. Combat tries to avoid the 2-steps dancing that Grimrock abused by giving enemies all sorts of behaviors, dodging or distance attacks. You'll need to move around a lot, tanking any enemy in this game is still guaranteed death.
Monsters lack variety and by the end of the game you'll wish you stopped encountering the basic ones such as spiders or turtles. I wish the devs added 3-4 more types. Loot isn't very varied but you'll find upgrades and better versions for all equipment; clearly, as you control a single character, this isn't the game's best strength.
Finally a word about dungeon design, which can make or break a game of this genre. I thought it was pretty average; some levels are better than others, but overall it's a very linear design. Every level is pretty much self-contained ( there are a few exceptions ) and follows the same pattern: get access to the exit by finding a key or unlocking a mechanism. The end-game levels get a bit better. Puzzles also get tougher. Some of them are really fun, others are pretty frustrating. Secret buttons / switches are pretty hard to spot and I wish there was a skill or something to help detecting them, because they're very hard to spot visually, so if you don't want to miss anything you'll spend far too much time glancing at every nook & cranny. It doesn't help that some of these buttons are mandatory to progress in the main story.
So the game is far from perfect but I definitely had tons of fun with it. A well polished, well focused experience, which can be pretty difficult at some times - well worth its price.

Nidhogg absolutely
