Released on my 12th birthday in 1996, although I am just now getting to play it.
The episode "TNT - Evilution" is really good and would stand on its own as the core content for this expansion. Most of the music is new and it's amazing. Lots of fun.
The episode "The Plutonia Experiment" uses old music from DOOM I & II and the presentation suffers for this. Most know it as not being as good as Evilution but it's also quite hard so I'll reserve criticisms until I've made more progress in it, but it's obviously a bit rushed. I've also heard it described as "undecorated".
I think the whole of Final DOOM would have been better had Plutonia not been included, or some additional content had been included to round the experience out. A commercial expansion of the time, "Perdition's Gate" was said to have been in the running for inclusion within Final DOOM, but I guess they didn't finish it fast enough and were told the window had closed, so they formed Wraith to sell it on their own. What I mean to say is that the Final DOOM package may seem to lack cohesion. I prefer to think of Final DOOM AS Evilution, and The Plutonia Experiment being just what it's called, an experiment, albeit less polished, that TNT showed to id, and id said "okay we'll buy that too." SO, bonus content, really, and nothing more.
I started with Plutonia, until I read a review on GOG mentioning for difficulty scaling, start with Evilution, since Plutonia is harder, and after heeding his advice, I find myself appreciating FInal DOOM quite a bit more.
As for the name, is this the be-all, end-all DOOM experience. The Final chapter? The best it ever gets? Nope, not at all. As officially licensed mod content made by a team who arguably have better megawads on the net for completely free, FInal DOOM is just the beginning. But if you're not one to ♥♥♥♥♥ about paying for a mod, it's a great introduction.
I recommend running this game in the GZDoom source port, with dynamic lighting enabled manually in the INI, and Sergeat_Mark_IV's Ketchup mod on default settings. For maximum immersion I also suggest using Eternal DOOM Status Bar by Team TNT, from one of their other megawads. You can use SmoothDoom as well but I can't be arsed to tell if it's working or not yet. And if you can find a mod that changes the music, but only for Plutonia, go ahead and do that too.
Go buy this game. It's good. It's more DOOM, and if you've played DOOM, you probly want more of it. Now if you'll excuse me I need to go practice shooting demons in the face for when I die and go to hell.

I havent reviewed anything in a very long time but I thought this game was worth saying something about.
I've seen a few bad reviews and some good ones. It's early access too so there are going to be some bugs but after playing the game most of the night here's my conclusions.
It's free. Truly free. No ingame market place crap. It's fun as hell. No it's not perfect. Zombies spawn behind you. I can't yet figure out hout to respawan with a different class, etc etc. Those issues aside, let me repeat...it's 100% free and fun as hell.
It's built on old technology - source engine it seems, but so is Left 4 Dead and sure the game isnt anywhere near as polished as L4D but it's and indie game.
The mission structure and presmise is good. Essentialy you attempt to infiltrate a hive of zombies, plant a bomb and then attempt to get out. As soon as you plant the bomb the clock is ticking and the zombies will do their best to make sure you dont make it out before the explosion. it makes for tense moments.
I have tried to play online but cant seem to join a room so i have played it alone in single player up until now but even that was fun. So, If you are a fan of past paced survival games like L4D & Killing Floor then youll like this. It plays like CS Source naturally so the controls are perfect. CS Nexon Zombies is another free game that merges oldschool counterstrike with zomibes but Codename Cure does it very differently.
If you want a perfect and slick Triple 'A' title then dont download this game...if you want some free no-strings fun with guns and zombies then do. I DIG IT.

GUNPOINT
-You play as Richard Conway, a professional spy who uses cool gear that lets him jump--or fall--incredible distances. Right from the start you get pulled into a murder mystery, one where you are the primary suspect. Your contact has been murdered and the camera feed only caught footage of you inside the building. You have to work to clear your name, and in the process you have to make a lot of tough decisions.
-You can choose your own dialogue, some of it actually making an impact on how the game plays out.
-Depending on your choices, there are different paths you can take in the story.
-Gameplay is a combination of stealth and hacking. You can rewire circuits to perform different actions--like a light-switch opening a door--and the game does a good job of giving you plenty of options when using it. There are multiple gadgets you can use throughout the game, but if you really wanted to you could go with soley your wits and your hacking tool.
-The music is jazzy and awesome.
-Despite having the limitations of retro-style graphics, it captures the noir feel quite well.
-My first playthrough was about two hours, but it looks like it would be worth playing again. Multiple endings and the ability to go either non-lethal or lethal reinforce the idea of picking it back up.
FINAL VERDICT
-Fans of noir and jazzy sounds will enjoy this title right away. It has great charm in its writing--the dialogue is my favorite part of this game--and the story is actually quite good. It feels like a plot to a classic noir film, but this game puts its own twist on things with a unique setting (some point in the future, I'm guessing, but it never really clarifies). Puzzle platformers and stealth enthusiasts will find a lot to like here. Gunpoint is a quick ride, but replayability and sheer quality make it worth the asking price.

I haven't played this game for too long, as you can probably see, however, there are a bunch of problems that I can see right away, without delving too deep into the game- but there's also potential and stuff that I liked.
Regard the "Do you recommend this game?" rating as temporary, as the game feels very unfinished and thus I won't recommend it yet.
So, first of all, I'll rant a bit about a few problems that I've encountered-
- No feedback for hitting someone: The game doesn't really tell you when you've hit an enemy? of course, sometimes there's a huge message in the upmost part of your screen, saying "You hit Name" or "You beat: Name"- which is pretty charming, but, it doesn't appear always, and without it there is no telling to whether or not you actually dealt any damage.
- Shooting doens't feel fun enough: Which is something that many games manage to nail. This is part of a game's "feel" which is something that the devs should probably look a bit into.
- The snail: In one map, (that was actually a pretty nice map, with a lot of verticallity and unique ideas) there was a snail, in the middle of the map- it was an item of some sort. And even though, if you check by pressing tab, holding the snail gives you points, the game tells you nothing about that. How am I supposed to play without a goal? also, you can't drop the damn snail :c
- Class swapping is not immediate in your team's base.
- Shooting sounds too repetitive-Note to devs: since I know this game is developed in Unity, or can assume so because of the launch screen, try to randomize the pitch a very slight bit, perhaps.
- Shooting sounds are also too loud when a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of people are shooting
- Some maps allow people to camp from spawn, in capture the flag game mode :/ which is pretty annoying
- Geysers/Launch pads don't show the direction in which they'll launch you.
- Couldn't enter mech because I was a bunny? that's racist brah
- Also 2 out of 3 of the classes really seem like they are from TF2, but they work well so it's OK.
- I haven't gotten any crates yet, which feels not that rewarding. Perhaps the crate system is uncomplete though.
However, there are certain stuff that I liked:
+ Has few classes that can be focused, unlike similar class-based-shooters.
+ classes seem to be pretty balanced.
+ fights are pretty fun, even though shooting is slightly feedbackless.
+ Dem graphics
+ Some maps are designed really well in my opinion (some aren't).
+ No sprinting- which is unique and so far, I like it (even though I wouldn't want people to not be able to sprint in every game)
So, overall, I'd wait for the game to fix some bugs and actually feel somewhat more finished before playing it.
However, I do think it has potential to be a pretty fun game to play- I could totally see me and a bunch of friends playing this together sometime.

Gameplay: 8/10
Plays like Halo. Creative like Minecraft. Murder Miners takes two great features of two great games and puts them together rather nicely. Combat feels exciting, construction feels easy and versatile. It's rather impressive how well things work when these two features have taken years on their own to perfect. Now, putting them together, it's almost unbelievable a development team could join them into one production in such a proficient manner. This is defintely a game worth picking up if you like either of these things.
For instance, if you prefer construction, you can jump into survival (PvE) or infected (PvP) games and build barricades against a zombie onslaught. If that's not your thing, jump into the standard PvP section that still allows for some construction, but is mostly geared towrads blowing your enemies brains out. There's something for everyone here.
Now, in regards to AI, it can be really stupid sometimes. They'll get really dumb at ladders, soemtimes run into walls, and a few other really dumb things that make the zombie survival a lot easier. However, once a zombie gets you, it's basically over. Not to mention, Zombies are pretty dumb already. I guess this could be a pass, but AI is still bad AI.
Sound: 7/10
Sound FX are decent, music is pretty good. The whole thing is rather fresh on the rotten meter. It's all sufficient enough to make for an engaging experience, but it's not all that varied in regards to general world interaction, guns, and zombie effects. Either way, it works.
Graphics:6/10
Standard indie retro feel. That, mixed with the blocky emulation of Minecraft, make for something that could turn many people off. However, for those who don't mind that, it's a pretty good set-up that works on the lowest grade potato computers. Some optimization issues may cause a little bit of lag at times, but that's a matter of it being ported from Xbox 360's Indie Game shelf. At this point, the game should be running fine. So many updates, and future plans for a sequel, this is definitely one company that's fun to support. They know how to make a good product and keep at it.
Also, to make one more mention on the art, the skyboxes look great.
Enjoyment:7/10
Pretty dang fun. I've played more hours on Xbox than on PC, but I plan on putting more hours in on this sucker. It's a lot of fun, and especially fun when playing with friends. With such a low price, it's totally worthy purchasing.

This is a real digital trading card game, which can mean positive and negative depending on your expectation and background.
In summary, HEX is one of a few deep strategy, digital trading card game on the market.  For good or bad, you need to think this game as Magic the Gathering.  Compare to it, this game has potential to play real draft for free, cheaper, and similar to Magic has potential resell value of acquired collection.  However, this is not a game where you invest $0 and become champion on construct tournament even if you are the best Magic player.  Gaining expensive card takes some initial monetary investment or alternatively, hundreds of hours investment.
I'd recommend this game for anyone who wants to play real digital trading card game for long run, and make one go to dTCG for you.  First, start PvE and just have a fun and get the feel of the game.  Then try some Frost Ring Arena to get enough golds, and purchase 2  booster packs.  Try play evolution gauntlet and see if you like it.  If you truly enjoy the game at that point (probably over 20 hours into the game at this point), then consider purchasing some cards as investment to speed up your Frost Ring Arena run, or alternatively make decent construct deck to earn more rewards from ladder.  If you decided to leave the game later, at least you got some fun to that point (hopefully) and potentially even sell your collection to get some of money you spent back.

Yep. This is just exactly just more of Doom 2.
Yep. this is the same amateur\sequel\add-on style of level design of that era, with trolling, random riddles and giant unending levels. With the main idea being shoot more stuff coz shoot more stuff. Compared to base Doom 2 it is not even artistically coherent\correct and very gamey. Visually levels are pretty plain, uneventful and not memorable. And of course final boss would be an icon of sin which was bad even in the original. If you want just to play more levels for doom without regards to quality — it is for you.
It starts very strong, with some new visuals and new music, but then it slows down at 2\5 mark to be as generic, trolly and poor as plutonia, after which it suddenly has a row of extremely short and plain levels. And overall Evilution is not thematically coherent, having you run around prisons, offices, warehouses, sewers and other boring real-life stuff. Though, sometimes you can find something truly amazing and great between them. Something which is very doom with all it's cultural zeitgeist and non-explicit references. Some parts are even surpassing both original Doom 2 and the Doom itself, some levels are legitimately artistically and technically great. And the final level is somewhat improved, with dumb puzzles, cyberdemon fight, and icon of sin (yes, again) being more combat heavy and sensible. I was on the verge of recommending it, but this release crashes in one place, and it doesn't display evilution text screens, instead it just uses plutonia ones, so you will never see the story of this add-on.
They tried so hard, and got so far, but in the end, it doesn't even matter. Some great stuff is spoiled with bad parts, after which it's ruined by the release, and on top of that there is the plutonia's dead weight.

Update 12/9/2016:
So I've played this game since alpha and invested hundreds of dollars into, and for the first time since this game was open to non-backers, I am tenatively moving my recommendation from no to Yes.
The (Still) Bad:
To be clear, two of my biggest complaints with the game remain, the game is still extremely expensive, and the AH ,which could have helped to mitigate that, is still so outdated (surpising for such a new game) and a chore to use that it ends up serving the opposite purpose, making it feel, at least for me, both considerably more annoying and considerably more expensive to collect the cards I want then in digital card games with no trading but a discenchant and craft system.  Whether or not you want to argue that this game can still be played F2P or not, if you want to get even close to everything, you better be willing to spend in the thousands of dollars, and if you just want one really good deck, you better be willing to spend a couple hundred dollars, then go back to having nothing when key cards from it rotate out.  Its business model at its core is still a less easy to ever cash out MTG model and the primary thing that always kept that game niche was the price point so they've forever limited themselves to the same niche of players it seems.
The (New) Good:
But enough doom and gloom retread, what has changed that's made me finally recommend this game?  Well for one, the PvE content is finally taking shape.  The second chapter is live, and with it, there is finally enough meat to PvE for me to recommend this game to some one for whom PvE is likely to be the only format they'll ever really want to play.  It won't sustain you forever, but it feels like a enough to be worth your time instead of ending abrubtly just as it was starting to get good as it had before.  Whats more, a number of the core frameworks of the game are now live, such as account leveling and the mercenary party system, which combined with the already very creative and cool equipment system I feel really seperates Hex from other similar DTCG and make it a worth while and unique DTCG experience.
I should note that the game still is MTG at its core, the gameplay and rules aren't just inspired by MTG, they were flat out lifted from it with only the most subtle of changes here and there, and whether or not thats a good thing to you will be determined by whether or not you like MTG, HOWEVER, they HAVE finally made another huge change I've begged for for years which has improved the gameplay experience exponentially in my estimation.  For the first time, the game makes use of the digital medium to reduce the rate of outlier opening hand draws.  Basically, whatever the most likely number of shards (lands for MTG players) you are to draw is based on your deck composition, the system makes you more likely to draw that number and less likely to get really unlucky and draw none or too many.  This has dramatically increased the number of matches which are not obviously lost at the opening hand, while still allowing them to keep in the Mulligan mechanic, since everything is still technically random, only the worst case scenarios have been reduced (though if you had a deck with only 5 shards in 60, it would actually make you LESS likely to ever draw them in your opponent hand since drawing a shard would be the unlikely event it would reduce but I think thats a good thing personally).
The (Still) Okay:
My last update to this review had been to talk about the addition of a free Ladder to PVP with rewards, and I still stand by the fact that this was an essential addition which will be very good for the health of the game long term.  Unfortunately, in the short term, perhaps because of the size of the player base (or at least the ones interested in PvP), the ladder is a murder's row, where I've played numerous top tier decks in a row at the lowest ranking of said ladder.  Unless your willing to spend money on limited formats, or spend money to build a top tier deck, PvP is probably not even worth your time, which is still rather sad.
Final Thoughts:
The game IS fun, both single player and multiplayer (if you can find some one of similar skill and card ownership, which unfortunately is pretty tricky right now unless your willing to spend big).  And for the first time, I can say there's enough fun here for most types of players, that its actually worth recommending.  It does stil have some significant core flaws, but if the AH is ever upgraded those may be mitigated at least a little.  Will this game ever be a good F2P game, thats debatable, some might argue it is already, but I'm not one of them, this game feels like it expects you to invest at least a little to really be able to enjoy it.  But maybe, just maybe thats okay, for the quality of experience Hex is providing if you do make that investment.

Dawn of War was very succesful game of its time. It had great campain, music, gameplay mechanics etc. After quite good Dark Crusade and medicore Soulstorm came time to introduce some new ideas into franchise.
Did it went well? In general, yes. Apart from improved graphics,the biggest change was in gameplay - quality over quantity. I'll start with the campaing - there's no more base of operation, no more huge armies or resource managment and unit production - instead you're charged with commanding small force (4 units). At first it seemed like a bad idea, but, it is done great: each of mentioned units consist of squad leader(who is also one of pivotal characters in plot) and two members - exeption is your force commander. Each of this squads has its own special abilities, which proper usage is your key to victory. Terrain and cover is now much more important - units without one are quickly anihilated. So, game is  therefore much more tactical than previous series - the closest mechanics is in Company of Heroes - same usage of buldings, cover, and vehicle armour.
In addition to that, campaing offers also RPG elements - your squad leaders level up, unlock new abilites and gain new equipment, which can be chosen before mission. That's where the more strategic approach is required: equiping proper gear is often a key to victory, as securing (and maintaing key asstets).
So, in general, campaing balances well all of mention elements. Plot itself is interesting (pivoting around Tyranid infestation of Blood Ravens recruting worlds), your sqaud leaders are well voiced and interesting - they're often give you theirs opinion or discuss with each other about recent or past events - the same can be said about other characters in the game. Paradocsaly, the most boring character is your own protagonist - Force Commander, whom you supposed to be - he is basicly mute, and I had an impression, that he's completly redundant in all that rabble - unfortunatly he is always present during missions.
Other aspects of game heavly supports multiplayer  - even skirmish with CPU is in Multiplayer Tab, which seems weird to me. Skirmishes resemble old Dawn of war in more ways than campaing - you have your base of operation where you can build yuor units using good ol' requisition and energy. You are no longer have to build multiple buildings to gain access to desired units - all of them are summond in your HQ - the more powerful ones must be firstly unlocked. On energy points can be built a station and generators - but beware - if enemy capturers your station, he also can gain your generators. Req. points cannot be however fortified - in addition, it generates much more supplies, the longer you hold it-  how's that works out? Game became very dynamic - to reflect that, you always have access to your HQ menu (F1 or appropirate button) and all your squads (listed on right part of HUD). Additionaly, before you start, you can choose one of three available commanders - each of them reflects some of gameplay aspects (offence, defence, support) and can be further customized in skirmish to meet your needs. New addition to game are special abilities - there are 4 of them for each faction, and they can be used if you have enough might points - which are gained by killing enemies.
Another multiplayer aspect of game is Last Stand, which is action hero co-op versus endless waves of enemies.
As for the more technical aspects - I am a little disapointed by menu tree - it could be done much better. I.e.: after CPU skirmish I cannot return to skirmish menu - why? What is the point of throwing me back to main menu? Options also aren't very good - apart from the basic changes, I couldn't do much more. Also I had some issues with to small font from time to time.
To sum up: DoW II is great game with superb campaing, and great gameplay - if your fan of both Company of Hearoes and WH40K universe, it is game definitly for you. As a single player oriented gamer I'm not very fond of lots of multiplayer additions (BTW, thats also reason why I'm concentrated on single player in this review), but that is quite understandable - after all it is core of RTS gaming.

FULL DISCLOSURE:
Yu-Gi-Oh! was one of the very first anime I watched as a kid, I created my first youtube account in 2007 to subscribe to Yu-Gi-Oh! Abidged, and I was active in the TCG until 2014 when they released Pendulum monsters. Needless to say, Yu-Gi-Oh! is my crack of choice, and Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Links scratches that itch.
The Good:
+A Limited card pool which, while it does use some of the newer cards/archetypes, completely excludes Synchro monsters, Xyz monsters, Pendulum monsters, and Link monsters. This makes the game feel a lot more accessible to newcomers or to people who have been out of the scene in a while.
+Duelist Skills are a fairly unintrusive way of making each player character feel unique without being *completely* game changing (at least until higher levels.) It's been fun using an old favorite like Neo the Magican Swordsman in my Yami Yugi deck and feeling like he actually had decent attack power due to Yugi's field spell Power of Dark.
+The returning English voice cast from the 4Kids series made me feel right at home. Kaiba and Bandit Keith especially have some quotable lines in this game.
+It's Yu-Gi-Oh!
The Bad:
-The interface is clearly designed for touchscreens and mobile phones, and can be frustrating to navigate sometimes. This gets most annoying in the deck builder, which needs a MAJOR UI overhaul.
-Like all F2P games, the grind is designed to slowly become more and more difficult/time consuming to incentivize you to spend real $ on the game. I have not spent any money on the game so far, and I was able to open Dark Magician of Chaos and Blue-Eyes Ultimate Dragon fairly quickly, but I'll be damned if I have anything resembling a competive PVP deck any time soon.
-On the same note, quests like "do 8 tribute summons in one duel against Tea" or "Raise your LP to more than 6000 in a duel against Ishizu and beat her using only effect damage" are not fun and only make me feel like I'm throwing garbage that has nothing to do with my actual deck into my deck just to complete them.
-currently no way to play as Duke Devlin

Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Links is a game that helped remind me how much I enjoyed Yu-Gi-Oh! growing up as a kid.
But then it reminded me of why I stopped playing Yu-Gi-Oh.
Duel Links (DL) has a compelling tutorial, giving players an opportunity to take control of one of the legendary duelists you watched growing up as a kid. Hearing Eric Stuart's voice as Seto Kaiba command a Blue Eyes White Dragon to lay waste to it's enemy is a cathartic experience, through and through. The whole of the voice actors do a great job in giving you that taste of Yu-Gi-Oh you've been quietly craving for a long time (though some certainly sound rusty). The beginning stages of the game do a fantastic job in getting you into it all, that spirit of "Let's DUEL". Granted, the AI at first does nothing but play lousy monsters in attack position, but it's still an exciting feeling, nonetheless.
The reduction of deck size to 20-30 cards is a stroke of genius. It shortens the duels, makes the starting hand that much more important, and still allows for flexible deck-building and strategies. The smaller field, while jarring, is a good addition to accompany the reduction in deck size, and increases the importance of effect zone usage. The duelist skills are also excellent ideas, because it gives players a chance to gain the edge in PvE and PvP modes. My preferred choice is Bandit Keith's "Sleight of Hand" skill, which gives the player a powerful equip spell, which can help turn around a pretty hopeless situation, and Seto Kaiba's "Beatdown", which buffs all your monsters for each Level 5 or higher monster Kaiba has on the field at any given point, giving you a potential 2700 combined attack point bonus.
A big draw to this game is that it seems like it's making an excellent gameplay choice, dumping off of a decade's worth of power creep that the TCG has gone through while keeping the effective rule changes, and it allows old duelists to slip into it all like an old dueling glove, while giving them something to learn and adapt to without text dumping them in oblivion, and current players to simply shift back their cards a few generations. However, this strategy hasn't eliminated the general playing styles of Yu-Gi-Oh PvP players: the spamming of Level 4 1900 attack point beaters and attack buffs, or running a powerful set of cards that have their effects happen so quickly you can lose track of what's even happening. So it makes playing PvP a dangerous roulette wheel of "fun" and "teeth-grinding aggravation". However, it is quite amusing to outplay someone using one of these strategies with your own, and it gives you a great feeling of accomplishment.
DL's PvE, however, begins running into the same sort of walls that all Yu-Gi-Oh games have when it's time to graduate into your mid-tier and high-tier AI decks. Meaning that instead of creating decks with a couple of strategies and supporting cards, they wield the dreaded "gimmick" decks, that rely on uncreative strategies that force all-round decks into corners because their one gimmick can only really be opposed with few, if any, serious strategies. At first, it's that Thousand Dragon deck with Time Wizard and Time Machine, then it's that Super Roboyaro fusion deck. Then you discover the world of hurt that is the "Reverse Trap" deck, and you're suddenly reminded why you stopped playing Yu-Gi-Oh games in the first place. There is just no counter to the gimmick decks, and you start to get tired of yet another PvP duel where your opponent is Joey with the "Field of Warriors" skill, spamming Mechicalchasers and X-Saber monsters with "Sword of Dragon's Soul".  It gets boring, and it gets frustrating, but that's a grind you're either up for, or not.
However, as a Free to Play game, with a very casual tone that most anyone can enjoy, I would still recommend this game to anyone who can stomach the grind. It's a visually acceptable game, and if you want to re-live your dueling days of old, this one is for you.

The most obvious comparison for this is Gone Home. Both are about young women coming back to a large house of eccentric design, filled with secret passages and hidden doors, and trying to find out what became of the family that lived there, using books and correspondence to discover clues.
While Edith Finch is a lot more visually imaginative (the comic book sequence, the cannery kingdom...) the gameplay is a lot more dull and straightforward. In Gone Home one feels like an amateur detective finding clues and piecing together a mystery but here all sense of agency is gone. Walk in to a room and the game directs you to what you should be looking at. Read a book and you're treated to essentially a one-button minigame. The cannery sequence might look great but gameplay-wise you're essentially just walking forward. If Gone Home felt like being part of an immersive theatre experience where one can rifle through the characters' things to find out more about them, this feels like an animated film where the W button must be held down to keep it playing.
There's a lot to like here and it's fun while it lasts but it doesn't feel anywhere near as satisfying a gameplay experience as a lot of similar games.

This game is absolutely brilliant. While only two of the four main characters are playable right now, those two are quite well polished, and not only do they have their own distinct playstyles, but separate personalities as well. Wyatt is, well, angry, angry at the goddesses for how they treat humans and angry at the demons and angels for working with them. Unlike many characters like him, his anger is also reflected in how he acts around his friends. He may not be attacking them or insulting them, but he speaks in small amounts and doesn't give off the feeling that he particularly likes pretty much anyone except for Reina, the other character that can be played right now. Reina, on the other hand, was raised as a monk and acts quite differently than Wyatt. Where Wyatt sees angels and demons and attacks them on sight, Reina will often ask them to let her pass first. She's more polite and more controlled, and often seems to wish that she could avoid many of the fights that happen.
As far as the gameplay goes, not only do the two offer very different playstyles from the start, but the unlockable weapons add more variation from there. My personal favorite was a bow and dagger that Wyatt could unlock- it couldn't break blocks nor could you block while using it, but the added range and speed worked very well with my playstyle, even more so when I upgraded the bow to poison targets. Overall, the game is very well done, particularly for a game that's still a work in progress. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes combat platformers.

Abyssal City is like a hack and slash Castlevania game with 4 different characters (each with different playstyles), 3 skill trees, and an attribute allocation based leveling system. With the skill trees and attribute points you can customize a character as you see fit. Specific gear you find is also based also caters to the three skill trees. This allows you to play in various different ways. Magic abilities also change their effects based on where you position them in your ability slots. So the same spell being placed in your Up+Magic Attack and Down+Magic Attack will have completely different actions.
The game has a story that seems to go throughout the game as well, and so far it isn't something to write home about but it's nice that its there. Overall the game has a very fun atmosphere and with 4 different difficulty settings you can easily find a nice place to set your own challenges. You'll also find mini-platform/time based challenges in some rooms that lead to huge rewards. Normally I find this sort of thing frustrating but I have found it to be an enjoyable challenge so far in this game. Boss fights can also be fun and unique as they seem to have their own very unique abilities and ways of defeating them.
With a controller the game handles very well and plays with very few problems. I have not tried the keyboard option but these games usually don't work well with one. The music is also pretty top notch.
I recommend this to anyone who enjoyed any of the Side-scrolling Castlevania games, especially if you like the idea of building your character the way you want.

The walking in this game drove me insane. This game took me 6 1/2 hours to complete, probably half of that time was fighting worthless enemies and boring backtracking. Vaporum is a very straight-forward 1st person dungeon crawl including all the standard features of the genre.  Here you will find pits, switches, puzzles, fireball traps, teleporters, and all the other goodies we have come to expect from games like this.  What sets it apart, then?
The setting and atmosphere.  Vaporum appears to have been heavily inspired by the original Bioshock,  with more steampunk thrown in for good measure.  The story of what happened in the abandoned facility is revealed to the player gradually through old notes left in text and, as was the case in Bioshock, recorded messages from various employees who worked there.  Thus far I am intruiged and curious to learn more, which is always a good sign.  I can also say there are a few moments that will get your heart pounding!
Combat is quite difficult on the default setting.  You will definitely have to be both nimble and clever if you intend to survive, for healing is in very short supply!  This brings me to one point I don't quite approve of:  If you run short of healing items, you may find yourself simply unable to continue.  The only remedy would be to start over from the beginning on a lower difficulty.  It is possible to gain access to vampiric attacks to help alleviate this, but the first opportunity for this is not until you are several hours into the game.
Overall, Vaporum is an excellent entry into the genre so long as you don't mind the difficulty!

Each class has a primary weapon and a secondary pistol (or pistols in the case of the Point-Man), and a utility. Support has a resupply crate that can also be used for cover. Specialist has a sentry gun that has infinite ammo, but must be picked up to heal it. Assault and Point-Man both have HE-Grenades for crowd control, and the Sniper has an incendiary that can be used for area denial.
Despite all that, the game lacks depth.
There are only 4 levels at the time of this writing, and they're decorated very sparsely.
A few crates here, a vending machine there, and always a zombie around each corner.
Each level has the same objective, go to bombsite, plant bomb, travel alternate route back to insertion point before bomb timer runs out and extract from the area. A pretty good objective, but if it's all we've got to play, it gets old after a while.
There are 2 types of zombies, the standard squishy type, and your stereotypical slow but tanky variety. There's no issue with that, but it seems like there are only 4 or 5 different models for the normal zombies, so frequently you find hordes of zombies that all look the same.
All in all, it's a pretty good game, definitely worth the lack of price.

I've just finished the game at 15 hours, and it was an enjoyable experience (mostly) throughout! I have a few gripes, but let's start with a list of Pro's and Con's and go into more detail a little later.
It was actually hard to come up with those cons, because the experience was a very positive one when looking back at it! That alone earns a recommendation, but I'd like to go into detail about some of the above notes. When I say that the
, I mean that in both combat and riddle-mancy! There's a block pushing puzzle in one of the first areas that totally blew my brain out; the solution wound up rather simple but it might have been better a little higher up in the levels. Similarly, there are a few enemies you fight at certain points that are very overwhelming and could probably use a difficulty pass. As I understand it, there's going to be one of those two days after I write this (in a patch), so maybe this will become moot!
As for the
the value only increases if you're the kind of person who likes to hunt for secrets diligently and/or do multiple playthroughs. There's an achievement to speedrun the game in 90 minutes, but I think even repeated playthroughs would still take 6 - 8 hours when you know where you're going and what to do (if you're taking your time). As for
, there are
that are chosen by something called a Rig at the beginning of the game.
One of them is Gadget-oriented, a bit like a mage, and you will pick up two Gadgets rather early on in the game to start you off. They do things like shoot lightning, launch fire forward, spit out poison, etcetera - more or less like spells, and they even use a mana-type system called Energy. At the time of writing, regenerating it can be a hassle and that makes Gadget-type playthroughs a little annoying... But that, again, is apparently going to be addressed in the upcoming patch.
The other two are combat- and then tank-oriented, with the combat-oriented Rig being my favorite. It causes every third attack to deal bonus damage, which makes it the cut-and-dry best in my opinion, but your mileage may vary. The tanking Rig causes you to reflect damage a percentage of the time and even ignore some of it while at low HP, but I didn't spend a lot of time at low HP, so... Not that great for my playstyle. Speaking of playstyles, they do throw in a few tricks that make the typical square-dance maneuver from Grimrock 1 (and some enemies in 2) difficult. I liked that!
As for the cons... There are three
that come to mind, and most of that is thanks to the lack of any kind of hint. Grimrock 2 was kind enough to give you a name for most puzzles that often times clued you in to their nature, but the storyline in this game sssort of prevents that kind of fourth wall breakage. That means you're sometimes left with whatever you can see with your eyes, and in one or two cases there didn't appear to be anything to see at all... I just had to bash my head against the wall until something worked. It still didn't detract from the experience a whole lot, though.
as mentioned above, which means they take a lot of hits before they go down and can be sort of annoying because of that. It does make you have to target-pick in large ambushes, as obviously you're not going to attack the giant sponge first and get yourself cornered. That part's fine, but they could do with a slight nerf (or your damage with a slight buff) in my opinion. There was only one enemy that felt like it had way too much HP, and that was a boss, so it's whatever.
The fact that it
might actually be a Pro for some people, but it's not for me. I don't really like crawling through an area I've already completed checking every wall for the secrets I've missed, so I... Didn't! I finished the game with about half of them found, and they were (to the developers' credit) mostly NOT those types of secrets. There are some that are more reliant on observational awareness. Things like, "Hey, that background pipe has a valve on it-- So does that one. I should turn these!" I liked those a lot.
Finally, there's
. That's fine and dandy, to be honest, and there's still plenty to work with, but yeah. You've got Blunt and Blade one-handers, then Blunt two-handers (Blade two-handers maybe incoming in a later patch?), Pistols, Rifles, and Shotguns. The Gadgets I mentioned before use your 1 - 4 hotkeys and are available to all Rigs, they're just flat better on the Gadget-oriented one. You can pull some wonky things are higher levels like dual-wielding two-handers and fun things like that. I suspect that's one of the stronger builds, but I'll have to test!
And I will, in my second run where I get all the secrets. It's a good game! Pick it up, for sure - the developers seem active on the Community Hub Discussion Board and similarly eager to patch the game around reviews like this one. It's got my recommendation!

You Must Build a Boat, or YMBAB, has a very similar concept and gameplay to the first game 10,000,000. In YMBAB, you have to link 3 of a kind in at grid box, by movint either a column or row, by clicking and moving the row or column. There are different kinds of blocks, namely: swords, staffs, shields, keys, crates, strong arms, and brains. You can also get items that drop and can be used along the way as well. The more in a row you link, the better the result. Using these blocks you have kill creatures and open chest to proceed through the 'dungeon'. At you home base/boat, you are able to upgrade these blocks or tiles, to enhance them, as well as being able to buy monsters to help you along the way. The main difference from the first game is the monsters, as well as the horn that allows the monsters to help you in the dungeon,  by stampeeding anything in their way. The horn is not triggered by the player, but rather has a bar that builds up until it is used. I have had lots of fun playing both this one and the first game, and it is a nice game to just enjoy as you kill everything in your path.

The game is a lot like Bayonetta in a good way, aside from the surface elements of scantily clad female protagonists, you've got a pretty similar setup for the gameplay and it even has something along the lines of witch time dodging on two of the characters. If you like over the top Japanese action games, you'll probably like this with a couple caveats.
PROS:
Crazy fun combat that has more depth to it than you might initially assume
Varied enemy design
Has the option for Japanese audio (and text even)
Strange but super fun music
CONS:
Huge info dump on how to do absolutely everything in the gameplay right when you start, you will not be able to memorize all of it at once and I'm not sure if there's a way to bring it back outside of restarting. I restarted and took pictures of the screens to use as reference for later.
Dialogue moves super slow and you can't speed it up without skipping it entirely, I usually end up doing that
Not a very high budget game so don't expect a lot of scripted action sequences outside of boss fights
Environments look like they belong on the PS2 (very low detail/resolution)
Some port problems, it runs fine for me but if you have a monitor greater than 1080p it will still only display at 1080
Enemies will sometimes get stuck in the geometry, this hasn't broke the game though since it just makes them very easy
NEUTRAL:

Vaporum, the steampunk dungeon crawler.
Vaporum showed up on my feed the day it came out which also happened to be my birthday, and being a dungeon crawler fan i thought hell yea lets give this a go. NOT AT ALL DISAPPOINTED THAT I DID!
Story. This game starts off with a great introduction into what to expect for the entire game. You cannot remember anything about who you are, how you got to where you did, or what this giant tower of steel and steam is. The door at the base opens, and thats where we take control. Immediately the tone is set. You're alone here, and the notes left behind by the former occupants of the tower are setting the stage for the tragedy that happened here. Things feel familiar to your character, but he has no idea why....
I will say, that i wasnt at all surprised by the ending, but i DID go out of my way to find as many of the notes spread throughout the tower and listened to all the audio logs (i love that stuff, its normally some of the most interesting things you can find in RPGs.)
Once you get past the first floor (a nice tutorial section to get acquainted with minor puzzles and combat) the real game begins. Combat can be frenetic and strategic, enemies have many different attack patterns, and the floors layouts will both help and hinder in coralling the enemies in. Expect to get standard dungeon crawler traps. Doors will close behind you when you enter a room, opening a chest will cause multiple enemies to spawn behind you, enemies will wait behind doors and boot you across the room when you open them, you get the idea. Most enemies movements and patterns are easy to read, and if you pay attention to your surroundings, you can usually avoid getting pinned in a corner. I say usually because the game is not always that fair about some encounters. Acid bugs are absurd, they have humongous damage potential, and their health is far too high for how quick they move and attack and how much damage they deal. They also continue to scale up with each floor, and are one of the most unfair enemies in the game. There are quite a few spots too, where you are forced to stand in puddles from them, becuase they come out in a hallway and you have no choice but to take the hits from them. The majority of the other enemies are varied, have decent telegraphs, and can be a lot of fun to deal with. Ranged battles are not free either, as many enemies have ranged attacks of their own, have ways to quickly close a gap, or in some cases, literally drag you across the map to them. You wont find yourself bored with combat overall.
Puzzles. This is a dungeon crawler. Expect standard dungeon crawler puzzles. Block pushing puzzles, button pushing puzzles, movement based puzzles, they are all present. I found many of them to be pretty interesting overall. There are a couple of obnoxious puzzles that are tedious, and one puzzle that is so bad, i told the developer we could no longer be friends over XD. If you are used to dungeon crawler puzzles, there isnt anything remarkably new or novel, but they are well executed, and i found myself never feeling so stuck that i couldnt progress.
There is ONE puzzle that i have absolutely no idea what i did to progress (a dark area with weird sounds behind a teleporter) but i got it in the end, and moved on feeling like, i have no idea what i did, but i did it. Overall puzzles are exactly what to expect from a dungeon crawler, and outside of a couple bad ones, will present a good challenge to most players.
I spoke with the devs about it on the fourms, but they pulled off a section of the game that changes the rules entirely and really makes the player react to situations entirely differently. It was one of my favorite sections in the entire game, and rather than spoil what it is or how it goes about it, i will say that those who have played the game know exactly what section i am referring to, and for new players you have something really fun to look forward to.
There is a lot of variety to how you can build your character, and while the upgrades in equipment are largely linear, the weapons do have different strengths and the games upgrade system causes the player to focus on a couple of skill paths. The variety in weapon types, as well as the options for sword & board, or dual wield, or two handing, or focusing entirely on "gadgets" there is enough variety here to warrant multiple playthroughs because the combat forces you to play differently simply based on what your build is. I do feel like a couple of skills are GROSSLY overpowered (armorer final skill im looking at you), the upgrades do give the player something to look forward to as opposed to just straight damage or armor uprades.
Overall, Vaporum does a fantastic job of adding a new entry into the dungeon crawling genre that sadly doesnt get enough entries these days. I might not be entirely correct, but i believe their team consisted of 4 people and they did an amazing job. I highly recommend that players who enjoy dungeon crawlers give this game a go. It doesnt change the playing field in massive ways, but it does add another strong entry into the genre, and it is priced fantastically for the content provided in the game.
I say this is a solid 8/10 and once some of the balance issues are fixed, this could easily be an 8.5 with potential for a 9 if they decide to add in any extra areas or expand on the weapons in the game (two hand swords please?)
This review is based off of the original release build of the game, and i know they have some balance patches coming in the near future which should address some of the bogus hp values and ridiculous damage output of some of the enemies.

TL:DR: An arguably unfair duo of MegaWADs that the hardcore fans might want to grit their teeth on for a challenge.
Final DOOM is a series of 2 32-level MegaWADs produced by members of Team TNT that were released by id Software as a full spinoff game to DOOM II. The first WAD, TNT: Evilution, was made by all the members of the team, while the second, Known as the Plutonia Experiment, were made solely by two people to add on to the product.
The question remans; is this game good? The answer: Somewhat.
Unlike the earlier Master Levels collection that kept things mostly manageable, Final Doom has levels that require insanely low kill-times to ensure your survival. While this can be done, the major problem remains in its rediculous amount of Chaingun-guys and Revenants that pepper you with bullets and homing rockets in areas with little to no cover. This could be awesome for those looking for a test of grit, to me it hamers down an otherwise solid set of levels and, in particular, TNT: Evilutions killer original soundtrack. Give this a go if you're looking for a WAD with a challenge or if it came in the affordable Doom bundle; otherwise, it can be left alone.

Top-notch visuals! Runs great in 4k (I had to enable hardware cursor, otherwise there was a tiny delay in mouse movement recognition.
Fantastic audio! Clanking gears, rushing water pipes, the tapping of mechanical legs against the floor, coming to hunt you down!
Story is sort of vague and generic, at least in the beginning. But a few minutes in, you start uncovering notes and audio logs, so you will be learning about the crew as you play.
Combat is real-time, with attacks having different cooldown periods. Even your basic swing of a knife or crowbar has a 1 or so second cooldown, meaning you can't spam click attack. Distance is measured in tiles. 1 tile for melee, and 3 or 4 for various ranged weapons.
Even though it is real-time, it's sort of "simulated real time". If you sit there and just keep clicking to attack while standing still, you and the enemy will pretty much be trading hits back and forth at a 1:1 ratio...(maybe not exactly 1:1, because different enemies do appear to have different attack speed, but so far from what I've seen, it's pretty close.)
Which leads me to my next point....
Movement! And well, map (or room) awareness. (Note: I have not played with the automap yet, so I can't speak for it, at least not yet.)
Attack Timing / Movement / Room awareness play a HUGE role in combat. Know your tiles, your enemy types/weapon types, and you will be much more successful.
For instance: The first type of enemy you come across is this flying mechanical thing that lunges to hit you. But it sort of "rears back" before lunging. Let it come to you. As soon as it gets within 1 tile, swing your melee weapon to hit it, then instantly back up 1 tile, and the thing will lunge at you and miss, then immediately step forward 1 tile again. Repeat this process with the right timing, and you will avoid 100% damage. At least from that enemy type.
Now, this enemy is easy once you get the hang of it. Different enemies move/attack faster, or maybe at range, or AoE, etc. Each new enemy will bring a new method of combat, and each have their own "best way" to take them down. The fast little spider things are best kited around in a square-like pattern. You can avoid damage from them, but it's a little more difficult to master than the flying thing.
Bottom line - I can't stress Attack timing / Movement / Map Awareness enough. Because you don't get repair kits that often, and you don't want to put yourself in a bad situation when you can't progress!

I remembered Aveyond not because I've played it (RPG isn't really my favorite genre but I can appreciate some of them) but because I was also looking for small games in order to add them into a database.
So, yeah, after some hesitation, I finally added all the games available on Steam (safe for the one that was just released). So here I am, after the big storm about achievements, guiding Mel, a young thief, that happened to be a descendant of an evil sorcerer, getting sucked into the evil plan of the Lord of the Twilight, a vampire ready to destroy your world. But well, Mel finds some allies in Edward, the Prince of Thais, in Stella, a girl that lost her memories, in Tej'Ilal, the sister of the Lord of the Twilight and in Galahad, her husband that refuses to admit that he's now dead and a vampire.
Aveyond 3-1: Lord of Twilight has ties with the previous games (Arhiman's Prophecy and Rhen's Quest if I'm not mistaken) and is the first chapter of 4 episodes. And despite being a chapter and ending a little abruptly for me, the story is well written and filled with humor. Mel is using sarcasm because of her life, Edward is very friendly and Stella is kinda naïve while Galahad is harboring a grudge towards Tej'Ilal, reminding him with sarcasm too of his condition, though she's more leaning for the peace than the destruction.
Also, this chapter is also set to learn about the mechanisms. As any good RPG, you can make a team, level them up thanks to combat (and well, even if not used, the characters are also leveling up), unlock spells for the mage and the healer, change their weapons or clothes so that their characteristics can be improved. You have also an inventory with scrolls, food, potions, etc.. to use during a battle (or not) to heal or to help hurting opponents in front of you. Some of them are tough - sometimes, the best is to come back later with a better team (the Poltergeist is an example).
Some quests needs to be done in order to advance in the story, while they're appearing as being a side-quest just for the money (like the tragic love story to find). Others are just bonus. But given the fact that you need money to buy stuff or to fast-travel, any quest is worthy to be done. Besides, when defeating enemies, you can loot them and find also money or items. You have also chests to open or bags to find.
Aveyond comes also with three difficulties: Easy where you're stronger and where most of the enemies don't spawn again after a defeat (yeah, I'm playing in this difficulty), Normal where every is balanced and Hard where you'll die more frequently - though even in Easy, I've been wiped. Well, if a character dies, you can ressucitate them but if your team is wiped, it's game over and it's up to you to load the auto-save (when entering a new screen) or a save of yours.
As I've said, the developer of Aveyond is well-known in the RPG Maker world and Aveyond is based on that. Don't forget that the game was released around 2009, so, it's normal to have these graphics that are very good but can sometimes give the feeling of "old game". The soundtrack is also correct.
I was very surprised to like the game and was disappointed when it ended. However, knowing that Gates of Night is the direct sequel and that my save at the end of Lord of Twilight can be found by the sequel and that I can continue like that is a great feature. Also, I was kinda asking myself when the game will end, because I felt like it was a long one. Indeed, it's taken me nearly 9 hours to reach the end, so yeah, while you can think that the price is high, I understand it.
Seriously Aveyond 3-1: Lord of Twilight is enough for newbies in the RPG world or people that don't like to micro-manage a character or having sheets without end. I understand now why Aveyond was a reference back then. Don't hesitate!

Angrily, you kick the wall and hurt your foot as your fellow marine laughs at you to your expense but suddenly the battle turns silent. You turn to your fellow marine who has a distressed look on her face as you signal to go in and rendezvous with your commander. This game builds of the roots of Legend of Grimrock. In that game, there was this weird combat loop where you could squaredance around an enemy to attack them without taking damage. Of course, this was a core part of the gameplay loop but it wasn't really expanded on and it was sort of an accidental result of the realtime gid-based movement, which didn't really serve the game.
On the other hand, Vaporum is designed around this mechanic. Different enemies have different kinds of attack patterns. For instance, one of the enemy types will summon a 9-tile damage attack on a cooldown of a couple seconds. When fighting this enemy, you have to be constantly thinking ahead a couple seconds ahead, making sure that when the next attack happens you have a safe tile to move to. Other enemy types have firearms and can instantaneously damage you from afar. When fihgting these enemies you have to keep track of where everybody is and maneuver yourself to avoid being in the line of sight of any of them. Other enemies hurl projectiles and create temporary damage floors, and there are also immobile turrets which can turn to face four directions and will fire after a short delay once you pass in front of them. On the one hand you have to make sure that when you cross this turret's path, you aren't blocked in from the other side, but you can also exploit this enemy to damage other enemies. All these combinations of enemies, fought in various types of combat spaces, make every encounter unique. It becomes a very strategic game, where you're in big trouble if you maneuver yourself wrong.
You yourself also have a few kinds of "spells" which have different damage patterns, like ranged atttacks, a fire attack which hits two tiles in the direction you're facing (inflictinga debuff which causes damage over time to themselves and any adjacent enemies), and different types of 9-tile AOE attacks (one does instant damage plus inflicting a damage over time debuff that also halves their damage, which is good for minimizing damage when you get surrounded, while another spell doesn't do direct damage but creates an acid floor in a 9-tile area, which continually damages your enemies, which can do more damage but only if your enemies stay in the acid for the whole duration). You can maximize your damage potential by using these attacks smartly, hitting as many enemies as possible while avoiding getting surrounded at the same time.
There are a few different builds you can try, changing your playstyle. The RPG side of things is pretty simplified, the focus of this game is really execution. It is a very skill-based game. It is also very difficult, putting you into many situations much tougher than what you get in Grimrock. Also, oftentimes an encounter will kick your♥♥♥♥♥multiple times until you realize there is a smarter way to approach the situation, for example, not aggroing every enemy at once, or using a set of double-doors to lure one enemy away from the others first, or using a turret to help damage your enemies. Oftentimes you could not have known the best way to approach an encounter the first time through. There are many encounters that are brutal if you were not already aware of the layout of the area and where the enemies come from. That's why I think this is a game where you should definitely save often. The game is hard enough where the encounters seem to be balanced around a player that already knows how the encounter plays out. Some of the fun is in figuring out how a particular encounter works, and conquering it after a few tries.
The game has no checkpoints, although it auto-saves at the beginning of each floor. There is an option, and corresponding achievement, which disables saving so you can only restart from the beginning of the level.
The graphics are quite good, although some walls look not so good. You can tell this was made by a small team, from things like how items don't have any models when placed on the ground (anything placed on the ground will appear as a sack containing your item, unlike in Grimrock where every item has a unique model). Some of the assets don't look great. But the lighting is nice, and mechanical enemies break apart into pieces when you destroy them which is pretty satisfying. The aesthetic is pretty good, I like the big clunky humanoids, it's just like bioshock again.

Codename CURE is a first person, co-operative zombie game with support for up to five players, providing immersive, fast-paced zombie fragging with fully dynamic and objective- based missions.
That’s how the developer/publisher Hoobalugalar_x describes his game. It’s really none of my business, but I don’t like the fact that this single guy gets both titles when other people worked on this game too. They really should have made a team name. They could have just said the developer and publisher was “Codename CURE Team” or something. People do that a lot, this guy with his terrible username decided that wouldn’t work for me. But, like I said it’s none of my business and it’s not relevant to the game itself, which is what I’m reviewing.
Let me start off by saying that this game is “early access” and even though quote on quote “There are a number of planned improvements for the game, including additional game mode(s), levels, and friendly AI improvements.” I’m still going to try to kick the♥♥♥♥♥of this modification for Half-Life 2.
Going into that, yes this game is obviously on the Source Engine hence the name of this video series. But, I’ve never seen a game on Steam that’s so blatantly on the Source Engine. The second I saw this banner on the Steam homepage I knew it was. Because of the models, textures and the skybox trees in the background that make the picture look incredibly lazy. The photo shopped muzzle flash and bullet streak didn’t hint that at me, but it hinted at the laziness.
Through my experience playing this game I didn’t notice any custom map textures or models. The only custom content you’ll see in this game is an X decal, the weapons, and the player models. The zombie models I’ve seen before. I could be wrong though, and the textures could be modified a bit, but the base model and texture are not theirs. The weapons look awfully familiar as well. The animations for some of the weapons are for sure not theirs, most are taken from Counter Strike Source. As for the playermodels, I’m a little stumped on that. I don’t want to search around Gamebanana, ModDB, or other games that would have soldier models to try to find these. I wouldn’t have commented on them with being taken from somewhere else if I didn’t see one soldier is actually a Chinese soldier, and the other one is a European or American soldier? The setting wouldn’t give that away, the game possess no atmosphere and no interesting level design. Its click a button, a door opens and you move on. You also have a Counter-Strike Source bomb activity that seems out of placed and just an easy way to add another objective activity rather than opening doors and moving forward in a very VERY linear space. The game claims to have advanced AI, but I didn’t see any difference to the AI then I would from any other Half-Life 2 mod with zombies. They see you and they move towards you. Then hit you. It’s not like they can jump or climb.
I don’t want to say, you’re better off playing this game, but you’re better playing Zombie Panic Source (which is free) left 4 dead or Contagion. This game is like a zombie movie that you’ve seen 1,000 of. Zombies are overused enough already, just pass on playing this game. I can’t recommend this game to anyone. But, if you want to try it out yourself though, it’s free and it’s only roughly 3 gig.
Its good but a little expensive. Fast pace games and great to play with other people. Can't see how this is fun if you play by yourself.

I got this game as part of the Humble Game Making bundle, and the best I can say about it is that it's a great template for what NOT to do when creating your own RPG.  The characters are cliche, the heroine unlikeable, and the plot is barely there.  Although there is an overworld map that you can stumble upon at times, it can't actually take you anywhere in this game, so the only way to progress is to either use the expensive and inconvenient fast-travel system, or resign yourself to endless bakctracking throughout the game world in an attempt to find out where you're supposed to go and what you're supposed to do next.
Even though this game, as an old-school RPG, begs to be played with a controller, you're far better off using the mouse.  This is because the game's terrain is designed with multiple twists, turns, and crooked paths, while the control scheme only permits you to move about in the 4 cardinal directions.  Therefore, it's much easier to just click a point of the map, and let the game take you there automatically, instead of rocking the joystick back and forth trying to get there yourself.
Although this was only part 1 of a 4 part game, I have no desire to play through the other three parts, nor through any other game in the series.  If I had paid the list price for this game, I'd be demanding my money back.

If 10,000,000 isn't enough, you get "You Must Build A Boat".
Just like it previous game, "You Must Build A Boat" is a match-3 puzzle game with an addition mix of RPG elements.  You goal is simple, you fight in the dungeon using match-3 to gain golds and materials, then use them to improve yourself and your boat, once you done with one area you onto the next, until you ungrade everything.
EightyEightGames did a really great job on improving the mechanic of this game.  Unlike the first game, the items you can use in this game is actually useful for many situations.  Also special magic tiles is now available to give you more choice on how to fight the monster.
The improvement come a little downside for me.  I feel the game became is a little too fast pace, most of the time, I end up trying to match whatever possible without looking the current objective.  It work most of the time but it take the fun away when it turn into just another match-3 puzzle.
If you do have a choice between this and the phone version, I would say get the phone one.  The game probably work better on a smaller screen.  Either way, for the listing price, I would definitely recommend this game to any causal player, phone or PC.

It's a simple and fun game where you hack-and-slash zombies.  The Movements are very flashy, it controls well, and has plenty of eye candy.  This is pretty much what Randy Pitchford would refer to as a "greasy cheesburger."  Not exactly fine dining, but you might enjoy it anyway.
As for the downsides this is a rather rough port.  There aren't any graphics options to scale for lower-end systems (like my laptop, I have to play this game on my PC).  Also the game seems to not do fullscreen very well as there is a black border around the picture.  On the gameplay end, combat is fun, but the level designs are amatuerish at best.  A series of rooms that have you fight one horde of enemies after the next without anything to break up the monotony.  This game is definitely an improvement, but still has a lot to learn from games like DMC, Bayonetta, or even Ninja Gaiden.
Overall, I recommend the game, but only if you are looking for a bit of fun from what is a budget title.  If you already own the PS4 version (like I do) or if you are looking for the next Bayonetta you should skip this game.

What Remains of Edith Finch is a unique game, I will give it that, but that does not save it from ultimately failing to entertain in a meaningful way. First off if you liked (or loved) Firewatch stop reading this and go buy the game as I am certain you will indeed love this game. However, be warned there are ZERO options in this game, meaning you cannot alter the character's experience in ANY way whatsoever. Also exploring is not possible, yes sometimes there are two routes to continue the story but only 10 seconds or so of different scenery transpire with nothing else to be gained. So this is a movie with small amounts of brilliant interaction.
That interaction can indeed be beautiful and is where the unique quality of the game surfaces, but after the second 'story' you see the formula that will be the entire game which weould have been fine except something is lacking which I will speak to below as it is a spoiler. My problem with this game lies heavily on the fact that the story telling style, characters, visuals and even music are so obvioulsy ripped off from the various Tim Burton films. By the end of this game, I was certain they would give credit to that, but no such thing transpired. The developers left one thing out though which is Burton's humor, so we get the heart aching tragedy and... more tragedy without a single morale to any of the stories. The only morale I can imagine to be had from this movie is don't be a crazy and often suicidal shut-in family.
So while the graphics are beautifu and the small amount of controls you will use are intuitive and never take you out of the story and the story TELLING is so well done, in the end the story itself is bleak, unimaginative and simply depressing as no closure, morales or point is left at the end of it to redeem what you saw. Here ends my non spoiler review and what follows are some thoughts on the stories themselves.
***** SPOILERS AHEAD *****
So this game revolves around a family (The Finches) who believe themselves cursed by some demonic plague which causes only one child to ever survive a generation. No detail is ever given why this is believed other than idiotic superstition. Even your main character shows gullability in possibly lending some of the recounted tales credence such as kids turning into monsters or cats. My assumption is that mental illness runs in the family as some of the deaths come from doing some very silly things like sailing a house across the sea or building a rickety metal slide many stories high. Yet suicide also runs in the family and the game makes no quams about at least two the Finches having offed themselves. That is some curse right there, of course this is all glorified in the Burtonesque story telling to look artsy, but in the end feels a bit disgusting as most of the family's lives were wasted.
By the time you are to the second room you realize you will be leading each character to their various deaths, which is fine I guess, but I was absolutely disgusted to have to purposely drown a baby by swimming down a drain in a tub all the while with the game making it into something 'beautiful', again if there was a point aside from enjoy your life while you have it maybe I could overlook this, probably not for that story at least.
The remainder of the stories are indeed interesting, but they all end with pointless deaths including the main character who I assume dies in child birth and then sends her child also back to the house for the uplifting experience of reviewing the suicidal and dimwitted relatives and their collection of untimely / disturbing demises. Why would anyone do that? Then again why would someone make this game without any redemption built in, if you are going to steal from Burton wholesale why leave out the humor and / or morales surrounding his original work. If you don't agree with me on how much Burton-borrowing is happening here go review his work, after all the Finch house itself which is the main character really is almost identicle to Jack Skellington's house in the Nightmare Before Christmas.
Ultimately what makes me give this a thumbs down though is how short it is - at two hours you end up paying ten dollars an hour for watching a movie as again you cannot alter the story in ANY way so there is no replayability. Did I like it as a story on its own? No it was too dark without any point for MY taste. Did I think it was brilliant story telling? Yeah it is as far as video games go, it got close to genius somewhere in ther invoking emotion and turmoil, but it fails in the end to escape its own weight and deliver something which transcends simply a shut-in suicidal sad family's story.

Run and gun platformer in the vein of Contra, but instead of frenetic and fun, I found it to be tedious, with pointless rocketing mini-game like levels mixed in to break up the tedium. While there were many great games I picked up in 2013, I'd like to say that this one was the biggest surprise of the lot. Valdis Story: Abyssal City is, at a glance, an action-y "Metroidvania" style side scroller with some appealing art design. But with smart RPG elements, a very responsive combat system, special events in the world and multiple characters, there's a lot to like about this game. I would personally highly recommend this game to individuals who are a fan of the genre and would still encourage any fans of side-scrollers to at least give the free demo a shot. As a side note, its soundtrack is excellent.
Criticizms would probably be a steep learning curve, events that you can overlook that can greatly impact your playthrough, and the fact that the game is rather short after 2-3 playthroughs; when you've become quite familiar with the general game path and have a solid grasp on combat, the game flies by.
All that said, though, bang for buck this is a truly excellent purchase that I cannot recommend enough.

What Remains of Edith Finch is a beautiful introspection on the meaning of life and loss.
If you can't stand walking simulators, avoid this game. However, if that doesn't deter you, you will find yourself absorbed in a story that haunts you long after you've stepped away from your PC.
Without getting into spoilers, you play as Edith Finch, a young woman who has returned to her ancestral island home. As you explore the house, you experience stories of her family members.
The stories take the form of minigames and serve as a mechanical departure from the rest of the game. Each minigame is relatively short and I found none lasted long enough to become stale.
The game is paced very well and I didn't find myself bored or struggling to find the next room.
The game performed well on my PC and I didn't experience any noticeable technical problems.
Jeff Russo's soundtrack transitions well between the main story and the smaller stories and succeeds in creating a unique sound for the different tones of each.
Lastly, the most common complaint regarding walking simulators is the length. A good walking sim, like a good film or a good novel, will succeed in captivating you and causing time to blur. I'm happy to say that I lost myself in exploring Edith's world and found myself truly immersed.
What Remains of Edith Finch is a masterpiece and I highly recommend you play this game.

I have some mixed feelings about this game. It is obviously... content driven. It revels in its art and theme with a silly world about anthropomorphic birds that have political and racial problems, including genocide. That's where the game shines. The art and theme of the game are really charming.
The gameplay on the other hand is lacking in thoughtfulness. It has its moments. At its best, the game is puzzle-platforming, including some simple platforming and crate-stacking. It also allows you to possess enemies in a method very reminiscent to "Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee," which is super enjoyable. There's nothing quite like gunning down bad guys that think you're friendly, taking all the risk with none of the.. risk. It's cool! But most of the rest of the gameplay, including the last boss, revolve around its sloppy gunplay.
At first it might not be so bad. Shoot a bad guy ~25 times and he dies. He juggles in the air with each shot until death which seems fun until the very moment when 2 or more bad guys are on screen. Your bullets will not go through flying bodies, which means if there are 3 guys stacked front-to-back, you will only hit the guy in front while the rest gun you down, knocking you off-screen to recover, at best, and at worst, stunlocking you until you die.
There is a sort of hiding / cover system in the form of a background layer you can move into at specified points, but this is ALWAYS [ALWAYS (ALWAYS)] omitted when you're in a difficult combat scenario. This means your only way of succeeding in the difficult combat sections is just retrying it until you get lucky and the enemy AI just doesn't shoot you as much as usual. Wow it's frustrating.
There are also combat sections that involve jetpacking around in the air shooting down enemies with jetpacks. This is kinda fun and feels much less luck-driven, but there's not much particularly challenging, as there's pretty much one strategy: Fly around and don't get shot while shooting. In a word: Shallow.
So all this said, there are good things in the game's aesthetic to experience but, for goodness sake, play it on Easy mode. There is absolutely nothing about the game's difficulty that is fun as it revolves entirely around a mechanic that you wish would just turn off.
