TLDR: I love it, give it a shot.
Overview:
Hex, is a wonderfully deep and occasionally frustration inducing card game from Cryptozoic, a company well versed in card and board games. It attempts to merge the trappings of an MMORPG with the infinite expansion of a TCG, and it is mostly successful. In the game’s current state, the MMO aspect is quite weak, while the TCG gameplay is quite strong. By being a digital only game, HEX can break some of the genre tropes and do crazy things like seeding an opponent’s deck with spiders that fight for you when drawn, or providing a small percentage chance that a card in your deck will enter the battlefield upon gaining health. Each set expansion has only made the gameplay more interesting and increased the creativity of the digital only aspect of the game.
The MMORPG Aspect:
What distinguishes HEX from other online TCGs is the MMORPG portion of its game. While HEX is an excellent RPG, the MMO aspect is lacking. There is no required player interaction, and no way to see other players within the world itself. The campaign feels like a strong single player RPG, but currently has no way for players to have any meaningful interaction beyond strategy discussions and card trading. You cannot see where are players are in the world, and all chat is done through a single chat channel, or through private conversations between friends. For an MMO it feels lonely.
That being said, the RPG aspect is great! The player travels through the world on a node based map, with each node being either a combat/story encounter or a town or dungeon. Towns serve little purpose, other than a place to gather and turn in quests. Dungeons are repeatable zones with their own unique maps and rewards for completion. Rewards for encounters and dungeons range from gold (usable on the auction house to purchase new cards) to new cards and equipment. Equipment is what truly sets HEX apart from the competition in terms of TCGs. Each piece of equipment affects a different card and can drastically change how it is used in combat. Equipment can only be used in the RPG portion of the game, and has no effect in PVP, as it would destabilize the careful balance going on there.
The TCG Aspect:
Anyone familiar with Magic, or the now defunct WoW TCG (not Hearthstone), will be able to immediately pickup HEX and grasp the core concepts. Players play resource cards to afford bigger and better cards until one player is crushed by the strength of the other. In HEX, each player takes on the role of a Champion from the greater HEX lore, each of which has their own unique special ability which can be triggered when certain conditions are met (similar to Hearthstone). Thus, a deck can be built around a specific champion, or a champion can be chosen to compliment a deck composition.
Where things get really interesting are in the different abilities that cards can have. Health stealing, instant attacking, and early striking are genre staples, but HEX introduces numerous abilities that are only really manageable in a computer run TCG. Escalation, the newest ability doubles a card’s printed numerical value (including its cost) but only while the card is still in hand. Tunneling allows a card to be placed on the field for a reduced cost, but with a timer until it is revealed and usable. My favorite abilities revolve around providing a stat boost to all cards of a specific type regardless of where they are located, in my hand, deck, graveyard, or field. This allows me to buff up cards that I have yet to play or even draw, allowing for a big surprise when I finally play a low cost troop with numerous buffs that result in a heavy hitter.
The PVP Aspect:
I have not taken the deep dive into the PVP aspect of the game, beyond some friendly matches against friends and a couple of tournaments. There are numerous way to play PVP and plenty of rewards for playing. It is common to get crushed by players who have spent hundreds of dollars on their decks, and that is the aspect which has kept me out of the TCG scene up until this point. For me, there is enough content, and opportunity to earn free cards in the RPG portion of the game, that I don’t need to rely on PVP.
Pros:
+ Strong RPG gameplay
+ Tough puzzles in the RPG (Require creative deck building)
+ Class and Race combos
+ Variety of gameplay styles
+ Easy to play completely free (though with a grind)
+ More content incoming
+ Encourages alt characters
Cons:
- Weak MMO implementation
- Pay to win PVP
- Class imbalance (Mage = hard mode, Cleric = easy mode)
- No guild system (Promised, but not yet implemented)
- No player interaction required (Promised, but not yet implemented)
- PVE can be a grind

Before I begin my actual review, I have to say one thing. The creators of this game deceived people who financially backed them. According to comments made by the developers during the game's creation:
Hex was promised to feature feasible methods of attaining cards through pve. At the moment, packs and cards through the campaign are few, far between, and (seemingly) highly limited.
Hex was promised to feature group pve--which we were told was "almost finished" a year ago. This was put on the back burner and the game launched without group pve.
Given that the game's philosophy has changed in favour of blatant money-grabs (despite the game's primary investors being its playership, no less) and given that this type of developer deception seems to be happening more and more lately, I'd feel morally obligated to give a negative review even if I felt this product were otherwise satifactory.
The single-player campaign (your only option for attaining cards without buying one of the lackluster starter decks or selling your organs, one by one, to roll the dice on randomized microtransactions) suffers from pacing problems. It's writing is nice enough, but there are so many encounters to get through any story arc. Each deck you fight is essentially the same as the last, with the only change being in your opponent's charge-based abilities. That wouldn't be so bad except 4/5 times an encounter's rewards are: 1/8 of a level and a handful of coins that have almost no value. Calling the Hex's grind tedious would be an understatement.
Hex's other appeal is as a clone of old school MTG and, I've gotta say, it succeeds on this front. The interface is very impressive and very clean, and I *would* praise it for offering a way to play MTG online with friends. The only problem is that anyone who's played MTG *knows* how expensive the habit can be. Buying packs is like the original microtransaction--but at least then you have a physical copy.
To bring that model online--to require your players to spend money for a *chance* to get 1 of the 4 copies of a card they need--is deplorable. It's one thing to steal a game's style to make it more accessible for people. You're still a thief but you're kind of a hero too, like Robin Hood. When you do it just to get a cut of the money, you're a thief and a scam artist.

This is a great follow-up to Doom II.  Unlike the Master Levels, it contains two full 32 level WADS that don't offer too much that is new in content except for exceptional level design.
The Plutonia Experiment is probably the hardest officially licensed DOOM experience ever created.  It has a few extra textures, but mainly uses stock art and music from DOOM/DOOM II.  A lot of the encounters consist of strong enemies in cramped areas, which is a welcome challenge after playing the previous DOOM games.  Some levels are inspired by DOOM II levels, and most are well-designed.
TNT: Evilution is much more different (new art & music) and is much more memorable IMO.  The overall levels have many different themes, from various techbases and hellish formations.  TNT is what you want to play when you want something a little different from DOOM/DOOM II, though difficulty is around the same, but much less than Plutonia.

I used to like mobile-centric games, back in 2013. It was a new frontier of gaming and a lot of new ideas were being used to figure out what could be done. However, I eventually became fatigued of the current running trend which is freemium everything. Freemium mechanics and business model, an extremely toxic and unenjoyable combination of ideas. It completely turned me off from trying new games for a while. It didn’t help that I felt like there weren’t any games being made for a core gamer such as myself. Games where I can sit down for more than five minutes and actually get a deeper, more challenging experience as I went along. Most of the time, the game shows its hand and I’ll get bored of it pretty quickly. A friend eventually cajoled me out of my negative attitude towards it and sharing a bunch he recommended. So, I decided to give Android another go, to look in the inner depths of the platform and find games that PC-centric gamers like myself might find interesting. It's true that You Must Build A Boat isn’t exactly a hidden gem. However, I think it’s a good starting point for me to start from. Let’s talk about building boats and killing monsters.
You Must Build A Boat is a combination of RPG, rogue-lite and match three mechanics. The player starts on a boat and is tasked with, well, building a much bigger boat. To accomplish this, he must run an endless procedurally generated dungeons, defeat monsters and acquire loot. Incrementally and eventually growing strong enough through capturing monsters, recruiting crewmates, finding relics and upgrading your capabilities to take on the challenges ahead. There are two phases to this game, running the dungeons and buying upgrades with the recently acquired loot. As this is a rogue-lite, the objective isn’t to “win” the dungeon, but get as far as you can and acquire as much material as possible. The RPG mechanics are in how you can upgrade your weapons, defense and spells that you can use in the dungeon. There’s a good tutorial that runs you through the various mechanics and currencies in the game.
The main portion of the game that the player will be playing in is the dungeon running. This side-scrolling endless dungeon has the player running to the right as long as they can. As soon as they get pushed off to the left, their run is done and they can either retry or return to the boat to acquire upgrades. This is the player’s health bar essentially. Each run will have an objective(s) that the player must strive to achieve. These objectives can unlock new shops on the ship, gold or power depending.  As you progress through the dungeon, there are procedurally generated enemies, chests and traps that will try to hinder your movement. You must match the appropriate tiles in order to defeat these obstacles. For enemies, this is usually matching sword or magic staff tiles to do damage. For chests, it’s key tiles. Traps and certain chests will have an icon associated to them telling the player what they must match to defeat them. Enemies won’t simply stand around and let you kill them, they’ll throw their own attacks that will knock the player farther to the left. You can match shield tiles to prevent “damage” but these must be refreshed pretty often to keep the shield up. There are three other tile sets as well: knowledge, strength and crates. Matching knowledge and strength tiles give you a currency for upgrades or recruiting “found” monsters which grant bonuses. Matching crates gives the player a chance to find items to sell or spells that can be used in the dungeon run at the player’s discretion. These spells vary from freezing spells to fireballs. While the player is running, they are constantly charging a horn spell that, when the horn is charged and the player is in danger, will clear the immediate screen of enemies. This can sometimes be a clutch play or completely wasted on a single enemy. It depends.
The general idea when you’re playing the match-three section is to have as many sword/staff/key matches available to deal with whatever obstacle you’ll run into. While the guy is running between obstacles, the player should clear the board of crate, strength and knowledge tiles as much as possible for their benefits and so they can have access to the sword/staff/key tiles. Matching four or five tiles in a row increases the potency of these tiles as well as tile multipliers that are unlocked later in the game. All the while, the player is up against a constantly changing timer due to the aforementioned “health” bar.
Upgrades can be purchased to improve the player’s sword, shield, staff, spells and even dungeon runs in general. There’s a choice of three different upgrades for most of these items but generally they are all stat upgrades with some having certain effects. All upgrades are worth getting, it’s just a matter of whether you can afford them.
You know, I rather enjoyed YMBAB. As far as mobile games go, it pushes the player to keep getting better at match-three. Since you’re up against a health bar timer where faster and better matches are constantly encouraged, it makes the player improve along with the character you’re playing as. Sometimes, runs can just be bad because you won’t get the natural matchups you need but more often than not, you can make it work. It’s about making the best of a difficult dungeon. Once I finished the campaign, I felt I had gotten enough of the experience but boy, it was a pretty darn good experience. While the upgrade/RPG mechanics aren’t exactly that deep, it at least gives you something else to think about and strive for in each run so that each subsequent run is that much better. It’s still a pretty simple experience when you get right down to it, but it’s got the right combination of mechanics, skill ceiling and ideas so that even someone like myself can enjoy it.
Honestly, I think You Must Build a Boat is a better experience on mobile devices. That’s not to say that the PC port is bad (it’s not). However, the mouse feels like a poor substitute for the touch-driven design. You could still play it with a mouse, but I think you’ll enjoy it more on your phone/tablet than on a PC. Still, this combination of fast-paced match-three mechanics and rogue-lite mechanics make for a fun time. And You Must Build A Boat is one that a decent amount of hidden depth for a mobile game. It keeps me interested despite its simplicity through its push to the player to keep getting better and faster at matching tiles together. So, give You Must Build A Boat a look.

is an interesting game and does have potential. You play as the Slayer, an implied Buffy expy who hangs out in a coffee shop with a gang of friends and occasionally goes out to hunt undead monsters. The game is very Buffy, even to the extent of dividing itself up into seasons and episodes - every mission is an episode, find and defeat the boss vamp, that's the end of the season. Move on to the next season and the next boss.
It isn't a bad premise and like I said it does have potential. The problem right now is the gameplay. Again, the idea isn't bad. It's basically the same combat and movement mechanics from
, but turned up a notch. There are RPG elements at play; you can't just expect 1-2 shot kills all the time like you could in
, instead enemies actually have HP and damage stats of their own.
And that's kind of the issue here.
is a hard game, and unfortunately it's not all for legitimate reasons. Despite what the game's Steam store page says stealth really isn't optional. Enemies tend to travel in large packs, they often take many hits to kill and they strike fast so evading isn't as easy as it was in
. If you're playing on anything above Easy difficulty open combat becomes suicidal, so you'll really need to rely on stealth to get by.
The problem is, the stealth doesn't work very well. You move so slow that trying to sneak up behind enemies while they're moving away from you is next to impossible, there is no grace period when you're spotted, and even with the perk that lets you deal additional damage on a backstab you're STILL looking at a protacted battle against most enemies.
Worse, enemies like to spawn in on top of you. I've seen enemies pop up two inches in front of my face as I was walking, and unlike
where you could stop spawns by not looting enemies, here there is NO WAY to stop new enemies from re-appearing constantly.
Basically,
is a good premise, executed poorly. The developers are still working on the game as of this writing, so hopefully they'll fix the stealth mechanics and the respawn problem. If they do then expect this review to be updated but for right now I can't really recommend this game in good faith.

It's very clear that Slayer Shock has the heart in the right place and it sticks head and shoulders above the metric boatloads of other crappy Steam First Person Horror Monster Shooters out there. Love and effort went into it to turn it into a respectable product. There are gameplay mechanics such as infestation, location based missions, different goals and objectives, a currency system and RPG upgrade mechanic, all polished up to a point where everything looks integrated into a coherent design and art style.
However, that won't make up for the fact that ALL of it is STILL incredibly rudimentary and with horribly low production values. Controls on keyboard and mouse are clunky and banal. Some of the plastic blob people and wooden monster animations are straight out of some of the worst titles out there. Hits still register on certain monsters unsatisfyingly and especially the flaming man is a confusing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who pops in and out of existence on anti-climatic whim. Maps, despite being procedurally generated, repeat quickly and after just 5 missions you've seen it all. If not for the 3D art and the likeable art style and music, it's the kind of game you could find on Newgrounds or as a Minecraft mod. It's a plucky little Indy title and it deserves SOME consideration for the amount of spunk it has, but not above the 4-6 bucks price line.
I can see the merits the title has, but as a steam game, it can't be considered as more than a lovable arts & crafts project that doesn't deserve hate, but doesn't do enough to be worth recommending either.

I wanted to like this game but I feel like there are some design choice that need to be revameped in order to make the experience more fun. The game is hard cause of any true difficulty but from mishandled mechanics.
The game has a rudimentary stealth system that it doesn't emphazise but is a necessity. Level contains loads of mobs that can easily swarm you and overpower you. The best way to handle enemies is to try to either sneak past them or to double tap them when they're unaware. The problem is, there is little to no way to gauge how hidden you are or an enemy line of sight. This problem is further acentuated in levels that are completely dark or have tall foliage that obscures your sight.
The early game combat is grueling and unfair even for rogue-like standards. Your starting weapon has almost no reach and does so little damage against the mobs. You get a range weapon after the tutorial, but it does little damage as well and you run out of ammo quickly. There are chests scattered throughout the levels for you to pick and receive a resupply, but this is still frustrating as enemies respawn but supplies don't. You can clear a whole room and use up your healing and ammo but on a return trip new mobs will be waiting.
Since supplies are scarce, it makes you think that you should focus on stealth. However, this has rpg elements and requires that players kill special mobs to get exp currency. While you receive some currency from completing missions, you miss out on bonus currency if you avoid combat. Worse, some mission require you to fight hard mobs at the very beginning of the game when you have no upgrades (the harrowing ritual to be exact).
The game bleeds atmosphere. It bleeds potential. But the game is anemic in terms of balance and developed mechanics. Stealth is too flimsy, early game combat too clunky, enemy spawn rates too unfair and design choices that make the game needlessly difficult. Granted, I only played for a lil over an hour but I felt from what I saw it did not look like the game would be worth the cost of admission.
If the dev updates the game to be more fleshed out and mechanically sound, I am willing to try it again. As is, playing the first hour was a frustrating beat down.

This game had potential, but it was quickly squandered.
First, the assets, my god the assets. As stated before, every model is ripped from Gamebanana, and all the textures in the maps are from Source engine games before. Graphically it has no origninality.
The maps are god-awful: wide-open with either too bright or too dark lighting, and textures, along with the basic cube geometry, and bland props,  that make the maps dull and simply not fun. The only chance they have is community mods, if somebody decides to add some.
The gameplay feels like a bad mix of L4D's arcadey-gunplay and No Room in Hell's tactics of slower pace and teamwork reliance. It doesn't mix well. The classes are imbalanced in different ways (Technician is basically superior to the Pointman), making the skill with Battlefield squad tactics feel... useless.  The weapons the classes have feel either too weak or too strong (the shotguns in particular are wonky: against normal zombies they die in one hit, but it takes maybe 6 shots to kill a damn zombie soldier), and the hit-detection is spotty at best, good luck if you're a sniper.
There's only 1 game-mode, which admittedly is kinda unique: you slowly clear room-to-room (except when zombies spawn behind your back all the time, the spawning system is terrible, it's no AI Director), until you reach a bombsite, plant a bomb, then haul♥♥♥♥♥on a time-limit to extraction, giving a L4D finale vibe, without the special enemies or weapons.
The zombies are clearly reskinned Half-Life 2 zombies, using zombie assets I have seen in Garry's Mod addons. They have no special abilities or anything that makes them very intimidating: they either move fast, move slow, or have body armor. That's it. As stated before, they also get spawned even in places you JUST visited because you don't look in that room for a few seconds, then you look back and... yeah, a dozen of them suddenly spawned from some cyber-void to make your life miserable.
Sound is very lacking. The zombie sounds are mostly just HL2 zombie sounds, and the music gets very old, very fast. The guns don't sound quite right either... usually too quiet for what they SHOULD sound like.
Since few servers are around, I played with the bots and beat every map (they're short, and only 4 of them), the bots aren't that great either. It makes the Left 4 Dead bots look good: they get in the way of gunfire (and zombies), make no attempt to get near supply boxes, and there's no Technician or Support bots (I guess the dev didn't want to take the time to have them drop their deployables). The basic maps INCLUDED with the game the bots struggle to navigate, often getting caught in ramps, staircases, or basic walls, and the game just lazily teleports them to you. In fact, they know that the bots are so bad, that they have them respawn every 30 seconds or so, right on top of you.
To summarize, this game does nothing new and seems like an amateurish mod. Trying to mimick L4D's co-op, but lacking in the feeling of suspense, tension, adrenaline-fueled gunplay, or even remotely any semblance of fun.
Perhaps if the Dev makes better maps (or the community makes some), with more game-modes and enemy types, with better bots and hit-detection (for guns and zombie attacks both), I would revisit it.
Oh, also, you can even spawn the HL2 NPCs, which is good for a chuckle.

This is a decent YGO online game if you're into fast duels. The game centers around the quick duel format and encourages you to have decks around 20ish cards rather than the usual 40 (although you can still use 40 I think) and you have 4K life points instead of 8K. Another thing that's new is the duelist skills, which are special perks you can designate for yourself and are one-time use abilities such as "Restart" which allows you to re-shuffle your opening hand at the beginning and draw a new opening hand. Things like that, which are a bit unnecessary in my opinion but you really got to grind to get some of the good ones so they aren't a big issue in the online duels yet.
As the game is still fairly new on PC, the card roster is likely lacking for many but there's enough in it at the moment that you can make some good decks to beat the AI or online opponents. I don't have a lot of hours in this game yet but so far I have never felt pressured to blow real money on the card packs or game currency to compete so I think that's a good sign. The game's grind is typical of most other freeiums so if you don't that kind of pace you aren't likely to enjoy this as like others, you can only do so much stuff before having to "wait" until you get more energy again or in this case, the game only has so many AI duelists you can face off against for a few hours. The legendary duelists such as Yugi, Kaiba, Mai and others can be dueled separately from the AI NPCs but they require their own resources you must spend to fight them and the typical way to get more of them is via the NPC duelists. Difficulty-wise, the AI is very lackluster starting out and only presents a real challenge when the AI gets those perfect draws any YGO gamer that has played other YGO games knows about that are insanely cheap while you draw nothing relevant.
As I said, if you enjoy the quick duel format you will likely get some enjoyment out of this once you start getting cards and dueling real people online. I prefer the traditional 40 card-8K LP format but playing with 20 cards does make things interesting when it comes to deck building and how the matches typically go. It's not for you, however, if you want something very intensive like Legacy of the Duelist that has the traditional format and a lot of cards. This game is still new and growing so there are a LOT of cards not in this yet.

A simple, short game about a spy with no allegiances who's just trying to keep himself from getting screwed over and make some money. Gunpoint's strategy with a stealth element and it's game mecahnics are what really makes the game unique. They are fascinating because they make you think in terms of open and closed circuts - e.g. object A does this which triggers object B and electrocutes a guard. While it's easy to catch on, it's not so easy that mental effort isn't required - I'd say medium on the challenging scale. If just doing the bare minimum, one can finish this game in a matter of hours, but there are extra achievements possible for doing levels with a specific style or speed if that's your kind of thing.
The dialogue is cute and made me laugh. While it's not an adventure game per say, you are given a few choices that will affect the game. And the ability to choose different dialogue options in between missions made me feel more invested in my character. (For example, I made my character as snarky as possible.) The music is well done and quite fitting, as is the 16-bit design; both really help to aid the cloak and dagger atmosphere for our spy protagonist.
All in all it's a cute little indie game that's definitely worth getting on sale.

Update 6/19/2017: I wanted to note they have added an account leveling system, so if you win games in any mode you will slowly gain account levels.  At certain levels the reward is a token to try some of the game's normally paid PVP modes (draft, Evo gauntlet).
Update 12/8/2016: I wanted to update this review in light of the recent major Hex update that added a second big PVE zone, Mercenaries, an additional class (Ranger), and a new asyncronous Draft PVP mode.  In short, this update is fantastic and really delivers on some of the potential this game has always had to make novel PVE content.
Original Review: If you like MTG, you'll like Hex.  Don't expect this game to be a F2P MTG, though, it's a true TCG, not a CCG.  If you want to play competitively, or accumulate valuable rare cards, you will have to spend money (or a lot of time).  BUT what you are buying can be resold if you quit, much like MTGO (and unlike Hearthstone).  I have friends who have decided they didn't have time to play anymore, and they were able to sell their collection for what they paid for it, though I would say that you usually should expect to take somewhat of a loss in that scenario unless you won a lot of cards through tournaments.
I don't want to say a bunch of things that have already been said, but I will say that some of the negative reviews of this game are just simply false.  You absolutely can beat the campaign without spending money (or grinding for 100 hrs).  I think people have even done without engaging with the player-run economy (i.e. Auction House), but its far easier if you realize that you can buy some synergistic cards for small amounts of gold (that you get from playing PVE).  Hopefully they will improve the AH and make it more obvious to new players.
There are also some very good negative reviews that point out legitimate flaws with the game, or ways that the game does not meet that player's expectations.  It's certainly not going to be for everyone.  I would encourage people to look at it as a much improved MTGO that also has a really innovative RPG-PVE component.  The PVE portion can now be played completely for free, some competitive PVP decks can be built for under $20, and the game is even more fun if you are interested in spending some money to play drafts and sealed tournaments.
Personally, I spend hundreds on MTG back in the day, so getting to play an even better game for far less money is fine by me.  I cashed out my MTG collection and spent 20% of that money on Hex for 1000s of hrs of fun (I play this game mostly without using the Steam client, so my actual hours are well over 1000).  I got this game for PVE, but found I really love playing Limited formats (Draft, Sealed, Gauntlet, etc).  Evo Sealed, in particular, is a blast.  I love the puzzle of figuring out the best deck to make out of a random pool of cards. The PVE stuff has been horribly delayed, but the recent update is delivering on the potential it's always had.
tl;dr Try it, keep an open mind, don't expect to competitively PVP without spending more (and use the Auction House if you do), engage with the community and ask questions, people are generally super nice and helpful.

I have mixed feelings about this game. On one hand it is one of the best TCG on the market. It's complex, fun, challenging and has a (mostly) helpful and dedicated community.
On the other hand it has many problems. Server issues on the steam release, Steep and unforgiving learning curve, unfinnished and unrefined PVE and a PvP that has far too many barriers for entry.
Let's start with the pvp and the barriars you'll face to enter. To be blunt, it costs money to participate in any meaningful pvp. Although this is standard practice in the TCG world, in the world of video games this will bewilder people and put many new players trying pvp particularly when they find that the skill gap between newer players and the players that are obviously dedicated to Hex and TCG's in general is huge. The strange thing is they don't seem to realise how good they are at the game. Even a experienced Magic card player like myself was pushed hard in contructed. Nevertheless as a digital card game trying to simulate the environment of real world TCG with it's rules and market place has left the game with an identity crises of being a F2P video game with a pay to participate TCG model.
However, paradoxically PVP is where the game truly shines. If you are an experienced TCGer I could not reccomend this game enough even if it is just to try. The game itself is reminiscent of MtG but with a few twists in the mechanics. Although at times it can get to obsurd levels with over 100 cards on the table in one of my games, it is great fun.
As for PVE. It's fairly basic although people complain about the difficulty, and in truth there are difficulty spikes all over the place, with practice and some research even f2p players can complete the campaign. However, I would not reccomend this game for players that are new to TCGs. It simply does not do a good job of teaching new players the game and does not open an easy gateway for new players to introduce themselves to PVP. To be frank, without a large playerbase with large population of low skilled players, this game will always struggle retain players trying to get into Hex.
But if you have a will of iron and a willing to improve yourself I would reccomend this game. If not, then this is definetely not the game for you.

Doom is quite simply the best shooter ever made and it's not just the nostalgia talking. The pure unadulterated ultra-violence is still as raw and visceral as it was when it was released in 1993. In terms of pure enjoyment in the form of fast paced action, this game delivers in spades. It is what every shooter today pretends not to be as they try to disguise themselves under thinly veiled attempts at plot and character development, a no-brainer all out gore fest. It gives us what we want from a shooter with no unnecessary bells and whistles too often used in modern FPS games to cover up the fact that the game play is simply lacking behind the masquerade of fancy graphics and tedious cut-scenes that ultimately get in the way of the fun, I'm looking at you Call of Duty. I love intricate stories and fully developed characters in games, notable examples of these are the Mass Effect and Witcher series, but this is a genre that has never been about that. This is a genre where the only time you should get a break from the action is the loading screen between levels. Moreover, thanks to the dedicated and thriving fan base there are a plethora of mods and custom WAD files that are constantly breathing new life in to this game. 21 years later and there are still multiplayer servers active, that alone is pretty impressive.

This is a wonderful little game that manages to stand out from the crowd of generic walk 'em ups by being actually well made and thought out. There's a story to be told about the Finches, and the developers have told it marvelously. From start to finish I was 100% engaged and invested in the the story unfolding before me.
Wondeful art and scenery, along with brilliant and vibrant enviroments make the game an absolute joy to walk through. Everthing is well thought out and interesting. I was constantly excited for what the game would pull out of it's hat next.
All of the stories about the family members are fantastically sad and beautiful, with two in particular really standing out (you'll know them when you get to them). All the voice acting is great too, which is a nice change of pace from the usual indie dev team budget voice acting.
If you like interesting stories being told in interesting ways, then you will like this game. Probably love it too. This isn't just another indie walking simulator story and even if you aren't a fan of the genre you'll find something to like about it here.
An easy recommend from me.

I don't often define the quality of a video game by how many awards it's won, but when I start losing the ability to count them on my hands, apparently I do. A good thing, too. Nidhogg is all kinds of awesome.
The concept is remarkably simple: 2 players go head-to-head in a half duel/half race to the death, both equipped with fencing swords and capable of more than a few tricks to give an edge in battle.
You begin facing your opponent in the 'middle' of a map, with an opening battle. Battles are fast and furious beyond imagining, often ending within a few seconds, which ties into the gameplay mechanic wonderfully: upon killing your opponent they'll need to wait a moment to respawn, allowing you to press forward toward your 'goal'.
Win a battle and you're given the 'goal light' allowing you to move forward further; lose, and your opponent gains it instead. So long as you maintain the previous kill you can pass-by your opponent without engaging and edge closer to your goal - should they fail to stop your approach.
This 'tug-o-war' mechanic is the single most endearing indie game element I've felt in a while. It's relentless, and the feeling of achievement after finally managing to push an opponent back to the end, before summarily being eaten by Nidhogg, is one of much glory and admiration. Simple, sure. But so very, very rewarding. Easy to learn, too, and likely near-impossible to master.
Single-Player Mode consists of fighting steadily more challenging opponents, one after another, on one of 4 maps. So, naturally, if you want to be playing Nidhogg for more than a few hours, you're going to need to go multiplayer.
Sadly, the online matchmaking within Steam isn't great. Assuming you can actually find a game, there's a good chance one of you will be lagging horribly — and when you're playing the type of game that you
play with even the slightest amount of lag, matches can often lead to aggravating experiences.
Assuming you have a few friends playing, and you're all within the same global region, this won't be a huge problem. And if you're lucky enough to have more than a few friends playing, then Tournament Mode will likely give you the greatest experience of all. I know, personally, playing live on Twitch, that this feature will make for 99% of all my time playing.
At $15~ I can only recommend a purchase here for players with friends planning to play with them - for now, at least. Which is largely a shame, as the gameplay offered in Nidhogg is truly exceptional.
Possible improvements include visual upgrades to characters to simulate some form of character progression; as it stands, every game is the same and with 4 maps there's limited variety. You'll be relying on your opponents to entertain you; if they do, you're going to love Nidhogg, if not, you're likely going to get very bored, very quick.

Commandos 2: Men of Courage combine the brutally long gameplay of its predecessors with modernized graphics. The game, while still maintaining the long mission length, somehow manages to be easier than Commandos 1.  There is more leeway for mistakes and as result Commandos 2 is less masochistic than its predecessor. That doesn’t mean this game will be easy on beginners though, in fact the tutorial and first few mission should hurt your ego if you think this game will be a cake walk. The graphic, sound effects and musical score are all very nice and varied. However, the game severely fails when it comes to clarity of objectives and pathetically easy enemy takedown patterns. In some missions the objectives are borderline invisible, so you may have killed all the enemies on the map, but if you can’t find the one specific npc, you will never leave the map. Overall a good entry level and modern commandos game, imo the best of the series regardless of a few negatives.

It's a Halo knockoff and a Minecraft knockoff with some genuinely unique ideas thrown into the mix. Even 1v1'ing with a friend is fun. Getting into a big match on a blocky recreation of CoD's Terminal map is just boatloads of fun.
The gunplay is surprisingly good, with every weapon feeling balanced and useful for a different playstyle. The hookshot and miner gun mix into the guns well and add a unique element to gunfights. You could shoot your enemies until they die as they try to do the same to you, or you could whip our your miner gun, open a pit beneath them and toss your grenades down it.
There are loads of original maps, but my favorite maps are the aforementioned block-based recreations of famous Halo, CoD, Counter Strike and Goldeneye maps. They all play like the originals, and many have secret passageways useful for sneaking up on an opponent. You can also build and destroy most of the blocks on the map, and save your bombarded/constructed variations into a brand new map.
There is no matchmaking system, and no way to invite people to a private match that I recall seeing. So getting into a game with just your friends is sometimes tricky. The graphics are obviously not max-resolution 4K swagology. But the art style is extremely charming.
Buy this game. It's only $2 at the time of writing, and you'll at the VERY least get a healthy serving of lols for your money. If you're like me, though, those $2 will get you a shooter you look forward to playing for hours whenever you hear someone else has a copy.

A mortar is an indirect fire weapon that fires shells at low velocities, short ranges, and high-arcing ballistic trajectories. It is typically muzzle-loading and has a barrel length less than 15 times its caliber.
A mortar is relatively simple and easy to operate. A modern mortar consists of a tube into which gunners drop a shell, which is usually referred to as a bomb. The shell contains a quantity of propellant. When it reaches the base of the tube it hits a firing pin, which detonates the propellant and fires the shell. Some larger caliber mortars have a string operated firing pin instead of a fixed one. The tube is generally set at between 45 and 85 degrees angle to the ground, with the higher angle giving shorter firing distances.

Dawn of War II much more closely resembles the table-top game in that you aren't focused on building a base and pumping out an entire army a-la Warcraft and Starcraft but instead you manage a small squad of 4 marines (in single player; multiplayer still has a bit of the base building gameplay) and cover is much more important in this than in the first game.
As with the original Dawn of War, the storyline is excellent. You face a number of enemies such as the Orks and Eldar from the first game as well as a new race that a lot of people missed in the original. The RPG elements that were in Dawn of War I and its expansions now extend to your entire squad and have been vastly improved. There are random loot drops and 4 different skill trees to level up as you progress. Customization is far from linear and there are multiple paths you can direct each of your soldiers to specialize them.
If you complete all of the side missions as well as the main story (not all missions are essential to win) DoW II easily gives you more than 12 hours of gameplay. I highly recommend getting the two expansions as not only do they have long campaigns of their own, their content also improves on the main campaign with new skills and weapons. In my mind, this is the game that the original Dawn of War should have been (though I enjoy it in its own right).

A simple, short game about a spy with no allegiances who's just trying to keep himself from getting screwed over and make some money. Gunpoint's strategy with a stealth element and it's game mecahnics are what really makes the game unique. They are fascinating because they make you think in terms of open and closed circuts - e.g. object A does this which triggers object B and electrocutes a guard. While it's easy to catch on, it's not so easy that mental effort isn't required - I'd say medium on the challenging scale. If just doing the bare minimum, one can finish this game in a matter of hours, but there are extra achievements possible for doing levels with a specific style or speed if that's your kind of thing.
The dialogue is cute and made me laugh. While it's not an adventure game per say, you are given a few choices that will affect the game. And the ability to choose different dialogue options in between missions made me feel more invested in my character. (For example, I made my character as snarky as possible.) The music is well done and quite fitting, as is the 16-bit design; both really help to aid the cloak and dagger atmosphere for our spy protagonist.
All in all it's a cute little indie game that's definitely worth getting on sale.

So this review is likely to be long.  But before I begin I want you to do something.  Type the word "vampire" into the search engine for Steam and see how many games come up.  Now, assuming you're a hardcore turbonerd like me, count how many -good- games there are that don't start with the words "Vampire the Masquerade:  Bloodlines".  Unless something changes in the near future the number of games is likely to be close to maybe either one or zero.
Now that you've done that, try counting how many games are basically a procedurally generated Buffy the Vampire simulator.  Betcha you're only going to see one!  Seriously, that alone makes the game worth it's weight in gold.  The concept is unique enough that the nostalgia factor might be worth it to some people.
So yeah.  Slayer Shock puts you in the role of a bracelet and hand obssessed "Slayer" straight out of one of Joss Whedon's famous TV series.  And by Slayer it's subtly implied that you were bitten and are a half vampire.  You'll start out weak and slow with nothing but a stake and a crappy nail gun and end each "series" a super fast katana wielding ninja that can outrun a car.
This isn't an entirely serious game.  Let's make this clear.  There's just as much tongue in cheek humour poking fun at the idea of the genre and setting as there is darker stuff.  One season I had protests occur at the school campus demanding more humane treatment of vampires that ironically ended with the vampires attacking the students.  The next had one of my shopkeeper NPC's get beaten so badly that she expired in the hospital a few days later.  I'd say it was dark, and it was!  But I got my revenge by hosing down a bunch of vampires with a super soaker filled with holy water.
Of course that's kind of the problem as well.  What the game does well (An at times tense and fast paced slugfest/stealth game through hordes of the ravenous undead.) it does extremely well.  I'll echo the sentiment from other reviews that at its heart the combat and mission running content of the game game hammers that part of your brain that loves to get minor, ultimately meaningless achievements.  It's got that potentially classic arcadey feel to it.
However there is a sticking point.  After the first few seasons it starts to get really repetitive.  The four or so levels only occasionally vary up into new configurations, the bosses never verge off into really unique traits outside of a series of "weak to this element, strong to this element" gameplay, the events are ultimately not that meaningful, there's only a few enemy types, and eventually the same events will keep occurring over and over and over and over and GODDAMNIT Kari you insufferable ♥♥♥♥♥ you've scared off our weaponsmith for the sixth time now with your snooty personality!
It doesn't get any easier to tolerate the lack of replayability once you complete a "series" of seasons and get legacy points.  Your would-be sire falls to your authentic hanzo steel, the game goes into the slow-mo mode you've become familiar with by now and...You wake up at the start all over again with new bosses + 15 "legacy points" while your mentor remarks that your nightmares post bite are getting even worse.  The game continues to get harder from there with every enemy getting damage and defense buffs.  That's it.  Same random events you'll be familiar with.  Same boss types (only with new names and new weaknesses and resistances.).  Same old same old.
So yeah.  If you're expecting a hugely interesting Whedon-esque story or for this to be the most mechanically "deep" game in terms of replayability at the moment you might be disappointed.  There's some neat stuff that could be done with what's there, but for a game that has so many random elements there's not as much as what probably -should- be there at the moment.  Keep that in mind.
I'm giving it a thumbs up because going off of an old post in Eldritch's forum the developer will likely continue to develop this with new content post release.  Supposedly Slayer Shock is a spiritual successor to Eldritch and it'll be much easier to develop content for.  Hopefully that means that it'll get many content updates as time goes by.  If not i'll probably have to edit this review and reassess whether the game is worth it or not.
Other than that?  The game's a gold mine.  It'll suck you in for a few hours and leave you wishing there was more of it.  If all this isn't worth $20 to you then pick it up on sale some time.

has simplified rules of the popular YGO card game.  To appeal to the casual gamer, various rule changes were made, a list of them is at the bottom of this review.
Now this is generally good news, as it makes the games much more simpler and quicker, were the game usually ends after 4 to 8 rounds, which is about 2-5 minutes. While in the orignal one, games could last much longer up to even 15 or 20 minutes. Meaning you are never going to be stuck in a game you are slowly losing and instead can move on to another.  The game itself has mouse support, however the UI wasn't changed for the PC port and there for can be very annoying to us and it has way to many pop-ups.
Card Collection wise this game is behind by quit a bit, it does not include the Synchro, XYZ or Pendulum cards, as of writing this review, however I noticed that a lot of cards released over the years, which were not cards like Tuners introduced exclusively for Sychro cards are already in the game meaning you have access to much more cards than just the older sets meaning you have a more wide range of cards to choose from. Personally I really liked the addion of Sychnro and XYZ cards, but I still had a good time. However that said it does limit the amount of decks you can build and one would presume these cards will be eventually added to the game.
Now lets jump into what you'll be doing every time you jump onto this game. When you first log in there will be a lot of pop-ups which will just overwhelm you, to sum it up; those are just about little events going on, which allow you to unlock certain cards a bit easier other than through packs. Than you jump into the tutorial, which will teach you the basics and I found it just good enough to do that. After that you are set free into Duel World, where you can do various activities.
There is your standard PvP with the usual ranking system (Rookie->Bronce->Silver->...), get to tier 5 to advance a rank, win 2 game to advance a tier. With a basic deck I already made it to silver, so right now lower tiers of ranking are noob friendly, which is really nice, as a lot of ranking system aren't in a lot of other games.
Matches were easy to find for me as I got one after just waiting 5 seconds.
Another key activy, which you'll probably doing most is duelling NPCs, they are just standing there waiting for you to beat them, usually they are very easy to beat and the game even gives you an auto-duel option, were a semi optimal AI plays for you and saves you some time. Deafting those is where you'll get most of your XP for your duellist from, which is important to unlock Skills and various Cards and Currency Items.
Now this got very tiring for me and but it is part of the grind everyone has to go through if they want be competitive and collect key cards, as certain cards are locked to certain AI dueslist you'll have to duel over and over to unlock them.
Lastly there is a shop where you can buy cards from card packs, you sadly can't unlock every card through the shop however, if you want to build certain decks, like Red Eyed Black Dragon Deck buying packs is key to buy them. Although a lot of top tier decks have mostly cards that are aquired by dueling certain dueslist. So I'd say its not that P2W as the usual Card Game.
Thus, in conclusion YGO Duel Links, is a more casual YGO, aimed at casual gamers or people, who want some nostaligia after watching YGO as kids, it's very grindy however and the UI is very tedious to play with. It'd say install it play it for a bit and just have fun with it, As it still is a mobile game.
Recommended!
The following major rule changes were made:
-> Life Points start at 4k
-> Monster & Magic/Trap zones are limited to 3 each now
-> Deck Size is 20 - 30 cards
-> Starter Hand is 4 cards (6 max)
-> Addition of Skills, which give the duellist a bonus such as, seeing the top card or starting of with Extra Cards on the field

Short Review: The game is a great game, but most of the stuff is taken from Half-Life 2, and mixed in a bit of CS things as well.
Long Review: The game is a simple game: Get from A to B, plant a bomb, get from B to A, escape, done. While this game is still early accsess, it still needs a bit of a while before it can really get it's shine. Most of the zombies textures (other then the zombie versions of your team which actually look alot taller then you guys are) are just normal citizens, just zombified and put into diffrent clothes. Most of the zombie animations (other then the 2nd zombie attack which is just really slapping you repeadatly.) are from HL2, heck even the burning animations. Bots are decent, but they only follow wherever you go and they don't really have a sense of exploration. And sometimes they just stand and shoot while being slapped repeadatly, or being slapped hard by zombies. Sometimes when an elevator is involved, bots will stand in the doorway and then die to the door closing. Health kits are from HL2. You have armor in this which uses the exact same armor charges from HL2. The music is pretty good. Also, the bots will teleport to you when you've gone too far without them. They also respawn. That's pretty much my review. (Notice how I emphasised slap in this review. Valve really likes slapping zombies.)
While the biggest weakness of this game is not being its predecessor it's also its greatest strength.

If you played Hearthstone and found it to lack depth then you can go to the other end of the spectrum and try Hex.
Hex, based heavily on Magic The gathering, improves a bit on the old formula by cleaning up the experience. It removes the need to track your land instead using a Threshold system where you burn a resource card to gain a resource. Colors are managed through the same system whereupon spending the resource card you can a gem of the matching color. Most cards have a "gem requirement" that you have to mee to play them. In addition, it makes great use of the digital aspect of the game in terms of card abilities. Examples of this are cards that randomly generate a troop of a certain from the whole game inventory of cards, something that would be impossible in a physical game. Another example is the keyword "Prophecy" which gives a boost to the next troop in your deck.
Beyond core gameplay, Hex does a great job of managing the player turns and windows of opportunity. Hearthstone addressed the challenges of a digital TCG by doing away with these windows. Hex has tried to preserve them but focused on making it very easy to stay aware of the♥♥♥♥♥for-tat back and forth of passing on your opponents turn.
What makes Hex special?
Besides being the best serious TCG in digital format (real life value of cards, streamlined play, unique setting, factions and art) Hex is unique because of its RPG elements.
There is a PvE campaign where your character levels up, gains skills/talents, and provides unique deck encounters.
Cards can be upgraded with Gems that give them unique abilities.
Your avatar can wear equipment which changes the function of cards in meaningful ways.
Hex's community is also the best in terms of engagement, helpfulness, and passion amongst all of the digital TCGs.
Bottom Line: If you like strategy and card games there is no better choice than Hex.

An Octave Higher is a very beautiful VN that establishes a wonderful Harry Potter/ Steampunk type world.   Except, with aspects of the Russian Revolution tossed in.   Muggles of the world Unite!  To me much more interesting than Harry Potter itself, I cannot complement the techno magic setting enough.  Seriously worth your time, the music is beautiful and I found the way they did the magical battles to be very well done.   The narrative shifts perspectives as you read, which is a little jarring at first, but I grew to really like it.    The characters are all interesting, and you easily will care for most of them.  The nice ones at least.
I did read the few negative reviews to try and understand where people were having issues.  I think one thing you should keep in mind when playing the game is that it takes a different track for a VN.  If you simply do the right thing, say the nice things, and do the polite things (like not going along with fights) you will end up having an average life and have a chance at a modest, but happy ending.   However, you won't find the secret of healing (fixing) objects or effect much of a change on the larger society.  But, if you take chances, speak out, fight, you have a chance at a making some change, and will see the "True"  ... but tragic end.   A true choose your own adventure, you don't see the entire story unless you try all the endings.   For me, I think I would opt for one of the happier ... but less heroic and meaningful ... endings.  True that things only get better for one or two people, you don't solve the big mystery and you don't improve the world that much as a whole.   But, you do get to be a little happy.  Kind of like real life.  But, it is so worthwhile to see what could have been ... if you don't play this like a typical VN.
Just keep in mind, if you do like we all do every day, and play it safe ... you WILL end up with a modest ending and easily miss 40% of the story.  Just don't expect to be happy if you really try to change the world.
Seriously, I was crushed by the ending of Life Is Strange and how poorly that was handled.   The developers of this game, strike the right note... so to speak... with the way they deal with multiple endings.    If you are looking for a great bargain during the steam sale... this is it.   My only regret is that I wish we would see more of this wonderful world.

I'm gonna keep this simple and cut straight to the chase. I am no veteran of card games, nor am I one of the die hard fans who backed this game on the kickstarter about 3 years ago. So if you want a more in depth perspective and backstory on development, feel free to ask someone from the community. They are remarkably kind and helpful.
This game is beautifully constructed. Lots of thought and effort went into building the lore, the PvE battles and cards. It brings new ideas into the card game genre, such as the Hero Equipment concept. You equip your champion with items that will enhance certain cards in your deck, allowing for lots of variation in deck building and (in theory) much more options than other card games.
In single player Campaign mode, you get to create your own champion, combining one of 8 races and 3 classes. There are 2 factions with 4 races each, and they all take place in the same world map with minor variation in events and location depending on which race you choose. The campaign is where you acquire most of your basic cards to use later in PvP if you wish to do so, although the game never pressures you to go for PvP.
You can just single player all day long and have fun by yourself.
However, as you progress through the campaign, you begin to realize that the cards you get from campaign rewards do not match the steep dificulty curve of the coming battles. The game throws everything in the kitchen sink at you, with enemy champions using clearly overpowered abilities and troops that require very specific card combinations and synergies to be countered. It's like if your boss at work tells you to "fix this copy machine" but does not give you the tools or finance you need to fix it.
Not only do you need more powerful cards to progress, you need them to synergize well with each other. Since the campaign gives you about 1 rare card for every 3 or 4 battles, and it's usually the same cards every time, you realize this whole situation was built as a grind fest with the ILLUSION of progress.
The only way to make actual progress through the campaign is to participate in the game's built in economy and start buying the advanced cards that synergize well with each other. And this is where the grind aspect becomes truly monstrous in proportion.
The community has even created a "guide" for new players advising them on how to grind the campaign and arena properly and progress through the game. I am not even kidding! When I first saw the guide, I genuinely felt sad for this community.
You can tell they are very passionate about the game because it has so much potential, and I truly sympathize with that. But a good community will never compensate for the fact that the game's economy is too convoluted, cumbersome and slow paced without spending real cash on it.
It was designed to frustrate the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you until you realize "If I want to make any kind of progress, I need to spend some real cash sooner or later". Unless you are playing 5-6 hours every day and get lucky with the campaign rewards, you will never feel like you have the freedom to create multiple functioning and sufficient decks for competitive (or even single player) gameplay. You will always be on the back foot with big holes in your inventory.
If you don't have the time to play all day long and get what you want, this game is not for you... unless you spend your money on it.
I will NOT call this game pay-to-win, because it's not that at all. The game does offer you a legitimate alternative to get the cards you want without paying real cash.
Instead, it's actually pay-to-avoid-endless-frustration-and-time-consumption. And that is something I do not like. Just my honest opinion.
I don't like when a "free-to-play" game torments you psychologically into spending your money on it. I prefer to spend money on the game because I LIKE IT AND WANT TO SUPPORT THE DEVELOPERS.
However, this game gives you no chance to sympathize with the developers. You are expected to pay in order to progress beyond the WALL OF TIME AND DIFFICULTY (WOTAD™), not because you actually feel good while playing. This is the major problem with "free-to-play" games these days. Until they fix this recurring syndrome, this game gets a 5 out of 10 from me.
5/10 Average game with great potential. Keep an eye on it as it improves... hopefully.
If you are like me and you don't have time to spend grinding through the game economy, I would not recommend it. Otherwise, go for it.

An Octave Higher was the first visual novel I've ever played and I was left with very conflicting feelings about it.
The game has amazing art. Music is great and visuals are beautifully drawn. I found some character models and expressions kinda stupid looking but it was a minor flaw in the context of overall picture.
Gameplay is very narrow and simplistic. The game changes character automatically at times. You don't have many decisions to make, but the ones you make determine the ending. It took me a while to understand how to achieve every ending but once I did it was a nice stroll through every storyline (I used the fast forward option to skip all scenes I had already seen and I made saves before every decision). I'd love to comment the "true ending" storyline but I don't want to spoil anything. I'll just conclude it by saying that it raised many kind of feelings...
The most conflicting part of the game is the story. The world is built in amazing detail and the plot is very believeable and well constructed. However, the game somehow doesn't live up to the expectations it manages to build. Maybe it is because the player is supposed to see things from the perspective of the main characters. After all, it is a story of four young people who all have very different backgrounds. Anyways, the game felt kinda short, or hollow, after all the world building.
Overall, An Octave Higher is a very nice stroll on a narrow street in the middle of a vast world.
I can recommend buying it on sale.

What Remains of Edith Finch... well, we'll find that out in its due course, won't we?
It's an Environmental Narrative tale of a strange, cursed family living in a house which becomes increasingly unwieldy over the years. The titular Edith returns to her family's home to find out the secrets of how and why they all met their strange ends. She may discover something about herself along the way...
This is an absolutely beautiful game, a pure joy to walk through and to see all sorts of sights. Like most Environmental Narrative games, it's hard to replay this as we know absolutely everything there is to know after finishing, but while you're here it's a real joy.
The story is told via Edith's voiceover, as well as text that swirls onto the screen and disappears idiosyncratically, sometimes flowing in the direction of your next destination, which is quite handy sometimes. Edith enters several flashbacks on her journey, some of which are much more involved than others, but most telling the stories of tortured, troubled people who met untimely ends.
I most definitely recommend this, as even on the mere 25% discount I got on this game ($14.99) I did not feel ripped off for only 2, 2 1/2 hours of gameplay. Check it out even at full price; I believe it's worth it! Support development of games with amazing storytelling!

Before reviewing this further I would just like to say that even though I have said "No" in the recommended category, if you were to get the game on a deep sale or in a bundle then I think it is worth trying it out just for the 1st Act at least.
It took me about 4 hours to get through Act1 and the ending I got, but a further 3 to 5 to complete the 2nd act and get the other achievements.
+ Nice visuals
+ 1st story arc is fine
+ Interesting concept to play through the role as 3 characters at once
+ Easy to save at pivotal times to go back to later
+ FastSkip function is well implemented and a godsend for further playthroughs
- Poor writing (needlessly long exposition/descriptions/world building with no real pay-off)
- Poorly developed characters and themes
- Playing 3 people at once doesn't work consistently depending on your choices
- The actual way the game switches you between who you are 'playing' is confusing at first, and then just irritating
This is 100% a Novel and not a game. You can make decisions in the story at 2 or 3 parts that will take the story down a different route to give the game replayability but other than that it is just there for the achievements and for a different "end slate".
The story essentially has 2 Acts in it. There are 6 Achievements that revolve around 5 possible endings. 2 of which I would consider to be the 2nd Act of the story and are utterly atrocious and appalling writing. On my first playthrough I made what I considered to be the sensible choices at the pivotal points of story arc and did not experience the 2nd Act of the story. When I replayed the story and made the choice that sends the story off down a deep spiral the writing and character development tanked.
Even during the 1st Act of the story but even more so in the 2nd the writer spends way too much time using exposition. Also some of the descriptions for certain aspects of the world building go into way more depth than is necessary. It would be fine if there was some mini-game, test or valid reason to know this information at some point, but there never is and I must have wasted a lot of my playtime reading through needless descriptions.
It feels to me like the writer does not know how to succinctly explain things (just like me with my reviews) and treats the reader like an imbecile. One particular character is used in that 'unknowing reader' role that is often used in games, but she has things explained to her a lot that don't make sense half of the time given her backstory and development and it seems forced.
There is a point during the 2nd Act of the story when you can say that you are interested in how a machine works and then the game launches into this crazy section where a character spends ages explaining it using diagrams and over explanation for no reason what so ever. It is not necessary to do this to progress, however I feel if they'd not wasted time doing things like this and concentrated more on the writing and character development the story would have worked better.
There are also several plotholes and ideas in the story that make no sense. People getting to places faster on foot than by transport. Objects/people conveniently ending up at certain locations. Main characters not knowing who other characters are even though those people are either famous, noteworthy, or even best friends with the characters father. At one point in the 2nd act we get an attempt to try and show how a potential bad guy may not be a bad guy after all, given to us by a character who hitherto seemed to have no interest or knowledge in politics yet suddenly becomes an expert. It just felt so forced and out of place.
Some of the character development, themes, and morals of the story in the 2nd act are perfectly fine, but for me personally the bad parts are too frequent and obvious and let the plot down.
I could go into more depth about how bad the storytelling and strange character development occurs but it would indeed go into spoiler territory so I will leave this here.
Overall I gave this game a 48%. Mostly due to the visuals, Act 1, and the games save/fastForward mechanics.

A friend of mine bought me this game for my birthday after I'd been admiring it. It was just the kind of story I enjoy!
Set in Overture (a city reminiscient of an 18th or 19th century modernising and revolutionary Europe) the story is told from the perspective of four main characters from different class backgrounds (an aristocrat, a couple of bourgeois students, and a worker from the proletarian class). This world, however, revolves around the use of magic in society.
The longer endings suddenly took a more dramatic and serious turn, but without the complete fulfilment of revenge I was hoping to see as one of the main characters became less relevant as the story went on. That would probably be my only complaint about the plot.
I loved the art style and the depth of the characters and most of all, I loved the soundtrack full of piano classics!
Since I don't seem to be very good at achieving good, or in this case 'true', endings on my own in any visual novel, I appreciate those who have made walkthrough guides for this game! I also appreciate the developers including a fast-forward option to skip over scenes and dialogue that have been already been played on previous run throughs.
If you enjoy visual novels, lovely art, an interesting story, and classical music, then give An Octave Higher a try!

An Octave Higher is a fantasy visual novel developed by Kidalang and published by AGM PLAYISM. This novel features a very intriguing narrative that swaps the reader between three different characters thus allowing you as the reader to experience multiple perspectives of the same story as it progresses. Given that the three protagonists range in status from high class, middle class to lower class society-wise, this gives one quite a unique viewpoint as you read. The story is very well written and features branching decisions peppered throughout the engrossing narrative which is always a plus in any good visual novel in my opinion.
Visually, this novel is a delight to behold. It features a beautiful art style that seems to be an amalgam of fantasy, anime and steam-punk. The colors are bright and cheerful and the sound quality is top notch as well. Also, the story takes you to an assortment of varied locations as the narrative plays out. In the end, I truly enjoyed the overall presentation of An Octave Higher with its gorgeous visuals and immersive sound effects.
An Octave Higher is one of the most enjoyable visual novels that I have read to date on Steam. The story has an abundant cast of interesting characters to interact with, the lore of Overture is fascinating and there are decisions to make that actually affect the stories outcome. Also, the title has some nice options available and there are six different endings so the replayability is quite high with this V.N.. There are Steam Achievements and Steam Trading Cards to collect as well as a basic and extended soundtrack. Visual novel fans will adore this title and I would also advise anyone looking to try a V.N. for the first time to start with this as it is definitely one of the better titles available. An Octave Higher is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to fans of the genre.

Slayer Shock seems woefully underbaked.
In Slayer Shock, you play through a series of missions, earning "Vampire Dust" with which to unlock new skills, weapons, and intel.  Missions take place in a series of procedurally generated levels that make up your town.  On each mission you sneak and fight your way across a map to complete an objective, which amounts to either "kill several elite vampires" or "walk to the following locations and press the use key".
As you complete missions, the town builds up terror and gradually shuts down in an Arkham Horror or X-Com-ish way.  Every mission the place you go to will go up or down depending on your success, two other places go up, and an event may throw some additional random-ness into the mix.  Eventually you die or research the final mission and complete it and the "season" ends.
Repeat this across five seasons of increasing difficulty with skills and equipment carried over, then start a new "generation" and repeat everything you've done before over again with an increased difficulty and a "rogue vampire" ally.
This all sounds quite good, but the problem is all of it is unsatisfying and bare bones.  None of it feels that good, has any depth, or possesses any of the variety and sense of discovery that made Eldritch compelling.
Maps are pretty much boring, linear canyons littered with obstacles, light sources, and structures in a way that doesn't come together in an interesting fashion.
Stealth feels half-baked.  Moreso, it's poorly explained and presented.  There's neither much of a visibility indicator nor much of a tutorial on how it works to let you figure that out absent explicit UI feedback.  You mostly have to assume that basic video game conventions apply.  Definitely don't run, don't be in front of enemies, stay out of light sources and be careful with your flashlight.  Noisy terrain bad?  Crouching good?  Smashing things make noise?  Cornfields provide visual cover?  No idea, although I've smashed some stuff pretty close to bad guys and haven't worken them so I'm guessing not all of those apply.
Ambiguity aside, there's just not enough interesting terrain, mechanics, or enemy behaviors to make sneaking particularly interesting.  Look at the map and the enemy patrol patterns, guess where you can avoid being too in front of the enemies, and go for it, and that's about it.  If you aren't on a hard enough difficulty to mandate it, you'll almost certainly find yourself sprinting across every map just to make it end faster.
Enemy variety is poor.  There are five kinds of enemies, and you'll likely see four of those on your first mission.  They vary slightly in what attack and evasion patterns you'll want to engage them with but are all dead simple.  Denser enemies on harder difficulties complicate matters, but that just means you'll need to be a little careful about aggro and kite a lot, or engage with the tedious stealth game.  The only remotely interesting thing here is that werewolves fight vampires, allowing you to use enemies against each other somewhat.
The game is also paired with incredibly uninteresting combat.  Weapons have minimal animation and sound effects, and enemies show no reaction to being struck until the killing blow.
Firing a crossbow, for example, consists of pulling the trigger, seeing a slow-moving smoke ring come off the front (I guess it's a gunpowder-powered crossbow?), and maybe your enemy drops about 15% of their health and notices you.  Sometimes it doesn't hurt them, and with no visible projectile it's hard to tell if that's due to inaccuracy or a range cap on the weapon.  Melee attacks are even worse- simple swipes with no sense of impact.
Mechanically, the situation is no better.  Other than whiffing at your opponent with your main weapon until their health bar is empty, combat offers some basic damage resistance mechanics to encourage you to mix up weapons, a push/stun, and if you sneak up on an enemy you can inflict double damage if you've researched the skill.  That's about the lot of it.
Overall, combat feels feels weightless and repetitive.
Previews of this game in the media made a big deal about the game being about learning about your enemies and figuring out how to defeat them, with phrases like "Ideally, you shouldn't succeed the first time you encounter a threat".  (from Rock, Paper, Shotgun)  This seems entirely absent from the game.  With the shallow monster pool you won't regularly be encountering anything new, and the bosses appear to be simply HP and attack rate buffed versions of a normal monster with different damage resistances.
Research consists of spending X dust and waiting for Y days to get info about the "big bad".  The first research tells you who and how many, which doesn't seem to do anything.  Then you can research three things in any order.  First, where the big bads are- presumably to avoid encountering them, although that's just a guess because encountering and beating them early doesn't seem to give you anything.  Secondly, you can learn the monster's vulnerabilities and resistances, which is obviously useful.  Finally, you can unlock the final mission which will let you end the game.
As I played Slayer Shock, my wife watched me play and said "This is an Early Access game, right?"  No, it's not and it costs $20, but it sure feels like somewhere between a very nicely polished free internet game, and an early access game that's got a solid framework in place but that hasn't been fleshed out at all.  I'd recommend you save your money.  There's little content and even less depth here.

It's a fast-paced two-player dueling game. You can fence madly, cartwheel away, throw your rapier, somersault through the air, snatch a rapier off the ground and skewer your opponent through the guts, you can rush unarmed at your opponent only to roll beneath his drawn rapier at the last moment, trip him with  a sweep of the leg, tear his heart out, grab his rapier and keep running. You can pull off all kinds of insane stunts, and I can't help but laugh every time. This gameplay is accompanied by an equally frenzied soundtrack and trippy neon graphics. The great art direction and style of this game is undeniable.
Multiplayer is online and local, and there is also a singleplayer mode where you fight a computer opponent. It's not as fun as desperately outsmarting a human opponent. The online multiplayer introduces a ton of lag and causes many maneuvers to be impossible to pull off. That said, I've been mainly playing online opponents (haven't had the chance to play local yet), and it's been some of the most exhilarating multiplayer gameplay I've experienced, despite the lag.
There aren't many games where you can do a somersault, but this is one of them. It feels great.
On the downside, there are only 4 stages. What you'll get out of this game will depend on how much you put into it and on the people you play against. Best suited for playing with friends, two controllers and a tv.
