You start off the game with the very homage-y named stake, Mr Pointy, and from your coffee shop base of operations with your team of randomly generated Scoobies you set out to save the town from the vampire threat.
Your team will fall in love, break up, get themselves killed unnecessarily and get you the best power ups so you send the army of the undead to the ash heap.
The graphics are simple but robust enough to complement the gameplay and the soundtrack is just spot on.
My only regret is I didn't spend my NMS preorder money on this game sooner.

This is a sequel to 1,000,000, building out on the leveling and RPG aspects while keeping the gameplay the same.  Which means you will continue to face frantic strategic match-three gameplay, as you try to make useful matches when encountering obstacles to be enemies and open chests. It's amazing how well the concept works; it really does feel like an action game more than a puzzle game, though it serves both purposes. It's not easy,  but the expanded options and purchases do give you a better shot, it seems. I was stuck on the last section for at least an hour (just not quite fast enough), and there's lots more replayability (you collect monsters, and several take special situations to get - I missed at least a half dozen in my playthrough). It's a weird mix of game styles, but it's very good at what it does.

I've been playing the Warhammer 40k tabletop game since 2002 (originally with Space Wolves, now rolling with Word Bearers and Astra Militarum) and I loved the original Dawn of War. Dawn of War II has more in common with Relic's Company of Heroes series then it does the original Dawn of War, in single-player games anyways, as you are only in command of small groups of Space Marines. No massive armies of vehicles, fliers and Squiggoths in this one.
Despite the reduced scale, Dawn of War II is still one of the best squad-based RTS games available. The graphics still look good, the music is the typical "epic" soundtrack and matches the grim dark setting. Control is perhaps the largest issue as it can be hard to get your squads to go into cover and it gets tough to pick out enemy characters.  Keyboard hotkeys help but it's still annoying.
All told, for the price, Dawn of War II is a great pick up if you want a small scale RTS or just a decent game in the 40k Universe.

I'd give DFUW a rating of 8/10 but that being said this is my favorite game and there just isn't any better for full loot PvP/sandbox gaming.
I've had an active sub for 2 months. I was inactive for the first 2 weeks due to computer issues. I've made it to 125k prowess and I feel strong. Its enough to max 3 weapon skills, my boosters in strength and dex, my base stats to 100str, 100dex, 70int, 80wis, 2 ults, a handful of leveled spells, and 2 crafting masteries. I'd say the key to get to where I am is to find at least one other solid player that you can farm with alot. Having a farming friend makes the spawns trigger faster, makes kills faster, and gives you a buddy to help you to your feet when you get knocked to the ground. Each of you pick a few different crafting skills to train (as this gives you self made gear whenever you want it, and also prowess) and trade each other for the things you need. Either way, the key is to have at least one trustworthy buddy to go farm with. Its also a decent way to make friends and get invited into a clan.
Running into other players:
I typically run into 3-12 instances of seeing other players doing♥♥♥♥♥♥per day I play. Requisitions, farming mobs, sea scrapping, etc (although its not uncommon for me to spot you, then slink off sneaky-like and get away) ((makes me wonder how many times I had unseen eyes looking me over)) keep in mind my playtime ranges from 3-10 hours per day depending on work and other IRL factors.
Status of the player base:
I see tons of new players joining. Near starting zones I see new players with less than 1k, less than 5k, and less than 20k (prowess) that I've never seen before running around (particularly Amurran, wolfland capital) *Note, Ork lands seemed fairly empty when I cruised through there. (a good place to start without alot of people killing you early on perhaps?)
Not to mention that players that took breaks or quit return often. New content draws people back, as does free-play days. Especially after the release of DUELS, (Tradeable 30-day subscriptions players can buy from AV and then sell for gold or loot to players) which allow people with too little cash or unintentionally expired subscriptions a shot at re-subbing for free (well, about 70-90k gold average)
Status of the community:
Oh dear. Read through the forums and you'll find all sorts of...strongly expressed opinions. Unfortunately most of those strongly expressing their opinions are also closed-minded to other opinions. So, be prepared for alot of loud and ignorant rants/complaints. Some are valid sure, but sift through those at your own risk and judgement. Anyway, I've read through a bunch and my opinionated summary is as such:
Darkfall is an ever changing game ran by an Indie and somewhat small time company called Adventurine. Its come a long way since Darkfall Online, DFUW's predecessor. AV hasn't always been the best with customer support but they're loads better now. People have always said AV doesn't listen to their customers well enough, but they have greatly improved. Keep in mind, that if you look through the forums you can find 100+ submissions for "How to improve" or "How to fix" things in darkfall. The trouble there is that there is 100+ posts! AND- reading through them myself, I saw many that were too poorly worded to follow fully, another handful that were terrible ideas (IMO), and another handful that I agree with but perhaps not the majority of players would, (or AV)
SO! You have alot of ♥♥♥♥♥ing, about things that bother a few people. But to fix it, you'd♥♥♥♥♥♥off a bunch more, so AV's hands are tied in these issues. Keep this in mind if you dare to sift through those posts. If you care to comment on them, take the time to speak clearly and consider how it would fit in with the rest of the game.
Dont be discouraged by these posts. And try and imagine from the content of the post, who the poster is. I see alot of rants that I'm assuming are just cry-hard kids. -- Not worth reading.
A Short Story of my start:
Start in Wolflands with my brother. Read a few guides, tested a few mob types, decided to wield greatswords. (whoops, IMO) Basically build for warrior type. Goals at this point are to get enough Rank Zero gear to not be naked, get spells like Vamp Strike, Power Attack, Barrage, Reinforce, Bandage so I can last longer (lots of damage buffs/lifesteal, some heals and a damage resist buff)
Why goblins? -They drop all Rank 0 armor and weapons, arrows, gold, reagents to cast spells, potions, food and some teliportation tools like portal shards and runestones. Also, killing goblins satisfies 5 feats at the same time: Humanoid, goblinoid, creep, varmint, freak feats, for lots of bonus prowess per kill once feats are complete (((Do not focus mastery feats, focus habitual feats. Habituals are earnable weekly, some daily, for bonus prowess for completing the habitual feat requirement. Focusing habituals will get you all your master feats in due time, its very time efficient)))
(@ 5k prowess)
Trouble is, goblins got boring and easy by the time I finished goblinoids and humanoids. So, I moved on to Gnolls, which drop way better. Avoid Gnoll vilegaunt/butcher spawns till 40k+ prow or with a friend or two. However the Gnoll shaman, tribesman, and fighters are all relatively easy and again they drop pretty sweet. (Coal, Rawhide, up to 3 piles of gold, teleport stuff, pots, plus all Rank Zero stuff) These classes of gnolls can be attempted almost at any prowess level, but I do recommend goblins first.
Then, it was on to Elementals. (I was 20k my brother 40k prowess)
Elementals, Ice, Earth, Air, and Fire -- all have their own feat plus the master elemental feat which all elementals count for. Ice, Earth, And air are all doable at 20k+ prow with a friend. Disclaimer- Elementals shrug off elemental magic, so mages are gonna have a unprofitable time casting spell after spell for little effect. Also, elementals hit hard with their spells and comparatively soft with their melee. Mages should consider equipping a shield and a favorite 1 handed weapon at this point and maxing that skill for elementals (and in general)
At this stage I was 40k prowess, and I started looking hungrily at the bigger gnolls. I'd already considered them best loot for easy kills/low prowess, and those big ones dropped much nicer and even expensive things! So, after buying more skills, upping their levels, and etc, My brother and I moved to Gnoll Vilegaunt spawns. Those ♥♥♥♥ers will be tough at first, so bring a friend or two. Their drops are great enough I still farm them as my favorite mobs (there are spawns that spawn Gnoll tribesman, shaman, fighter, butcher and vilegaunts, with an additional vilegaunt/butcher spawn ON TOP OF the 5-pack spawn, so lots of the tough guys often = fast loot when you can kill em all) Also, I should add that mobs can hit each other, so make them do that alot and crouch behind cover to avoid arrows (big mobs in your face count as cover from the ones behind them, they'll shoot their buddies while trying to hit you)
I killed a handful of other mob types, (look up the troll dungeon for more easy prow with decent loot (but a decent chance to run into other people) I wont tell you my full story with every mob I've killed in detail but I can say -- look at the PvE feats and target some mobs that have good rewards. There are guides elsewhere that breakdown their ease-of-kill and drops. Read those if you want more info than this long♥♥♥♥♥post.
Making Friends:
So, the best thing you can have in DF is a buddy! I've stated so already, you'll grow super slow solo. How to make friends? Well, there is the recruitment sections, you could try that, or invite friends to play darkfall, or... Go knock people over! But, instead of ganking them and looting their grave, Revive them and invite them to farm or hang out.

This game is a graphical upgrade. It does have more content. It does run smoother. But I found the insincere "You Win!" after every run, the stretched, unskippable mini-cutscenes, the insipid tutorial, the shallowness of play, too distracting to notice the things it made better... Until I went back to the original and found I really couldn't enjoy that anymore either.
I had hoped it would be so much more. It could have been so much more, if it was presented differently. Perhaps if it took some of the moments it spent intrducing pixel paper people with shallow and meaningless one-liners and used it instead to contextualize our search for the legendary artifacts that can allow us to build, not just a boat, but a FLYING SHIP.
In my heart of hearts, I am disappointed.

Small Town Terrors Pilgrim's Hook is putting you in the shoes of Vera, a young woman in her thirties, whose twin brother called for help, as he came back to their native island of Pilgrim's Hook. Now moved by the need to save him, she returns there to discover that there is a surnatural entity that wants her...
The plot of the game is well-written: you're first there to save your brother Arthur and you end up to be wanted by a surnatural entity that is terrorizing somewhere the inhabitants that stayed. You don't know why it wants you but it's not set at all to kill you... Given the fact that you're the only one that is resisting its power, maybe it thinks that you may become an apprentice or something like that.
Anyway, it promises a dark setting and indeed, between the village kinda dead, fogs or even abandoned houses (yours among them), the scenes are really well drawned. The soundtrack is good too.
But I've kinda a problem with the gameplay. I mean, it's great to find items but in some scenes, you have to move so much stuff that it can be quite boring after a while. Besides, as I played in French, some words used weren't familiar to me. I took minutes to find a single item, resorting to click on any items. And some of them weren't really easy to spot. But the puzzles are well balanced.
As it's a CE, it means bonus. So, you have a bonus chapter, concept arts, etc... Also, there are in-game achievements that could have been without problems on Steam, as they're the usual ones: finish a scene in less than a minute, don't use hints, find Cestor's creatures (kind of beyond objects), etc..
If I find 15 euros a little too much for the games as there are some of the same type (Collector's Edition) that are a little above in terms of quality and that are less expensive, it's still worthy of your wallet. Go for it.

"Pilgrim's Hook" is the second installment of "Small Town Terrors" game series. Previous game in this series: Livingston
There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're amazingly well done. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio. The visual and audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu.
There are three different game difficulty modes to choose from: Casual, Expert and Hardcore.
There are fifteen different achievements can be earned during gameplay. Some of these achievements do have certain requirements before they can be unlocked.
There is a notebook holds all story events that had happened in the game.
There is an objective panel inside the notebook. Click on the tab it will bring up the objective panel.
The interactive map allows the player to fast travel between each location quickly. It also indicates there are tasks that needs to be done at certain locations. The map can be accessed through the notebook and outside of it. Please note that the map isn't given immediately when the game started.
Most of the hidden object scenes consists of find "x" amount of an item and traditional word list. Some of them do require little or no interaction.
Most of the game's puzzles are rather easy to solve without much difficulty. For most of these puzzles there's a reset button. However, there's definitely a skip button, for all of the puzzles. These two features are only present in "Casual" game difficulty mode.
There are twenty-five collectible sea creatures. They're scattered throughout the entire game.
Since this is a collector's edition game, there's a bonus chapter, but it can be unlocked only after the main story of the game's completed. The bonus chapter is the pre-sequel to the main story.
There's a built-in strategy guide for the game. It can be access anytime during gameplay.
In the Bonus Content section: nine concept art; six wallpapers; collectibles: whale bones and sea creatures; Arthur's Journal; Achievements and Bonus Chapter.
[Please note that Arthur's Journal and Whale Bones sections can't be accessed right away.]
Final thoughts, I definitely enjoying playing this game all the way through to the end. However, there's one thing that would make traveling less tedious is having a map that fast travel ability. As for the replay value I would say is low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

For some HO gamers this game will be entertaining and enticing, for others it will be annoying and dumb.  Once the rather contrived supernatural aspects are accepted even the "weirdness" that occurs is amenable.
The Story:  Vera receives a cryptic phone call from her estranged younger twin Arthur asking/begging her to come back to their childhood home, Pilgrim's Hook, a remote ex-whaling island village off Nantucket, Massachuesetts (USA).  (This fictional place would be off the coast of Boston, Cape Cod, or Martha's Vintage in Massachusetts for trivia lovers.)  By the time she gets there her brother is missing and she must find him.  Relatively typical storyline, except for the fact she finds him by chapter two.  Meanwhile, an evil lurking Cthulhu-like octopus starts talking to Vera through water puddles and flat reflective surfaces.  Creepy, and just exactly why does it want Vera?  This is actual storyline: the mystery of island and why it is there.  The evil denizen of the deep is left rather open to interpretation, however, its motives are not. It clearly states them.  However, why it considered Vera to be a good candidate is well ... simply a poor choice of its part.
The gameplay:  This is where the gamer will love or hate the game.   If a straight forward linear hunt, search and find is your thing, then this game is not it.  The gameplay is "open world".  What I mean by this is the gamer can go anyway, look, hunt, search, find objects, and do puzzles in no given order.  What can be done is limited to the clues given, items found and objects available in the inventory.  This will cause "confusion" for linear thinkers, and complaints from those who dislike "wandering".  (There is a built in walkthrough that is set up in a linear progression and a fast travel map.)  The game "bottle necks" at certain points and the player can not progress until all objects needed to be found are found and the tasks needed to be done are completed.  (Personally I consider these points to be self checks, if I cannot proceed I missed something somewhere.)
Puzzles: There are two types of HOs.  1) Straight forward HO scenes with at least one cleverly hidden object. (Not the type that makes one say "jerks" but the type that make one say "oh there it is, wow how did I miss that"  2) Find x amount of objects.  Usually 3 different objects of different amounts.
There is a variety of other puzzle types some harder then others, one requires a lot of patience and one ultra classic I have not seen in years.  (Some of those oldies will stump today's audience and this one will probably stump some players.)
There are two sets of Hidden Finds: Castor's Collection (fading in and out sea life) found throughout the main storyline, and the Whale's Bones, only available after finishing the bonus chapter.
Overall: Not a deep storyline and one that leaves a lot of room for intrepretation and unanswered questions if one thinks about it too much.  "Open world" game style.  A variety of puzzles (at least one ultra classic) and HO scenes.  This a relatively short game, too, compared to more recent games.
One last thing: Achievements.  All in-game achievements can be achieved in a single playthrough and some achievements are quite different from the usual achievement fare.  If steam achievements and trading cards is the only reason you play then do not play this game, this game has neither.  However, if you play HOs for the sheer joy of playing a decent story with decent HO scenes and puzzles then play this game.

Hex COULD be a really good game, but instead it's just a really frustrating RNG exercise.
Huge flaw in the core mechanic of the game is that the resources that you need to play cards...are also cards!
You stack your deck with different types of gems, which you need to have enter your hand (via drawing a card once per turn) so that you can play them in order to unlock a threshold that allows you to play other cards.  So let's say a sapphire card requires that you have 2 sapphires unlocked, but you keep drawing every other type of gem - or you don't draw any gem cards and just draw combat cards.
Vice versa you keep drawing gem cards and can't draw any combat cards.  You'll just sit there and watch your hero quickly killed while you can't do anything about it.  So you'll enter the deck builder and increase the number of gem cards that are in your deck, therefore increasing the likelyhood that you can draw some gems, which will allow you to play combat cards.  Then you'll start drawing nothing but gem cards and have no combat cards in your hand with which to attack or defend.  Or the combat cards you can draw require more gems than you can draw. You could literally be killed by a single 1/1 card hitting you down to 0 health because you can't play anything.
Basically this game requires your RNG to grant you the perfect mix of resource cards and combat cards, which is very unique (see: flawed and stupid).  There's a reason that most other card games don't do this - IT DOESN'T WORK.
Great artwork, neat campaign and story, cards feel reasonably balanced, you can tell a lot of work and care went into making this game, but it's fatally flawed.

I found Tölva to be quite enjoyable, and well worth my time.  As many other reviewers have mentioned, it's not a thrill-a-minute nonstop cavalcade of action, but there's enough combat to keep things lively enough for my tastes.  There's a fair amount of walking around, but the level design is quite beautiful and a treat to look at.  Apart from a few open plains-like areas towards the end of the game, travel times are mitigated quite well by the ability to fast-travel to bunkers and spawn points.
The combat itself veers from extremely satisfying to underwhelming, depending on circumstance.  An otherwise well-thought-out plan of attack can get derailed by unexpected flanking or having patrol groups show up at inopportune times, and it can be quite fun when you can successfully take over a bunker and survive in the middle of that chaos.  At other times your drone can feel like a lumbering ox getting torn apart without a good chance to retaliate.
The game does get a bit repetitive towards the end, especially if you're one to try and 100% it.  Some indication on the map of which areas contain missing items / signal data wouldn't have gone amiss.  But the game doesn't overstay its welcome, and it was only the last hour or so which I felt a little unenthused about cleaning out the last remaining map icons.
The ending itself is abrupt, and leaves a good amount unspoken, but IMO it works well enough in the context of the game.  The story text (in the form of "signal data") is serviceable enough, and there's a surprisingly lengthy and thorough "Lorebook" available to flesh out the universe, if you're intersted.
In the end, it's an enigmatic and beautiful world Big Robot's created with Tölva, and I'd definitely recommend checking it out.

First of all, I would like to say I got this game for 50 eurocents via a coupon of a friend. I saw this game had achievements and even trading cards, so I mainly hoped for something decent or maybe even good. I didn't find what I was hoping for.
Plazma Being is a puzzle platformer in which you control a flame thing from space that can change forms. That about sums up the whole depth of this game. I was REALLY hoping I would find more depth, but as I continued to level 10 and beat the game (yes the game is that short), I barely got any. The only depth you will find in this game is beginning with 2 forms and ending with 4(!) forms to change between as you progress through the game, 3 very lackluster bosses, which required only a slight bit of thinking and generally 1 ability (with a bit of luck) and some sort of collectibles in the form of energy bubbles which enable you to progress, depending on if you play on the teleporter charger mode (if I say this right). If you play on the other mode (on which I fully forgot the name, sorry!) you don't need to collect the energy bubbles.
Now I can almost hear you thinking; 'Well what did you expect for 2 euro's (or in your case 50 eurocents)?' To be honest, I didn't expect a really unique indie game or anything like that, but I did expect a fun platformer to have a couple of hours of fun. Well, it would be fun if the above written (part about the depth of the game) was all I had to nag about. Instead I got steadily more frustrated as I played on. I am not gonna list every negative point, as my hands already hurt from playing this game with the controls it gave to me.
Pro's
- Cheap, especially with coupon(s).
- Easy to understand, although the game doesn't have a tutorial, it's clear in every level what you are supossed to do and even if you missed energy bulbs (which the game also makes clear at some point during the game).
- Clear indicator when placing/freezing blocks midair, so that you can see when you can jump onto the block or not.
- Your character sometimes make some slightly cute noise.
Con's
- Buggy. Sometimes you can't jump for some reason, sometimes you can't go under blocks you placed/freezed midair for no reason (unless your hitbox suddenly grows at that exact point *cough*), sometimes blocks shoot away when you are trying to displace them with your powerups, and so on. First this isn't that bad as you can reset via a nearby checkpoint, but it happened so many times (at the very least 2 times per level with me) it really ruins the game.
- The controls. I picked up my xbox controller when booting up the game, didn't work. Ok, then with keyboard. A and D to move, W to jump, L to restart (from a checkpoint) and mouse for your powerups (scrolling alternates between powerups and clicking left or right mouse button uses them). The main character controls like a piece of rock tied to a persons leg. Very sluggish, but once you get moving stopping is a bit... wonky...
- The bosses, which I mentioned earlier. Obvious spoiler alert: the bosses are very simple and require a slight bit of skill. Fighting the bosses consist of doing one action, sometimes multiple times. Reflecting a laser, bouncing a bomb back and sitting on top of the boss describe all the 3 bosses and how to beat them in one sentence.
- The game mechanics and "puzzles". When trying to use your powers to displace objects with your mouse in this game, you get a clear circle of the extend to which you can displace objects. Problem is, when you move objects, the circle gets smaller the faster you move them to prevent you from throwing objects farther away then you should be able to. If you try to move an object just a little bit to the sides of your circle, good luck, because your object will fall into a void (which means restarting!~). There are some more minor issues with mechanics, but I will leave it for you (the reader) to discover. The puzzles however, are godawful sometimes. The puzzles that require you to think are sometimes challenging, but other times just downright annoying. Luckily you can skip entire puzzles whilst asking yourself; '...Was I supossed to do that...?'. Eventually I got stuck at one puzzle, looked it up on youtube and the guy who "solved" the puzzle literally said the same thing I thought; 'Was that the solution or did I do this wrong?'.
- Lastly, the feel of this game. I simply feel the developer just lost interest halfway through the game and finished it in a hurry, which explain the bugs and the ways you can cheat yourself through puzzles.
I wouldn't even mind if this game was released in an even slightly worse state, but it just almost sickens me that the developer even asked money for this, when it doesn't even feel full effort (again, MAINLY in terms of bugs and puzzles) was put into this game. I can search on kongregate for more fun platformers which will entertain me more and longer for free, which also give me the feeling more effort was put into it.
TL:DR
You would be better of playing a fun platformer on kongregate for free, I really think the developer of this game shouldn't have even asked for money for this game.

This is a different kind of strategy game. There's no silly basebuilding, resource gathering, or other superflous stuff. You get your points, you buy your units, and you tear your opponents apart for the objectives. Making up for this lack of BS is an incredibly detailed unit and gameplay system. Armor combat is realistically modeled in this game, with penetration value, sloped armor, angles, and location-specific damage taken into account. Oh, and did I mention you can directly control any unit in this game, allowing you to pull off those daring tactics that the AI sometimes just isn't realiable enough for?
That aside, this is essentially similar to Men of War, but missing a substantial SP component. Its multiplayer is a very refined, distilled version of MoW's great multiplayer, and is very well balanced overall. If you don't mind the realism or intense micro, this is a game worth checking out, at least.

Final Doom is a stand-alone huge mission pack based on Doom 2 in 1996. Or more exactly, it consist of two big IWADs, both having 32 levels, both fan-made, both not bringing anything new or changing core gameplay. And both are harder than your average Doom 2. The names of these two level packs are TNT Evilution and Plutonia Experiement.
It also had a PS1 port, which takes only some of Final Doom levels, puts some levels from Master Levels, toned down difficulty and then applied a dark horror-like atmoshpere to it, with low brightness and ambient music. I feel that it's much superior experience for those who aren't complete Doom 2 fans, instead of dragging thorugh 64 levels.
As usual, Steam version was handled in same way as other Steam versions of classic Doom games. That means "badly".
Once again you have to edit "ddraw" line to "opengl" in conf files to make DosBox run without lags. Adn once again setup.exe wasn't included, so you have to manually edit cfg files for controls and music. Yes, uses Soundblaster by default too. At least Steam still gives you option between "classic" and "with mouse" control scheme when launching game.
Specially for Final Doom, configuration isn't the only thing that got screwed up. You see, in Steam version both level packs use same exe file. And that exe is from Plutonia. Not every data is kept in wad file, some were in exe too. What it means is that TNT Evilution uses Plutonia's story for occasional text intermission and it shows Plutonia's level name on same slot on level's automap.
Oh, and they share save slots too. Loading another's pack save crashes the game. You better be careful not to screw up progress by overwriting wrong save is you are beating both packs.
Now, for gameplay of those two packs themselves:
Made me want to yank Chaingunners out of Doom mappers hands, along with their arms. 10/10
Just kidding. Well, at least this common complaint it true for both packs.
TNT Evilution is slightly harder than Doom 2 and is uncertain of what kind of level style it wants to have. It's quite a mix, not exactly all fun one. It can't decide if it wants to have tricky "gotcha" maps, hard crowd stuff, linear layout or confusing mazes. Maps 19 and 20 are really something, as they get out from Doom's abstract style and look like a real place, with office rooms, truck, what looks like actual warehouse boxes processing. It's actually quite nice. And then pack will throw you into huge empty level. So yes, uncertain. It does make use of new textures though, here and there, most memoriable being blood patches on occasional wall. It also includes new music, which helps to give it a personality. They aren't bad either.
Plutonia Experiement is a different beast, that wants to rip you apart. It's more in line with Doom 2 style, only slightly less dull and brown. Mazes are also complex, but in a good way, it doesn't make you run over map in search for a hidden button. It also rarely uses new textures of green color, as well as reuses Doom 1 music. So, in some ways it's a bit better than Doom 2 when it comes to level design. Heck, it even has a map that is maze, filled with archviles that are aware of your existance, hunting you down as you figure out the ways that various doors are opened.
And it's also hard. It's a main point of this IWAD actually, to be hard. And cheap, occasionally, not going to forget situation where I was teleport in front of two teleporting archviles, that you can't break a line of sight from unless you decide to just run away into near pit and try to snipe from down there. So yes, it's very hard, which in PC gaming with saving means abusing quicksaves every few seconds, not the most pleasent grinding.
Multiplayer doesn't seem to be supported by Steam version. You should use Zandronum source port for that. Eh, you will figure it out by yourself.
I actually wanted to not recommend this game at first, since it's kinda more of same Doom 2 but harder, didn't see appeal of playing 60 more freaking levels that hate you. But that was before I properly played it in single-player.
After beating it, I can say that Doom 2 gameplay is still fun, even if using Super Shotgun on everything and having Chaingunner in every room gets repetive. So yes, Doom nuts should get this one.

If you're into desolately beautiful landscapes, this game is worth buying for the scenery alone. The level design and graphics are unlike anything I've ever seen before. The graphics are rich but subtle, and detailed without being noisy, if that makes sense. The time of day changes in real time, and there are some truly beautiful moments, such as when the shadow of a cliff sweeps across a valley, or night turns to dawn. As regards performance, for the most part it ran smoothly at high settings/4K on my machine.
The weapon selection is limited to a pistol, automatic rifles, the lightning gun from Quake, and railguns. They're very weak to start with, and only towards the end of the game can you buy ones that have satisfactory damage/reload stats. A more varied weapon selection, like mines, remotely-detonated bombs, mortars, rocket launchers, etc. would have made the game a lot more fun. I've lost count of the number of times I had enemies chasing me through narrow passages and wishing the game had mines. The railguns aren't very effective as sniper rifles -- the range isn't nearly long enough, and only a few of them have anything like a proper scope. The reticles are bright and sci-fi looking, which is fine in the daytime, but at night they tend to make targets hard to see.
Combat, unfortunately, is very basic and boring. Movement is slow and clunky, which to me seems like a wasted opportunity -- when your character is a robot, it's practically a license to make movement as fast and agile as you want it to be. Disappointingly, the most effective combat tactic I found was to lure enemies near a spawn point, and then keep respawning as many times as it took to finish them all off (there's no penalty for dying except having to trudge back to where you need to be).
You can recruit other bots of your faction to accompany you, but the device that lets you do that takes up one weapon slot, and the bots are only effective as cannon fodder to distract enemies from you, so I chose to go solo instead.
The game makes you walk a lot. Dying in a place where the nearest spawn point is far away, and having to trudge all the way back to where you need to be gets old very quickly.
One of the most annoying sequences for me was the puzzle in the 'Dirac Undulation' region. It's incredibly frustrating and doesn't add anything to the gameplay.
Overall, definitely worth buying for the level design alone. I'd very much like to see a sequel with the flaws ironed out.

Don't let the graphics decieve you into thinking this is an inferior game. This is actually one of the best one-on-one multiplayer games and makes for some intensely entertaining matches. The graphics just drive the point that the gameplay is simple and could have, indeed have been done several years ago. The type of game that makes you say "why hasn't anyone done this before?" This is one of the simplest controls in a fighting-style game, yet despite its simplicity there is a lot of depth and split second strategy involved. It's easy to see what your opponent did and say "Oh, now I know I can do that next time" without thinking which button to press.
This is like a Versus fighting /  sidescroller where both opponents start in the middle and try to fight / run their way to their victory side. Like American Football one team is able to proceed at a time while the other acts on defense to keep you from moving forward. A kill means you can go forward to your goal. You're in the constant frontline of a battle between yellow and orange. Do you go in slowly picking out each of your opponents one by one? Or did you see an opportunity to throw your sword and dash like hell to the next screen? High, medium, and low sword attacks for poking (lower goes furthest) move your sword between the three positions with up/down keys, switching position to an attacking sword parrys it away. You can roll underneath a mid-high sword while low sword pokes a rolling opponent in the eye. You can jump and divekick your opponent to make them drop their sword, while they can throw their sword at you for an easy in-air hit. Thrown swords can be blocked in mid and high position... Very simple in motion and with an answer to everything a very well balanced breakfast. I give it 5 stars.

Dear god, what a disappointment this was.  I enjoyed 1000000, but this game is like someone decided to draw it out as long as possible while removing half the things that made the original tolerable.  Oh right and when I beat the last quest the game softlocked.  GOOD JOB.
The drink system is absolute rubbish now, with mostly-useless effects and less flexibility- drinks last a set number of runs so once you drink one you're stuck with it for that amount of time.
Monsters have a large variety of effects, which means for the most part there's no strategy for taking them out.  You just have to match attack tiles in general.
Upgrades are now basically worthless for the gold they cost, and you have almost no gold income aside from quest rewards until the very end of the game!  This means you can't grind until then, and when you DO get there, you HAVE TO grind, because the last quest is ABSOLUTELY RIDICULOUS.
Oh right, quests.  Instead of collecting resources to unlock upgrade types, you have to do quests, which usually involve satisfying some unique action during a dungeon run.  That's generally fine, though some rely on blind luck.  However, their main purpose seems to be roadblocking upgrades.  After a certain point, the equipment upgrades all require "silver" which only drops from quest rewards until you get an upgrade near the end of the game that lets you get it from matching crate tiles.  Thus, silver restricts what upgrades you can get, which makes grinding mostly useless.  Furthermore, base stat upgrades are hard-locked to completing "monster capture" quests, so you can't grind for them at all.
Take the combination of the following factors:
1) Traps are so punishing you have to have a variety of tiles ready to match at all times, which requires luck.
2) The RNG is streaky which means you get a lot of garbage or a lot of accidental match chains, which can either roadblock you or make progress smooth.
3) Quest items are looted from boxes which require a lot of matches of specific tiles.
4) The last quest item is put so deep in the dungeon you have like 10 seconds to match the required tiles.  The dungeon is pushing you back just that fast.
5) Dungeon effects are randomly generated, but they stay the same until you complete a quest.
6) Monsters near the end of the game take like 5 or 6 attacks to kill and have no weaknesses for the most part.
7) Items can be stockpiled for emergencies between runs once you get the upgrade that allows it, but all items STAY IN THE GRID, GETTING IN THE WAY.
All these factors combined means that if you get a bad roll for your last set of dungeon effects, the final quest becomes PURE LUCK.

Valdis Story: Abyssal City is one of the best games i've played so far, i've been so hooked on to it that i have yet to become bored of doing the game over and over, it feels like each playthrough is a challenge and the hardest difficulty which is unlocked after your first playthrough really puts your skills to the test.
The storyline is quite a fun turn of events as neither hell or heaven is the good guy here!
You start off on a ship with your crew then some giant monster comes and crashes your ship and you all sink and end up in Abyssal City which is deep under the sea, it turns out that you have been caught up in the middle of a war between angels and demons and your only way out is to battle your way through hordes of angels and demons as you search for your missing crew!
Currently there are 2 playable characters out of 4 which will be available in an upcoming patch. The 2 currently available characters have very different playstyles, one of them is a monk which starts by using only fists while the other starts with a sword, both have their strengths and weaknesses which makes it really fun to play through the game a second time.
I started out playing the swords man in the hardest difficulty and finished the game and it was quite rewarding as i had to put some effort in to it, later i decided i was going to try out the monk and oh my did i get a surprise, it was like playing a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT GAME! i died a couple of times to bosses here and there which i had considered mastered, but because of the different playstyle and spells it really shook me up and made me have another blast through the game!
The game also features a leveling system and a talent tree system which is pretty rare for a sidescroller, it brings out allot of possibilities while leveling on what path you wish to take and what  stats you require for your skill tree... Want to be a MONK MAGE?! no problem... Want to be a barehanded swordsman!? again no problem... the game is very well built to give you the different options of choosing what ever path suites you best!
The item system in the game is very pleasing, it's not to complex and not to simple, you will grind enemies along your travels and they will drop a variation of items for you, later in the game you will be able to use the items obtained to upgrade your weapons or armor as you see fit or even expand your mana or health pool.
This really brought out the good old RPG feeling in me and made me want to try to obtain all the items in the game in my first playthrough, i then realised that there are some items in the game that are only obtainable from chests and you will have to think wisely before you upgrade your weapons or armors as you may not be able to upgrade any other weapon or armor in your current playthrough!
While gliding through the game you will fight vicious bosses that will show you no mercy at all, you will struggle and enjoy the sensation of progressing them til you finally deliver the final blow! you will be required to try out various combinations of armors or spells in order to find out what the best possible way to kill the bosses are.
Every boss in the game has some sort of weakness and it's yours to figure out!
The game it self is well designed, the story is great, has beautiful graphics which are all hand drawn as well as amazing music that really puts you in the zone when fighting bosses or while you are exploring the world of Valdis Story!
Pros:
- Playable multiple times
- Very fun combat system
- Challenging boss fights
- Multiple characters to choose from
- Great leveling system with a unique leveling tree
- Difficulties made to please the average player to hardcore player
- Upgrading system
Cons:
- Map can be frustrating for beginners who have not played the game yet
- You will become hooked to the game and not want to leave your computer!

Valdis story : Abyssal City is a Metroidvania type of game with quite interesting backround story and setting but shadowed a littlebit by frustratingly hard bosses. The game begins with your character dumped into an underwater city along with your now lost crew and point is to try search all of them and find out just what is going on.
Population of the games world is split into 2 main factions which are Angels and demons, both sides trying to obliterate the other. Humans are minor third faction whose existance is comparable to fodder for both larger factions and their souls are used to bolster ranks of angels and demons. In Abyssal city another side called Ferals come into this equation, dangerous species who skulk around the Abyssal city and ruthlessly kill any who come in their way but for some reason they specifically hunt only angels and demons.
You are a freedom fighter demi-human, a leader of your little crew consisting characters from all 3 factions. Every crewmember has, for personal reasons, pledged to your cause to fight both angels and demons. Each member gives you either an ability to summon him to aid you in a fight, work for you as a vendor in specific place in the game or teach powerful, castable finisher attacks to improve your combat performance.
The game itself is basically sidescrolling hack and slash coloured with more or less difficult enemies, occasionally somewhat tough platforming and just insanely difficult bosses who are likely to have your hide several times until you figure their patterns and weaknesses. Thinking how you place your hard earned skill and stat points along with upgrading your picked up gear is imperative to make it to the end and using spells and buffs is occasionally a matter of life and death. For example an Ice buff against fire type enemies or bosses might actually save your controller/keyboard from immediate obliteration caused by momentual lack of better judgement due frustration.
As it is, combat is very fluid, magic system works very well with melee combat system, weapons, armors and assistants are more than worthwhile to level up and with cooperation of skill trees and stats posses heavy effect to your combat style while allowing you to build, at least almost, the kind of fighter you want.. be it counter attacking warrior or backstabbing assasin type.. or just yolo going megacrit maniac.
Valdis story has few game time connected events and doing something before its too late actually affects the later parts of the game. You are likely to waste much more time on your first playthrough but if you think it as a mere training run before the actual fun begins on the 2nd run, it makes Valdis Story : Abyssal City much more satisfying experience.

Lame Magic the Gathering ripoff, without the design chops that make Magic fun. There are so many TCGs out there that are actually creative, and bring something new to the table, often for much less money than HEX demands you spend.
Basically, if you have the money and you're looking for a deep, strategic experience, Magic is still your best bet. If you're looking for something cheaper or more accessible, there's Hearthstone, Spellweaver, SolForge, Card Hunter... and a ton more I'm probably forgetting. An absolutely excellent experience so far. Haven't finished it yet, but its totally engaging, especially if you read the (very engaging and quite cerebral) content as you progress. It draws you right into a sci-fi mystery with timescale spanning eons... long after any meatware was on the scene.

It also doesn't hold your hand too much. You need to figure out your tactics, use of different view modes to understand how to complete the various puzzles and allow you to progress further.
Sound and music is very poignant / relaxing and dramatic as it needs to be, as I said earlier creating an excellent atmosphere and seamless experience. Works great on ultrawide screen, also plays really nicely with a controller or mouse and keyboard.

Last but not least I recommend watching the gameplay videos on the store page. They really sold me on it, and gave me an excellent idea of the gameplay without ruining the mystery.

If you want a hidden object game which offers exactly what you assume in this genre, Pilgrim’s Hook won’t disappoint you. It may be unoriginal, but it is also a solid hidden object puzzle title.
Small Town Terrors 2 is the kind of hidden object game that tries to remain in the genre’s comfort zone, which works as much to its advantage as against it.
The story offers little surprises: while searching for a loved one you find yourself in a small town haunted by something evil, which of course you promptly destroy before the end credits. There is next to no supporting cast, and the voice acting is kind of a hit and miss.
Same goes for the puzzles: we don’t meet a single one that wasn’t seen before, but they offer a large variety and a good difficulty curve– although the hidden object scenes tend to rely on the ‘find x amount of said object’ gimmick. The only really conspicuous flaw is the usual dumb adventurer syndrome, where you instantly throw away a useful object even if you would need it three scenes later.
Despite these small issues Pilgrim’s Hook is still a good pick that won’t really disappoint any hidden object game fans.

Factions of Android "drones" are fighting an infantry war over the surface of the planet Tölva (which is emitting a wierd signal that attreacted them in the first place).  You play as a hacker who hijacks these drones to take control of their bodies in order to infiltrate their organization, and use their bodies to scan the various signal generating anomolies on the surface.
The gameplay loop is a rather addictive explore, fight, loot , repeat.  It's like an indie scale version of the fallout 4 loop, bare bones but pushing all the same buttons.  Tölva is one large, seamless, open world It manages to make it's anomalies mysterious and a puzzle I genuinly want to unravel.  There is some paradoxical architecture in structures on the planet, which is something i've not seen since the Stanly Parable and ties your brain in knot.
The combat seems basic, but serviceable.  There only seems to be a very limited variety of basic guns, in an assortment of minor variations, slight incremental upgrades that you can unlock as you advance.   Any time you're killed or you just want to bug out you can just hijack another drone at one of the various bunkers you capture during your exploration.
I cannot tell if the world is hand crafted from a limited set of assets or if it's a really well done procedural generation. Either way it's enough to make me want to explore Tölva.

Final DooM, aptly named, is the final essential game from the DooM franchise, created by Team TNT and the Casali Brothers over a course of 4 months and split into two episodes. The levels featured in this standalone 'expansion' were designed in mind for people who had completed the original two DooM games on Ultra-Violence and were looking for more of a challenge.
Final DooM not only achieved what they set out to do but did it with class. There are some terrifically obscure masterpieces among this collection and the difficulty these maps provide generally doesn't come from swamping the player with massive hordes of enemies, but from cheap/clever monster placement.
This offers a far greater challenge seen in the original two games, so much so that if you were comfortable with completing the originals on Ultra-Violence without 'Save Scumming' or dying once throughout entire playthroughs this would be sure to kick your♥♥♥♥♥atleast a few times... hard... While there are a few maps here I disliked slightly, the good ones far overshadow them and progression welcomes you to new, unique challenging combat situations which bear a demonic grin while trying to brutally slaughter you.
Final DooM should be played on Ultra-Violence or higher, playing it on anything easier defeats the purpose, if you feel it's too hard, rather practice with the originals until you get good enough to do so to appreciate and experience the full terror and panic the level designers have laid out for you. All in all some brilliant levels and high challenge is the centre point of this game, of which it achieves flawlessly. Play it Now.

I dont really know, how I should think about this game. While I played Dawn of War for its multiplayer, and Dark Crusade for its campaign (and multiplayer), Dawn of War 2 is like the two side of a blade.
The campaign was...well...more than great, it was awesome! While you had simple unit progression in Dark Crusade, you had now the control over small squads you were able to level up, skill and equip!
The campaign story itself wasnt that great sadly. The multiplayer is a desaster!
Playing as the Bloodravens again, you have to defend their home system against a big horde of orcs and later tyranids.
The campaign works like a round strategy game, where you equip your squads, control your planets and choose missions based on their urgency, difficulty and reward.
Choosing a mission, the real game begins in RTS style and you have up to four unit groups to control. Every group is lead by a hero unit, that has special abilitys and weapons.
Mostly fighting against overwelming enemy forces, you often have to fight tricky and stealthy, use good tactics and know, how to use your forces abilitys.
With every mission you get XP and items and can specialize your troops on melee or ranged combat, health and ability points. You get new weapons and new equipment, and sometimes gamechanger like the terminator armor, that awesomely upgrades your troops (except the scout of course) and gave me a big wtf with the upgraded Space Marine Stormtroopers, with teleport and big hammers. Awesome!
Having 4 units in every mission but a lot more usable units in your rooster, you can choose, which units you use in a mission, desiding on their abilitys and firepower and the enemys you will face.
Now two things shall be said:
The campaign is theoretically endless. You can play as many missions as you want. No pressure to do the final missions. You just have to hold down the enemys enough to keep the Xenos Infection low.
The whole campaign is coop. Instead of 4 units, each player controls 2. Nothing more to say.
Now the big bad:
Beside the campaign, there wasnt really anything useful left in this game. I tried the multiplayer, but was highly disappointed. Buildings are completely gone in this game. You only have a main building and troops. Confusing, frustrating and totaly not RTS like. I played Dawn of War for a long time and I played Starcraft and Age of Empires 2 and I couldnt get any fun in the Dawn of War 2 multiplayer.
I would like to give this game a good rating for its awesome campaign, but it hasnt much to offer beside it. It is like a HD version of Dawn of War without RTS gameplay. Why not making a complete Shooter out of...wait they already did that and it was awful...
It's so fun! I recommend to everyone!

Regarding to false promises, this has none. Whatever the description states, it delivers; which is commendable unto itself.
The game sports very fast-paced gameplay, incorporating well into itself teamplay and requires communication among the team; the constant hordes of enemies enforces teamplay further, discouraging lone-wolf players.
The classes include a large degree of specificity, as they each boast different gameplay styles and each add a different dynamic to the team. Each dynamic that each class offers in-game gives the team a certain diversity that allows the group to prevent failure from a variety of situations, that may jeopardize the success of the mission.
Each class is given specific weaponry and abilities that allow them to bring their title to fruition, certain classes are effective within specific engagement ranges, while other classes are effective in others. Failure to keep any one of the team-members places the rest of the team in a disadvantage against whichever role they lost.
Although the type of gameplay is well established, the variability of the situations your team might face is lacking. Although map design is fair, the lack of consistant updates, modding and the Workshop will eventually make the game suffer.
It is fun to try out, however the game does not offer much to continually satisfy the player. Also, there is a lack of original content of which the developers of the game does not credit the creators. This has potential, but the product currently does not place itself near what potential quality and content it could contain.
The game is free, give it a try and help the developers by supplying them suggestions and critiques.

This is Dawn of War II, while I do recommend this game, bare in mind it is NOT like its predecessor, I would call Dawn of  War a classical RTS with a base-capture element, while this is more of a action-oriented tactical RPG with more units. The Campaign is the best mode in my opinion or the online area modes and you won't be constructing buildings at all, all you will do in the regular 1 vs 1 mode is producing units. Controlling units, bases and manage economy but there are no build orders you just upgrade your current base to build more units.
A lot of people, myself included did not like this change. I am a big fan of 4X, strategy and RTS games, but this is more of a RPG, I would say the campaign itself is totally worth it if you buy it on a sale, then go ahead, and get ready to gear up your own space marine squad.
And the customization in the campaign is awesome, you want to give Terminator Armour to Assault Marines? They pick up the Thunder Hammers, give it to your marines and they turn into regular old Terminators, want some extra range for your assault gun-carrying Termies? Then give 'em the good cyclone missle launcher and let loose havoc.
The campaign really is the peak of this game and it lets you play from many different angles, but do keep in mind from an RTS point of view, Dawn of War I is the better multiplayer online game. But DoW also lets you play co-op in the campaign so if you just want to enjoy the Epic Space Marine bad assery with friends then totally pick this game up.

I have been searching for something new in the MMO genre for a long long time. I was a vanilla WoW player.. I really loved the world pvp in that era of world of warcraft. I have always felt instances and battlegrounds etc ruin the immersion and potential fun of pvping in mmos.
Enter Darkfall: Unholy Wars. There are no instances. It is a PVP based mmo where every bit of pvp that happens in the game is somewhere in the world. PVP is cutthroat like those games of yesteryear. When you kill someone all of their loot drops on the ground. It is a sandbox mmo... you can go anywhere and do just about anything... you can customize your class as much as you want. There are not levels, just incremental "prowess" of which you only need about 30k-40k to be pvp viable. At time of writing this review I have 46k prowess and I have killed people with as much as 200k prowess. It took me about a week to get to this high in prowess which consisted mostly of killing different camps of monsters throughout the game.
I could go on describing the game, but I think anyone reading this review will know if the game is for them or not. Gaining prowess is a grind, I find it far superior to questing which there isnt a single one of in this game.  Combat is completely skill based (no tab targeting what so ever.) meaning you will need to be comfortable playing first person shooters to enjoy this game.
I see myself playing this game for a long time to come... I just wished I had discovered it a lot sooner.

I was watching the show RWBY with a bunch of friends the other day and when Yang got hit by a Big Mech though a concrete pillar everyone suddenly shouted: “OMG!! She turned super Saiyan!!
As it should be for everyone around the world that grown up from the rise of anime age, everyone knows Dragon ball Z and Saiyan became a new specialized fictional race of monkey boy (men) that have tails and spiky hair which can turn golden sparky and instantly became super cool.
This game is one of the more recent one that was made from the franchise. It’s a 3D fast pace fighting game with simple controls and cool animations. Instead of going through the regular Dragon ball Z story line with main story hero such as Goku, in this game you are a time patroller recruit that was enlisted by Trunks (the time traveler from original story) and Supreme Kai of time in a setting of Time and Dimensional Monitoring and Interfering Agency. Your Job is fix the time line and make sure the story of Dragon ball Z doesn’t get changed by other time travelers. So you will appears out of nowhere in different dragon ball Z time period to help the good guys and even sometime bad guys.
The Storyline stay quite true to the original storyline with added time traveler plot that’s quite simple and merged well together. Graphic is decent and most of the design and animation stayed very true to the original manga/TV drawing while turning it 3D.
Voice acting of both English and Japanese used original voice acting from TV show as much as possible. For dedicated fan it’s awesome to hear many of those super memorable line from the original show.
Difficulty is quite easy and you do need to customize your character well. (Equipment, Skills, Items and Plus attribute of level up). If you run into some problem with certain story level go back to your base and grind some parallel quest to gain better skills and EXP.
Multiplayer is one of my complain for this game as a real in game chat system is not there and you have to depend on Steam chat or voice chat to organize and arrange multiplayer game. There are much fewer people playing multiplayer for this game now and if you sampling making a game room you will wait for hours before you meet anyone randomly wandering in.
Achievements are all quite simple to get, 1/4 of them simple story related, 1/4 of them require grinding for skill drops, 1/4 of them require you train with different story masters, 1/4 of them multiplayer. IF you invest around 40-50 hours in grinding you should be able to get everything except those multiplayer related ones. With 2 friends those multiplayer related achievements should be attained within the hour. (A Steam forum friend helped me and I am sure you can find others to help you.)
8.5/10 would be my rating and I would rate it 9.5 if the multiplayer was better designed. Get it and play it if you are a dragon ball Z fan, fighting game fan or both.
PS:
1.	There is a Xenoverse 2 came out last year and it seems like the samething. I will try it when I get the game later.
2.	For those of you that having trouble getting some certain skill to drop just have elder kai (DLC3) as your master and talk to him to have him tell your fortune. If you luck is not at best or he refuse to tell fortune just go to a parallel quest’s character select screen and then back out. The RNG will be reset. As long as he tell you that your fortune is at the best than skill will sure drop as long as you can reach ultimate finish. (Thanks to the utube for teaching me that.)
3.	If you have trouble getting dragon balls you can have both regular Shenron character as your teammate and that will increase your drop rate to 100%.

This game is hard!  Frustratingly so!  Some of the bosses are cheap - and I mean extremely cheap.
Others are ... pathetic. You can stand in one spot the entire time and the boss basically doesn't do anything but jump all around the screen and eventually get near you so you whack the crap out of them.
Neat story though confusing as sin when you first start the game. Some missables (meaning you'll never have a chance to go back and get them if you don't in the "right time" or at the "particular point in the game.")
The game is not designed really for the idea of 100% complete in all sections.  It is meant to be played over and over again.
Update:
So, I started to play this game again in 2015 - it has been patched a lot from my first play through.  It is more polished, there are some bugs, but not as many as when I first played. It is _a lot_ better now.  It is still "about as finished" as when I first played though, they added a few more bosses. I am more consistent at getting "S Rank" on boss fights this time around as I understand the mechanics and the general "path" to follow to complete the game 100%.
There is only one area that I found was a true missable the last time I was in there and there are only a couple items/crew you can miss. So, 95% of the game is not "missable."
You can either find it or not and a good portion is "unmissable."
Some of the "upgrading" is a bit warped - takes waaay to many materials to upgrade so I think that is a bug or a re-balancing issue.
Certain builds (all or nothing) types are enthusiastically OP. If you don't build that way though... you will not have a good time. Or well, you will have a much harder game to complete. I really enjoyed my all stat/skill points in Luck Build that seems like one of the most OP builds in the game currently.
I don't find the game as hard as I use - after configuring my controller a bit more to a more generic playstyle it is significantly easier than using a keyboard.

As someone who has only a light history of serious tcg playing, I find Hex to be the type of game I've always been looking for. It fills a nice niche that isn't really in the market atm. At least not with the same quality as Hex has.
Pros:
1. Insanely fun and well designed sets. Limited and constructed are clearly well thought out, and every set brings interesting new mechanics.
2. Unique mechanics only possible in the digital space. Hex sets itself apart by doing crazy things that are not possible in real-life TCGs. Modifying troops, filling an enemies deck with hundeds of spiders, and lots of other fun little things.
3. Possible to play the whole game for free. It will take some work on the part of the player, especially a new one, but I was able to amass a pretty respectable collection in during my time as a f2p player. Constructed pvp is a bit harder to f2p, but then again, Constructed is the most expensive mode in all TCGs.
4. Great Developers and great Community. The devs and players all seem to really care about this game, and they generally are very generous and respectful towards other players.
5. Real value. Hex strives to marry the qualities of real life TCGs and videogames, and as a result, cards in Hex have real money value. (In particular, rares and legendaries, as commons and uncommons are in such high supply.) Cards can be invested in and sold for Platinum (premium currency) or Gold.  If you decide to invest some money in Hex and a few months later, you don't want to play anymore, you can still sell your cards to others through a third party, allowing you to at least get some of your money back (and if you are very lucky and get the timing right, more).
Cons:
1. Starting out can be rough. Between a lack of experience and a small collection, playing the game as a f2p can appear quite daunting. This early phase will require some patience and research to get a good deck for farming the arena, but once it's done, you'll be able to play the game as a true f2p player, especially now that Evo gauntlet is out.
2. Some bugs. They have been getting much better with these, but there are still a few noticable bugs in the game. Nothing extremely bad though.

On the surface everything it fine with this game, however the more time you spend with it you start see more and more problems. Some commenters already pointed them already but here are the main issues from my point of view:
- The "free to play" label is misleading because after just the first day you realise you need to invest real cash and/or lot of grind time to actually make any progression (expanding your card collection). A new player has no chance to finish the first PVE chapter without buying some extra cards or having an insane luck (read "tons of frustration" until it happens).
- The development of the game started years ago and even the crowdfunding was very successful (based on their MMOTCG vision) they delivered just a really short chapter with almost no interactions with other players (at this point you can only chat and buy/sell cards via AH). Other than that it is a single player experience.
- In order to participate to PVP events you need to buy tickets (with platinum). You can buy platinum directly from the cash shop or grind gold (invest in a good deck) and convert it to items (cards, boosters or equipment) and sell those via AH for platinum.
-The strategy of Cryptozoic is focused on luring new people into playing and don't care too much about retaining them. This was visible from the starting campaign when they offered ridiculous overpowered rewards for backers. Too bad for the others. Later when community was screaming for PVE content they preferred on heavily investing and promoting their PVP tournament. Some bugs are present unfixed since alpha (eg Forge of Cadoc) and in addition things that were fine are broken after updates (eg. Arena challenges rewards). My general impression is they bite more than they can chew.
To be fair I would like to add also some positive comments:
- Even if their roots are visible connected with the MtG on the launching set, they put serious efforts to differentiate from those by creating new mechanics and exploiting the digital aspect of the cards.
- The game looks polish and in general the quality of artworks is quite high (except the character portraits who look a bit rushed).
- It is a great idea with huge potential, I still hope they will take this more seriously and eventually (IN A REASONABLE TIMEFRAME) achieve what they promised in the beginning.
I could have made this as a "positive" review but I just want them to keep the developers with the feets on the ground and point (once again) that this is NOT a finished product.

TL;DR If the premise interests you, you like visual novels with few choices and endings, and are not affraid of blood and sudden tone shifts, then give the game a try when it's on sale for at least half off. I give it a 5 out of 10.
GAMEPLAY  3 out of 10
This is a visual novel, so I know the only "gameplay" is reading and picking an option. But even by visual novel standards, there were surprisingly few choices. There was about an hour of story before the first choice selection was presented. On top of that, the beauty of a visual novel is that all of your choices have an affect on the story. While the game fulfills that purpose during the first half, choices in the second half felt like they had little effect on anything. I swear that a big  chunk of the dialogue from the two second half endings is almost word-for-word the same.
SOUND  5 out of 10
The music isn't terrible, but it's hardly spectacular. Honestly, it got annoyingly repetitive after a while and the songs didn't always fit the tone of the scene. For a game that so heavily references music, it was a little disappointing.
VISUALS 7 out of 10
The backgrounds are lovely and certain scenes are particularly well drawn. The faces sometimes look wierd, but overall everything looks fine. Nothing spectacular, but not unappealing.
STORY AND CHARACTERS  7 out of 10 for the 1st half, 3 out of 10 for the 2nd half
The game is divided into two distinct halves, with the second half taking place after a 5 year timeskip. There are a total of six endings, four in the first half and two in the second half. Although, the generic ending from the first half has no achievements
so it hardly counts.
The first half was great. The setting is unique, the characters are both believable and relatable, and the story is fairly well-written. There are some adult themes and as I mentioned there is visible blood, so if that bothers you then I suggest steering clear of the second half.
Speak of the devil, the sudden tone shift leading into the second half felt forced. After the time skip, the story really goes down the drain. The charcters are different. Not in a believable "I've changed over the years" way, but a "the story demands I act this way" fashion.

ACHIEVEMENTS
There are a total of six achievements--five for each real ending and one hidden achievement. If you don't really care about such things, then I suggest you ignore that hidden achievement
If you insist on getting all six achievements, then good luck. That hidden achievement is... I don't even have words to describe it. Actually, I do: idiotic and childish.
IN SUMMARY
I personally have no intention of playing the game again. I played all the way through only because I had already paid for it, but I honestly wish that I hadn't bought this game. If it had only been the first half of the story then I might have enjoyed it, but the second half left a bitter taste. I give it a  5 out of 10.

is a sci-fi FPS largely bent on exploration. The unfortunate part of this is that it isn't that interesting to explore. Nor is the shooting that great. It's functional. There is some lite faction warfare, seemingly the bot species has different aspirations and goals. Some outposts will be overtaken after you occupy them. Making you need to head back and defend them.
You'll earn scrap from exploring that will net you the ability to purchase new upgrades for the robot chassis as well as new weapons and other AoE style augments.

The combat is actually rather formulaic and repetitive. I found only 2 methods of dealing with enemies to be an alright way of going about things. One, snipe everything from afar after marking them with the binoculars. You might be familiar with that one. And two, use pop shots from the rifle so they activate their shields and then take them down -- The AI doesn't seem that intelligent. The shields drain from your battery and the AI doesn't seem to care for appropriately making the most of them. They tend to let them drain completely once activated. Giving you time to hide, reload for a full charge and then unload on them while their battery recharges. If that failed, I had a drone I could launch to aggro their attention away from me as their shields were drained. Now, that might seem like 	there is a lot going on. But when you have to do that same thing 6 or 7 times per encounter – it gets real old, real fast. The less than exciting exploration as the icing on the cake so to speak is just not enough to look over those aspects.

Just for frames of reference, I've played the following card games: MtG, YuGiOh, HearthStone, and Net Runner.
HEX: Shards of Fate is a digital tcg that has a single player vs AI component as well.
As a competitive tcg the play is very fun and the mechanics are a natural extension of the mechanics of traditional physical card games. Competitive play will cost money (either buying cards), or paying to enter limited tournaments, but if you're a tcg fan, the experience is everything you'd expect and hope for.
As a single player game vs AI the game is quite fun as well. There is a campaign mode that tells a story as you progress through, grow a character, and gain new cards for future encounters.
Some general pros and cons that I have are:
Pros:
Very fun mechanics both in the traditional tcg sense, but also the campaign in which you have characters that can level in the realm of a card game.
Free to play system in which you can earn rewards and sell them on the auction house to other players.
Continued development! More tcg sets and more missions in the campagin.
Cons:
The campaign story telling is a little sad. Characters sometimes respond the same way even with different races, and it doesn't make much sense. In the initial introductory mission, you feel like the races are different, but then when the other missions take place it feels very generic.
The auction house needs some work. It works for now, but it's pretty clunky.
As the game is still young and is in active growing development, there are some growing pains. If you're a patient person and can deal with this from time to time, I would actually say that this is a good thing (they are constantly improving!)
----
Overall, if you've played any trading or collectable card games I would highly recommend this game.
If you've never played one before, I think HEX is actually one of the best places to start because you can play vs the AI in a nice and relaxed environment free of the stress (because the AI doesn't care).
Would definitely recommend!

Thank you to the developer and publisher, Big Robot Ltd., for making a game for me to escape, explore and enjoy.
You will see everything The Signal of Tolva has to offer in probably less than :20 and in some ways it feels like a demo or concept but exploring the beautiful surface of Tolva and the fun of having your own band of expendable robot brothers made it a worthy journey to undertake.  
The Signal fo Tolva begins with you being dropped into a pretty good sized open world in search of, you guessed it, a signal. The signal is a mystery, is it doom? is it enlightenment? O boy i really wish i cared. As you explore you will receive brief messages from the mother ship but most is just simply go here, why, mission completed jargon. You will also be on the lookout for 60 orbs that will add context to the story. Luckily on the hub there is an indicator telling you when an orb is close. My problem with the orbs are it tells the story out of sequence and after i collected about 30 i had no clue what was going on and basically gave up. There are actually 2 signals and both with a different abrupt cinematic conclusion to the game. I really like the idea and the opening set up is good, but my interest for the story faded quickly.
Once you begin your quest you are given a brief tutorial on shooting, collecting resources, hacking signals,using your radar, lights and taking over a base. This is the crutch of the entire game. The open world is free to explore but at the start some regions will be blocked by contamination. You will not be able to traverse these locations until you complete certain mission which will unlock defense upgrades. Resources that are basically rocks scattered across wreck sites and the landscape are used to buy upgrades for guns and there is a level up system which will unlock tiers of weapons and other upgrades. There is limited inventory space which sort of forces you to play a certain way. Myself, i enjoyed using the sniper rifle and the tool that allows you to recruit allies to your team(Allies, and yourself, kind of look like the droids from The Star wars series). The higher your level the better tool you can equip which will allow you to recruit more allies. Allies and the AI overall is pretty good and hearing one of your robots laugh after a victory or death is pretty funny. You can also position your allies for fights(ala Mass Effect), but they were always more than capable of handling themselves and they were never afraid to mix it up. If i wanted to go solo swapping out the recruitment tool for a shotgun or assault rifle with better shield make firefights more difficult, but manageable.
The game is presented with a hand painted aesthetic which is very different for a FPS but it looks great and the use of a day/ night cycle showed off some beautiful scenery. For the most part the game ran ok, but i did have a few hard crashes. If using an AMD card make sure drivers are up to date as performance will be at an almost unplayable state if not done. Also another highlight is the sound design with the robots, guns and soundtrack all very impressive.
The Signal of Tolva is very vanilla and in some ways unoriginal. It lacks content, everything is pretty basic, and im really dissapointed in how the story is presented but traversing the beautiful landscape of Tolva with you allies was just fun. Its overpriced at $20 but if you can catch it for $10, as i did, I think that’s a fair price. Hopefully this is just the start of a bigger project for Big Robot Ltd. because I really enjoyed my time on Tolva and would like to see the idea expanded with more locations, deeper progression systems and a better way to communicate the story.
