What a bargain.  You Must Build A Boat gets a wholehearted recommendation from me.  Gameplay is terrific.  Timed match-3 is fast paced and rewards you even when you don't succeed with your run-goals.  Actually, they say you won each run, even if you failed your objectives, because you still collect treasure, gold, etc. that comes back to your boat where different vendors you've picked up along your travels will sell you upgrades to melee & magic weapons, spells, shield and more.  The chip tune music is catchy (I could listen to it for hours-long game stints without tiring of it) and matches the game perfectly.  This game mixes luck (random tiles) with skill (your timing, choice of attack, strategy against different foes, etc) which is nice because it doesn't get boring.  The RPG elements of upgrading your equipment and run bonuses are great. Plazma Being has an enjoyable, albeit simple, storyline and some innovative platform/puzzle mechanics. There are multiple character modes which allow you different options to interact with the environment. These modes, when they are initially found, will trigger small tutorial pop-ups, followed by a simple puzzle that requires the use of the new ability. This is an excellent feature and greatly assists with the learning curve of the game.
The music/sound effects are simple and generally relaxing.
Graphics are simple and highly suitable to a platform game.
Controls are typical WASD for movement with the scroll wheel of the mouse being the default to cycle through the character modes/types. Overally they are generally responsive, however, I have found there does seem to be some delay in jumping which can result in one "skidding off" the edge of a given platform.
The implemented physics are above average for games of this type and generally make logical sense. However, velocity of blocks et al. can be unexpectedly fast at times--with what one would consider a minor movement resulting in a block flying off the screen.
There are two tiers of saves. A general save slot which stores one's overall progress and waypoints within given levels. As the puzzles are very specific (although there is generally more than one solution--intentioned or not given the physics in the game) you will find yourself reloading to waypoints akin to Groundhog Day. This can, as with any waypoint system, become very tedious, with otherwise simple puzzles becomming more of a chore depending on finesse level. The waypoints are, however, common enough, as to generally make any reattempts quick.
I have enjoyed Plazma Being as a relaxed platform/puzzle game and originally purchased this when discounted. I have, enjoyed the game enough that when the opportunity presented to get a free key I responded to the forum post for such and have since given out two copies(I was given 2 keys not just one) of Plazma being to other individuals.
The game can be frustrating in that Groundhog Day/Edge of Tomorrow sort of way. However, taken in small bites, it is a very well designed platformer and well worth it's price point (which is very often discounted by coupons or general sales).

I've never played Final Doom before. I've only played Doom 1, but I've seen gameplays of Final Doom on YouTube and that already made it my favorite Doom game, because it has the weapons and demons from Doom II and still takes place on another planet, other than Earth, so I had to play it for myself. But I was planning to install the Brutal Doom mod to it, anyway. So, I installed the source port, Zandronum, to my computer, then copied and pasted the .WAD files of Final Doom to the Zandronum folder, and then extracted the files of Brutal Doom to the Zandronum folder, and not only did Brutal Doom work on Final Doom, but Zandronum also made Final Doom much more playable, making it much easier to start up, getting rid of the lagging, fixing the doors, and adding way more options in the Options menu, including options for the controls, so now, I can actually have fun, playing Final Doom with or without Brutal Doom. And it's still my favorite Doom game.

I'm not too big on squad based RTSs, though this one was so fun that I couldn't put it down.

There are two points of interest / buildings on each map that you can capture to increase your squads’ abilities, though you’ll only be able to capture one of them in a sitting.  Don’t worry, you’ll often come back to these maps (optional or not) in which case you can capture the other one you missed.  Capturing them goes a long way into making your team that much more formidable.

There’s a lot more that I didn’t cover…squad types, gear slots, factions, special items, and etc.  I will say however that the game is seriously worth the money, especially now that it’s come down in price since launch.  My only complaint is the lack of variety in gear, though “Chaos Rising” offers a bit more in that department.  This is one squad management / strategy game that you won’t want to miss.

If you have some local friends to play with, this game is excellent. The combat is surprisingly deep and even after a few days I still find it really fun to play in a local setting. Spectating people chanting and cheering when someone is disarmed and slain is one of the things that just can't be coded in to the game. Eight player tournaments are also spectacular, but this is an even less likely scenario for most prospective buyers. There is a single player game that is adequate for times where you'd like to play but have no one to play with for the moment, but this mode is not nearly as interesting as battling with other humans.
Yes, there is an option to play online. However, online multiplayer still has a lot of issues that seem to vary between being "fine" and "massive desync; abort everything". It's a shame, but I can't recommend this game that doesn't treat this game as a local multiplayer game the time being. There may be a day where that's untrue, maybe even soon, where it'll be absolutely fine online. Until then, consider this game only if you have at least one other person to play with. If you are willing to slog through some horrible connection problems with some people, there may be some fun matches to have, but the cost-benefit of that could potentially be very low.
In short: great game for local multiplayer. Very interesting and fun mechanics. Promising online multiplayer that is currently very unreliable.

An Octave Higher is a difficult game for me to review properly. Playing through the endings, with the exception of a few points in each, I really enjoyed the game. However, as the mixed review status of this VN may have hinted, the game isn’t without its flaws. Strengths in universe-building and the magic system are contrasted by a somewhat shaky plot and flat leads. But at the end of the day, I liked this VN a lot. For me, An Octave Higher is a nostalgic work. It reminds me of the sorts of artistic narrative-driven games I used to play as a child, like the Professor Layton series. It’s not perfect, but compared to a lot of other cheap VNs available on this site, it’s fairly good. While I find it does deserve a lot of the criticism I’ve seen other reviewers throw at it, it also deserves a chance.
After playing through all 7 endings, here are my thoughts:
Pros (+)
+Interesting primary universe. Overture shines as a fantasy city.
+Fascinating magic system. Applying science to magic makes it an actual, comprehensible field that makes readers feel a very real connection to it.
+Gorgeous background art and lighting choices breathe life into Overture.
+Soundtrack is great, especially the main theme
+Fights are clever and well-paced, as well as accompanied by relevant visual aid. Although nothing is strictly animated, the fights never ceased to have me on the edge of my seat.
+Thorough economic system, and clever world-building around a magic-based technological society. This especially as expanded by Janis Woolf in
+Addresses the good/evil divide in a more complex manner than simply claiming one side right and the other wrong. For a fantasy work, it’s a refreshing change.
+Characters are likeable despite a few flaws in their writing.
+As far as tradables go, this game does pretty well. Cards are pretty fair quality, although a bit expensive. Emoticons are pretty average, nothing amazing but nothing totally worthless either. What really shines is the backgrounds. Hope you get lucky and land one of the rares. And even if you don’t the common backgrounds are still really pretty.
+Everything following the timeskip in
is really good.
+Easy to get 100% achievements. Always a nice touch.
Neutral (•)
•A few other reviews cite the lack of music-related magic or the importance of music in the story as a major complaint. While they’re not wrong, most of this criticism is unfounded. Beyond the title (which is likely only used for dramatic effect) there’s no promise that music will be the unifying force of this story. And, quite appropriately, it’s not. Although in the
ending it does ending up playing a bigger role.
•The
, and
are all parallel endings, with only minor variations between them. They also completely miss out on the back half of the game (post timeskip). If you get one of these endings, I urge you to keep playing for one of the others.
•Somewhat unsurprisingly, the true ending is objectively the best one.
Cons (-)
-Out of the 7 endings, all but 2
come about abruptly and are mostly unsatisfying. In each of these cases, after a certain event the story just…ends. A lot of loose ends are disregarded or swept under the rug, and you’re left with these sense of missing so much from the story and the universe.
-The ending for
was especially disappointing, especially given some tasteless and honestly out of place “fanservice” snuck in at the end.
-The two main leads – Franz and Elise – are pretty flat characters. Hints of potential development are scattered throughout the story, but unfortunately aren’t explored. While not unlikeable, on many occasions they only serve to advance the story.
-On the topic of flat characters, Franz didn’t get nearly enough development, or even express enough of an opinion about the bourgeoisie/proletariat divide
More development would have been appreciated.
-The plot involving
that drives our 4 mains together doesn’t pan out in any but the
ending. After all of the buildup, the outcome was pretty disappointing.
- The Libertad’s establishing characterization is weak. A greater connection to the initial plot or one of the main characters would have been appreciated. However, they do improve significantly after the timeskip in
-No back button for dialogue. While there is a text log accessible through the menu, there’s no effective rewind button beyond loading old saves.
-The fast forward option for dialogue chooses what to skip through based on what text you as a player have or haven’t seen before, even if dialogue between different endings (given slightly different choices) is basically the same. A comprehensive, or at least less conditional, skip function would be appreciated.
Despite these, An Octave Higher is still a very good game. I urge you to give it a shot. However, as mentioned previously, buy it on sale.

Well, I almost got to the end before I just had to stop. Where do I start with this review? Perhaps with a content warning: I'm going to talk about racism, pedarasty and sexual assault (as portrayed in the game). But tl;dr: the game has an interesting setting and an extremely enticing premise, and beautiful art, but is ultimately capitalist propaganda, has unsettling cardboard cutouts of female characters, and has a dry story. It's a letdown. I'll get into it in depth now.
So, the promise of the game is pretty cool. "Welcome to Overture – The capital city of a great empire that has discovered and uses magic in its daily life... But, in a world where magic defines your status, rumors of a revolution are stirring, and the city is uneasy. Already there is unrest and talks of a rogue faction, determined to bring order and equality to the classes."
Immediately, I was really attracted to the premise - you get to follow three characters in the face of an impending revolution. In a game which literally uses a bourgeois/proletariate class system, I was expecting an anticapitalist or anti-imperialist critique of an empire - and to some extent I wasn't entirely disappointed.
The setting had a class divide and suitable tensions. It also hinted at how the empire functions on the back of slave labor. Specifically, enslaved black people from the south. This is briefly mentioned, and then completely ignored, and no black characters appeared in the story. The only character of color was a highly orientalist portrayal of an Arab man named Gesang. Portraying class struggle as almost entirely a white on white struggle, especially in the context of an empire with explicit colonialism and slavery, is utterly ahistorical, and I mean ahistorical in the context of making a video game for consumption on planet earth. Google the Thermian argument.
Additionally, the anticapitalist struggle was quite contradictory. Clearly the authors of the game didn't pay much attention to what actual anticapitalist struggle looks like - the revolutionary leader called for both a stateless society as well as a society with a "government by and for the people." Did you know that the "dictatorship of the proletariate" as a concept was popularized by *statist* communists during the Bolshevik revolution?
But it almost doesn't matter, because the game immediately characterizes the revolution with only three characters, one of whom is kind (as well as the only person of color), and two of whom are rapists, or at least are pretty ready to sexually assault a random woman before the police can stop them. But fine, the portrayal of anticapitalist struggle is pretty much the most ahistorical and whitewashed strawman you can think of, fine. You could toss this out as only a political critique. But I am, in fact, only getting started.
[And as an aside, I am actually not ok with the lack of warnings on this game. A young girl is almost sexually assaulted and there aren't adult content warnings on this game]
I actually really liked the premise of the setting - a scientific magic system which was loosely fleshed out - was pretty cool. The not really focused on tension between scientific magic and traditional, "magical" magic was pretty interesting, and as an aside, the art direction was excellent. Too bad we have to experience the setting through these ♥♥♥♥♥♥ three characters.
Let's see - we have Franz, Frederic, and Elise. Franz is kind of an impotent character, having almost no characterization except his loose committment to his research. Listen, as someone who does actual scientific research, I can say that we aren't actually all dry boring men. Franz could have easily been more compelling or interesting  (the game sets up a potential tension by how Franz is clearly not fulfilling an ideal of masculinity, especially compared to Frederic - but then never explores it)- but he basically just quietly advanced the plot in a disinterested manner. After playing it for a while, I really have no idea what Franz wants, or likes, or dislikes.  His friend Aretha at least is pretty interesting - if sexually overbearing and domineering.  I would have rather played her to be honest, because at least she seems to want something, even if it is only to get into Franz' pants. And Franz is supposed to be the main character, I guess, because you're forced to play him most of the time. Other characters feels like an afterthought really. Overall, uninteresting. (As an aside, I guess he's supposed to be 17, but I felt like he was 22, like, a senior in college, from both his societal position and characterization, and so the idea of him dating Elise, a 15 year old, makes me deeply uncomfortable)
Frederic comes off as a banal privileged prick at first. And then he sexually harasses and nearly assaults Elise, a fifteen year old girl, and then the story, incredibly, tries to humanize him and make him sympathetic. It fails.  I'm actually not too bothered by his characterization - he has clear likes, dislikes, wants, and fears. We understand that he is, in fact, a basic ♥♥♥♥boy. And the story succeeds in portraying him as such. The problem is, I don't want to play a ♥♥♥♥boy, and it was the most I could do to simply click through his parts after I figured this all out.
I suppose I'm actually the most disappointed about Elise. She is by far the most interesting character in the story - I mean, I am quite bothered by the premise of her story being that she is, essentially, being trafficked as a minor. And that the story doesn't really pay much attention to that, except to maybe put forward that the anticapitalist faction is complicit in this. I suppose I would be more horrified, but the game seems underwhelmed at the whole thing.
Now, sex work is work, and all labor is coerced, and so I find problems with how the *only* portrayals of labor come in the form of the factory, which is never critiqued, and the brothel, which trafficks minors and is funded/protected by the anticapitalist faction. It's almost as though the game wants me to decide that the anticapitalists are just bad people, and that it doesn't want me to critique the capitalists.
But fine. Elise is 15. Her dialogue reads like she's 10. And she's the object of male love interest, by the game's own system, by men who are definitely characterized as adults. Honestly, that's not ok, but fine. Her story reads like torture porn (being orphaned, being on the streets, being forced into child labor and eventual prostitution). She has little to no characterization (she likes pianos and is... happy sometimes). And you get to play her almost never. Remarkably, after all of this, she was actually the most compelling character to play, and I was actually really disappointed that I didn't get to see more of her.
My biggest problem with her was that her entire story was men enacting things onto her. Frederic sees her and decides he wants her. Franz spots her and decides to recruit her for a magic project. The anticapitalist faction guy Gesang sees her suffering and buys her lunch. She is an object for these men to enact their dry, uninteresting stories upon, and frankly she deserves better.
So that's my take.  In conclusion, this game demonstrates an absolutely disregard for portraying a realistic anticapitalist struggle, or realistic female characters or characters of color. It focuses on two overbearing uninteresting dudes and follows them and their petty stories. I spoiled the endings and saw that you could join the anticapitalist faction at the end, but honestly, I played up until the final fight and I have no idea why you would, after all the game screams at you to tell you not to. Don't buy it, just go read the Communist Manifesto - I assure you it has a better narrative than this drivel.
This game doesn't deserve the tags cute or female protagonist. Though I suppose it does deserve surreal.
Overall: F-. See me after class.
Edit: I requested a refund.

An Octave Higher is a visual novel that takes place in the fictional world of Overture where magic exists and a person's place in society depends on if/how they can use magic as well as that person's financial wealth. Imagine that the setting of this game is similar to the US in the 19th century Industral Revolution except that magic actually exists and you'll get the idea of the premise here. Basically, you play as three different characters-Frederic, Franz, and Elise-and they are rotated accordingly in the story. As this is a visual novel, choices do matter. Depending on the choices you make, you can find yourself aligned with certain characters. For example, if you play as Franz, you can make decisions that align him closer to Elise or to Aretha, Franz's friend. Also, decisions regarding whether Franz and Frederic get along determine whether more of the story becomes revealed (and thus, the true path gets told) or it ends. Although the first half of the story reveals this, the second half reveals it even more-that there is huge class disparity between the aristocracy/bourgeoisie and the proletariat-and magic plays a role in this class division. That's basically all I will say without revealing more although I will say that the true path is the most tragic so be warned.
There are a total of 6 different endings although one of those endings doesn't show up as a Steam achievement. The art is beautiful and I especially love the music in this game. I'm a huge fan of music from the classical and Romanticism eras and the selected pieces fit really well at certain moments. Of course, there is original music as well and it was equally enjoyable.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game if you're a fan of visual novels and love a good story. There isn't really any romance in this game but the story is so good that it isn't necessary. After all, all visual novels don't need to have romance to make them enjoyable. Also, I'd recommend getting the soundtracks (in DLC format), as I found the music tracks very enjoyable and soothing to listen to. I'm certainly looking forward to the prequel-One Small Fire at a Time-and hope to be able to play it in the near future. ^^

There's a lot to like here, from the amusing magical science classes that look like they leapt out of my software engineering classes, to character interactions and story concepts (heavily alluding to Indonesian class struggles and historical riots. You don't have to possess any knowledge on the topics, but those who kow will appreciate the added depth).
As fellow reviewers had noted, the pace-tone shift might be somewhat jarring (between the first and second act), and I can see why it could seem like two different games. However, despite a few plotholes here and there, An Octave Higher offers you a world worthy to experience. I like that this Visual Novel does not try to force-advance character relationships romantically, instead focusing on their roles in the story.
The writers tried to give nuanced personality to every character so none appeared particularly good or bad, but somewhere in the gray area. A commendable effort, though some might come across as being 'tryhard'. Perhaps the prequel would make up for this.
For those who like their stories tied up neatly, however, An Octave Higher might leave you wanting. The ending is open to interpretation, and some plot points were loosely let go.

I enjoyed this game for what it was, and what it was wasnt 100% of what it could be.
Story: You are from a special corporation attempting to figure out what is happening on the planet of Tolva. You do not have machines of your own, so instead you take over machines on the planet that you can use for your own will, and while inhabiting this corporations machines you are tasked with finding "The Signal From Tölva".
Combat: The combat in this game is actually very well done for what it is, it is perfectly balanced with nobody having an unfair upperhand and nobody being to weak. The playing ground is made fair for everyone. You can lean to get a better firing angle on your enemies, while they can do the same to you, you can flank your enemies, but they can also flank you at the same time, you can use a squad of 3 other machines to help you, but the enemies will also use their numbers against you at the same time, you can use your special abilities, but they can also use their special abilities. Its all even and pretty fair.
AI Enemies & Allies: Now in this game you have 3 factions who are all competing on this one planet. They all have different looks but the same abilites and levels as eachother, but different preferences. The Bandits like their machines guns and rifles, while the Zealots like their heavier weaponry and machine guns, while your faction uses pretty much whatever they want. You can chose from any weapons you unlock through the story, while also gaining better weapons with your higher tiers of your machine body. You can upgrade very quickly by doing ingame missions which were allowed to game to keep you always on a task whenever you needed one. Now your enemies also have different tiers, along with your own faction, the higher the robot tier, the better they seem to act. A tier 1 unit will go right into the fray and be killed very quickly, a tier 2 unit will take some more hits and pick them off from father ranges or use better strategy depending on the weapon. A tier 3 will actually begin to use available cover, along with all the abilites and options it can use while also being a better soldier. The higher the tier the better they seem to act, and the better they seem to operate as an available unit. The higher your tier, the better you will get, the better gear you will get, and you will be able to have a larger squad of units that are the same tier, or lower tier then you.
Weapons: The game has a suprisingly good range of weapons.
Random Encounters: You can find a random encampent of enemies or allies out in the wilds of the land, you can find a dropod falling from orbit to kill you or your allies, you can find lore pieces scattered all across the world, but not to close together, and you can enjoy yourself some nice battles here and there along with capturing a fort along the way.
Traversal Of Terrain: Thank god for fast travel, even though the game is more about exporation of the amazing landscape it has a large amount of walking that will be annoying when your trying to defend or capture a fort.
Overall: The game is an 7/10 game it feels like, it could use a whole lot more added to it like a better way to implement the story, but this game overall will not grab you and make you wish for more and more and more. Its walking is a little tiring after awhile but is understandable, its not made by a company of gods, and etc that shows why this game is good but why it is also bad. 7/10.

I have not always considered myself a carebear.  I cut my teeth like a lot of people on games like Ultima Online, which will always hold a special place in my heart.  The constant danger from both the environment and other players made life precious and your actions have weight.  A simple trip to go mine ore could often become a danger filled epic as you struggle against both PK's, Enemies of your clan and even your own personal nemesis from time to time.  Along came Everquest a few years after UO to instead focus in on working with your community members rather then fighting them.  While nothing works 100%, players gradually stopped killing each other in favor of deeper loots.  Still something was lost to us UO fans.  Danger was no longer quite as "Real"  Since then I have treadmilled through im sure just about every major AAA MMO release trying to find a home to bring back that excitement, I had always steered clear of DF because frankly I was pretty sure I would get my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me.  I was right! About 2 weeks ago though, I decided why not give it a try.  After all, at one point I use to handle myself and I did still PvP in games like WoW for instance.  I am no coward, in real life having retired from military service and some real life experiences that would make half these hardcore gamers wet themselves in fear.  I could handle this.  Boy was I about to be suprised. (in a good way)
Okay, so anyone who has played Darkfall Online:Unholy Wars, or its original incarnation knows one thing about it.  It is a very unforgiving, political, no handholding environment.  You start off in the newbie area related to your race (which sadly has been turned into humanesque models for hit box purposes) choice is by far as close to a handholding experience as you will get.  A very almost subtle tutorial (very reminiciscent in feel to EVE Online's Turtorial) will guide you through the basic ways to gain prowess in the game, which is accomplished by completing certain feats within the game (think achievements for all you console junkies out there)  The thing I love is, right off the bat with very little effort you can build yourself up well enough to create just about anything you initially need.  Virtually everything you do gives you prowess so just playing the game and setting out on planned adventures can help you get to certain goals.  There are no levels in Darkfall, you literally just  build the character you want through the skill and power choices you make.  The only skill you really have to grind at are the crafting skills which to be honest are just like any other crafting skill in other titles, its all about harvesting the resources and creating objects.  A salvage system lets you take even the loot you get off creatures and turn into something useable.
So my first few days in Darkfall were pretty uneventful.  The global chat is filled with the usual batch of idiots with nothing to say, and the smattering actual helpful people.  I will say this with absolute conviction, you will not find much help out of global.  No, global chat is pretty much redundant.  Trade chat is much more focused however.  Where I think AV did it right is, they instead implemented the Mentor program.  With the mentor program you will actually have a older player assigned to you, to help you with advice and  some have even been known to do more then that.  That being said, my only expectation was knowledge and my mentor gave me that in droves.  I did do a bit of research prior to coming in the game on the clans present and had already chosen my clan before coming in, but from what I understand, a lot of folks end up joining the clan of the mentor.  Either way, you will have to type and actually communicate with people if you want half a chance of getting anywhere in DF.
I made myself some chain armor a crappy greataxe and decided to see what the PvE is all about in Darkfall.  I found it suprisingly fun and pretty evenly balanced in terms of my characters abilities to handle, and you figure out real quick if a creature is beyond your abilities in DF.  Again no hand holding.  There is no level marker to tell, you simply have to go in and give it a go.  To be honest, I LOVE THIS.  It has brought exploration back into my gaming world.  The world is a dark and sinister place and Agon, filled with fallen ruins, serene environments and caverns and holes in various places does its best to push that envelope.  I even managed to find places that veterans of the game were unaware of.  That is pretty awesome.
The only thing I have had a hard time with has been managing to stay on the hit box.  I am partially handicapped and my reflexes are somewhat impeded but once I got some practice in, it is easy enough to stay on target.  PvP though provides a whole different dimension to combat.  The custom roles patch that just went in effect has certainly made things interesting.  Now gone is a lot of the cookie cutter class runs of the past as players new and old are trying to figure out what they feel comfortable with.  I am sure it will not take long for the flavor of the month meta gamers to start touting ultimate builds, but for now everyone is kind of playing around with the improved options which honestly give a TON OF FLAVOR to character building.
To fans of old school DaoC, I would highly encourage you to check out DF:UW.  It really has that old frontier feel that a lot of us were big fans of.  It also does one thing that very few PvP games do.  It gives me a better reason to want to defend my clans holdings, to expand them.  I am motivated beyond just racking up points so I can prestige etc.  I have a stake in this world, and I think that is important, because even DaoC to some extent failed to bring that to the table for me.  Yes, I have spent most of my gaming time as a carebear, more interested in the crafting and pve content then pvp.  But Darkfall has changed that for me.  While I am still not 100% hardcore into PvP, I do like mixing it up and I feel a real reason to do so.  There is something to be said for that in a game.  So this has been a old carebears review of why I think Darkfall Online:Unholy Wars deserves a second look, a third look.  Yes it is tough, but thats good, challenge yourself.  If you just put the time and effort in you will not regret it.  Now is a great time to jump on board as well, not only is the playing field slightly more even as everyone figures out the impact of the custom roles patch but AV is running a new player special as well.
I hope this mini review is helpful to others like me that sit somewhere in the middle between hardcore gamer and casual gamer.

Spelling is so not inportant...Congulation you found me review. We look at The Last Hope to see if the game is good based on a pro/ con style and end with my final conclusion. Also spelling is important but the intro to the review is a joke...
Pro:
I laughed. It was funny playing the game because of how bad it was. The audio for the skeletons were zombie sounds that seemed like stock sound effects or poorly made by the developer. Both are very believeable options.
Con: (Everything)
Why is each level long. The 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th level is progressively long. The thing is the dev probably tried to to make an adventure game but forgot to add more visual things to look at. The world is baren and dull to look at. If the world was smaller then the player can face the game's dull nature in bite sizes.
The game is poorly optimized. At very frequent moments in the game the frame rate drops to power point levels of frames. This could be many factors but my guess is that game running a massively sized world with many particles, and AI is a bad idea.
The audio is repetitive and annoying. The footstep sound effect stays rather constant through the entire game regardless of walking on wood, grass, sand or water. Then there are the moments that the game plays the audio of octoberfest constantly through the level and the raining sound effect even if it s not raining.
Enemies have no animations. I really dont want to talk about it but it looks very lazy.
Why is there bars for hp, hunger, and thirst is there is no visual indicators besides numbers? It is a nitpick but the point is that the white text blends in with the background in most levles very well that it is hard to see what hp the player has. Do these stats do anything? There is not much in the world to help these stats so it is a useless mechanic to add.
Why is the sword not properly connected to the character and does nothing to enemies? Im too lazy to go into details on this but at many times the sword would disconnect from the play when they move. When the player tries to attack an enemy the enemy still does hit damage.
Why is there so many gameplay mechanics placed in the game? Besides the others i mentioned prior there is also driving which is a buggy mess and flying a plane... it does not add anything to the game. It feels completely out of placed and not needed.
Later in octoberfest level the ground looks like
It is very odd and feels like the developer was lazy so made some weird ground object.
The story was boring. It never felt tied in with much of anything but another thing shoehorned into the game to fill some sort of checklist.
The world direction is odd. Sometimes the player will need to fumble around for some time if they get lost in order to find their way back on the progression path. Getting lost is never a good thing.
Text at points were messed up. There were some moments in which there was spelling mistakes and other moments in which the text ran off the screen.
Nice to see controls..not keywords but what about controls for the controller? I was playing with the controller and had to press random buttons in order to understand what they do. Didnt know the controller had a sprint button till halfway through the game. Thanks developer!
Conclusion:
I had to shorten the cons on the review because the game was a mess and just typing out criticism of the game was very fatiguing. There was pretty much nothing the game does right. My guess is that it was a student project and that they felt it was a good idea to show off all the things that they could probably do in unity but on the oppisite end display how they couldnt master those same mechanics. Also thought it was a good idea to sell the game for money. Now there are some good student games out there somewhere but this was just an awful game. I can not reccomend the game to anyone. Even free I felt cheated haha. Also i dont know what was the developers facination in adding texting emotions in the story dialogue. That is just odd.

There's been a bit of fuss, apparently, about how "dark" this interactive visual novel allegedly is; and while it's not wholly undeserving of that reputation, it's also not "Salo" or Lars von Trier's "Antichrist". It should only prove genuinely shocking to those whose idea of mature entertainment is Marvel movies...though there's no denying it has its "moments".
And no, it's not quite as "romantic" or "girly" as it might first appear, so if that's the kind of story you're in the market for, there's a good many VNs out there that should serve you better. That said, it probably is a slightly more "feminine" than masculine proposition in its general appeal.
Technically-speaking, it also has more visual and aural tricks up its sleeve than most interactive novels, and the music is quite lovely too. It also has an unusual mechanic for an interactive novel - or ANY video game, for that matter - in that the choices you make are not directly on the behalf of the protagonist, but a third party with an interest in seeing how the story unravels (I won't spoil it beyond that).
All told, a very decent quality product going for the bafflingly low price of FREE, so if it sounds like it's of even the slightest interest to you, there's no reason not to indulge. I'm not exactly the type to dive straight back in to get more story paths and endings, but it appears to be quite generous in those areas, so even I might return for a second helping in years to come.
Verdict: 8/10.

Cupid is an absolutely beautiful “game” and definitely one of the jewels of the visual novel genre.
It’s polished, with a consistent and visually gorgeous art style, great readable font/dialogue windows and an awesome soundtrack. The story runs smoothly and the reading isn’t at all tedious, the dialogues are short and engaging and there are options to start at a chapter or skip to a choice if you really hate reading, but this game is far too good to skip through all of it!
The story is dark and devious, and definitely fun if you love gothic tales of twisted minds, or just want to spend an hour or so in a nicely drawn world where there are no happy endings, despite the candy coloured art style. The choices in this game somewhat matter to unlock endings and some achievements, though there’s few options and no way to play “good” if you play games like this for role play or immersion.

A street urchin with a voice in her head, a prodigy, cheeky and lively pianist and a suspicious but elegant Marquis stage this beautifully crafted visual novel full of twists and turns about love, need and vengeance.
The story is dark and cruel but the characters are very credible. Cupid is pretty unique in that the emotions of the characters are carved along the story, in the present, without overusing flashbacks. Another original feature is that you don't directly choose the actions of the protagonist, but instead, you choose what the voice in her head will tell her. You probably have already noticed that the artwork was carefully prepared; that is true and consistent throughout the game. What you might not yet know is that the text is also a delight to read and melts in perfectly with the atmosphere.
There are many, many choices and 4 endings, plus a secret one (endings 1 and 4 were particularly good!). Achievements are rather natural, but some of them will require a guide. Talking about achievements, there are 67 in total, which I found somewhat excessive. Linux port is sort of flawed due to RenPy Engine problems, but can be workarounded.
This novel does not deserve to be free. If the devs are reading this: add a DLC with artwork and music from the game for a few dollars to act as "donation". This is not all that uncommon.

I'm a Twitch streamer. Hex has been my main game to stream for over two years, and I would not cast a game for that long that I didn't personally enjoy. However, Hex may not be for everyone. Read on, and let's see if the game is something you'd be interested in.
If you are looking for a card game, where the primary focus on the game are rich and strategic interactions between cards, Hex might be a game for you. Especially if you enjoy deckbuilding and brewing. With over 1300 cards available and all sorts of effects and synergies spanning all its modes, there is already many cards to take in and explore. Though, if discovering cards and deckbuilding sounds like a chore, perhaps it isn't for you.
If you enjoy card games, and like to compete against other players, Hex might be a game for you. The PvP is modeled like many competitive Trading Card Games in its tabletop roots. A small entry fee and some luck and skill can turn into awesome prizes. And at the highest level of play? Perhaps you'll win a qualifier and play in an Invitational tournament in front of an audience for a large cash prize! But if you don't like PvP play, this won't be a compelling reason for you.
On the other end of the spectrum, if you don't like the pressure of competing against other players, and just want to play out your amazing combo, Hex also has you covered. Its single player PvE play, in the form of a RPG-inspired campaign to explore and grow your own champions (that will be expanded upon in the coming years!) and an Arena mode to take on a gauntlet with a fully-geared deck. An experienced player should find about 10 hours for a single once-through playthrough. Cards, equipment, gold, loot to gain, and this is all free! But some aren't interested in single-player modes, if that is you, then feel free to ignore this section.
Do you like collecting stuff? Does the prospect of turning extra things into stuff you want sound compelling? The T in TCG stands for Trading, and Hex prides itself on its economy. The terrible feeling of getting an extra of an amazing thing, and being unable to trade it, is not in this game. Open a legendary in a pack, get a rare dungeon drop, or receive an exclusive promo in an event... and find someone who wants it in the Hex Auction House. Turn your extras, tournament winnings, farmed gold or bought platinum into anything you can find a buy or trade for. Though, if economy is not your thing, then it's not.
Well, there's a bunch of reasons I have for liking Hex. If you've read through, and one or more of those reasons intrigue you, give Hex a try. It's free to make an account, the campaign and PvE is free and you get stuff, random PVP games are free, and you have full ability to buy packs of cards if that's the kind of TCG player you are.
Hex has given me over 2 years of fun, and will likely continue to. And if you're like me, you'll like Hex too.

One of the most interesting and well put together VNs I've played: it is good in a lot of different ways (story telling, characters, character interactions, world, the sets of choices, music etc), and didn't have anything I really disliked (other than Fredrick being a bit annoying at the beginning).
An Octave Higher is good story dabbling in familiar topics (science, engineering, politics) in surprising depth and relevance while being in a fun magical world. Attempts to do this are often poorly done, but An Octave Higher is an exception: for example it was actually interesting as social commentary in some cases, though I would not say that was the main value.
The story is told from several perspectives, through interesting (tho in once case a bit annoying) characters who's relations you get to influence to a good degree (you can make people hate the annoying guy, or not for example) that have interesting consequences. There are enough different branches and endings to be interesting, but few enough you can explore them all pretty easily: I think its about right in that regard.
The game is unvoiced, but the music is very well done throughout, and there is a lot of good and well used custom artwork.
For full completion (which I recommend to get all the story) its about 9 hours (I read slow though, and did reread some parts: might as well enjoy it).
I recommend reading the keyboard shortcuts listed in the settings (L for log, and F for skip/fast-forward mainly): they are far faster than their menu setup, and not the same keys I'm used to in some other VNs.

Dragonball Xenoverse let you finally be a part of the Dragonball universe by creating your own time patroller, who has been summoned to stop time from being manipulated.
Growing up watching these fights it was super fun to be able to join in and pummel Freeza, Cell and Majin Buu along with all their henchmen, although I’m not sure how I managed to make a Super Saiyan Yamcha (who still managed to get killed).
I found the story to be good, the side missions to be fun (for a while) and the mastery system fun as well.
I found the game to become repetitive if you are trying to grind out certain skills or item drops (it relies on RNG and certain conditions to be meet in the stage, like beating Vegeta first, or letting Krillin die). The Grinding is painful, and some of the last missions are insanely difficult (I’m looking at you mission where I must fight every Saiyan 3 at a time). These can be easier if you have a good player joining you, but the AI tends to get destroyed (and you must share your items with the AI, where as another player gets their own items).
I also found the game very unbalanced (at least for single player)- depending on race and sex of your character the game can either be easy or difficult (female Saiyan with max super will destroy almost any boss(s) in 1 hit, making battles a matter of charging up the meter and spamming the same move.
Multiplayer was still active when I played (not sure now), and was quite good- lagged heavily a few times but that never stopped me or caused a loss.
If you are prepared to spend time grinding for a 100% and have a few people you can coax into playing with you than a 100% achievement isn’t too hard to get (just time consuming).
The DLC brings extra skills, missions and masters into the game (and a skill which ignores Kamehameha’s, which is nearly a must in the later game) and will required if you are chasing 100%
The game has its issues, but is enjoyable and If you liked watching Dragonball Z then you should pick this up.

I think I was supposed to walk away from this game feeling like I had been part of something big. Too bad that didn't work.
I finished the game thinking, "What the hell just happened?"
Signal is a complex story rolled into a simple game. You navigate the map doing find-the-items and capturing control points, while every once in a while getting into a fight with AI opponents that are spry but uninspiring. The weapons are frustrating and limited. The ally-recruitment is so costly in time and security, and works so poorly that it simply isn't worth it, so an entire game mechanic gets pretty much ignored. The map is visually 3-dimensional, but in reality your movements are more or less constrained to a 2d surface.  You can't jump on top of ledges to get the drop on opponents, for instance.
The story pieces, when you finally slog through to them are sometimes interesting and there are some rather epic environmental things going on. But even when you find something, the best you get from the story is a few lines of gibberish.
Did I mention there's a giant PDF file attached to the game that alleges to explain the whole backstory? No? Well, there is. But it isn't going to help you understand the story.
Nothing will help you understand the story.
Still... it was 11 hours worth of seeing someone else's world, which was kind of nice. But now that I've seen the world, I don't think I actually got anything out of it. I certainly see no reason to go back in.
I don't consider my time and money spent on this game wasted, but of those 11 hours, I could stand to have six back. I really wish there was a middle ground on Steam recommendations, because this game is a solid 'meh'. I wouldn't recommend it to someone I still want to be my friend, but I can't help thinking that someone able to give more of themselves to the story would actually get something more out of the experience.  If you're that person, well, this might be the game for you.

I am a huge fan of the Warhammer 40,000 universe. My first exposure to this world was the original Dawn of War franchise, and I loved how they tweaked the traditional RTS style with a new squad based style.
With Dawn of War 2 they did it again; the game wasn't going to adhere to standardised conventions. While never fully either an RTS or RPG, it contained the best of these elements. Think party based RPG with loot drops!
The game allows you to appreaciate the Space Marine as it should be - a small squad of super human soldiers cutting its way through a multitude of enemies to achieve its objective. No hunkering behind defenses, no building a bigger army than necessary. You are dropped in the centre of the action and you have to literally carve your way through with bolter and chainsword.
The story is relatively straight forward, but you will be constantly drawn back to the high paced visceral action and adrenaline rushing music. Nothing can relieve stress as effectively as dropping your assault marines on top of a cluster of enemies and making them go splash.
Although this game has potential, it is ruined by a poor interface and bad new player experience.

I Kickstarted this one and it finally got Greenlit on Steam.  This game is tough and I'm playing it on normal.  It hearkens more to the mega man days where movement is very stop and go, and taking damage will completely destroy your momentum.   The non-combat timed puzzles are brutal and require nothing less than perfection.  I spent a lot of time repeating them over and over to get them right.
Combat is pretty complex, combining light and heavy attacks, along with a block, dodge (cancel), and parry system.  It takes a bit to get used to, learning when to heavy attack to break a block, or block yourself.  There's a lot of trial and error in discovering exactly which attacks can even be blocked or which ones you should use the "Cancel" dodge.  But like the non-combat puzzles, every boss or enemy has a pattern, and this is one of those games that gives you warm fuzzies when you finally get the pattern and beat the boss after the tenth time.  Until you figure it out, expect frustration and what will feel like cheap hits.  Also, it keeps things fresh when you backtrack through previous areas because the enemies level with you and gain new abilities to attack you with as your progress through the game.
Along with that is a fairly deep magic system and your customization through both stat increases and a talent tree, that definitely changes the way you play your character in many places.
The graphics have a nice retro sprite feel, without reverting to the overdone 8-Bit style so prevalent, lately, falling somewhere between the quality of the PS1 and PS2.  The soundtrack is superb, combining a lot of retro synth, metal guitars, and symphonic instruments and spans something like four hours.
This is one of those games that will challenge you, but reward you when you succeed and I'm really digging it.  It really does feel more like the toughness of the original Super Metroid or Symphony of the Night to me than most games in the genre have presented lately.  And I'm just playing it on the easiest of four modes... O_O

I have very mixed feelings about this game, and those feelings are pretty distinctly centralized around each half of the game. It's difficult to boil this down to a short list, but I'll try to make a TL;DR version for those who don't want to read my full opinion.
Long version:
This game has six different endings, all of which are mutually exclusive. Three of these are based on characters maxing out their relationships, and the fourth is a generic ending if none of the others are triggered. These are all what I call "first half" endings, in that they are endings received when the second half of the story is not triggered.
Now, I think of this first half as entirely distinct, as the tone and the focus is entirely different from the second half. The first half is fairly slow-paced, with a lot of worldbuilding, character exposition, and other introductory fluff. It can be a bore to read, but it's an interesting take on steampunk magic which I haven't seen before (though I'm hardly an expert). The characters are great in the first part, I think. It's a fairly short first arc, but there's enough personality that I kept going just to see more interactions between these characters. There's a fair amount of comedy, and it was pleasant and lighthearted for the most part. I wish that the first four endings overlapped more (They're relationship-based. That's this game's best part. You can't tell me that they couldn't have done more with this.), but I did appreciate how casual the endings were. We got a snippet of life after the story, and it was more than the usual "happily ever after" stuff. I just wish that there was more to this whole arc, both in the story and the endings. It cuts off fairly abruptly, and the conflict of the first arc is solved maybe five minutes before the end, leaving the last bit feeling incredibly rushed. But to be fair, that's probably because you're meant to continue past that, onto the "true" endings.
And that's where the story falls apart. The single choice that sends you onward to the last two endings takes the cheery tone and chucks it out the car window, then backs over it for good measure. There's one word that comes to mind for me when I see the transition: edgy.
, which seems unrealistic and doesn't really fit other than as a reason for the characters to act the way they do in the second half. In fact, everything changes in the second half. The characters aren't nearly as likeable, and the game makes the mistake of making an antagonist of the more likeable of the two characters involved in that spoiler, and the one you'd expect to be the antagonist becomes the closest thing to a protagonist. By that, I mean that no one's really a protagonist. There are just a bunch of morally grey people who barely resemble the characters we grew attached to in the first half. I'm convinced this part was written by a teenager, because it's less competently written and it's unnecessarily dark and the tonal shift was violent enough to give me whiplash. To be honest, I only finished the second act for the completion bonus. I didn't really give a damn about anyone by this point, because they were all so bland and lifeless compared to the first arc.
All this said, I still really liked the first arc. I don't think this game is worth full price (hence my rating), but if it's half-price or less, it's worth considering. I bought it at half-price, IIRC, and I'm not sure if the second half ruined it for me or not. If I had played just the first half, I would be satisfied with paying the $6 or so for it. Whether it's worth purchasing even then is your call, and it depends on what you want from a visual novel. If you like solid character dynamics, I'd recommend this. If it takes ten hours or more of enjoyable story to get you to part with your cash, then this is probably not for you.
TL;DR
Pros:
-Good first arc
-Interesting worldbuilding
-Good character dynamics and interactions
-Fair amount of comedy
-Lighthearted tone
-Fairly satisfying endings (even if I wasn't really invested in the last two)
Cons:
-Crappy second arc
-Feels little like the first arc
-Characters act very differently
-Dull, drab tone in an attempt at bleakness
Bottom line:
Probably too short for full price, but might be worth it at a discount if you're interested. I recommend the first half; play on at your own discretion.

I'm a long time trading card game player and this review is primarily addressed to players already familiar with classic paper trading card games.
If you want a digital trading card game that retains the complexity of classic trading card games then HEX is for you.
Almost everything within the game is tradable which means that everything in your collection has a real world value. The game offers a great ruleset that allows a huge set of interactions, veteran card players are going to feel at home with familiar concepts like The Chain (The Chain in WoW TCG, The Stack in MTG), activated abilities, triggered abilities, combat and resource systems similar to MTG, and a lot of other things. HEX also innovates a lot in the digital space; modifiers on cards can be tracked throughout different zones (even in zones hidden for players, like your deck), cards can interact with zones without revealing/shuffling/searching or other shenanigans, effects allowing you to see cards in your opponents hand without them knowing, transforming cards into other cards, etc.
The game offers a great PVP experience with both constructed and limited formats (draft-like, sealed), and as in classic trading card games, you get to keep all cards and packs obtained in these game modes which justifies the small entry fee. There is also a PVE part of the game that is completely free to play, at the moment this includes a campaign with character progression, talent tree, dungeons, quests, equipment, mercenaries, and card rewards.
There are two ladders in the game, one for limited and one for constructed. The ladder resets every two months, and the top 64 players from each ladder are invited to a tournament with cash prices. There's is also two tournaments every weekend with $1000 cash in the prize pool, one for constructed and one for limited.
HEX has a superb economy with two different currencies: Platinum and Gold. Platinum is bought with real world money, while Gold is given as a reward in PVE. Entries to PVP tournaments has a small Platinum fee, but opening packs yields Chests which in turn needs Gold. This results in paying players needing Gold, and since everything is tradable the paying players lists cards and items on the Auction House for Gold, hence everything in the game can be obtained by just playing for free (however there is a lot of grinding involved to get the most expensive cards).
An important thing to note is that buying and selling in-game items for real world cash is not prohibited like in many other games. If you no longer want to play the game, you can just sell all your stuff to the different stores available, alternatively you can sell off some expensive alternative art cards that you might've won in a tournament or similar.
All in all, HEX is a great game with a great future! Give it a try!

2. Followed the story from start to finish allowing me to reinact all the fights from the battle.
3. When you use a supermove/finisher, the world alters (ie. if frieza uses his finisher, the world turns to lava)
With that said, Xenoverse is the first game since that's come close to providing that kind of experience. Unfortunately it does not let you reinact the fights but at least you get to experience them from a different view. Character selection isn't as great as it used to be and some forms just have shortcuts. Yes it hampers the experience quiet a bit but the fight style really makes up for it. It almost feels like I'm playing DBZ the way it's shown in the anime.
There's a little more customzation that goes on and the story seems kind of silly but I would still recommend this to any DBZ fan. My expectation in story and character selection is quite high and some may just find it to be repeatitive. I do wish the arena's change when a super move lands but I can live without it.

I've been playing Far Cry 2 again at the same time, so I have to compare them. In Tolva, you go around capturing bunkers for you and your allies to use, but you're not just sweeping the map for icons. Bunkers are some of your spawn points, but also your main source of allied soldiers. Other factions can actually retake them, and do so in real time. Because instead of enemies seeming to randomly respawn in the same spots (or driving up and down the same stretch of road for all eternity, until you finally decide to blow their predictable @$$ up with a landmine) like in Far Cry, the robots in Tolva actually do things. They patrol sectors, investigate sounds of distant gunfire, move to reinforce under-defended bunkers, etc. It's a level of reactivity that is really needed for an open world game, and it makes fights that much more interesting, too.
All too often, open world games are designed and written in a way that fights against their nature; usually with a linear cinematic story that takes away whatever freedom you're given in the rest of the game (Assassin's Creed, I'm looking at you especially), or endless swathes of pointless collectibles. In Tolva, the collectibles tie into the core systems of the game. The story is told as you find it in the world they've built. Very few games seem to get this sort of open world design  and story-telling right. I feel like Crackdown did, Saint's Row did, maybe a couple of others. Tolva's not a large game, but it's a tightly designed one that knows what it is.

I felt compelled to write a review. It's one of those games that make you feel that way as it is easily misunderstood.
This game is more about exploration than about shooting. In fact, the combat almost feels like a minigame to secure your progress. I believe this is important to mention and clear up: This game is not going to give you a deep combat experience if you are looking for a combat title. Buyers who want layers of combat material will certainly be disappointed in what TSFT offers. But this is not a shoot 'em up. This game is more about mysterious written story, traversing new environments, and searching for hidden items. In that, there is a neat experience waiting to be played.
Let me tell you first about the combat. Nearly all battle objectives are the same; all enemies behave essentially the same. There are only three gun types you or your enemies can wield, and the weapon progression simply consists of the same guns with increased damage, range, reload time, and so forth. You can defeat nearly any squad of enemies easily by taking cover behind a large rock and popping out to destroy them as they walk closer.
Stick with me here, I know it sounds bad. It's not to say I didn't have some fun with shooting; there were a few epic moments of close encounters and triumph. After a while, it can certainly get repetitive or stale. But it is not "bad" as in poorly designed, executed, or buggy. The combat is what might be called "lacking" or "more to be desired," neither the best nor worst I've seen. But as I mentioned earlier, TSFT is not ultimately about fighting.
The real substance of this game is found in its element of discovery - this is what I'll remember this game for. You are pitched into a large map that is not procedurally generated. Your task is to explore it. Your goal is to collect information, which are your clues to the truth that no one has been able to find about this planet. Turn the lights off, and put on a good headset, because you may miss out on the tense atmoshere that this game can create.
The people who say you need to read everything are right. And, read the "player manual" too. You'll pass by everything wondering what this game is about if you don't take the time to delve into it. If you reach the end without picking apart the story I can almost guarantee you will be lost and disappointed. This might be a minor spoiler so I'll hide it, but
You will ask questions about this game. It will make you think. And that, I believe, is what the developers have intended to do with this story.
No, this game is not the embodiment of gaming perfection. There are things that I can think about and say, "I wish this was better." But there is much to appreciate and enjoy in this title for the ~11 hours it provides, and it was overall a positive experience that I can recommend as long as you know what kind of game this is.

Even though is old, it is so much fun!
The game was released year 1996 (According to Steam) which is a great reason to the pixelated, Psyche-3D graphics.
However, because the game is old also comes with positive sides. For example:
- Lossless gameplay
- Nostalgia
- (Pretty) Simple game controls.
Lossless gameplay:
Means that the game has nothing that breaks the gameplay at any point. You press "New Game", then you're already in the game. Nothing in the middle at all. And that's how the game is all the way until the end (Because then you've finished it).
Nostalgia:
It speaks for itself. If you're familiar with the 90's FPS games, this will have effect. As the game was released in 1996 (As I said before), the way the game looks like and is played is like all the other game from the 90's. Note that the game has a lot of secrets and tricks. These will help when you need it, but you need to find them first (The best way is to just mash space at all the walls in the room).
(Pretty) Simple game controls:
The buttons used aren't many. Arrow keys, W, A, S, D, Control (Ctrl), Shift, Alternative (Alt), Space. If you want (Highly recommended), you can activate the mouse by pressing the scroll wheel. Then you can look around with the mouse and shoot with Left Click. You'll find this really useful, as it's easier to aim at the enemy with this setup.
Also, the game is really hard. But here's some helpful hints you can have use of:
- Move. Like an idiot. The most lethal shots are not instant, and sends a projectile that can be avoided.
- Use multiple save slots. Using only one can get you in trouble.
- Scavenge. If you're low on health, go back and try to pick up stimpacks and first aid kits left behind. Try also to find secrets.
- Pay attention to sounds. If you do, you can sometimes foresee if there's an enemy behind a door or not.
- Save frequetly. Every time you've cleaned a room, save. If you're low on health, save in a different save slot.
This is not necessary, but I recommend using ZDoom instead of the original game. Why is because it runs much smoother and looks much better. ZDoom is also free, but requires you to buy the original game first (Otherwise it doesn't have the files required to run the game).

It'll take you on a short but very uplifting ride through the life of a girl who struggles to even exist. The only thing she thinks is what keeps her sane is the lingering but also daunting memory of her Mother whom with few memories she had of besides that of memories of abuse. Yet she clings to her Mother. Clings hopelessly to the thought that through it all her Mother still loved her somewhere deep down. This girl goes by Rosa. She is given the name by people who take her in, give her new meaning to life, to love. But this is dangerous..  because now Rosa is hungry for it. Hungry for what these people have given her. The counselling memory of her Mother sooner becomes that of what leads Rosa down darker and darker paths. Leaving her sanity to be the very thing that breaks her in two. Oh yeah and it's got some weird succubus witchcraft thing going and ends off with it being incest. Overall, would definitely recommend if you are looking to get yourself steamed up for a short time then let your soul soak in holy water for about 20 minutes, then rinse and repeat.

you find yourself at the final stage. You throw your sword in an all out attempt to dispatch your enemy and advance, but he throws his as well. With victory within reach you run and roll into your opponent hoping to sweep and knock him down, leaving him vulnerable. This game is almost complete, utter trash, but it had the potential to be one of the greats.
If you're coming in to this pile of garbage expecting full-scale, warzone-style PvP with no instances and just tons of chaotic no-BS fun, then you are going to want to take a complete 180 and forget the words "Darkfall Unholy Wars" entirely. Seriously, do it. The next time you hear any of those three words in the same sentence you are going to think of this pile of crap, and it will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. So, take my advice: do whatever you can to forget about it, because it's -that- bad.
Again though, it could have been good, and that's what sucks the most about the entire experience. First of all, the game should have simply been called Runescape 2.0, because that's what it is: Runescape 2.0. Want to play an MMORPG and PvP and just have a fun experience? Y'know, like what video games were originally intended for? Fun? Yeah, no, buddy, not here. You're instantly greeted by some of the worst graphics this world has ever seen plus one of the worst and most simplistic character creation tools imaginable, and then poof--you are dropped into -the absolute worst- "tutorial" level for a video game IN EXISTENCE. I am not even trolling, but I admit that I am exaggerating. It's still pretty bad, nonetheless. It accomplishes the basics--gives you the controls, shows you what the tiny little icons that were meant for ants are for, etc., but then it just fails, hard. It's so utterly-gosh-damned boring it will drive you insane. If you actually DO manage to finish the abysmal hold-your-hand level, well then congratulations, your reward shall be even more ungodly torture: upon start of the "real" game, you are dropped dead center of the newbie "town" (which consists of about three and a half buildings and two NPCs) and left COMPLETELY TO YOUR OWN DEVICES. I was still confused about 90% of the stuff in the tutorial and now I am suddenly expected to just accomplish everything in the game on my own.
Nah, we're not doing that. Garbage. Stay away.

Murder Miners is an intense and action-packed Halo CE inspired multiplayer game keeping you on the edge of your seat every time you play it! There's always people disgusing as blocks of the map and you just go past them when they suddenly stab you in the back with an energy sword!

Also, every Wednesday, the community gets together and servers get packed and new servers have to be made. This means that there's gonna be extreme violence and 30-player action!
Murder Miners is the best multiplayer game I've ever played, and I recommend you try it.

Darkfall Unholy Wars review from a new player (started playing beginning of Feb 2014):
The main purpose of this review is to help you determine whether or not darkfall is for you, as I understand this game is not for everyone. Will YOU enjoy it? Read below and find out!
First of all, you need to understand Darkfall is a pure HARDCORE PVP game.
Apart from the starting/safe zones. you can attack anyone / anytime / anywhere (even party members and guildies!)
When you kill a player, you can loot anything that is currently on him (BUT items deposited in banks are safe).
That being said, in order to enjoy this game you need to:
1. Love PVP in its most cruel & hardcore form
2. Love world PVP as there are no BG's or arenas.
3. Join a guild (a clan) as roaming alone will get you nowhere (at first). Only by joining a clan you will understand the true purpose of the game.
4. Be ready to do a bit of grinding in order to level (acquire prowess) - being in a clan will help you become PVP ready much faster as guildies can help you with feats/lend you fishing trawlers (to powerlevel)/and provide you with tips and better understand of the game.
5. Rebind you keys to your liking.
6. Get over the odd interface.
IF your focus is PVE or questing or if you dislike PVP or are a very casual player or a loner by all mean stay away from this game!
Do I personally enjoy the game? Here's my experience:
I started playing this game about a month ago. The first time I logged on I was a bit turned off by the controls and the interface. With proper keybinding I was able to get over this. I then started doing a bit of reading in order to understand better the game and learned how to build my caracther (a skirmisher). I then started gathering prowess by all possible means (mobs grinding & skinning, gathering, crafting, explorations, prowess monolith, feats, etc...)
At this point I was getting more confortable with the game and felt it was time for me to start PVPing. I tried roaming around the world by myself but without success. Either i'd meet over geared player and would get crushed or I would simply not find anyone to fight...
Until I joined a clan (Zerg), got summoned to my clan keep, hoped on Teamspeak... and started raiding other clan keeps!
I can now say that I'm truly having a blast playing Darkfall, as nothing beats the feeling of running around with a dozen guidlies / traveling by boats in order to lay an attack on other clans.
I still have a lot to discover & understand but so far as a PVPer by heart I'm really enjoying this game.
SUMMARY:
This game is great IF you enjoy HARCORE WOLD PVP and if you are ready to take the time to understand the game, join a clan and farm/grind a bit in order to become pvp ready (you'lll need around 15k-30k prowess, which is easily attainable within a week or two with proper clan support - lots of clans are currently recruiting new players - ie: Zerg clan). Trawling (fishing on a boat is for example a very fast way to gain prowess, but beware of pirates!).
I hope you will find this review helpefull, hope to see you in game,

Symphony of the Night meets Devil May Cry. One of the best metroidvania 'genre' games ive played.
It pulls at all the good aspects of recent Castlevania games that are expected and loved:
RPG progression via level ups, new/better abilities, aquiring new spells, better gear, item drop hunting, etc. It also has a nice variety of scenes, ranging from the typical gothic castle to lush poison filled gardens, to dank unstable caves.
Explore the areas in semi linear semi plot breaking segment jumping; allowing you to branch off and do other parts of the game early, or in different order if you feel brave and clever.
Good ol backtracking; going back to previous areas to find those hard to reach goodies and secrets. The whole story and design is done well enough that it doesnt seem "too tedious" to go back through previous areas to get to the next link in the plot, or to treasure hunt.
The music is superb; ranging from enriching piano/organ symphony, to some more upbeat / urgent sounds that remind you more of a megaman/metroid platformer stage.
The written parts of the story are well done, and it iven has a nice 'lore' section later in the game that further unlocks entries as you progress, giving you great backstory and even loot drop details of enemies. Some parts seem a little "Im just standing here for the heck of it" plot thin..... but the overall arch keeps you interested in whats happening next.
A very engaging story of events that make sense, rather than a "generic enemy villians vs you" story, without being overly dramatic or complicated.
Its a game that gives you all the basics you need for a great rpg / action platformer , without trying to add 'interesting new game mechanics' for the sake of trying to be different in the crowd. It knows what it wants to be, and it sticks with it.
A must have for Castlevania fans, and the like.

TL;DR at bottom
This game, like many other zombie survival knockoffs of GOOd zombie games such as Left for Dead, fails immensly at EVERYTHING it has to offer.
First, I will begin with the sound design and music. While me and my friend were playing this game, we noticed that there was only one sound that played when a "horde" would rush you. To emulate the sound, Take something Super mario would say and reverse it and slow it down by 70%, now shove some broken glass in your ears and there you go. Other than that, the reload sounds aren't TOO bad but the pistol is by far the worst offender. Its like shooting a pistol from 40 feet away with ultra ear muffs on and pixelation effects on the sound.
Next, I will adress textures and gameplay. The zombie models dont look half bad, but I'm fairly certain they are "borrowed" from CS zombies or whatever it's called. However, they can group spaswn so when you look down a hallway, you see about 80 zombies coming at you all synchronized in animation, which is once again "borrowed" from HL. This wouldn't be so bad if when the zombies attack, they grow claws like the ones from HL. The gameplay itself consists of 5 or so classes each with different guns. Although I'm not sure how a sniper would come in handy in case of a zombie apocolypse. The classes aren't really a key element in winning its more of just "Oooh I like ShotGuns more than SMGs so I'll pick him!" You run around bland environment after bland environment shooting zombies with WAY too much health and pushing buttons. And pushing buttons, and pushing buttons. Pretty much all you do is run around like a♥♥♥♥♥♥pushing buttons to get to more buttons. The goal in each of the *wait for it* FOUR levels is to get to the center, plant a bomb and run away. But that's okay right guys? It can't get repetitive there are only FOUR LEVELS.
TL;DR
In conclusion, This game sucks, it really does. But hey, it's early acess and its free and still its not worth it. My advice to you, the viewer is don't waste your time on this atrocity, instead go get TF2 or LFD2. Thanks for reading!

When you play a 'charge' (land), you get a threshold - and certain cards require a number of different colored thresholds but otherwise you can spend any type of 'mana'. The best way I can relate this difference to magic is with an example like this:
1) You have 10 Islands and 2 Forests.
2) You want to play two primeval titans (cost 4GG)
3) In Magic, you wouldn't be able to do this because you only have enough green mana for one.
4) In Hex, you can do this. As long as you have enough mana, you only need to have the two forests (threshold counters).
Still liking it.
