This game is a must play in my opinion.
The price tag may be a tiny bit hefty for the playtime but that by no means should stop you from experiencing this game and this historic journey through the past of the Finch family.
Each tale of death and darkness is lit up by its own personality and enlightenment, this is in no way glamourising the tragic stories of death, whether it's caused by the mistakes and punishment of parents or an unlucky train coming your way, every person seems unusually content in their end. It's almost like they want this in a sort of sinister way.
Each person explored in this game makes you feel connected to them as you play through their final moments and wonder,"Where did this go wrong?".
As predictable as the ending is the bulk of the game has you on your toes wondering what you'll find around the corner and who on the family tree is next.
This game is a complex story of tragic, unfortunate, horrible deaths of a historic family but it puts them in a light which makes each one more meaningful then the next, it doesn't spare any details. This game is a must play as it is a game as much as an artistic account of life entering death with the most incredible atmosphere and grace.
What Remains of Edith Finch is a masterpiece of modern day storytelling and writing, if you haven't played it yet go ahead and do it, you won't regret it. I promise you that you will get more of an experience than anything else from this game.

Ok, so this game gets a lot more flak than it deserves. It IS understandable though why most people wouldn't enjoy it. It's a game that take a LOT of time to get use to, and what most people don't know is the true purpose of this game. It was meant to be a role playing game that is player driven, with quests that players created, and players would specialize in 1-2 skills and be that way. The gameplay is a slow progression, and I mean slow, but is pretty nice with friends. I have only played it with one friend, and he's really endowed into this game, and I am pretty into it as well. The theming is great, as is the art and concept of the tools. However, the combat is a different story. The combat is twitch based, which is great for PvP, as I play on the PvP server (There is a PvP and PvE server). However, it's not that way with enemies such as creatures. The creatures attack way too fast, and do way too much damage for how fast they attack. Some enemies called Revenants use the Twitch based combat, but as I said, they attack with too much damage for how fast they swing. Once you get used to the combat, you'll be able to progress from small critters to mediocre critters, to medium creatures and critters, and large/deadly critters/creatures. I level them by their HP and Attack strength. The building system is phenominal, you're able to create these pretty nice structures, however you'll need to increase your skills to build better things, as expected. The cooking system is great, the cookable objects have flavors which you need to balance out to make a fully nutritious food item without penalties (Food effectiveness reduction). As said though, you will need dedication for some skills, such as some craft skills, as you'll need to effectively grind EXP manually, which can be time consuming, so you'll need some time to kill. If you have a friend, it'll be great. You can adventure together, and you can create quests together. The tutorial is pretty time consuming, and if you want better help and explanations, you should ask people in the chat. All in all, great game, it's ashame but partially understandable the amount of flak it has been recieving.

An Octave Higher is slightly different from your average Visual Novel, and although not excessive it is quite enjoyable. It is not voiced, which can be seen as a poor point - but I don't think so. No erotic content.
Pros:
+ New mechanics: unlike the traditional Visual Novel you can decide the choices of 3 different characters, giving a new dimension to the tree of choices.
+ Great music - even if the OST is not at the edge of excellence it is written with care and emotion, and the collection of classical music is well chosen.
+ I appreciated the courage to talk about uncomfortable topics like paupery, social balance and so on, not as a mean to differentiate eroge characters but as a central topic.
+ Round characters, with charisma and realism.
+ I know it sounds kind of n00b-ish, but... AFFECTION POINTS DISPLAY! THANK YOU!
+ Presence of easter eggs...
Cons:
- ... that seem to have been added forcefully, sticking out a little too much for my taste.
- The storywriting style is sometimes too innatural: especially lessons and explanations seem to have been written just to provide the reader with some lore background, and their style is poorly matched with the context in which it is put.
- Short, too short. Given the mechanics explained above, it would have been a great deal to have complex tree branching with multiple side-effects, it would have given the story a greater complexity and would result in a more enjoyable game. Maybe next time.
The overall impression is that this game was made "on a budget", but for the budget, a very good experience! Try it at least when it's on sale!

Truth be told, I don't really want to say anything like "stay away from this game, it's terrible, blah blah blah" because it's really not. It's a visual novel with multiple endings (although most of the story is the same between the paths, apart from the true ending with its two paths). There is no additional gameplay element beyond the game being a VN, so don't look for that kind of thing. Of course, that's not a problem. It's a VN.
Anyways, as a VN, it can be judged for its art, characters, story, and music. Art is fine, characters are mostly fine, music is interesting and fairly classical...
And the story had so much potential... And fell so flat on its face. The true path is literally the worst path among all the paths.
However, the magic system was innovative. This game was clearly partly designed by an influence of engineers in its writing, with a magic system driven by applying functions and magic being a series of equations; but also referring to control systems, and really heavy reference to digital logic / digital design on the engineering side of things. It's smart! It's really smart. And then some questions are asked... then Libertad comes in and leaves ALL other questions unanswered, while also leaving their own set of questions unanswered.
Libertad and the revolution literally sinks the story completely. It just doesn't have a proper ending... and it doesn't have a direction. It just has a message, one that doesn't really know where it's going, considering the problem it asks ISN'T SHOWN TO BE RESOLVED. Barely ever have I seen a true path both heartlessly cruel and also unsatisfying due to the complete lack of closure.
So:
- PROS:
--- interesting world, innovative magic system (in terms of world design), in-depth explanation of how magic drives things (how the omnibuses fly and stuff, it's really cool)
--- fancy classical music
--- fun characters (excluding true path where everyone is either too verbose, naive, annoying or just stupid), Aretha is best girl
--- many interesting questions asked with a lot of intelligent facts thrown into the debate, there are quite a few things in here that are legitimately smart.
- CONS:
--- Libertad, anything in the story that has to do with Libertad, and therefore everything in the true path
--- Due to the excessive amounts of Libertad in the story, most other main questions are left unanswered, and the Libertad plot leaves even more questions to be answered that are left unanswered
- VERDICT:
--- If you like VNs, this one is set in a world that's driven by a REALLY interesting magic system, mostly based on engineering facts and aspects taken from the real world while also merging it the aspect of emotional intelligence. So it's worth checking out just for that.
--- The true ending is sunk by Libertad and is complete garbage from start to finish with no direction.
Overall? Worth checking out... I'd recommend to, actually, just for the magic system. It's an interesting thing to see Amplify(Transform(Willpower)) + Amplify(Transform(Courage)) as a means of casting Meteor.
But the endings might leave you frustrated, without a sense of closure. You ask, "wait, that's it? What the hell was the point? Why did that even happen? Did that achieve anything? Does anything change? Also, what was up with..." and you get no answers.
In the end, while the VN is pretty interesting, this review is a warning that the endings might not be something you like, and might not be something you expect, and you might not get the answers you are looking for. There's a bunch of other cool things here though! So don't be put off too hard by my warning.
---------
UPDATED VERDICT ABOUT 8 MONTHS LATER:
- Buy it on a sale. But the "true ending" path left us with a bitter taste. Even now, after 8 months, all I can remember is just how frustrated we were by the "true ending": a bitter emotion.
So with a minor spoiler here, the true ending is the one where you are a complete douché to literally everyone around you. Then there's a 5-year time-skip and all writing goes down the drain. You should probably avoid that path, because it sucks. If you avoid the "true ending" path, the game is pretty nice. Just don't expect to get answers to all your questions, because you don't. You wouldn't get those answers in the true path anyways, just more questions.

TL;DR: Like grindy games? Play. Don’t like grindy games? Don’t play.
As I stand at the edge of a small peninsula located between two waterfalls that cascade down into the valley below I marvel at the beauty of the – for a nooby rather dangerous –surroundings of the aptly named two-man community “Twin Fall Town”.
The idyllic spot – that was chosen for beauty rather than functionality – is, to say the least, a bit of a challenge, and a struggle at most. Wild bears, hostile hounds, over-sized racoons (maybe the radiation has something to do with that?), and savage coyotes often interrupt the flow of our day while we’re trying – after 19+ hours in-game – to still finish the crude barricade around our soon-to-be-town, that will hopefully one day save our lives a few times in the future. For now, however, it is a long and slow battle against nature where we are the unwelcome guests.
Welcome to Xsyon; an Early Access Post-Apocalyptic Open-World Online Survival game with Role-Playing elements. That’s a whole mouthful and the time it takes to pronounce this gives you a rough idea of the length of the game.
Before you read any further, however: if you don’t appreciate a (very rewarding) grind-game: close the tab, delete this game from your wish list and move on.
If you do enjoy a slow-paced game in a huge open world with survival, building, crafting, and battling the elements (or other players on the PvP server) whilst having tons of recipes to discover and stats to improve – and most important of all; you don’t mind grinding it full-on – than look no further: this is the game for you.
Xsyon is still in early access which does mean you’ll have to deal with the odd bugs – such as not being able to run up a steep hill, while a bear or racoon easily walks up a vertical waterfall (obviously, a horizontal waterfall is called a river) – and updates are not released very often as it is being made by a small team.
But the game is enjoyable! The amount of content it already has (which seems to be expanding a lot over the next few months) is astonishing. The grind – although at times you really feel you should do something else in between before you start going crazy – is actually quite spot on; you don’t build a village in a day, you don’t learn all recipes in three hours, and you don’t catch a fish every time you throw out your line, right?
If you’re reading this I’m assuming you’ve got some affinity with survival games, too, so you’ll be familiar with the hunger/thirst aspect of this genre. Whereas many survival games (I’m looking at you, The Black Death) have a hunger-rate that goes down faster than a fat kid on a seesaw, Xsyon seems to have found a rather good balance, and a nice addition is that you shouldn’t “fill up” on food or water until your bar is at 100% as this will affect your character (and not in a good way).
Also the day/night cycle takes a lot longer than in many other (early access) survival games. Beyond Despair is a dark setting anyway, but the nights seem to last forever; The Black Death (sorry, I’m still a huge fan of this game) has finally added a day/night cycle to their game, too, which is long and pitch-black; Xsyon has 9-hour in-game days. That’s pretty long, and in my opinion enjoyable, too, because of the game’s “grindy-ness”. You really need that time to scavenge for resources and you’d get really cranky if every 20 minutes the world goes dark for a friggin’ hour.
In other words; Xsyon most definitely has added the survival aspect, but has implemented it in such a delicate way that you at some point think: “It’s been a while; my character might be a bit hungry, let’s break the grind and go fishing instead.” rather than “I’d like to go to [location] but I have to eat 15 apples, 2 loaves of bread and a basket of sour grapes and then scavenge for food first before I… Oh now it’s dark again; better wait till morning.”
I do recommend playing with a friend if you want to start a tribe of your own, or you may want to join an existing tribe before setting off on your own so you can level up your skills first. In my experience the players on PvE (Peaceful) are very polite and helpful and will give new players some basic free gifts just to help them on their way (a few pouches and a basket, which you can’t make at the start of the game, are very welcome gifts).
Xsyon may not be the most beautiful game on the market (graphically), the game needs performance updates as at times it runs quite poorly in forests, and some of the character’s movements are a bit wonky at times (running can be almost “slow-motion-like” on certain surfaces, while walking anywhere seems as if your character’s legs have been placed in spleens and he/she was then refused to use crutches), but none of this matters as you slowly grind away trying to make something of your life in the wilderness before winter arrives and you’re going to be royally [......].

while playing this ending. Yeah, I know this game has a ton of negative reviews and mine is no different, but I wouldn't exactly call this a "bad game" now that it has a few very easy achievements added to it, which gives a little incentive to try this game out.  True,
is in dire need of polish, but I found it had quite a bit of charm in some areas.
is a game about walking to a destination which you have to discover while making sure you survive to meet it.  During your quest, you will need to maintain your health, hunger, and thirst...which can become quite a challenge in various areas (this limit is removed the moment you board the plane to the USA, which makes the experience more casual and enjoyable).  The overall objective is to push a small object a short distance (like nudging it off a cliff), but with a very long run towards the destination.
The enemy AI ranges from path wandering (like mindless drones that are just a very very very mild "ooga booga" spooky...like a bedsheet ghost) to stationary enemies that you can (for most of the time) step around...though sometimes it's unavoidable.  I wouldn't call the enemies scary or threatening, but they do take a small chunk of your health after being touched.  After losing all your hunger and/or thirst, you'll start losing health...so avoid enemies if you can.
I found early game (inlcuding both UK and Norway routes) and late game to be quite casual and a bit charming.  However, I will say that I loathed the Russia level with a passion.  Due to the lack of visibility and scarce food/water/health kits, you may find this area to be quite a pain...especially if you end up falling into the water (meaning it'll be a pain to get back on land...and no, it doesn't quench thirst).  Not only this, but in Russia, you'll have a massive and nasty lag until you reach the cave.  It's also worth noting that the driving segment is completely awful and you'll find yourself resetting it often.
Overall, I wouldn't say
is an awful game since there are many worse games I've played, but it does need some polishing, some lighting, better AI, better story telling, and some better balancing. I hesitate to write a review so early in the piece, but I was very pleasantly surprised by my first session of Darkfall.  I knew what I was getting into because I played Mortal Online for about a year in about 2010, when the game was very buggy and had broken features.  I'm told MO has improved since.  These independent, shoestring budget operations are works in progress, but I encountered no glitches in Darkfall.  The interfaces all worked, the crafting made sense, and the PvE combat was as it should be: I died to mobs at first but then started to get the hang of things.  The environment looks empty, but that's the nature of these games.  People try to stay hidden out of safe zones unless they are looking for action or have nothing to lose.  I played during the Aussie day on the US server, and there were plenty of players around in the town, and a couple in the wild to.  One, who came upon me trying my hand on Goblins and who I basically fled from until I realised he wasn't going to pinch my meagre noob stash, ended up inviting me to his guild.
These styles of game are superb, fantastically immersive, and great fun whether you like to play a killer, an empire builder, or a running away artisan like myself.  I hope you decide to buy this game and graduate from themeparks into a world where you can truly leave your mark.

Because there are many free to play TCG out there, I wanted to explain their F2P model, rather than review the game itself, so you could decide if this game is worth your time. There are certain people I'd recommend this game to and others I would not.
If you are looking for a casual experience and aren't worried about competing in tournaments, the free to play campaign mode is probably one of the best TCG experiences you'll find. If this is all your looking for then I'd recommend spending a few hours in the campaign to see if you like the mechanics. If you were a MTG fan, you'll almost certainly like the game play. I'm not going to weigh the pros and cons of the game mechanics, balancing issues or AI. Check another review if you want to know more about those details, but for me, all things consider the game play is extremely fun.
I wanted to address this more towards the potential new competitive players. There are many questions to consider before jumping into a game like this and I wanted to shed as much light as possible on those questions. How is the free to play experience compared to users who pay? How much time will you need to invest to compete for free? How much of an advantage will people who spend money have over you?
The game has two in game currencies, platinum and gold. Gold is earned from farming PvE modes, either the campaign or arena. Platinum is purchased with real money. However, there is an auction house where you can sell your cards or equipment for either gold or platinum. Platinum can be bought at the rate of 100 per dollar. I earn about 7,000 in gold for completing a PvE arena run, which usually takes me 30-45 minutes per run.
To compete in a tournament you need two things, packs and platinum. You can buy packs from the game itself for 200 platinum ($2 dollars) or you can buy them off the auction house, right now they go for 175 plat or 22,000 gold. I've only ever paid for packs with gold. Considering you also get loot you can sell on the AH, I usually earn enough gold to buy 1 pack every hour and a half or so.
There are different types of touraments. Drafting requires 3 packs and 100 plat entry fee. Sealed requires 6 packs and 100 plat fee. Constructed requires you to build a deck with cards you own + a 500 plat fee.
Without farming for gold, you'll be looking at $7 draft, $13 for sealed and a one time fee of $50+ for a deck + $5 per tournament for constructed. IMO, these prices are not worth it. While our community is big enough to see your cards move on the AH, it is too small to justify sinking that kind of cash into this game. Also worth noting, you do win packs for winning a tournament, but in order to play completely off your winnings you'd need to get mostly 1st, so you can sell your surplus for the entry fee. Back when I played MTG, I had a DCI score of 1,800. At my skill level, it would be unreasonable for me to expect to win consisently enough to play entirely off my winnings.
That said, if you are okay with a little gold farming to compete then I would recommend this game to you. Count on playing a 3 to 4 hour draft for every 4 or 5 hours you spend farming the Arena. You'll also want to plan on selling your pulled cards or winnings on the AH for platinum to cover future tournament fees. You will be able to get by on less farming as you do better in tournaments. If you play in anything but contructed other users who pay money will have no advantage over you. If you want to play constructed, expect an unfair pay to win experience (the same goes for MTG though). If you are a new player and want to farm gold then I would recommend spending $10ish to build a viable and quick PvE deck to run the Arena. While this isn't necessary, you will need to spend quite a bit of time in the campaign mode, building up a collection, before you'll be able to run the Arena as quickly as I do. IMO, this one time fee is well worth the time saved to immediately start farming. Bare in mind, that most viable speed arena decks will cost more than that. I will post a budget version of a deck that can get perfect and quick runs in the arena in the spoilers below. If you are feeling creative you can build your own, but you will need to get creative to spend as little as $10. Arena farming isn't just about winning, but winning quickly.
TL:DR This game isn't worth it if you want to pay to play competitive PvP. I'd recommend it to just about anyone else though. Farming for drafts is viable with about 4 hours of PvE per draft and smart use of the AH. Casual players will have a lot of fun with the PvE campaign mode.

While there is nothing inherently wrong with Gnomes Garden, it is simply just decent time management game that you will most likely forget five minutes after finishing it.
Gnomes Garden is a typical casual time/resource management game: you have 1-3 workers, whose task is to gather resources (food, wood, stone, and crystals) to spend on production facilities and on clearing road obstacles that prevent you from reaching the end of the stage.
Problem is, the developers knew how the core mechanics of such a game work, but they had serious issues with the details. All gameplay elements are introduced in the starting stages, leaving nothing than endless repetition for the majority of its 49 levels. At least reaching gold times on them is a challenging task; maybe a bit too much, I regularly had about 1-3 seconds left on the clock.
Interestingly, the game uses 3D models, meaning it is more demanding than most titles in this genre. But that is not why it has such a mediocre score, but because it does absolutely nothing to stand out in the sea of similar time management games: there is next to no story, the atmosphere is generic fairy tale, the whole game is… bland. Good enough for a casual game, but not even the least bit memorable.

OK, so i finished this game about a month ago and I figured it's time i get up off my butt and give something back to society.  Or something like that.  Supposedly it's good for my soul or karma or at least my butt.

Anyway, I've been playing video games for a VERY long time.  I've never been much of a fan of "action" games (The Thief series being a HUGE exception) I've always been more of the adventure gaming type.  And in this genre i am continually amazed at how much better and better the actual writing for these games has gotten over the last, say, decade or so.  I mean, some of these games are better written than books my very popular authors.   Which is really fortunate for us gamers because, let's face it...  after some practice, most programmers/SW Engineers can figure out how to make really cool graphics and gameplay and all of that.  But it takes an actual WRITER to create a compelling story and figure out how to tell it withn this medium.  And that's what we remember when the game is over and the bells and whistles and the flash bangs are done...  we remember the story.
My point is... Edith Finch is another great example of terrific graphics, sound design and gameplay wrapped around an intriguing and original STORY.   And the combination of all of these things works very well.  I will not give away too many details...  i think the way that the stories of each of the family members is told is wholly clever and original and, in fact, the manner and style of the way each of these stories is told actually closely matches the personality of each person.  See, this is what i mean - this is really smart writing.
The ending was a little bit of a shocker, i'm not sure if it was meant to be a twist or if I'm just an idiot.  Which, apparently, as I've been told, has been known to happen... I don't see it, but, whatever - All opinions are welcome, this is a safe space, there is a lot of love in the room, and feel freeeeee to be yourself.
Pfft, whatever.
But yeah, the ending.   I actually went back and watched parts of the beginning again just to see if i really understood the ending.  I've done that many times with a movie, TV show, or a book.  But never, that I can recall, with a game.   See what I mean about the writing?
Anyway, go buy the game and play it and love it already, would you?

An Octave Higher is an excellent visual novel about magic, friendship, a broken piano, and class war between the proletariat and the bourgeoisie in a capitalist society. It's set in the grand city of Overture, where magic has become a science that's fuelling an industrial revolution, resulting in the mass-scale production of magical machines. Since magic is used to do everything from cooking to driving, being able to afford the necessary mana potions is what separates the upper class from the lower class. Some reviews complain that it's too heavy on lore and explanations, but I really appreciate the detail, which is interesting and provided in context.
The story is told through the alternating perspectives of three main characters: Frederic Godwin, an aristocrat/GIANT D.O.U.C.H.E.B.A.G; Franz Byron, a student/researcher at the Conservatoire; and Elise Shelley, an orphaned factory worker who quickly captures Franz's attention with her special compassion magic abilities. It's supported by a number of minor characters, such as Frederic's overbearing father, Lord Joff Godwin, who founded the Magical Mechanical factory where Elise works; Franz's Professor Johann Poe; Commander Janis Woolf of the Dragoon police unit; Franz's best friend, Aretha Blyton (who is my favourite character because she's smart and funny and likes to bust Franz's balls) and her psychiatrist mother, Alanis; Elise's best friend, Jude; and members of Libertad, a radical proletariat group who are leading the uprising.
The narrative is well-written, the plot is engaging, the art style is beautiful, and the classical soundtrack is fitting. There are a number of decisions that need to be made along the way, and the first path that I followed (which gave me the Egregia♥♥♥♥♥laude achievement!) led to Franz and Aretha graduating from the Conservatoire with honours (despite Franz's research project not going quite as well as it could have) and the defeat of Libertad by the ruling class. A bunch of other stuff happened as well, but I don't want to give it all away! There are six possible endings, so I'm eager to play through it again, partly because I'm addicted to getting Steam achievements, but mostly because I want to see Franz and Aretha fall in love... and I'm hoping for a revolution ^.^

NOTE: just following the core of the tutorial and generally figure out the UI will take about 2 hours by itself. You may or may not come to a conclusion about it within those 2 hours; I didn't.
This review is based on a measly 4 hours of play. My normal "likes" are Fallout 4, 7 Days to Die, Empyrion:  open-world sandbox games with a strong creative/builder component.
So I should love this game, right?
In a nutshell, it just wasn't fun for me. As they say, "your mileage may vary".  I champion the
of the game, but the implementation just doesn't work for me.
Yes, I read the reviews that cautioned that this game is Grindy^11, but I didn't fully appreciate that. You start with a 20-slot backpack, which is already about 2/3 full with the starter stuff, and which quickly fills. You see you have slots for other containers, but you don't generally get recipes for creating them. You have to (for example) level up your basketcraft by picking about a thousand pieces of grass (I don't think this is an exaggeration), and making grass thread, grass string, grass rope, etc. until you unlock the grass container recipe.
I cannot emphasize enough how DULL that is. It sounds acceptable in the abstract, but it is pretty painful.
Many other sandbox/builder games, like Empyrion and 7 Days to Die, have skill unlocks and prerequisites to be able to make better things; Xsyon is a whole 'nother plane of existence in that regard.
The UI doesn't help in this (or any) regard: you'll regularly need 3-4 panels open at any time to accomplish anything. That grass you're collecting? You can only hold 4 bundles at a time, and you can't for some unimaginable reason transfer it to your backpack, so you have to stop every 4 bundles and craft something with it, which of course requires several panes to be open.
I ultimately, uh, sad-quit because a humanoid NPC killed me and took my starting weapon and clothes. The clothes I can replace, after a fashion; the weapon would probably take me dozens of hours to make, or have enough cash to buy.
I've been waiting a long time to get into one of these types of games (along with Life is Feudal and a few others on my watchlist); I was willing to take a chance on Xsyon since it was on sale. I regret my purchase.
THE GOOD:
On the PvE server (Peace), the community seemed friendly and helpful, if not small.
The movement controls are pretty standard. The map (there's one for PvE and one for PvP) are huge, but everywhere I went seemed very rugged and mountainous (apparently based on the Lake Tahoe area).
Let me add one final note: I can see why some people enjoy this game. Building a simple hut is a major accomplishment, and you feel you've accomplished a lot in doing so; I get that, I really do. But the journey is really, really long and tedious. If you want to follow that long road, and some subset of you folks WILL enjoy it, you have my admiration.

The story had a little bit too much math involved than I cared for (hated that subject), but luckily, you don't have to actually do any of it. The story was engaging regardless, and I am now aiming to see all other endings. TRIGGER WARNING for some: There is a mild♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt scene. The characters were likeable, with the exception to one in particular. The music got a little repetitive, but if you're a classical music fan, you will be thrilled by some surprise pieces. Over all, I give this game a yes. I would perhaps wait until it's on sale like I did.

Imagine a 19th century setting where industrial revolution was initiated thanks to magic instead of coal/vapor.
Magic is omnipresent,  used in machines and powerful magicians are enrolled in the army/police. The only constraint to use magic is the consumption of mana potions, unfortunately the market is regulated by the state who maintains artificially high prices which means only the richer classes and the corporations are able to acquire them. The only employement possibility for the lower classes is heavy factory work (using magic) where they provided with barely enough mana to work through their shift.
The main part of the story concerns Franz, a student who has been assigned a difficult (if not impossible) thesis project to find practical applications of "compassion" magic which is primarily use to heal and give energy to living beings.
Lured by a candidate sponsor in the poorest part of the city, he stumbles on a young girl, Elise, while she was trying to revive a broken piano using compassion magic. Seeing some potential for his thesis, he convince her and his mentor to employ her as his assistant... In parallel you'll witness a growing revolution led by a underground group called Libertad which aims to break lower class's dependency to the bourgeoisie for the access to mana potions.
This VN will keep you busy for 8-10h (I'm a fast reader) with a enjoyable story and 5 different endings. They extensively explain the various magic concepts (formulas, systems, machines...) and the depiction of magic duels is very dynamic.
The art is pretty and original and the characters have a large set of facial expressions. Special mention for the classical music soundtrack with a very catchy main theme.

Short review: Fun game. You can compare it to 10,000,000 but it added some new mechanics that my draw in new players.
Long review:
NEXT PART CONTAINS SPOILERS (for as much as this game has any)
Let me go a bit more indepth now. On the surface the gameplay between both games is exactly the same, you go in a dungeon with Explorer and do the puzzle shoving and solving with the 'match-three'-game. Meanwhile you will beat enemies, get gold and other goodies. Gold is basically used for the same thing as in the previous game, you buy upgrades with it. One thing changed in that perspective. If you played 10,000,000 you know you collected wood and stone to upgrade your shops and things like that. However in this game, you will unlock your shops through getting certain achievements in the dungeon. And you have way more shops then in the first game, also you will catch some loot like random rings and stuff. Eventually you will unlock someone you can sell that stuff to for gold.
So with the wood and stone collection gone, you have three new tiles. You have a 'Meat', 'Power' & 'Crate'-tile added to the mix of your normal staff, sword, key and shield. 'Meat' & 'Power' are basically for the best new addition to the game, namely the monster buddies. Completing objectives and achievements will unlock certain monsters, which you can eventually purchase. These monsters are basically your upgrades for certain things. Like +10 Staff Power or +10 Trap Time and stuff like that. These become very useful eventually also in later dungeons. What remains are the 'Crate'-tiles. These basically replace the item-slots you got when opening chests in the first game. Nothing special, only thing is they take up a place on your board. This can be a bit annoying when shoving around but it will help you immensly.
How about the gameplay then? Like I said it didn't chance much, they added some tweaks and turns. But on the surface it's exactly the same as 10,000,000. Only thing I like better in this game then the previous one is the fact that you have more then one dungeon. You basically travel with your boat (starting of as a simple rowing boat) down the stream and go plunder the dungeons along the way. Completed all the objectives in one dungeon, you travel on. For me personally I like this better. In 10,000,000 I usually had no problem beating the first level of the dungeon, but came across trouble beating the next levels, which essential made me put down the game. Here you can just go and keep on doing the same dungeon over and over. Ofcourse eventually you will run into higher speed and difficult enemies. But it won't block you, cause you will start on Lvl 1 of every dungeon and you will not travel futher and get more challenging objectives before you beaten the dungeon, basically serving as a watchman for your difficulty. Only downside I see to this is, that if you eventually encounter a dungeon that's to hard for you, you can't go back to the previous. I would love to have seen this to be added, but I can see why they didn't.
Overall a very positive vibe from this game. It's much like 10,000,000 and if you liked that one, you more then likely are gonna like this one. If you didn't like the first one, you can always give it a shot. Because the game added enough new content to try and be an 'upgrade' from the first one.

You Must Build A Boat (YMBAB) is a fast paced tile-based puzzle game. It wants to have the feel of an older game, as one can tell by the minimalist pixel art style and the 8-bit music. Your objective: run through a temple, gather treasure while fighting monsters, and use your gold to progress upriver by... building a boat. Who knew...
To it's credit, YMBAB works well with its chosen style. Old games are, on the whole, more challenging than most new releases. And you will find that YMBAB is challenging... it will take awhile to master.
As you continue you gain crew members who make you stronger and give you a place to spend gold... you even collect monsters to help you.
However, many players may be turned off after about an hour or two of gameplay due to repetition. Runs are essentially identical, different places are really just palette swaps, and too many times you will try to complete a quest only to just not be given the proper tiles. That's my major gripe with this game. How random things are, often times preventing you from advancing to the next area simply because the tiles won't line up right. I'm sorry, but I can't predict if a cascade will get me my mandatory 4th triple match of the run before I get pushed off screen to start over.
Also, I've noticed only two music tracks in the game: one for your boat, one for going on a run. I'm not against 8-bit music, but only two tracks is aggrevating.
I have yet to reach the end of this game, and maybe I never will. Perhaps all that's there is a "GOOD JORB BUDDY" sign and a button to start again. I don't recommend YMBAB, but go ahead and play it if you want... just be aware of the grind you are about to suffer through.

This is one the most unique games I've ever laid my hands on.. so to speak.
You play as super cool ultra spy man. With the ability to jump to absurd heights and stick on anything, walls and ceilings included. Each mission has some preamble to give some context and is very clever and quite funny. Your objectives include (mostly hacking into a monitor) or picking up laptops.
The crux of the gameplay is staying out of sight. Turning off lights, hanging off the ceiling and tackling the guards. One simple punch should do the trick. Preceding to the objective and extracting. Buts that not all. You soon discover that you are magic.. or least have the ability to connect things electrically from great distances. This process is called crosslink. You can switch between regular vision and crosslink with a simple flick of your mouse wheel. There are multiple colors which basically identify the different circuits in the building or buildings on the map. You can try things like connecting a switch to a door so that when flicked it operates the door. I'd elaborate but experimenting is its own reward, the proverbial 'EMMERGENT GAMEPLAY' that marketing teams get so excited about. There are sockets, alarms, cameras, sound detectors, elevators among other things for you to experiment with. These are sometimes puzzle-esk but mostly serve as tools to infiltrate undetected.
You die real fast. One shot one kill but what's great is restarting is almost instantaneous making experimenting really fun and interesting. You can even choose to start at different intervals some seconds away from when you met your demise. There are also gadgets that require batteries that can can aid you in infiltration and those things are fun but the best way to play is to get real familiar with and into crosslink to prevail, the most rewarding way if I was to give a suggestion. Arguably, the ability to crash through windows silently may be a bit over powered but that ability is mitigated by using a lot of your batteries.

The King felt ill! The kingdom seems in disarray! It's up to you, his daughter, to restore the kingdom to its former glory!
Like for 12 Labours of Hercules, the main character isn't helping at all. In other words, it's the servants that are doing all the work. Gnomes Garden is a casual time management game where you have workers that are gathering resources needed (food, wood, stone and crystals), building mines (for the stone and crystals), farms and windmills (for the food), workshop (for the wood), upgrading these for a better production and  repairing routes and other objectives (like light a fire or activate portals). However, the servants can be helped by witches (needed for some objectives) and firemen (helping objective plants to grow or to scare the little monster that will incapacitate your witch or servant from doing their jobs for a few seconds). And you'll repeat that  for 50 levels.
However, there are temporary bonus, regenerating over time, that can be activated : run faster (your minions move faster), work faster (less time for the building to give the resources) and stop time (the timer is frozen for a limited time). And these are very handy if you want to reach the three stars. Indeed, you have a timer. If you go past a star, you're loosing it. The less time you spent, the more likely you'll keep three stars. And as it's an achievement, you're also motivated. Nothing is wrong to loose one or two in the first run, so that you can try different strategies for the level. However, keep in mind that sometimes, you need to manage tightly your resources: you may be lacking some of them when they're needed and can't advance anymore (example: no more stones for a hole in the road - the building that could have given you the resource is behind this hole and there is no other road to it - you're doomed to restart). One of the good points is that you're not limited in the tasks done by the servant, if you want to gather 3 woods and 2 foods, you can check them without restriction (compared to 12 Labours of Hercules where you couldn't indicate more than 3 tasks).
As you can see, the gameplay isn't hard per se, it's just a matter of being efficient and to make the right choices (no need to upgrade a building to the maximum if the current level is sufficient or to upgrade the house - I've made the majority of the levels with two workers only). However, you don't have any other characters that can help. It's just the minions, not even the princess is present in the level to do something.
The graphics aren't bad in itself, they're cute, however, the HUD could have been more reflecting this and the list of objectives less confusing. The soundtrack was also good.
However, Gnomes Garden, while being still enjoyable, didn't have the same magic than 12 Labours of Hercules. You have more stuff to manage, true, but you can't choose your difficulty, the map is poorly designed and there, you don't have really any help from an heroin, contrary to Hercules and Megara, that were present and needed for some tasks. For the price, 12 Labours of Hercules proposes more fun for less money spent. But Gnomes Garden is still a good little game. Wait for a discount or for a bundle.

The game itself is decent enough for a TCG. Given that there are bucket loads of games out there in the genre, having good mechanics and well thought out cards is mandatory. The game gives you that. It also gives you a campaign that is fun and addictive until you beat it a few times.
You've actually got to adjust your deck for the campaign to beat certain challenges. I dig that. Makes you think beyond using the same old deck every time.
You also get to wear equipment to boost certain cards, and you level up a character to give you certain perks, much like hero powers in other popular card games.
Note that you only level up your character to level 9 in the campaign. There is no character devleopment outside of the campaign and you don't use campaign characters vs other players. The campaign is not finished and there is only 1 "act" to go through. Also, only half the classes are implemented at the time of this writing.
That's all great....for a week or so. Then the bad starts.
You will not have enough cards from the campaign or currency, which is gold collected as you play the ai, to build a decent deck. Despite what other player's in thier community want you to believe, going into this game FTP is going to cost you weeks of time before you even get enough to get your first booster, much less play a competive deck against a human being.
People will argue this to their death and point you at various guides...all of which I did for 75+ hours. I still have yet to have enough gold to get my first booster pack. They expect you to buy cards with the gold you earn in the campaign to progress through the latter parts of the campaign. Many of the cards you will be after cost 20 to 30k gold, while you are earning around 2k per evening. They then want you to sell cards you got in the campaign, which do not sell, because everyone wants to sell the cards from the campaign. They then want you to buy packs from other players. which currently cost around 19k gold, draft, win, open reward packs, repeat. Not feasible. Not at all.
The biggest downer is the market model. You cannot spend gold directly to get _anything_ from the game. They sell everything for platinum, which is real money currency. The one and only thing gold is used for is to roll bonsues on booster packs for a chance to win extra cards....those booster packs being bought by someone else or won in tournaments of course. There is nothing in the game you can get from playing that _someone_ didn't had to pay for.
Yes, you can trade on their auction house, but as a new player, expect that 98% of the cards you get in the campaign do not sell, or sell so low that it isn't even worth clicking your mouse. Why would they? Everyone is playing the campaign and already has those cards.
Which brings me to the other downer. The cards you win in the campaign are not randomly drawn from all cards in the game. There is a specific set of cards in the adventure packs that are drawn from. You get the same rares based on your class/race for challenges. So expect the market to be flooded with those particular cards. They only have a bit of value if they take 10+ hours to get...and I mean little value.
This model of not having the game directly give players any product for the currency earned with their playtime will leave you having to replay the campaign several times and that gets damn boring. Then you might, and I say might, just come up with something that you can progress to the arena with. YOu then have to play that Arena over and over for countless hours with a deck you are bored of playing to acquire enough gold to buy packs from other players to draft with. Good luck following the guides! They all contain cards that cost at least 30k gold that you will have to buy via auction house from other players.
The game is clearly built to hook you, bait you, then frustrate and bore you until you fork over your cash.
I wouldn't have a problem with forking over $50-$100 for a few months of fun, but it's going to cost _alot_ more than that to get anywhere. They want MTG money. Not having a means to spend gold directly to buy boosters makes that obivous.
Don't listen to thier community. They get pissy when you argue it's taking too long to get anywhere without spending money. I spent 75+ hours on this game and have been successful in many online and paper TCGs. I am not about to go and spend thousands on another one. Never again after Magic.
It is not 1990 and most of us should know better than to get involved in the old TCG model of spending hundreds on cards just to continue playing.
We have viable alternatives now. Living card games for paper and many many TCGs out there that reward you cards for play, with minimal investment for a tournament every now and again.
It's too bad, because I like the campaign and the AI challanges so far.

This is essentially Magic: The Gathering with a few additional mechanics that wouldn't be easily implemented in a physical format card game. The game flow is almost exactly the same as MTG with the major differences being:
- Mana (gems in Hex) have a smoother curve overall and there is less management of it.
- There are heroes similar to what you have in Hearthstone with unique abilities, health totals and so forth.
Aside from that you are more or less playing Magic. Even the gem colors/strategies are copied from Magic so if you like to play Red/White Aggro in MTG then R/W Aggro is going to be pretty damn similar in Hex. Blue control? Yep, it's here. All of the general tendencies and basic strategies are very similar across both games.
Now, I like MTG. I played it for years. The MTGO client has always been a bit... special and it definitely isn't as beginner friendly as Hex because there is single player campaign mode. Even the standalone annual MTG games can't compare to the campaign mode in Hex. That said, Hex doesn't have that great of a client either. It's slow and not particularly responsive. The store is clunky and the auction/marketplace is downright painful to use.
Hex also lacks in the format department in comparison to MTG, so don't expect a lot of options outside of basic drafting and constructed. You won't see anything like EDH in Hex, at least not yet.
To sum up: Do you like Magic: The Gathering? Yes? Then you will like Hex. It's cheaper and the client is slightly better. No? Move along and give SolForge or Hearthstone a try. (Definitely try SolForge. It's a great game and it plays FAST.)

Good level design with lots of renewable resources, so the strategy is mainly in figuring out when to build and upgrade production centers. I missed getting three stars on about a third of the levels the first time around, and liked the game enough to want to go back and replay them.
Major downsides:
The sides are cut off in fullscreen mode on a 4:3 monitor, occasionally cutting off things you need to click on. It mostly works in windowed mode, but the resources needed tooltips are sometimes cut off, so you have to guess what you need, and the window's too small to play comfortably. (Or maybe I just need new glasses.)
A bug with the same achievement popping up every five seconds when I replayed levels after completing the game. Irritating enough to make the game unplayable unless I turn off the sound.
Clickable areas aren't well defined and are sometimes misaligned, so when objects are close together, it can be difficult to click on the right thing.
I had enough fun with the game to recommend it despite these issues, but they might be dealbreakers for someone else.

Hello!
I am writing this review to let everyone know just how much I like this game.
AND It seems very odd to me that Xsyon is so underrated and unknown!
This game has so much to offer a player like me. I am older, in my 60's but have played mmo's since they first came out.
I have played all the major old school mmo's like Everquest, and many of the newer class of games like Allods, terra and the like. Im a huge fan of seamless 3d environments, and really like the feel of Xsyon.
One thing I really like, is that I don't have to rush to the "end" here. With so many skills to work with and so many things to craft and build, I reckon i'll be here for years.
Oh, and speaking of building, you should see the amazing things people build in this game! I have been on a walk about all over, and have seen things like full sized castles, indoor swimming pools, paddocks for animals, and cool little villages. I have not don't much building yet but from what i gather from players, its a module style building system, with things like wall, truss, and roof parts that you can put together in many different combos. Plenty of styles to choose from as well.
I've done a fair bit of crafting so far and it is pretty typical of other games. I do like the way this game provides the baski tools you need to give it a go. I learned the hard way that the first thing you should do with your starter tools is make more starter tools!  I reckon my next project will be to make me some armour.
The community in this game is true blue. Always helpful and willing to keep ya going. Like, they warned me not to mess with "revs" yet till I was a bit more experienced. Once I found them at an abandoned homestead, I know what they meant. Imagine sick starkers running around trying to kill you and you have the picture. Most had twice the hit points I had and I had to run away not to die. I have'nt even tried animals yet, but I'm sure that day will come.
All in all, this game may not be your cuppa, but if you enjoy a good community, and time to make your mark, then you are gonna love this game. Please don't take my word for it though, just go all in and try it mate!  You won't regret it!

Birds. Guns. Two great tastes that taste great together! Especially considering this game costs about as much as a large pizza or half a movie ticket. Rocketbirds is a very entertaining little adventure that has you as...well, a chicken (a really badass one) aiming to liberate the world of the evil penguin regime. Damn penguins...
The controls take a bit of getting used to, but it throws in various aspects in gaming in well together. There's violence, puzzles, and most important... JETPACTION! Yeah, you get to fly around in a jetpack, which is probably the best part of the game cause you get to blow things up in a jetpack. I mean what else could you want in life? Seriously.
The difficulty is mostly balanced as well, though you definitely need to be quick on that trigger finger when you got baddies on both sides, thankfully the game is pretty generous with health and ammo in tough situations, including the jetpack sequences. Did I mention how awesome those are? You're a chicken flying around in a jetpack with a machine gun shooting at penguins flying around on jetpacks with machine guns! Just...picture that in your head. Now imagine that being a million times more awesome than that could possibly sound.
Um...what else...oh yeah! The cutscenes are pretty rad too. Nothing that will question everything you ever stood for in life or cry tears for hours, but they help set the tone, the tone being "Duke Nuke if he was a chicken but with twice the asskickery". The music is also sweet. It's indie, but it's not "in-your-face" indie. It's just...y'know music that goes well with the game!
No more spoilers from me, though. If you want a fun way to kill a lonely Saturday night or just love birds flying around unconventionally while wielding weaponry, then drop a Hamilton on this game and just see for yourself!

I took about 6 hours to get every ending, as well as the special achievement. I have to say, I thoroughly recommend this game, I enjoyed every second.

Minor spoilers:
The first four endings are pretty lighthearted. In fact, if you only played the game through once you could be forgiven for thinking that An Octave Higher builds up a story in which the core issue is never really tackled. However, you have to make a certain few decisions to unlock the second half of the game. There, it quickly gets dark.
It is for this reason that I advise anyone contemplating suicide to avoid this game, as it deals heavily with this subject matter in the second half. However, if you are stable enough, the final endings are truly amazing.

I picked up this game because I wanted to see if I'd like the visual novel medium. It was on sale so it seemed like a safe choice.
The game has a good story set in a very captivating world, the characters are unique and memorable, and the choices are simple but meaningful. You experience the story through three character's different perspectives, which is a bit of a theme of the game. It's a good mix of humor, drama, and friendship. It not a tear jerker, but it has its moments.
The art is good, aside from a couple minor things here and there. Though I never really liked steampunk, I really enjoyed the art style. Maybe I never really gave it the chance before.
The music is great and really fits the game's setting.
There are tools for skipping already read dialogue, which is extremely useful for finding the different endings. The text log is very useful too. Saving/loading works perfectly and I never had any technical issues while playing.
Judging by the non-sale price, I was hoping for about 10 hours of entertainment, which I got.
All in all, An Octave Higher is exactly the kind of experience I was looking for. I'd highly recommend it.

This game, despite its odd name, is a sequel to 10,000,000, which came out a couple years ago on Mobile and PC. On a micro level, it's pretty much exactly the same game with as few minor changes. The first is that some of the match-3 icons have changed. Staves, Swords, Keys and shields remain, and do the same things as before. Crates have changed in that they now drop items on the board (rather into discrete item slots off to the side), while Stone and Gold have changed to Power and Mind icons. You will now gain gold from opening treasure chests in your runs, and selling loot afterwards.
The other change in the game is the end goal. In 10,000,000, you are presented with a simple goal - score 10,000,000 points in a single run. In You Must Build a Boat, your objective is to finish every quest in the game. You will go from location to location, moving to the next after you complete every quest in a location. Quests are similar to those in 10,000,000 - kill X enemy before he hits you, open 5 chests in a run, etc.
These differences are largely trivial, however, as the game plays out pretty much exactly the same in the end. The final quest requires you to go on a solid long run with a powered-up character, more or less in line with the point goal in the last game.
The presentation is a little nicer, but the view gets very cluttered as you increase the size of your boat and add NPCs to it. The other main negative I'd point out is that some of the art on the tiles looks pretty bad, and the crates take a long time to get used to seeing on the board and matching. Other than that it's a solid game and a worthy follow-up to the excellent 10,000,000.

First of all, beware of the spoilers in the video and screenshots on the store page. I didn't watch the video until after I played the game, and I was amazed at how many solutions to puzzles that it contained. Now onto the review.
This game was a hidden gem for me. I was in the mood for a game that I could comfortably play in a weekend. I liked the idea and the look of the graphics of this, so I gave it a shot. I ended up enjoying this far more than I thought I would. It also took a bit longer to play than I was expecting, but that was mostly due to me getting stuck on a couple of puzzles. I got a great sense of satisfaction when I did figure out the solutions, and they always felt reasonable and logical. If I stopped playing and came back to it later with a fresh set of eyes, most of the solutions seemed obvious.
Generally the game is all about using your brain to solve puzzles, but there some parts that test your platforming skills. It had a good progression of adding abilities to keep the levels fresh. It was impressive how well the puzzles were made to use all the abilities, and even at one stage had a puzzle based on
. Some people have complained about the short length of the game, but I don't think that adding any more levels would have resulted in any new type of puzzle. I was quite happy with the way the game ended.
The game plays perfectly on my netbook powered by a 1GHz dual core AMD C-50 processor at 1024x600 (below the minimum spec). The minimum resolution is 800x600 (why don't system requirements ever state this) and it supports windowed mode. It also worked surprisingly well using a trackpad instead of a mouse, although I did my full play through on my desktop system so I only tested the trackpad on the first few levels.

FINAL DOOM is a package of two highly acclaimed “megawads” or collections of fan-made levels. In all you get 60 very well-designed levels, which equals about twice the length of DOOM II, or nearly the combined length of DOOM II and THE ULTIMATE DOOM. It’s highly recommended you play those two games before touching this one.
FINAL DOOM adds literally no new mechanics or anything to the table. It’s kind of just an extension of DOOM II -- sort of like the difference between SUPER MARIO BROS. and SUPER MARIO BROS. 2 THE LOST LEVELS. Another reason the comparison is apt is because of FINAL DOOM’s increased difficulty over id Software’s original creations.
What makes the maps in FINAL DOOM so good is that they were designed specifically for people who’ve already completed the first two games and are thus already highly accustomed to how DOOM works. The fan levels manipulate enemies, items, and the gimmicks of DOOM in ways beyond what id explored.
Between the two megawads, “TNT Evilution” in particular manages to feel tough but fair. It spends a lot of time using enemies in ways DOOM and DOOM II didn’t prepare you for, messing with preconceived notions and tactics that may have gotten you through those games.
You may end up in tight quarters with a Hell Knight or a corridor with a Revenant, subverting how you usually fight against them. Despite stuff like this, the levels are designed to where you can always find new ways to deal with old problems. In this way TNT manages to always keep you guessing.
The other megawad -- “The Plutonia Experiment” -- on the other hand, feels a little bit cheap in my opinion. It definitely feels possible to beat, but ramps up the difficulty pretty much as soon as you begin and puts you in a lot of downright crappy situations without warning. Whereas TNT gradually ramps up the grade of enemies and weapons, Plutonia throws Revenants and Mancubuses at you on its first level. I also think it overuses chaingunners. If you’re a stubborn kind of gamer you can still enjoy it, but it’s noticeably more frustrating than TNT.
FINAL DOOM is sort of like an ultimate mastery of old school DOOM, its levels making the most of DOOM’s mechanics and requiring the most of the skills you developed in the original two games. That, and being basically twice the content of an actual official DOOM game, make it one the most valuable collections of commercial fan content around.

Wow. Simply spectacular. Consider it a combination of Receiver, Hotline Miami, and Bushido Blade. The goal is simple. Reach your endzone after passing through multiple screens. This is one of those excellent games where you can make your own game with a little imagination and elbow grease. Try king of the hill, or a super-sudden-death slo-mo game mode where the only possible attack is to throw your boomerang sword. Wow. I can't stop saying wow. If you liked Hotline Miami--seriously, pick this up. It's a lot of that games greatest concepts distilled into a plotless breeding ground for couch co-op and epic 6-player tourneys.

I'm going to go ahead and say this at the beginning of my review: 11/10 Would buy twice. What does this game have to offer you may ask. Answer: No less than pixelated face/gut/crotch-stabbing 1v1 FUN!!! The entire game is a tug-off-war scenario where each player spawns at the center of the map, his objective to move forward towards his enemy's side of the map. Both players are armed with swords and there are several different levels of combat. Literally.
Your sword can be held in 4 different stances: Crotch-level, Gut-evel, Face-level and Olympic Torch-level. The first three allow you to stab your opponent in either the aforementioned areas and the last one (held over the head) primes your sword for throwing. Yes, you can chuck your sword at your enemies.
For those times when you lack a sword, you can go up close and personal for some ol'-fashion ninja combat!!! Crouch to get under your opponent's guard where you can trip him and, when he falls down, break his neck! You can jump to perform a diving kick (which also plants your enemy firmly on the ground, neck-breaking ensues if desired). You can run up walls, hang off ledges and parkour your way past your enemies.
Remember though, the ultimate objective is to get to the opposite side of the map and prevent your opponent from doing the same. It is true that sometimes the better part of valour is flight. Coincidentally, the best part of valour is victory. So if you can avoid your enemies, do so. Just remember to watch out for any swords thrown your way (they travel faster than you, so you should probably duck).
Multiplayer is sparse at the moment, but someone is usually online. The action is fast, frantic and absolutely hilarious! The AI in singleplayer is smart and the further you progress the smarter (and towards the very end) and faster it gets. A good game to play with friends over the internet (you can send invites directly to your Steam friends from within the matchmaker). All in all, I'd say it's worth the price if you manage to get your friends to get it as well.

As soon as I seen people saying this was the Yu-Gi-Oh! game aimed at the older fans of the original series who used to play years ago I jumped at it hoping to relive some of those childhood memories and for a first number of duels I enjoyed it, I saw hints of 'pay2win' but it's a card game and I can't for the life of me name one without some pay2win elements so I completely let it slide but after just a few hours of play it begins.
The exact same nonsense that put me off Yu-Gi-Oh! in the first place; Those turns that last 10 minutes with cards popping in and out of the deck and graveyard like there's no tomorrow, I can understand the technical skill needed for pull these off consistently but it sucks the fun right out of it for me and was the main reason I was so happy to see a game aimed at the older fans as I thought there would only be little bits of it.
I was wrong. I played a game earlier where my opponent chained cards and effects for quite some time until he had cleared my board entirely and some traps) and got himself a formidable board at the same time and then the turn ended and it came up with 'opponents turn'. He went through about half his deck flicking cards in and out of there, the field and the grave in MY TURN. Now I know long chains like this have always existed in Yu-Gi-Oh! but I was hoping so badly that it wouldn't be as prominent in this game as sitting there doing nothing while you watch your opponent take longer than you in your own turns is just a bit boring for me.
That however is a somewhat personal rant as I know people do love to pull these off so it's on the players rather than the game I guess. The only faults with the game I've found are that the port could do with a little polish, a real 'fullscreen' option and some more bits to fiddle with on the settings as masterrace always demands.
Overall it does what it does very well but if you want the old school casual Yu-Gi-Oh! experience you'll need to invite a friend to play with or keep searching as unless you just want to play vs ai over and over you'll eventually find that you spend most of your in-game hours sat watching half an hour of set up each time you enter a duel.

Highly ambitious and promising, I havnt been this excited to see a game grow in a long time. Now is the time to buy, create your settler, and find a place in the game. It's amazing to watch this barren wilderness being settled by a growing number of player tribes, everything from trading centers to small campsites. The game world is already quite large, so I can't wait to see what the full map holds when the game exits early access.
Can't recommend it enough. Have some patience during your first few hours, take the time to familiarize yourself with the different skill options and crafting menus, join one of the many tribes who go above and beyond to help new players learn and settle in, the game will suck you in.
EDIT: While I am still excited for the possibilities of this game's future, some of the initial enthusiasm has died down. The devs have been worryingly inactive in the steam community and xsyon forums. Exploring further in the game world has also let me see just how much the player base has lost some major players. there are several extremely large tribes that have control over huge areas off land, have built and terraformed massive settlements, and then vanished, leaving behind these ghost settlements. While it could be cool at first to see the "ruins" of a lost tribe, these areas are locking down large plots of land, making them unusable for active players. even more so, many of these old super-tribes were very destructive in the way they gathered resources, meaning there are less forests, valuable junk piles have been used up, and all these resources are just sitting on these old tribes' lands, useless. On the opposite end of the spectrum but equally annoying is all the random "tribes" scattered around that were created by 1 player who played for 1 day then quit. these lands are also unusable for active players, often having not a single thing built on them besides the tribe totem pole.
I have read elsewhere that tribes are removed if they are inactive for over 3 months. this needs changing. this is far too generous for a single-person tribe, and is useless to help against the large old tribes, which may have 200+ members gone for a year or more, but 1 person keeps logging in, which means that tribe gets to keep all that land. players should be auto-kicked from their tribe if inactive, so that way the tribe will lose that extra land and be reduced to a size that matches the actual number of active members.

What Remains of Edith Finch is 2 hours of fantastic content. An interactive first person experience more than a game in the traditional sense, it reminds me of the greats in the genre like The Beginner's Guide and the Stanley Parable, with perhaps a bit more polish and scale than those ones.
Telling the story of a cursed family, you follow Edith Finch, the last surviving member of said family, as she explores her childhood home, and recounts the last moments of her extended family. This story is incredibly sombre and at times macabre, but the story is told with a sense of wit and humour that makes the game fun to play despite the subject material.
The game is very linear and short, so if that's a dealbreaker for you, try another game. But in this genre, you are paying for a well told story that can be experienced in an afternoon, so if you're happy with that, by all means buy it, as it is worth every penny. But if you are on a tight budget, definitely wait until there is a sale.
I hesitated at first when confronted with the $19.99 price tag, but I bought it on a whim and I do not regret it at all. I hope a lot more people get to experience this story.

Okay this is the first time I reviewed a VN (I did one before with A Kiss for the Petals though that's not a 'proper' review imo) on Steam so bear with me, okay?
I count myself among the minority seeking out for more narrative-driven games and for better narratives within them.  And in this sense, I adore visual novels genre. So, when this gem showed up on my recommendation list, I wasn't expecting much. Maybe some average story, a couple silly characters, that sort of thing. What I got, instead, was a journey to an entirely new and exciting world that left me with a feeling of intrigue and a longing to someday return. A story about how circumstances can divide people.
Set in the city of Overture, a large city in the midst of an industrial revolution spurned by the discovery and implementation of magic, An Octave Higher comprises a nest of concrete and steel itself governed by the marriage of science and magic... that you might even call it magical science. From scientific theory to engineered machines, mana and the powers it provides Overture in its entirety. As you can probably tell, the story revolves around magic, where it is the key to it all: education, industries, to the country’s militia, and is even used in everyday livelihoods for the upper districts and for those who can afford mana potions. Anyone with a mana potion can cast spells, and must do so if they want to live comfortably. Heated water? That calls for fire magic, born from the Courage attribute. Want healing? Summon your Compassion. Omnibuses, the flying taxis of the city, operate on wind and gravity magic (Faith and Willpower).
But magic is far from a catch-all solution if not without costs... It’s borne problems of its own as the city is divided into a three-class system. The Aristocrats on top are the wealthiest, living in their manors and are in charge of most industries of any and all magic machines. The Bourgeois are the middle class where most can afford to use magic and to go to schools that teach the usage of magic. They primarily live in the middle city that takes care of itself. Lastly, the Proles, who make up the poor class that you will usually see in dead-end jobs, are rotting in the shanty towns that make up the lower quarters of Overture. Where the lower class is consistently in awe of the magic and machinery that the rich take for granted, the upper-class look down upon the proles, who grow more and more resentful. Poor citizens are reduced to being compared to simple parts in a machine, and at a certain point in the game we overhear a conversation among factory owners who weigh costs between buying new machinery or hiring more workers.
And this is where we meet our three main protagonists and their respective roles in society. There's Frederic, an aristocrat brat who is pretty much awful to everyone he interacts with despite being a great sorcer player. Soon after, we meet Franz, a well-off student and researcher at the local university. And finally Elise, a young factory worker who lives at a brothel and in a few short months is expected to join the ranks. The narrative jumps around between these three characters liberally and it does effectively convey what everyone is thinking about in any particular situation.
At this point, I can't say enough about the writing. The pacing is excellent, and it encapsulates world building to an almost perfect point. In every instance, the writers find ways to explain details to players. Questions such as: what does the average factory worker's day entail? How does this machine work? What are the rules of the arena sports game, Sorcer? All of these details are provided in context. Another aspect of the game I really loved was the complex theories of magic layered within it. I have no doubt that the game developers spent many hours getting the magic theories down to a science (like its clever use of using magic theories in place of real mathematics), and the end result presented to us definitely allowed me to further immerse myself in the rich fantastical world of Overture. I do wish there was voice-acting in the game though, as that would have definitely aided in the immersion experience.
The music, while a bit lacking in variety, is pleasant and soothing. This gives gameplay a relaxing and calming effect, which in turn causes the hours of playtime to quietly float by. Sound effects within the game have a tendency to fall flat, but they aren't distracting and don't take away from the experience.
Overall, I really enjoyed playing this visual novel and it is undoubtedly one of the better visual novels I've played in recent memory. I grew really fond of the game's setting and characters by the end of the story, and I believe that the game's world still has a lot of potential left to be explored. This visual novel is one that fans of fantasy stories should definitely give a try! And by the way, the developer, Kidalang, already announced a prequel to this game called
so make sure to look out for it!
