I received this game as my second review copy (wohoo!) and was very excited to try it because I love match games – in particular, Puzzle Quest. I was very satisfied with my gameplay experience.
If you like match games, RPG-lite elements, grinding, and retro pixel-style graphics, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are simple and nice – the variation in monster/character sprites is decent and the amount of detail in the game is good. As you progress through the game, you will encounter new crewmembers, resulting in new rooms being added to your ship (increasing its size). Eventually, you will transform your tiny dingy into an awesome pirate ship. Whenever you complete an area, you will travel to a new one, complete with different backgrounds and “water.” The music and sounds are decent and remniscent of the old-school retro games era, however, I muted it after an hour of playing in favor of my own.
Controls are entirely mouse-based and very easy to learn. There is a mobile version of this game, and you will quickly notice how the game is meant to be played with a touch interface. That being said, the PC version is still very playable and fun. There is a helpful tutorial, however, I noticed that it does not seem to be skip-able – which can be a bit annoying when you start a new game again and have to go through the text dialogue multiple times. The learning curve is mostly minimal, however, will have to do a fair bit of grinding in order to progress (even if you happen to be the best match gamer in the world). Enemies become stronger as you progress, and the game continues until you are knocked off the screen – which is hastened whenever you are attacked or take time to open chests. I like this system because it is indicative of your remaining health – so at max health, you will be running at the very right end of the screen.
Gameplay consists of you matching various tiles (minimum of 3) while your character runs through a dungeon. Different tiles execute actions like attack (magic or physical), open locks, and shield (prevents damage and refills health – allowing your character to run further to the right). There are also brain and muscle icons, which act as a form of currency to purchase things like attack/spell upgrades and hire crewmembers. Crate tiles take up space, however, destroying them will sometimes yield useful items or spells (ex: a fireball spell that pierces all visible enemies). You get bonuses for matching more than 3 tiles, matching different tile types simultaneously, and chaining matches. Grinding plays a critical role in this game because enemies will start to do massive damage to you if you are not upgrading things like your defence (health) and attack.
Whenever you start a dungeon run, you can add missions (a maximum of 3 once you invest in the ability) – each one adding to the dungeon difficulty and loot chance. Completing missions will give you resources, as well as things like new crewmembers (monsters) to recruit. Recruiting monsters will provide you with a particular bonus (ex: increased critical attack chance), and recruiting all monsters in a “set” will give you an extra bonus. Monsters that have been recruited will appear on your ship, roaming around and looking ferocious. Once you have run a specific distance, the difficulty of the dungeon will increase and you will enter the next level of the dungeon area. Completing all levels of the dungeon will allow you to progress to the next area. It is always advised to progress as soon as you can because loot rate/rarity (and monster difficulty) will increase significantly, allowing for more efficient grinding.
Eventually, you will encounter “traps,” which must be disarmed by matching the appropriate tile. If you fail to do this within a small window, you will activate the trap – the worse one being a freeze trap that renders all of your actions invalid until you thaw out (very easy to lose if this happens to you at later stages). Sometimes, you will find food in your play area – clicking it will refill your health substantially. Treasure chests will also increase in difficulty (requiring you to match key tiles 3 or more times), however, you can offset this by matching 4 or 5 tiles instead of the minimum 3. A nice thing about the game is how it says: You Win! whenever you get knocked off the screen. The tutorial even explains that you cannot truly “lose” the game.
Once you complete the game, you can restart in a new game+; I tried this for a short while until moving on to other things.
Overall, the game plays very well, and can be extremely enjoyable if you are a fan of the match-3 genre. I got ~7 hours out of this game, and have played it into the wee hours of the morning just because I wanted to finish a stupid mission.
Recommend!

I've played it to 100% completion, and I must say that this visual novel is marvelous!
An Octave Higher is set in a world where magic is science. In fact, they even have an education major called Magical Science, however contradictory that sounds. The story takes place in Overture, a kingdom where the people are divided into three different classes: Aristocrats, Bourguoises, and Proletariats. You will experience the story from three different perspective, with each character coming from a different class, and therefore has different way of thinking, knowledge, or even belief.
It tells a deeply compelling story about friendship, conflict, betrayal, and hope. It's very hard to point out the good points without spoiling anything, but if you're looking for a non-anime/non-cliche story with high emotional stakes, look no further. An Octave Higher will give you a hell of a ride, one that won't be easily forgotten.
By the way, the game has SIX endings: 1 premature ending, 3 "relationship" endings, 1 true ending, and 1 alternate/bad ending. Playism has an official guide in their website, and I suggest you get them all. Especially the true ending route, because only then you'll see the complete story.
10/10 you won't regret your purchase.

Captivating and beautiful. Really a series of short powerful experiences, each with a distinct art and interaction style. Creative and experimental, yet quite refined and fluid. Extremely linear story, but you will attribute that to fate, rather than poor design. You will be touched by this story in a way that is deeper than any linear media can.

Only 2-3 hours of gameplay, the controls are a bit unintuitive, twitchy, and difficult to master, and it's not particularly exciting. In addition, recognition of which objects can be interacted with in which ways is very difficult, leaving an average player quietly perplexed with the lacking game design.
But the mechanics are solid, and a few of the puzzles are quite elegant and satisfying to solve. Imagine starting out on a simple platformer, having the powers of the wizard in Trine. Later you gain the Trine thief's grappling hook, and a limited ability to teleport into certain objects. None of these additional powers are explored to their full potential.
I give it a positive review because it's worth playing around with, if only for the unique feel of the game and its combination of mechanics. However this game has a lot of wasted potential. If the developer were to come out with additional, more complex puzzles, with better level design, and more variety to the environmental mechanics, or open it up to user-created levels somehow, it could be a beautiful thing, a la 2D Portal.

NOTE: This review only focusses on single-player.
Dawn of War 2 is a highly enjoyable game. You play a Marine Commander and a selection of squads, and you level them up and get new items and abilities for them. Story is fairly solid and keeps you involved in the campaign. Time is a factor in the campaign - take too long and you can lose sector resources, making the game harder and harder.
You have to choose the squads you'll take on most of the missions, and the equipment you take, and these choices can make the difference between crushing victory and crushing defeat. Try to keep your squad leaders alive, as losing them impacts on your mission score, making the next missions harder (get a good score, and you may be able to deploy to multiple missions per game day, allowing you to keep ahead of the 'issues' in the sector).
Missions themsleves are mostly enjoyable, with some tricky firefights. Make good use of cover, flanking, and your squads abilities and equipment to prevail. Recommended.

The Signal From Tolva is a First Person Shooter where the player controls a robot, who has travelled to the planet Tolva to investigate a strange signal. The main objective is to travel around the small open world map, finding and scanning several artefacts, to learn more about the origin of the mysterious signal.
The planet is also inhabited by a number of friendly and enemy robots. Some of these robots are wandering around, possibly on the same mission as yourself, while others are defending small bases. If you clear a base of enemy defenders, the friendly faction will take control, and the base will serve you as a fast travel / respawn point. You can also collect resources that are scattered around the map, and use them as a currency to buy new weapons at a base.
After a couple of hours you’ll unlock a command module that allows you to recruit between two and four friendly robots, to follow you into combat. Its an interesting option, but I personally didn’t find it very useful. Apart from the fact that your allies die very quickly, the major drawback is that you only get two weapon slots (I’m ignoring a permanently equipped pistol which is very weak), so if you equip the command module, you only have one offensive weapon. Ideally in an open world game, I want to equip an assault rifle for short/medium range, and a sniper rifle for long range. You do also get an area of effect special attack, but this takes a while to recharge.
Of course, when fighting alone you can easily get outnumbered, sometimes encountering up to six enemies simultaneously, but as an FPS veteran, I enjoyed the challenge. And occasionally you’ll be able to fight alongside a friendly patrol who are heading to your objective anyway, so you get the best of both worlds. There isn’t a great deal of enemy variety, but they do have fairly good AI, retreating when damaged to buy time for their shields to recharge, and attempting to flank you.
Unfortunately, The Signal From Tolva is let down by its technical performance. Even though I was well above 60 fps, mostly in the 80-100 range, it doesn’t always feel smooth. There are frequent microstutters, where the action kind of freezes for half a second – especially when collecting resources. It doesn’t make the game unplayable, and I never felt like it negatively affected my aim, but its still annoying. There have been other reports of this problem on the forum, but as far as I could see, nobody has found a reliable solution.
Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard. I finished the game in just under 7 hours. Without going into spoilers, the story is not very detailed.
Ultimately, Signal From Tolva is a fun, but flawed game. And whilst not an essential purchase, it could entertain you for a few hours, but you should wait for a sale.

Dragon Ball Xenoverse is a simple, yet entertaining Dragon Ball Simulator. This concept is important: take into account that this is not a traditional fighting game, but a Dragon Ball game with a Dragon Ball-based combat system including air combats, flying and diving, fireball blasts, rushes and special attacks. If this is not the type of game you are lloing for, you may want to check other alternatives, but if the description above looks like it could entertain you, you are into ~20 hours of fun and entertainment.
General game aspects:
So, where to start with DBXV? Maybe we could begin explaining that in this game, you will create a character that will serve as your avatar in the game and will carry on all missions. Later, you will be able to team up with other DB characters as you unlock them and even get them teach you some skills thanks to the master system (no, not the Sega console). As you defeat foes and complete missions, you will unlock new skills and in-game currency and experience points are gained. These experience points will be used to level up your character and distributing points into some attributes, giving DBXV an rpg-esque touch. Note that there are different races in the game, each with their own abilities, strenghts and weaknesses. This feature adds some replayablity to the game as there are several builds to try on your character(s), so kudos to that. BTW, the game calls for specialized approaches so don't be shy to consult a guide or FAQ before spending some points on yout character upgrades.
About the story:
Trunks, a time patroller (an specialized squad who watches over time to fix any possible disruptions) has summoned you to help him with his tasks. With such a simple beginning point, you'll be thrown into battles, revisiting all the Dragon Ball Z arcs and unlocking side quests (or as the game names them, parallel quests). Side quests are interesting in the aspect that your actions may trigger alternative win conditions and alter the development of the mission, and thinking about what to do in order to unlock those alternatives can be quite enticing. Also, they are mandatory in order to obtain some juicy rewards.
Sound and Graphics:
Beatiful and colorful cell shading graphics are present through all the game. Animations run smoothly and areas are well-designed. They are not top-notch graphics (this is a 2013 game) but they do the job just fine. The soundtrack is quite good and all characters are voiced by their original voice actors (at least, in the japanese audio).
Gameplay and controls:
First things first: a gamepad is highly recommended.
It doesn't really take much time to get used to DBXV combat system: you have two attack buttons (light and strong), a ki blast button (fireball spamming), a block button, a flying button, a tragetting button, etc. By combining any of these buttons with the triggers you gain access to special attacks and ultimate attacks, both of them being kinds of attacks that consume your "ki" meter. There is also a "stamina" meter that is consumed when you dash or block.
Consumable items with different effects (healing and boost effects, mainly) can be equipped.
All in all, the combat is pretty simplistic but fun and it doesn't get repetitive too soon, taking into account that your fighting style will also depend on your character build. There are no major camera issues and team battles are pretty common in this game, so the targetting system is appreciated.
Lasting appeal:
It took me 22h to complete the main story of the game and all parallel quests. Taking into account that there are a couple more parallel quests to beat after the game and a new arc that is unlocked after meeting certain conditions, I guess about ~25 hours could easily be spent in the game.
Final words:
DBXV is a good Dragon Ball game. It attempts something different and it does it quite well. We are not talking about GOTY material here bu certainly an enjoyable pseudo hack-and-slash game that will be loved by Dragon Ball fans and will be attractive to casuals as well.
I give it a 7/10

PROS:
• Engaging gameplay.  Similar to MtG, but with enough unique features to gameplay (like being able to track changes to cards, having full cards generated instead of just token, the champion/avatar system) that make HEX games just fun to play.
•  HEX has AMAZING art.  Each card has exceptional art.  I was around in MtG's early days and HEX is nothing like that.  In fact, HEX art now in many cases is a step above what MtG currently has.
• A pretty welcoming community.  Being a game that was Kickstarted means that there are already some veterans in the game since the beta that are always looking out to help their fellow players.
CONS:
• The biggest complaint I can leverage is that development seems to be a little slow.  The game shows great promise (and as mentioned, beautiful), but new features seem to come along a bit slow considering the genre.
• While marketed as F2P, it really isn't.  It is very cheap for a trading card game, but a significant investment of time would be required for a person to play the PvP sections without ever spending a dime.  It's possible, but probably not the best way the game should be played.
Overall, though, I heartily recommend the game and I think that it will only increase in quality with time.

First Impressions review after a few days;
Yu-Gi-Oh, what's not to love? overall what could go wrong?...
It's not a bad attempt. ( Considering there's has been alot of attempts, should really tell you something )
-Many of the rules are changed since the good old days. (Board is only  3 cards wide, so only 3 set cards and 3 monsters, no second phase, are just a few i've noticed and these are not positive changes)
-The lay out sucks. ( Designed it seems mostly for mobiles devices, the play field is smaller as described above, and is squished into the middle third of your screen, with an enormous play log and card description dominating the other quadrants)
-Deck size is reduced to between 20 and 30 cards per deck. ( Severaly limits options and kinda takes fun out of complex deck compositions )
-Field spells do not change the graphic of the board.
Some positives, yes they got somethings right.
- Play mats / card sleeves options.
-Ability to play with a character avatar, fully voiced is amazing, go go go Dr. C!
-Ability to earn cards and gems to grind rewards is pretty fair, I guess.
-Some visual representation of monsters and summons is actually nice, and a positive addition.
-Voice acting as ever is top notch.
Overall, the negatives detract from the game in my opinion. I find games that stream line themselves annoyingly rarely if ever do so for the better. "Dumbing" down the old PC version / card game for console and now even further for mobile is just weird.
If they released the old PC CD version with online play, character choice, rewards, mats and sleeves and god forbid TRADING (Gasp, yes I like interacting with players beyond simply wondering through a lonely click and play random match up system where card values count for little, except to prove some land whale floated their daddy's company so they can purchase complete top end decks) , then I would give it 10/10.
Instead it ends with a fair 6.5 / 10.
Also, side note, beware spending too much, it would'nt be the first time a Yugi card game and been unplugged and everyone loses all their cards.....

This game started out to be alot of fun.  General platforming and some good quality toilet humor along the way to overthrowing the penguin dictator.
It has some good things going for it, like lots of chicken on penguin violence and lots of penguin on penguin violence.  I like  that you can exercise mind control on enemy penguins and make them commit fratricide.  After you've used them up like a spent prophylactic you can throw them away by making them commit suicide.  It's quite entertaining.
The animation is top notch and the controls are a bit clunky but it rarely gets in the way.  There are a few levels where you strap on a jetpack and do some dogfighting, which breaks up the platforming nicely.
There are a few things that drag this game down though.
Artificial difficulty.  At points in the game they just throw enemies at you from both directions (it's 2D).   Therefore to execute your attack, turn around and execute another attack in time is darn near impossible before those guys just surround you and spam you with gunfire so you can't do anything but sit there and flop around getting shot until they drain all your health.  It gets very annoying.
The puzzles never change, you must find this keycard to open that door and advance in the level.  The further you get through the story the less intuitive the keycard quests become.  Here is the formula to figure out the path; if you kill a penguin standing somewhere and he is immediately replaced by another you're suppose to take control of him to do your dirty work, ie open a door or move a platform and take out a few of his teammates in the process.  However to do this you have to throw a....lets call it a "mind control grenade".... so as the story goes on they crowbar in more artificial difficulty by making you throw it through smaller windows, bank it off a wall, or make the guy pace around etc.
Overall it's a decent game, however I'm about 2/3 through it and I believe I've reached the point of diminishing returns regarding entertainment vs frustration due to ramping artificial difficulty.

Rating: 8/10 ("Very good")
Recommended for: People who enjoy VNs, mystery readers, people who like a little darkness to their fairytale. I would recommend this for a first time VN-reader.
My route order: Ending 3 > Ending 4 > Ending 2 > Ending 1 > Secret Ending. I can't decide if I liked ending 1 or 2 the most.
Overall, CUPID is a very solid visual novel with an interesting premise. This is a "mystery" VN done much better than Root Letter -- the story actually manages to be captivating instead of draggy and long. It took me about 4 hours to complete all the endings (skipping already read dialogue), which is decent, especially for a free game. That being said, the story felt so fascinating that I would not have minded spending some money on this game. It deserves it.
Of importance to note is that the novel is not told in chronological order. There are time skips and time jumps; the narration goes back in time, then shoots back to the present. This can occasionally make it difficult to follow, but a little persistence and thought should clear things up quite easily. In addition, reading through the novel again from the beginning after completing it makes a world of difference.
The art is often hit-or-miss; sometimes, it is very pretty. Other times, it leaves something to be desired. It is simplistic but gets the job done. It also manages to be creepy when it needs to be, which was a nice surprise.
The soundtrack was selected well and complimented the scenes in the visual novel. It never felt repetitive or poorly timed.
The characters in CUPID were all very interesting and well-written. The novel exchanges POV with each of its three main characters -- Rosa, Catherine, and Guilleme -- though its main focus is Rosa and Guilleme. This is an effective way of telling the story that kept me interested in the game. The prose is also overall very enjoyable to read and never felt stilted or overly amateurish.
In the novel, you primarily "play" as the voice in Rosa's head, her "mother". Your choices do have an effect on the endings and the way Rosa reacts in certain situations. It would be pertinent to note that the character you play as is actually rather malicious and negative -- the majority of choices simply temper how poorly you, as a voice, treat Rosa. This was an interesting design choice where the majority of protagonists appear to be "good", so it was a nice surprise if a little jarring at first.
In the end, CUPID is absolutely a must-read, especially for a free visual novel. It is memorable, with interesting themes and concepts, and fascinating characters.

Back in the day, this game was great. The graphics were good, features were nice, and there was plenty of developers building this game up. This game had an actual fighting chance in the game industry when compared to others in its genre. It was known as Wurm Online 2. I even purchased the game when you had to buy it and pay a monthly subscription with it. Speaking of the payment model, many times the player base and myself talked about how the payment model was bad idea and how it can potentially kill the game or not allow it to get anywhere. I continued to play anyway because I liked the game’s ideas, the genre, and so on.
What got me to quit was that I had a guide spawn hostile mobs near me and get me killed because of it, basically abusing their powers. When I confronted him, he said he didn’t do anything and just teleported away. I then afterwards got into an argument with the forum manager who was trying to censor my criticism of the game when providing feedback. At that point I just didn’t want anything to do with the game anymore. The game developer was alright, never seem to cause problems besides making overall poor choices when it came to staff hiring and the payment model.
After a while the game went free to play using Wurm Online’s payment model where you had restrictions until you payed somehow, don’t remember exactly if it was a subscription or what. I gave it a try and little to nothing changed. Years after not playing, almost nothing changed, no amazing features, no mounts, no improved combat, just nothing exciting and worth playing. Now the game went to the payment model I wanted from the beginning and so I gave it a try. It’s still the same thing. No real changes, graphics are now outdated, and it appears there is only one developer on the game.
At this point, there are two competitors, Wurm Unlimited and Life is Feudal: Your Own. This game just simply doesn’t stand a chance with them, where they’re fully staffed, have better graphics, are more stable, and have far more features. I wanted to like this game, I tried to do my part. The player base is tiny, because the developer made overall poor choices like having terrible staff and having a terrible payment model. The damage has been done, maybe the developer can dig himself out of the hole he’s in. I hope he does, but this game doesn’t appear to have a future. I hope I’m wrong, but I wouldn’t be surprised seeing this game die off soon enough.

Suffice to say, this game, while being a shooter/action game at heart, also has puzzles every once in a while as a break from the action.
I guess that is what I like so much about this game, that it tells a rather messed up story using irony and moments of hilarity to minimize the effect. A worthy follow-up to 10000000.  One of the few games where I made sure to 100% the achievements.  Going through the story mode will take ~7.5 hours, and around ~25 hours to get all the achievements.
Pros:
- Lots more to do.
- Building the boat is a more obvious form of player advancement than the counter in 10000000.
- Plenty of hidden extras all over the place.
- You can always make a match, so failure is (almost) always your fault.
Cons:
- Sometimes when you find a crate, you'll have none of the tiles you need on board, so you'll be frantically matching while you slide off into oblivion.  Can get frustrating at higher levels.
- Can get frustrating when random level modifiers boost enemies in unfair ways.
- The UX is a bit of a step back in some ways.  The game seems to have been designed for touch, and you'll often do something and be left with an item on screen with no clue that you're supposed to just click the living crap out of it.  The busywork clicking is annoying and out-of-place with the rest of the game.
- When you restart at a higher difficulty, you have to redo the tutorial.  The developer said on Twitter that fixing this is on his TODO list.

Gameplay always comes first, beyond story or visuals. Gameplay is what makes a game tick.
And gameplay is where Nidhogg shines.
It's tense tactical game where your skills as a player matter as much as your ability to lure and trick your opponent.
It's a subtle give and take, of establishing patterns only to break them, of intimate moments of stillness and caution as the two of you step back and forth anticipating the first strike.
It's a game where all are equally matched, where true skill decides the victor rather than the perks, upgrades, boosters of so many other games
The simplicity of the controls hide a surprisingly tense and strategic game. One hit kills and there's a wide range of moves and maneuvers at your disposal. While I love Samurai Gunn's lightning fast speed and more varied maps, Nidhogg's slower paced, more cerebral challenge is absolutely addicting. And while you may be able to leap through the air with ease in Samurai Gunn, your moveset is far more versatile in Nidhogg. The smooth animations give each fight a fluid dynamic feel.
Not that the visuals are bad either. The surreal graphics and chunky pixels give the game a style all its own. And while the number of maps may seem small, it's definitely a case of quality over quanity. Each map is unique, with its own eccentricities to be mastered from the concealing high grass of the Wilds to the collapsing bridges in Clouds. Not only that, each map consists of several areas as you and your opponent push back and forth to victory. Epic 20 minute duels are not uncommon
I rarely play online games, but Nidhogg has me hooked. This is a must play
It's fun but not for long. 30 minutes was enough for me. Completed maps on Casual difficulty. Too hard on Average difficulty.

You can take my recommendation for Doom 2 and more or less apply to this, word for word. However, there are a few things that make Final Doom stand out from Doom II and Ultimate Doom that deserve pointing out.
One, this pair of megaWAD's (yes, you get two 32-level games in Final Doom) wasn't made by iD Software. Rather, they were developed by TeamTNT and published by iD Software.
Second, those who are bothered (for whatever reason) by the more abstract level design found in The Ultimate Doom and Doom 2 will find that the level design for Final Doom (especially Evilution) resembles real buildings and places. This doesn't take away or detract from the fast-paced gameplay the series is known for, in my opinion.
Third and finally, if you thought the difficulty was too easy in Ultimate Doom and/or Doom 2, then Final Doom should remedy this. This is especially true for Plutonia Experiment, where you're facing tougher monsters and lots of them early on.
I'm obviously quite biased when it comes to the Doom franchise. However, I'd still recommend getting this. Again, it's more of the same, but that's not a bad thing especially if you like fast-paced, hard hitting twitch shooters like I do. :)

I used to click through VN's just to get the achievements. I was ready to do that again with CUPID, but for some odd reason I was hooked by the first line of the story.
The first scene tugged at my heart and I had to know what happened to the protagonist in the past and where her story is going.
I found the writing excellent, plenty of little funny whimsical moments; and as the story progressed, very deep dialogues that were extremely interesting to read through. Their description of going through grief truly tore me up inside and I found myself crying and sympathizing with the painful experience I was reading,
Playing with mature filter off meant I was surprised by a VERY graphic detail of a sex scene, I had no idea it was coming and it was pretty... intense to read through.
The best part of the story for me was how they kept it exciting all the way to the end, throwing in twists and turns that threw me off what I thought was a straight forward story.
Music, storyline, story telling, character development and visual art were all fantastic.
The only part that was lacking was the occasional use of language that didn't fit the era of the story (I believe it is set in the 1700's if I'm not mistaken.)
For a free to play game there sure was a lot of time and effort put into it, and I recommend it if you're not afraid of dark, sexual, creepy material (heavy on the incest implications; I didn't know this before playing and it would've probably made me not pick this game).

An Octave Higher is a really good story about music, magic, and class conflict set in an interesting steampunk-ish world that reminds me quite a bit of The Legend of the Korra. The story is told from the alternating perspectives of three characters brought together by an unusual research project: Frederic, a narcissistic aristocrat; Franz, a brilliant but asocial student of magic; and Elise, a factory worker who dreams of being a musician.
While the story can be heavy on exposition at times, it's necessary to explain the complex and unique way magic works in the city of Overture in order for the plot to make sense. And aside from a bit of awkwardness when it comes to fitting those details into conversation, the story is really well-written. It's full of original ideas and morally complex characters, and while it's mostly pretty serious and dramatic, it has its moments of comedy as well.
Overall, I really enjoyed it, and I recommend it to anyone else who wants a good visual novel that's not too long. Make sure you don't stop after one ending, as there are several, some of which involve a much longer story than the others. I'd love it if the creators wrote more stories that take place in this world.

I've had about 1500hrs in Xsyon before it hit steam. - Tribe/village/homestead construction with many options (pvp/storage safety in home tribe)
- Cosy, postapocalypse environment (the graphics adds to the charm)
- Honing skills (if you like grinding)
- Intricate crafting system
- Entertaining melee combat system (if you can fight and got the equipment)
CONs:
- Few players to interact with (does add to the postapoc feeling)
- Lots of grinding (if you dislike it)
- Steep learning curve (most newbs need to ask questions to learn the basics, but there is usually someone online to help)
- Recipy system (requires grinding to randomly unlock crafting recipes, or scavenging/buying schematics/blueprints frm others to learn how to make most things)
- No firearms in a postmodern apocalypse, currently only melee combat (archery is planned, eta sometime before never).

I don't normally write reviews, but I feel compelled to write one for this game, because it deserves no less than that. So, here goes.
Before I begin though, I must admit that I only played this game due to the recent Steam Summer Sale, in which one of the daily quests was to Get an Achievement. As almost everyone familiar with Steam games are aware, visual novels are one of the easiest genre of games to obtain achievements, and this one just happened to be a random pick of mine for that very purpose.
But oh, what an awesome pick that turned out to be. CUPID, despite its simple name and brief, unassuming description on the store page, turned out to be one of the best visual novels I have ever played and indeed, will ever play. And I have played quite a few visual novels in my time.
As the game's blurb goes, CUPID is set against the backdrop of 18th century France, and it centres around four main characters: the protagonist of the game, Rosa, a beautiful but shy, timid girl living on the streets as a rose vendor, Rosa's long-deceased Mother who guides her every move as a voice in her mind, Catherine Emilia Perride, a musical child prodigy and Rosa's best friend, who gave her a home and grew up together with her, and a Marquis known as Guilleme Michel de Gul, a dashing, charismatic character infamous for his string of alleged romantic conquests that were as short-lived as they were sensational, and the wild rumours that followed in the wake of their destruction.
You play the role of the aforementioned Mother, whose face is never shown in the game, but whose psychic directions to Rosa can drastically impact the outcome of the story.
Right off the bat, the game makes it clear to the player that it is no ordinary slice-of-life, feel-good visual novel, as many recent ones are wont to be (not that that's a bad thing, mind you). Rather, you as the player, are immediately challenged with what initially appears to be a confusing narrative, made up of both gentle love and cruel abuse, emanating from the same flawed character.
This may be discomforting to most people (myself included), who may be unaccustomed to such a dark, and indeed, twisted theme. But if you soldier on, you will find that there is indeed a reason to the apparent madness, though it may take a while to reveal itself.
The child Rosa encounters a similarly-aged Catherine at the grounds of Guilleme's mansion in the beginning of the game, and Catherine is immediately and somewhat inexplicably drawn to her. Although the Perride family isn't ostensibly wealthy, Catherine manages to convince her father to take Rosa in and provide for her. Thus begins a friendship that lasts until Catherine's death (I hope this isn't a spoiler since it is already mentioned in the game's store page description), and now Rosa must find out what, and who, really caused her death.
While this general storyline may sound interesting enough to some readers, if not a little cliché, it is *how* CUPID tells its story, and not what it is, that sets it apart from many lesser visual novels. The prose and dialogue is simply marvellous; fluid, natural, totally believable. It is terse in moments when it needs to be for emotional impact, and wordier in others when the tension and mood is lighter. At no point did I feel that the conversations were forced, or the prose jarring; everything just seemed to flow and read as naturally as one would expect of real human interactions.
It is peppered throughout with statements that made me stop and ponder over them, at the same time marvelling over how simply they seemed to fit into whatever dialogue or narrative was being said at the moment. Here are a few choice ones I can recall off the top of my head:
- "You can't fake sacrifice"
- "Friendships are a shallow kind of relationship"
- "You cannot take love without giving it"
- "Generosity is the only saving grace of the dying"
And impressively, it accomplishes this without resorting to "big words", the way some other novels may attempt to in order to present an illusion of profoundness.
As for the art in the game, it is simple but beautiful, nonetheless. Plenty of care was given to the facial expressions of each character, and they change frequently and appropriately to reflect the vacillating emotions of their owners during each conversation. The background art also deserves a mention here. While they might not win any awards, they are tastefully done and complement each scene well. The music is a little subdued however, and is comprised almost entirely of piano pieces.
Together, they are weaved beautifully to provide the player with an experience that is both thought-provoking and emotionally impactful. Just as there are elements of horror in the game, with one scene being particularly bone-chilling to me, there are also heart-warming moments that soothe the soul, with one exchange between Rosa and Catherine being particularly poignant and memorable. This range of emotions it invoked in me then, is one of the largest I have felt in any game before, and I believe, is probably what its creators set out to achieve as well.
While some players may feel discomfort in the central theme and the dark overall mood of the game, I would argue that that cannot be held as a black mark against the game, and rather that it should be judged on how well it delivers its content to the player. And in this respect, it delivers in spades.
There is well over ten hours of gameplay here, if the player is interested in obtaining all endings and unlocking all CGs and achievements. Speaking of achievements, there is an astounding 67 (!) of them here, and I know of no other free game on Steam that rivals this amount. So then, even in the realm of replayability, an area most visual novels are notoriously poor in, the game scores well among its peers.
With all that being said, CUPID is certainly not a game for children, or even young teenagers. The theme of twisted love and abuse may also hit too close to home for some people. The game apparently has a PG-17+ rating and fully deserves it, not only as a deterrent for younger players, but also because those without the required maturity levels would likely not be able to adequately appreciate it.
In summary, this game is an easy recommendation for those who can appreciate a good story, even if it is streaked with darkness. Lovingly crafted and masterfully told, its only price tag is your time. I am simply astounded that a game of this quality is absolutely free of charge.
Thank you Fervent Studios, for this work of art.

My old Tribe leader noticed me in chat and sure enugh the tribe was still kiking and had simply moved. My first real multi-story structure was started on a Saturday morning. By Sunday evening I was about to ram Xsyon up somone's a**. that building caused me more grief than the IRS. The short version:
Xsyon is a great game and if you're a fan of player made worlds, interesting crafting/building systems, or post-apocalyptic survival games, it's definitely worth checking out.
The long version:
I started playing Xsyon back in 2011, before the game was available on Steam. The game is early access, but don't let that scare you away - in it's current state, the game offers enough content to keep you busy indefinitely. Early access games have been known to contain game-breaking bugs and unfinished features, but that's not the case with Xsyon, as the features that are in the game work. I have encountered bugs from time to time (as in any game), but I have to say that once reported, they are fixed - fast. I've seen the game's dev come into the game and talk with me personally to fix one. The game's team of moderators (guides) are active in not only helping players out with any issues or even questions about the gameplay, but they also hold events and generally seem interested in what they're doing. There have been many major patches rolling out important new features since I've been playing.
There is a skill system in place leading to the gathering, crafting, food and building systems. The crafting system allows you to create a ton of different armors, weapons, and utility gear (carts, tools, etc) from materials gathered in the world. The building system allows you to take crafted and gathered objects and build structures in the game (other players can see and interact with the structures, and you and even let them work with you in building them). The building is extremely interesting and has a large array of pieces available, allowing players to create anything from small tents and huts to immense palaces and castles (I have to admit that I personally spend a LOT of time building with my friends in the game - by the time I finish 1 project I have 5 more ideas that I want to try out). The food system allows players to hunt, fish and grow and forage lots of different things, and cook them to make food - it's easy to do the minimum, but players that really invest themselves in this system can create very powerful food items that can help in every day things. The skill system as a whole works well - it's easy to throw yourself in one skill and master it, but harder to master 2 skills, and so on. Playing solo is possible, but the game is much easier playing as a group, allowing you to focus on your chosen skill(s) without worrying about the others.
The game is definitely worth checking out - I know I've spent a lot of time playing it (I only connected my Steam and Xsyon accounts a few months ago, even though I started playing in 2011, and am at over 600 hours on Steam) and will continue to play it for a long time.

What Remains of Edith Finch is both simple and extremely interesting. At the start it feels like something that will be close to, say, Gone Home - story-driven ambient exploration game. And it is. But the way that it tells it's story, or more specifically - many stories, - is where it gets interesting. The game, also with a lot of horror and mystery elements at the core of the stories, tells a tale of a history of a rather peculiar family, full of people who ended their life in an unusual and sometimes gruesome, but also very non-surprising way. To the point, where they were believed to be cursed, something that some of them tried to avoid, and some embrace.
What is the most interesting aspect of the game is not just the way that it gives a very different tone and voice to each of those family member stories, but also how it almost always tries to enhance the story it tells through how you live through that story. Some of it is simple, some of it is stunningly effective. With the best example story being something that, if just told or shown, without any interactive element, would not have a very strong effect on the audience. But when told through the interaction, and quite simple, actually, it makes you connect to that story so much more. And the fact that those actions are actually quite simple, but yet work so well to tell the story is what sets it apart from similar attempts, like, say, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, that had more classic adventure game puzzles. And makes a lot of the actions you do in the game more meaningful.
Which is not to say, that the game was all solid or all stories were similarly good. It is a bit disappointing how slightly more abruptly the game ends, even if it works like that intentionally, that I wish it did. Some of the stories it tells are a simple or too long. And exploratory bits had those slightly annoying parts where scripted animation takes priority in forcing you to walk somewhere or look a certain way. Which was understandable, but felt more restrictive than a lot of the smart bits, where such direction was instead enhancing the experience and helping the pace. Either way, I would highly recommend checking this game whenever you have 2-3 hours as it definitely worth it.

This is a direct sequel to the game 10,000,000. It is a Match 3 dungeon runner with RPG elements made famous by Puzzle Quest. It uses the take on match 3 where you drag a whole row or column at a time and it continues from the other side of the play area when it gets to either end. Match 3 or more of a tile and they break, filling in from above and giving an effect based on what tiles were broken. There is also a 'dungeon' above the play area that shows your little pixel dungeon runner moving forward until they encounter either a monster or a chest.
Gone are the locked doors from 10,000,000, but instead you will encounter little flying traps that will fly in over the top of whatever you're encountering. The trap has a tile type displayed in it which shows you what type of tile you need to break before it drops on you and also tells you what the effect will be if you don't. The traps add a bit more complexity as they force you to either deal with their effects or break them before they drop on you while still trying to deal with the monster or chest in front of you.
Also changed from 10,000,000 is the items which now spawn directly on the play area and you click them to use them. This can present a problem as they are essentially dead weight until you use them, but they aren't useful in every situation. You don't want to use a damage item if you're on a chest for example. Another example is certain monsters are weak, strong, or immune to certain items, so saving them for that monster or not using them when they'd have less effect is important, but you also can't match with them so they reduce the amount of available matches on the board.
I know you're also wondering, what's up with that title? Well rather than the stark dungeon rooms of 10,000,000 you are instead gradually building a large sailing ship, though you start with a basic rowboat. The ship automatically expands as you gather more NPC's to buy upgrades from and once you've gotten all the quests done in an area you sail on to the next part of the map, which is a new dungeon.
Quests are essentially the same. They form the backbone of progression in the game and give rewards for doing specific tasks along the way. Some quest rewards are just gold, some are key items which give other passive bonus effects, some are new NPC's, some are captured monsters (more on that in a second). The difference from 10,000,000 is that you can select how many quests you want to have for each run. Each quest you take increases the difficulty and rewards available on that run. They also sometimes come with their own modifiers to that dungeon.
As you progress through the dungeon levels, it will either add a modifier, or reroll an existing one if it already has 4. These can be things like chests with more locks, monsters with more HP or damage output, or even visiual effects like mist or darkness that covers the right half of the dungeon.
The basic NPC's are there, sword upgrades, staff upgrades, shield upgrades, potion vendor eventually. The new ones are for the replaced tile types. Wood and Stone have been replaced with Muscle and Mind. Instead of using them to unlock rooms or upgrade them, you use them to unlock small passive bonus effects in the form of captured monsters or to eventually upgrade your spells. Also since XP tiles aren't around anymore there's a vendor later that sells you those static effects for other forms of currency instead. There's even an NPC much much later that will allow you to invest gold now for a random chance of gaining more gold back after you've gone a certain distance in dungeon runs (cumulative over multiple runs). Seems like an odd choice for how late you get it, but it takes some of the grinding away potentially in the late game where stuff costs a ton of gold.
This is a pretty good sequel. No bugs that I saw, better options for audio and video this time, feels like a full PC game rather than a mobile port. There are a lot of lessons learned evident in the design of the systems and it feels mature in comparison to 10,000,00. It can be picked up and put down pretty easily and still feel like you're making progress. The game isn't super long if you're just playing through all the quests, which isn't a bad thing in my eyes. My playtime represents how long it took me (approximately) to beat the game for the first time. There is an option to reset and play through again with an increase in difficulty if you're looking for a challenge or some replay value. I did not unlock everything, but I didn't feel the urge to do so. That's not a knock against the game's appeal, it shows that you don't need to grind out every upgrade in order to win.

This is one of those times I wish I could simply leave a review as 'Mixed'.
You... And who Else? is a grindy strategy based game with an emphasis on micro managing gear and selecting the right general at the right time in your wave based battles. The story is somewhat in the backdrop, consisting of a hero trying to head north and recruit local talent in nearby kingdoms to fight back against a threat. That said, there's usually little dialogue to be had, as the game's focus is the wave based battles, defined in the game's description as 'places to explore'.
_Pros_
+ Lots of general to control, each with their specific minions. It can make for some interesting combos. You get these generals by beating them in their kingdoms, usually after a long fight. I found this to be rewarding.
+ Art. The images used for monsters and generals are pretty good. Not quite anime, but it has a slight style in that direction.
_Cons_
- Way too many details to remember and manage. You have to quickly learn which enemy does what and is fazed by what kind of attack. You also have to figure out what your abilities do (the shorthand descriptions aren't always useful) and you use medals to micromanage details in how your generals level up outside of combat, which can result in their minions also leveling or gaining new abilities, but it doesn't tell you unless you access a certain menu combination back at a town. Why?
- Excessively difficult. While strategy is highly important, your characters are simply... kinda weak. Certain generals vs certain enemies will win battles quickly, but your resources are pitifully low, leading your generals to run out of gas quickly. Running out of magic points is common, there's few places to grind, xp is extremely minimal... you can't finesse your way through this game, but it doesn't really enable you to get much stronger either.
- Fights are monotonous and take far too long. Fighting 22+ waves, consisting of 1-5 enemies apiece is a drag and this is most of the game, to be frank. Fail a single wave and you have to start at the very beginning of the gauntlet. Most people do not like having all their progress dashed on a bad decision or poor RNG. The trial and error nature of things is sloggish.
- No personality. Most characters don't talk beyond their defiance to join your side or mutter a generic 'for king and country' type line when chosen for battle. An RPG style game without conversation and personality is not a good design. You never get behind anyone, they're ultimately just meat puppets with stats.
- Music. Disable it. It's basically a single short track on endless repeat.
- Clunky menus. This was a big sticking point for me. The menu system is a complete convoluted disaster. You can't simply equip/status check your generals. Instead, you have to bring them into your party and then check them, despite they're on your immediate roster. Their minions are completely inaccessible to do anything with until you order a formation at a safe town, something I had no idea was even a thing until I screwed around. Then there's annoying little things like leaving a town breaks up your party back to the roster area again. It's just a headache that badly needs optimizing.
Conclusion: I want to like this game, but it gets no updates or support of any kind that I can determine. The UI is a mess, the battles are tiresome, rewards are few, and there's just not a lot to this game. There IS a good concept here, but the execution is rather poor and unwieldly.

This game was a lot of fun! Get it!
I really could leave it there but I also enjoy it when people find my reviews useful so I do believe that I will have to add more…
Gameplay
So many times when a game developer works out a nice formula for a fun game they are able to tweak it a bit here and there to keep future installments of that game fun! I remember I played the first bridge constructor when it came out years ago as a free flash game when I was in university. I absolutely loved it and played quite a few of the other games but then forgot about the franchise for a while. Then I saw the bundle offer and then simply had to have it.
As I was saying earlier, many developers do find it hard to present their games in a new and fresh way but I believe that “Bridge Constructor: Medieval” has done this with flying colors. The first few levels are what you’d expect, build a strong bridge with limited resources, a bridge strong enough to transport heavy carts, equipment and men.
After that it gets very creative, for example in one set of levels you have to make the bridge strong enough to make the enemy go to the middle of the bridge but weak enough that it breaks when they get there, destroying the enemy. There are other such creative level sets but I won’t mention them so that there are more pleasant surprises for you to have.
Story/Writing
The game has a story! It is correct and brings the story together well enough. Not a story rich game (obviously) but it is nice to have that story that brings everything together.
Music/Audio
Pleasant medieval fare, not too distracting and sets the tone correctly! The SFX are excellent, very accurate and also very entertaining. One really sits at the edge of one’s seat when they hear the bridge beginning to break.
Art
Good quality and immersive. At no point do you feel that you are playing a cheap game or that anything is particularly subpar. The material textures are very well done and the character sprites are cute.
Physics Engine
Excellent, seems very realistic and very fair.
Conclusion
It’s a fun game for anyone that loves these physics games and a very unique and clever twist on the genre.
Recommended 8/10

There are the types of FPS players who don't care about that and choose to focus on improving their skills on games that lived and died on balanced mechanics and muscle memory. There are also FPS players who focus less on this to grind out objectives and built-in achievements into the game. Maybe there's some crossover, but it leads me to question whether the lively community in this game is nostalgic, falls into the first category of FPS players, or both.
Anyways, the core mechanics, maps, and community of this game - it's the perfect trifecta that keeps the life of Valve games. On sale, it'll give you a few hours of fun - maybe more if you enjoy the classic FPS genre.

I have been playing Hex for a little over two years now. I had never kickstarted a game before, never played a beta let alone an alpha, so this was quite an interesting experience for me. I came to this game because I love TCGs, and I needed convenience to play one. I had played Magic when it first came out, but as a kid, I never understood how big it would get. Later in life I would try to play the WoW tcg, but quickly found that being a physical game had restrictions when you had adult responsibilities to adhere too. Hex allows me to have all that I love in TCG, and play in big tournaments from home.
But the game has become so much more then that. The community of the game is some of the best I have ever had the pleasure of being apart of. I really like a lot of the streamers, and people that I interact with on a weekly basis. The game does innovative things, because it exists solely in a digital environment without physical restrictions. The game has a passionate team that communicate with us, and drive the game through amazing leaps and bounds, always getting better then it was before. Hex provides a free to play Player verse Environment area where people can win cards, equipment, and gold to continually improve their decks, and collections. Staunch grinders can reputedly make enough gold, to actually draft now and then furthering their collection. Talented draft players and auction has savvy individuals have been able to go infinite, and amass a collection without having to drop money into the game all the time. Streamers and community members do giveaways, and help new people out, as they enter into the game and start learning what the game has to offer.
The game offers up options for several kinds of players. Collectors, competitive players, free to play players, and you can just play the campaign for fun.
This isn't to say that the game doesn't have flaws.
Hex is a small company, with a limited staff, trying to do huge amazing things, in a variety of areas. This is a huge under taking. Because of this production time can be slow at times, communication can sometimes become strained, and vague. Sometimes they will make choices that people don't agree with. The tutorial and introduction to hex has grown by leaps and bounds but still sometimes confuses people. Lastly, many of the promises from the kickstarter have yet to be delivered, and that scares new people, and infuriates some older people. The initial campaign is a little short, and the replay-ability is not as good as it could be.
Despite these flaws the game is well worth while. The company continues to add staff, and create a foundation, that makes the next step easier, smoother and more efficient. Production time, and deadlines are getting faster, and I have faith will eventually work like a well oiled machine, producing PVP, PVE and events in a fashion that at the very least every couple of months something new is happening. As new people come in, and talk to veterans, staff members, the helpful Nobles, and talk on our forums, the game will improve. Kickstarter rewards are slowly being checked off, and the majority of the Kickstarters have accepted the delay with grace and poise, while still letting them know they don't want to be forgotten, and Hex continues to prove that we won't be. When they make a mistake and the people talk to them in reasonable ways, letting them know how they feel, they consider our words very carefully. If it was indeed a mistake, then they are quick to find a solution, always putting us first. Sometimes they make a choice that we don't agree with, and after careful consideration they stand firm. I personally have experienced this, and feel that in those edge cases, they are doing what they think is right, and I believe that they can see the bigger picture then I can, so I put my faith in them. The adventure zones will continues to come, enhancing and expanding the game, the focus will broaden, and the secrets that are hidden in the lore, will slowly come to the surface. Choices will go from making small effects in small places, to large effects that ripple through the story.
Lastly I want to stress something that I think is often missed in a game like this. If you find the campaign short, if you love playing draft casually but maybe don't like the meta. Walk away, and take a break. I have through these two years, had to for one reason or another slow down, or take a break from the game. When something new draws me back, I am always excited to jump into the new tasty treats with gusto. Sometimes though, you just got to take a break. That doesn't mean you have to leave forever. Come back when your not burned out, when something new excites you, or whatever.
Remember the game is free to download, free to try, free to talk to others who are playing. Taste it, and see if Hex is right for you.

I love Aldorea rpgs and would have played more than 50 hours for each rpg.
However, after playing 11 hours on this rpg/strategy game, I am feeling really bored and tired of the large amount of micromanagement. I am wondering if any other player is feeling the same as I do.
Lets look at the micromanagement.
In this game you can have yourself and a team of 8 generals (from a total of 20).
Each general can have up to 3 additional troops, so your team have up to 36 troops.
When you get new weapons and armors (which happens all thetime), you have to spend time distributing to your team of 36 troops (out of 84 troops). There is not even an "optimize" feature in the equipment manual, and I have to manually check each of the 5 slots for the 36 troops.
The game world is large with a lot of enemies and castles to attacks.
Each attacks is broken down into an ever increasing number of "waves".
Each waves comes with it group of new enemies.
I have only started playing since yesterday and am already fighting 20-30 waves per battle in the nearby towns.
The whole mechanics of this strategy game is just very tiring and boring.
Unlike other strategy games like Civilization, Master of Orion, or Rise of Nations, etc, which really draws you in, this game just became a series of boring micromanagement action, one after another. I have already spend 11 hours in this game, and feel like giving up due to excessive boredom.
Please note that I love Aldorlea RPGs and have 20-30 different Aldorea games. Some of the Aldorlea games, I have played 50 to 100 hours too, and love it.
However, I am not feeling the same level of enthusiasm for this game.
As a result, I do not recommend this Aldorlea game.

A lot of the mechanics are fairly unique and would only work well with a PC version of a card game - the art is wildly varied and pretty fun to look at. The decks feel familiar with regards to color, but also do have their own bits of nuance.
Most of all, though, I personally love the addition of a 'character' atop it all - complete with talents and equipment that affect your cards, troops, etc. Clerics are biased towards blessings and buffs, Mages are big on actions/instants, and Warriors bolster troops nicely.
There's also a seemingly pretty robust single player campaign, which rewards you with cards and boosters as you go along - and they don't appear to be totally static as far as what you get.
My only complaint is some of the UI/click actions are a hint delayed feeling and sluggish, but that's really it. Again, the neat mechanics are what make it for me - stacking buffs to the next card of a certain type you draw, cards that scoot up in your deck as turns pass, creation of 'random' cards (any card, not just ones you own), etc.
There's also a nuance in their resource system - it's essentially like MTG with one big difference. In Hex, cards just have a flat cost, i.e. 4 'resource', much like MTG. In MTG however, you might need a total of 3, but two had to be blue. In Hex, you may only have gotten two blue 'resources', but all your resource is lumped into an overall pool, and the colors add a 'threshold.'
Meaning that if you had gotten 2 blue and 5 white, you'd have a total of 7 resource, with a 5 threshold on white and a 2 threshold on blue. As such, you can cast two cards that cost 3 each, even if both require 2 blue, because you meet the 'threshold' amount for those cards. It's a subtle difference but it makes decks a lot friendlier to multicolor and you don't end up getting cornered by needing one more of a color or another as desperately. Most cards I've seen only need one or two threshold, so a multicolor deck can easily squeeze by with just one or two of a resource with a bit of bad luck far longer than you could in MTG!
All in all very fun, great art, lots of interesting mechanics. Solid recommend in my opinion!

Pros:
- The graphical update is really good overall. Most of the original sprites were faithfully redrawn and apart from a few missteps (some towns look like cheap 3D models on the adventure map, a few unit card backgrounds look like they were merely touched up with an upscale filter).
- You can swtich between the updated and the original look.
- The game itself is H3 Restoration of Erathia in its fully original form as it was released back in 1999... nostalgia!
- There is an HDE mod which introduces some features from the expansions: you can revisit structures without moving your hero by pressing Space, if you also own the original H3 Complete you have access to the random map generator and expansion scenarios can be converted from the original game too.
- Steam multiplayer functionality.
Cons:
- The game itself is H3 Restoration of Erathia in its fully original form as it was released back in 1999... and that means that you don't get the content from the two expansions (Armageddons Blade, The Shadow of Death) and Heroes Chronicles, the 8 episode campaign expansion. Overall you lose a lot of stuff compared to H3 Complete (around 70 campaign missions, countless scenarios, a lot of heroes and artfiacts), a game you can pick up for 10 bucks on GOG.
- The sounds and the soundtrack were not remastered.
- The pre-rendered cutscenes have a noticably lower quality than what you see in the original game.
- The user interface of the original game was not improved in any shape or form. This is a letdown as the UI is fairly archaic compared to modern standards and you have access to a mod called HoMM3 HD for H3 Complete that not only adds widescreen functionality with XBRZ image scaling (nice, sharp image quality) but also expands the original UI a lot. Compared to H3 Complete with the HoMM3 HD mod installed the game is a chore to play sometimes because of this.
- No extra content. This may seem like a weird one to appear among the negatives but it would have been nice to get something that is exclusive to the HD Edition, a new campaign for example.
Overall this is a serviceable remaster that loses most of its appeal because of the missing content, the lackluster UI and the fact that the original version has a large community that spent almost two decades of improving and expanding an already fantastic game. If you really like the new graphics or you desperately want to play multiplayer through Steam then pick it up but under any other circumstance just steer clear of this release.

It's a fun online card game with room for improvements on the F2P side.
Pros:
+Gorgeous card artwork (like MTG)
+Has PVE (Campaign and player vs AI arena)

Cons:
-Questionable stability of the campaign server, suffers from constant downtimes.
-The in-game currency from the PVE content (Gold) is nearly useless, without major uses other than seek trade with other players for Platinum.
-Limited access to most of the cards in the game for F2P players. Most of the cards obtained in campaign can't be used for PVP.
-Availability of useful cards and equipment in the Auction House of the game is VERY limited if using Gold for currency. Highly inflated pricings.
-Game is extremely challenging on the PVP side if you don't spend cash to get Platinum and buy Packs/Cards.
-Most tournaments require an entry fee to participate, that leaves F2P players out of most of the PVP content of the game.

This was truly a big surprise. I like visual novels despite that a fair amount of them have weak storylines, but this visual novel's story was not weak at all. It was surprisingly well-done and just awesome. Honestly, it could've made a decent storyline for a RPG, but I know indie companies don't always have the money for that.
The point-of-view switches between three different characters. I like this because it allows the reader to see from different story perspectives. It also doesn't cater to one character's biased interpretations of events. After playing through the game a lot, I must say that I think Elise is supposed to be the main character of the three.
The achievements for this game comprise of 5 endings and 1 easter egg. There is also a 6th ending that doesn't yield an achievement (because it's neutral/generic). The easter egg is hilarious, by the way.
The artwork of this game is impressive. Although, sometimes the characters look a bit awkward in how they're drawn.
The music is lovely. Quite lovely. This is to be expected considering the title of the game.
I definitely recommend this game for those who like visual novels! It might also serve to be a good game to introduce someone to visual novels, since it's definitely one of the better ones out there.

Finding a solid VN with all the elements of an absorbing and worthwhile game is a tall order, and while Kidalang Studio’s An Octave Higher is far from the perfect experience, it’s just different enough to be worth sinking some time into.

[Author has received a review copy of An Octave Higher]
An Octave Higher is one of the newest additions to Steam’s growing library of OELVNs (Original English Language Visual Novels), which I have something of a love hate relationship with. On one hand, getting access to visual novels without having to wait for translation sounds fantastic, but on the other the majority of these new titles lack the funding and quality of story to stand up to their Japanese counterparts. While An Octave Higher is not the OELVN we’ve all been waiting for, it’s most definitely a step in the right direction, boasting a novel and intriguing setting in addition to exploring moral issues that are both interesting and relevant.
Whatever complaints I may have had, I enjoyed my time with An Octave Higher. I loved the setting and the scientific representations of magic, and even cared about the characters by the time the story had reached its end. However, I felt that the routes didn’t conclude in a satisfying way and failed to tie up the various plot threads meaningfully (though the bits before the endings were still enjoyable). The technical aspects, while not impressive, aren’t deal-breaking and have their own charm. All-in-all, An Octave Higher sits on the better side of the fence of available OELVNs and if it sounds like the setting or story would interest you then you should definitely give it a go.

This is a fantastic game with a fantastic story.
It's a long visual novel, a single playthrough with the non-canon ending was three hours, and it's not like most games (even most visual novels that I've played) in that you make very few decisions. I believe, on my first playthrough, that my first decision didn't take place until about 45 minutes or an hour into the game.
Which brings me to my larger point: this is a game for people who like to read and really enjoy a story. Decisions are fundamental to the game and many of them directly impact which ending you're going to experience, but you won't be choosing little things all the time. You'll be making big decisions, the narrative will be allowing the characters to make the small decisions.
That said, and it's said simply to inform so as to help those who might buy the game to avoid any confusion or frustration with the style of the game, and as I said before: the story is fantastic. There was a great deal of care and consideration put into the writing of this work, there are moral and social quandaries and complexities which are shown to the player and, depending on player choices, the player gets to see the difficult (and not wrong) decisions and opinions formed based entirely on the perspective of the character.
As one character says in the game, in a battle there are no good guys and bad guys. We all go through life convinced that we're right. Those of us who fight do so because we believe we'll get justice. Gilligan suggested that all violence is created by people seeking justice who believe they deserve something which they're being deprived of: be it respect, objects, or any number of other complex social equations. Violence is the attempt to replace feelings of shame and inadequacy with pride and worth. The writing in this game is good enough that it successfully creates multi-faceted characters who always have reasons for whatever violence they might create, and the game creates such a complex social tapestry that it's easy to see how the individuals (on both sides of the conflict) are, in their own way and with their own limited perspectives, right.

New Xsyon player here, and here is what I think of this game in just seven hours.  I will update this review as I continue to work in the game.
Simple question: "Should I buy this game?"
General answer: if you like sandbox free-to-do-as-you-please types, then yes.  It's worth the investment.  You can tell a lot of effort has been put into this game, though it's fairly underdeveloped.  The developer still seems actively involved in the community, but the community is lacking.  Nice people, just few of them on.  Expect to solo while you learn, and that's totally fine.
This game is crafting heavy, but it takes a lot of time (and boring clicking and clicking and clicking) to get what you want done.  I mean a lot of time!  Not even so much that it's a lot of time, but that it's super slow-going, and very little instruction in-game, with a fairly generic tutorial.
To have the best chance to start enjoying this game, I advise you make basket making your primary starting hobby.  This will help you get to the baskets you'll need to start developing resources without spending ten hours figuring out that you need to do this, and five more leveling it by farming grass and making thread and so on.  Once you have baskets, you're golden to start working the land.
My advice further:  Safely navigate around the lake.  Find an area off the lake that has trees, rocks, and access to the lake.  Set up a tribe.  Start developing your totem area (aka learning your crafts).  Get to know the ten players in the game at any given time.  Eventually join their tribe just so you have something to build onto.  Or keep developing your own.
By doing this, you will be in a safe zone for learning the basics. This game is a 20% safe area game, with the other 80% all PvP.
In the game, you can choose to be an Elementalist(Mage), Warrior(Melee), Skirmisher(Ranger), or Primalist(Healer). You also have the choice to train your skills in all of them and switch between what you want to be. But it takes time to swap between classes, so you can only be one at a time, and not switch up in combat.
For everything you do in this game, you gain something equal to experience, but it's called Prowess.
Prowess is used as a form of currency and is used to spend on your skills. So spend wisely.
Players do not have a combat level, or skill total level, they have a prowess level. The amount of prowess a player has, can determine on how strong they are. But just remember, they might of spent it all on gathering skills and not their combat skills, so you might have a chance. Thats the exciting part. A player with 15k prowess could kill a player with 100k prowess. depending on what each player spends their prowess on. :)
The game is focused around clans, and taking over cities and villages, with a huge PvP based world. Everything outside of the safe zone is all for all. Anyone you see in the wilderness, you can attack. But be careful, you might annoy a clan, and they might track you down with spies.
The wilderness in this game has five levels of wilderness plus the safe zone areas. As soon as you step out of the safe zone, you have 30 seconds before your character is unsafe. What you have on you, you will lose if you die. Except your three basic wepons; your bow, staff and sword. The lowest of all wepons that every player in the game has.
The deeper the wilderness, the harder the NPC monsters will be, and the more loot they will drop. This also goes for trees, rocks, and other gathering noads.
You've got the freedom to do what you wish in the game.
You can gather items to get your crafting skills up, Eg; mine iron ore and smelt that into Iron Ignots, to make armour or wepons, or just to sell to other players to gain Gold Coins.
Or you could choose to PvE, and kill NPC monsters to loot items and skin them with a skinning tool to get leather(to craft) and other items.
Or you could go out and PvP for money, or work together in a clan to keep your cities under protection and fight for them.
Other features on this game include player mounts, player boats, ships and also player houses.

The Signal From Tölva gives you more robots than you’ll know what to do with. This story-based shooter drops you onto a planet full of robots clashing with other robots… who are clashing with still more robots, all of whom are looking for the source of a strange signal. There is a mystery to solve and some interesting AI systems to manipulate in the 10 hours you’ll spend playing, but there’s a lot of slow-paced walking time to get to the good stuff. This is no Doom or Wolfenstien.
Your character is sort of a mystery itself. An outside organization, who you only hear about through a dispatcher named The Broker, has sent you to infiltrate the Surveyors, a robot faction who is probing the planet Tölva for secrets. This allows you to commandeer robot drones on the planet’s surface, effectively warping around in a vast computer network. It’s a smart way to implement a respawn and fast-travel system, and you can use it to cut down on some of the walking.
This is a great casual robot shooter, to the point you wish there was more to it. If the devs at Big Robot take the idea of The Signal From Tölva and over all added to the game, they could have a classic for the ages.
If you're NOT looking for a fast paced shooter with a mega skill tree and a plethora of weapons. Then get this game and find out what exactly is The Signal From Tölva.
