If you enjoyed 10000000, you will enjoy You Must Build a Boat. It is essentially more of the same, with some additional layers of complexity which help the experience feel more rounded.
You will probably not be surprised that your primary goal is to build a boat. You do this mostly by clearing dungeons, which is generally accomplished by executing a variety of match-3's in an experience that mirrors an endless runner. You'll have a variety of ways to attack your enemies, you'll gather loot, and you'll use that loot to upgrade your ship. The dungeon goals feel a little tougher this time around. While this adds a welcome level of complexity (and hoarding spells to hurl at fireball at a frozen enemy does feel mighty fine), these more complicated goals can sometimes stall your experience. There was one dungeon objective which was so poorly explained that I was stuck for at least an hour before I finally Googled to find out what I was supposed to be doing. When a similarly difficult objective came again a little later, I didn't waste as much time before looking up the answer. Still, plenty of run goals are accomplished simply by entering the dungeon and matching away. As you upgrade your weapons, spells, and shield, you'll find allies to aid your journey and your runs will become longer as you master the matching mechanics.
You Must Build a Boat suffers from being extremely repetitive. You are going to be doing the same matches again and again. You will go through dungeons that all look fairly similar and face lots of similar enemies that want to kill you. It is a grind, and while it is well-executed, you will probably not be able to play the game in one sitting. My mouse hand grew numb during more than one play session, and the visual strain of staring at the screen to discern matches can be tiring. Still, I absolutely recommend the experience for its high level of creativity and clever execution. I have always enjoyed endless runners, and this is among the best of them.

After spending ½ an hour playing The Last Hope, it had made me question a lot of things. (As if the description wasn’t confusing enough!)
We are thrown into the game without any proper guidance or tutorial on how to play. The controls are established in the beginning, then we are given our 1st mission. You will playing as a Viking and explore in different areas all of which have no specific name or description. You could waste a good 10 minutes of your time wandering the first area (space ship?) before finally reaching your objective. Then the rest of your gameplay is you running around
.
You will also be completing various objectives that aid in finding the time machine. But, some of the methods lack explanation, or just didn’t make any sense. (E.x Why are the portals only activated by our shield, exactly? Where did we even get the shield from, and why are we playing as a Viking for all the areas?)
The game has nowhere near AAA graphics, yet I am constantly struck with lag and delays in movements through the game play. This was likely the worst part of my experience playing. Its art would be great if, considering it had some unity in it. In this case, it didn’t. When you approach the first area: a field of aliens, dinosaurs, military tanks and … other things I can’t comprehend. Textures and shading are also messy and doesn’t really flow well within the map. At times you may encounter blurred or a cut-off of the environment, which looks like a bug. A theme just wasn’t established clearly in this game, nor was it properly organized. As a result, it looked messy and questionable on nearly all aspects visible.
Effects and animations are also minimal. None of the monsters will even attack the character, and majority of them are as dead as a statue. The only way to die is if you literally run head-on into one, which will trigger the “Try Again” screen.
Little to no audio are used in the game. 90% of the time you’ll be hearing nothing else but your footsteps. The remaining part includes other atmospheric sounds that trigger upon interaction or setting foot in a new environment. The footsteps become irritating over time, and the volume should have been lowered so that we are more in-tune with the environment.
Overall, the Last Hope was chaotic at its best. Too much was implemented into a Time-travelling game with too little organization. The graphics need polishing, the story and concept needs more detail and explanation, and the text should be revised. I’ve spotted more than a few grammatical errors coming across the story dialogues. I do not recommend playing this game.

I don't normally write reviews, but I feel compelled to write one for this game, because it deserves no less than that. So, here goes.
Before I begin though, I must admit that I only played this game due to the recent Steam Summer Sale, in which one of the daily quests was to Get an Achievement. As almost everyone familiar with Steam games are aware, visual novels are one of the easiest genre of games to obtain achievements, and this one just happened to be a random pick of mine for that very purpose.
But oh, what an awesome pick that turned out to be. CUPID, despite its simple name and brief, unassuming description on the store page, turned out to be one of the best visual novels I have ever played and indeed, will ever play. And I have played quite a few visual novels in my time.
As the game's blurb goes, CUPID is set against the backdrop of 18th century France, and it centres around four main characters: the protagonist of the game, Rosa, a beautiful but shy, timid girl living on the streets as a rose vendor, Rosa's long-deceased Mother who guides her every move as a voice in her mind, Catherine Emilia Perride, a musical child prodigy and Rosa's best friend, who gave her a home and grew up together with her, and a Marquis known as Guilleme Michel de Gul, a dashing, charismatic character infamous for his string of alleged romantic conquests that were as short-lived as they were sensational, and the wild rumours that followed in the wake of their destruction.
You play the role of the aforementioned Mother, whose face is never shown in the game, but whose psychic directions to Rosa can drastically impact the outcome of the story.
Right off the bat, the game makes it clear to the player that it is no ordinary slice-of-life, feel-good visual novel, as many recent ones are wont to be (not that that's a bad thing, mind you). Rather, you as the player, are immediately challenged with what initially appears to be a confusing narrative, made up of both gentle love and cruel abuse, emanating from the same flawed character.
This may be discomforting to most people (myself included), who may be unaccustomed to such a dark, and indeed, twisted theme. But if you soldier on, you will find that there is indeed a reason to the apparent madness, though it may take a while to reveal itself.
The child Rosa encounters a similarly-aged Catherine at the grounds of Guilleme's mansion in the beginning of the game, and Catherine is immediately and somewhat inexplicably drawn to her. Although the Perride family isn't ostensibly wealthy, Catherine manages to convince her father to take Rosa in and provide for her. Thus begins a friendship that lasts until Catherine's death (I hope this isn't a spoiler since it is already mentioned in the game's store page description), and now Rosa must find out what, and who, really caused her death.
While this general storyline may sound interesting enough to some readers, if not a little cliché, it is *how* CUPID tells its story, and not what it is, that sets it apart from many lesser visual novels. The prose and dialogue is simply marvellous; fluid, natural, totally believable. It is terse in moments when it needs to be for emotional impact, and wordier in others when the tension and mood is lighter. At no point did I feel that the conversations were forced, or the prose jarring; everything just seemed to flow and read as naturally as one would expect of real human interactions.
It is peppered throughout with statements that made me stop and ponder over them, at the same time marvelling over how simply they seemed to fit into whatever dialogue or narrative was being said at the moment. Here are a few choice ones I can recall off the top of my head:
- "You can't fake sacrifice"
- "Friendships are a shallow kind of relationship"
- "You cannot take love without giving it"
- "Generosity is the only saving grace of the dying"
And impressively, it accomplishes this without resorting to "big words", the way some other novels may attempt to in order to present an illusion of profoundness.
As for the art in the game, it is simple but beautiful, nonetheless. Plenty of care was given to the facial expressions of each character, and they change frequently and appropriately to reflect the vacillating emotions of their owners during each conversation. The background art also deserves a mention here. While they might not win any awards, they are tastefully done and complement each scene well. The music is a little subdued however, and is comprised almost entirely of piano pieces.
Together, they are weaved beautifully to provide the player with an experience that is both thought-provoking and emotionally impactful. Just as there are elements of horror in the game, with one scene being particularly bone-chilling to me, there are also heart-warming moments that soothe the soul, with one exchange between Rosa and Catherine being particularly poignant and memorable. This range of emotions it invoked in me then, is one of the largest I have felt in any game before, and I believe, is probably what its creators set out to achieve as well.
While some players may feel discomfort in the central theme and the dark overall mood of the game, I would argue that that cannot be held as a black mark against the game, and rather that it should be judged on how well it delivers its content to the player. And in this respect, it delivers in spades.
There is well over ten hours of gameplay here, if the player is interested in obtaining all endings and unlocking all CGs and achievements. Speaking of achievements, there is an astounding 67 (!) of them here, and I know of no other free game on Steam that rivals this amount. So then, even in the realm of replayability, an area most visual novels are notoriously poor in, the game scores well among its peers.
With all that being said, CUPID is certainly not a game for children, or even young teenagers. The theme of twisted love and abuse may also hit too close to home for some people. The game apparently has a PG-17+ rating and fully deserves it, not only as a deterrent for younger players, but also because those without the required maturity levels would likely not be able to adequately appreciate it.
In summary, this game is an easy recommendation for those who can appreciate a good story, even if it is streaked with darkness. Lovingly crafted and masterfully told, its only price tag is your time. I am simply astounded that a game of this quality is absolutely free of charge.
Thank you Fervent Studios, for this work of art.

If you want to play Magic: The Gathering with different cards, this is your game.  The game copies the ruleset of Magic: The Gathering to the letter, just changes the words for certain things (Sorceries become Basic Actions, Instants become Quick Actions, Enchantments are Constants, Artifacts are... still Artifacts, actually).  The upside to this is that if you already know how to play Magic, you know how to play Hex.  The downside is that mana screw/flood is still an issue.  However, Hex does have character abilities (like Vanguard in M:TG) and skill trees that may help (I lost interest too soon to find out; mana screw was one of the main reasons I quit playing Magic).  So, there's a little more depth than Magic, but it's basically the same game.
At least it doesn't have completely random effects like Hearthstone.  That game is so good until someone plays one of many random effects and then it becomes "Flip a coin to see who wins."  At least mana screw doesn't let you have the illusion of winning.

Overall this is a fairly decent game. I personally wish that the devs spent more time on the character art (its honestly pretty bad) especially when they've showed off such detailed and interesting backgrounds throughout the game. The devs also beat you over the head with their rules of magic. They make sure to point out at every opportunity that something is powered or created using magic. They go into such depth about random clocks and carriages that it suspends the narrative to circle-jerk over their own created universe. As far as VN's go, An Octave Higher also lacks many of the bells and whistles that other VN's have such as gesture controls, smart skipping and as far as I can tell, branching story lines based on choice.
Now, on the positive side (and please bear in mind that I am only 25% of the way through). The story is good enough for what you pay. You take on the perspective of 3 separate and very different characters. Each one offers an interesting perspective on the brewing class-war, and each offers up their own unique feel and backstory. As far as choice, there hasn't been much, but I believe that the story is fine without it at this point. The world is interesting enough, the conflict (while slow to emerge) is an archetypal classic, and I am truly interested to read more and more into the story to see how life develops for the main characters.
7.5/10 Get it on sale and it's worth every penny.
EDIT: I have now played through the majority of the endings and this game is incredible. There is an entire second act that has to be discovered before you can fully experience the true story of this game. That story is engrossing, gritty and can end a few different ways (Although i personally don't prefer the true ending). I was wrong about the bells and whistles, the game automatically skips all previously read text, pauses at choices whenever they appear and there are a TON of them. The endings are truly different endings, not just 'slightly changed' outcomes (looking at you ME3), and each one is either an 'awe' or 'woah' moment.
After having finished this game through and through (still working towards one missing ending) I have to give this game props as well as upgrade its Llama rating.
8.5/10 Great game all-around and a wonderful story (if you choose the right paths)

Bold and offensive in all the best ways, Rocketbirds has more personality than just about any other game of its kind. As unexpectedly serious in tone as the story is, what's even more surprising is how well it comes together. I genuinely began to empathize with our hero's plight to free his country from the oppressive reign of the Penguins, which is no small feat for a game starring a machinegun toting chicken. The stilted, self aware voice acting and dialog add a darkly humorous overtone onto this which when taken in tandem is a completely unique and entertaining narrative that outdoes the straightforward tale underneath.
Gameplay is a side-scrolling shooter stripped to its bare fundamentals, involving little more than rolling from room to room guns blazing and shooting anyone dumb enough to try and stop you. Interspersed are a few sections strapping you into a jetpack for aerial combat, but for the most part the developer chose to keep things simple and uncomplicated, which I think the game is better off for. My only complaint are the somewhat stiff and clunky controls, whether using KB&M or a gamepad (though I would definitely advise using the later if you have the option). You can only shoot directly in front of you, but switching directions takes a split second too long and allows for a bunch of cheap shots from enemies, and can get you into some tight spots during later levels. I did get a hang of them eventually, but they could certainly be improved.
But cumbersome controls are in no way able to bring the game down. The art style which places animated 2D character models against realistic, slightly offset 3D backgrounds is brilliant, and the kickbutt soundtrack is impeccable to say the least. Despite being extremely brief the campaign is exciting and full of action, with solid (though entirely habitual) gameplay and a creative, excellently constructed presentation that sets it apart from the rest. More than anything else though Rocketbirds is simply very, very cool and an adventure well worth taking.

About 1.5 hours into the game at the point of this review.. and I will update my review as needed as I get further into this visual novel game.
The game lets you save your progress at any point it seems, I've never had a problem saving or loading anywhere.
It's a fantasy novel of rich magic users and the poor living in rags and how they cross paths into each other.  It isn't a plausible story with all of its sorcery and magic spells, but also seems to be a lot less fantistical then the sort of dragon and giant spider fighting fantasy stories you might expect as well.
So far, the writing seems well done, and the art work is really nice.  I am impressed both visually with the art and the writing so far, about 15% through the game.  (You can check your progress at any point from the main menu)
Considering I am reading this story for my YouTube videos so far, and I am pace for about 10 hours, most people not reading the dialogue aloud will probably read at least twice as fast.  I'd guess this is a 3 to 5 hour game for most people, which will depend greatly on the user naturally with how fast they read or 'skim over' the writing.
Be advised at I just barely got into some pretty mature and very sexual-in-nature content at the 15% mark.  I was kind of surprised by this and the fact that there was no mention anywhere that I saw that this game/novel included sexual or adult content.  No nude art as of yet, but pretty mature sexually natured dialogue, and I can see that it might get much more graphic in the near future.  I will update this as I play through, but BE ADVISED THAT THIS GAME MAY NOT BE SUITABLE FOR CHILDREN/MINORS ESPECIALLY YOUNGER CHILDRED UNDER THE AGE OF 14 OR SO.
So far, I have enjoyed it, so at this early point I will give it a thumbs up with the understanding that I may change this entire review and even my recommendation at any time.  But right now, with the amount of content, the quality of the writing, the entertainment value, and the really nice artwork, I'd give this a thumbs up to anyone who enjoys this kind of game and/or novel.
At this point 15% in, there has been NO choices, and NO gameplay at all.  It's just reading and clicking the screen to move forward.  This is fine for me, as I'm sure choices will be made at some point, but I realize this might upset some people, which is why I have pointed this out.

New review summed up by this thread on their official forums:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Disregard my played time so far, I've been playing this game as one of the earliest Kickstarter backers and have hundreds if not over a thousand hours ingame outside the Steam client.  Simply, this game is EVERYTHING I have wanted in a TCG.
- The community is amazing.  It is by far the most helpful and friendly of any game I've played.  Clearly things may change with the massive influx this new platform will bring, but the core playerbase (supported by the devs) has cultivated something truely special.
- Similarly, the developers have done right by the community the vast majority of the time.  It's clear and apparent they care deeply about building a strong ethical reputation with their playerbase.
- It plays similar to MTG, but the digital only realm vastly expands available mechanics, interactions, and future potential.
- Free to play PVE currency (gold) actually has a valuable transaction rate to premium currency (platnum). With some patience and understanding of the economy you can easily transition into buying packs, tournament entires etc.  In game assets can be purchased with EITHER currency as reasonable prices through the in-game auction house.
- The art and audio are fantastic, the atmosphere is stellar.
- This game has unfortunately suffered from multiple delays development wise.  While this is certainly a negative, I feel that the attention, and try and do right by the players attitude mitigates my frustrations with the slow development place.  I anticipate future PVE and PVP releases to be at a much more acceptable cadence.
- Some of the lore is...discordant.  I enjoy the vast majority of it, however there are certain aspects that seem out of place or that I don't personally care for.  This is clearly in the eye of the beholder but some players may be slightly turned off by it.  I do not recommend the Hex novel.
- As of yet unimplemented features.  The potential is there and the rest of the game is SO good, that it makes waiting for promised but un-implemented features all the more painful.  Per above, I"m hopeful development and release speed should improve dramatically.
All said and done, I would (and have) recommended this game to a wide and diverse set of people.  It's worth spending at least a few hours ingame before forming your opinion as much of the game really starts to shine once you have an appreciation for how all the systems interact.
DEFINATELY TRY THIS GAME.

The sound, the music choices, the narration, the story, the special narration effects, the graphics.. everything. The synergy between all these aspects help make this one of my favourite games in a long time of playing games.

If you love these kinds of games (as I do), you really should consider looking into this one. I share my more detailed thoughts on Xsyon in the following video for those interested ;)
If you play these kinds of games, you will understand many of the things they have in common, from Crafting gear, to building up your home/settlement/tribe. But here are some things I really enjoy about Xsyon you won't see in most (if any) others like it (so not an exhaustive list - just stuff I really like)...
- Make a quest... what are you looking for and what are you rewarding someone with for completing it? Add these details to your quest, and anyone can complete it!
- When a settlement is abandoned, the structures left behind can be torn down easily. More importantly, when the supported structures are gone, the terrain (any terraforming done) returns pretty quickly to its natural state! How awesome is that?!
- Not only do the skills you use increase as you use them, but at the same time you are doing things (crafting, etc) you are filling an XP bar. When full, you get points to spend on ANY other skills as well. It's a nice combo giving you some options without it being a straight free-for-all.
- This takes place in post-apocalyptic Lake Tahoe. The "world" is the mountainous area surrounding the lake. Things get more dangerous (and rewarding) the farther you explore away from the lake. Native American influences are heavy here and the combination of that with the apoc setting give this really cool "return to the old world" feel that is really compelling for me.

Can't say this game is revolutionary (although it is about a revolution). Just a very well executed platformer. Fun gameplay with a bit of variety, good graphics, good soundtrack, good story.
